I have discovered an unexpected operation in this element; for although I purified it through distillation and manifold rectification until it reached a most lucid splendor, it nevertheless possessed such an affinity with darkness that, in a short space of time, it contracted its old and pristine obscurity and blackness, quickly losing its transparency and the beauty of its luster. This matter brought to my memory the saying of a wise man named Artephius <note>A legendary 12th-century alchemist often cited in Hermetic texts</note>, who, in his book titled *The Greater Key of Wisdom*, says: *Perhaps there are certain infirmities to which the Devil joins himself by means of a humor emerging from the temperament and disturbing health itself; and this happens most especially in infirmities arising from choler <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors, associated with fire</note>, the cause of which is this: because the nature of choler itself is hot and dry like fire. Now, the body of the Devil is composed of two things, namely fire and air. And we have said (he says) in preceding passages, that every subtle thing may enter into every gross thing. It is manifest, therefore, since fire is subtler than air, that the apparent part of the Devil's body is air, but its hidden part is fire; and this is the cause of his concealment from human sight, since the medium through which we see all things is air, which is joined to our eye. Since, therefore, the interior of the Devil is of the nature of fire, it is manifest that he is opposed and contrary to the nature of the soul itself, which is of a nature of equality <note>Balance or harmony</note>. When, therefore, some choleric sickness invades the body (since Choler is the Devil’s hidden part), it appears clearly that he joins himself most easily with Choler, and thus his dominion over the other humors is increased; indeed, that humor can predominate so much that the soul withdraws from the body and is utterly separated from it.* Thus he spoke.

For this reason (I say), the Devil is suited by natural instinct to insinuate and join himself into this element of fire. From which we can diligently observe that just as God, the King of Light, works through celestial fire toward life and preservation, so plainly on the contrary does this Prince of Darkness—who has his dominion in the sublunary elements—act through this corruptible fire toward death and destruction. Hence it is that this spirit of privation, wandering and roaming everywhere by the impulse of the darkness he contracted (by which he has been vexed and agitated since his defection; that is, compelled to hide the lucid rays of his first-born creation behind a dark veil as punishment for his ambition and disobedience), now shows himself ready to demonstrate through effects the affinity or consanguinity that exists between him and the choleric humor; from which even the good air suffers.

From this it follows that a man, by the force of this element predominating in him, turns out to be a Lunatic and distracted from his senses; dark impressions blunt the clearest edge of his intellect and cloud the rays of his mind, while terrible and deceptive chimeras lead his imagination astray and make a mockery of it. Indeed, the Devil is accustomed to converse with many in this way in manifold forms, and disturbs them with monstrous visions. Hence it is also that the life of a man laboring under a burning fever, or a disease arising from a gnawing melancholy, is infested either with delirium, or insomnia, or despair, or lycanthropy <note>The delusion of being a wolf</note>, insanity, and for the most part by melancholy vapors procreated from the flatulent smoke emanating from this sulfurous element. This fiery smoke likewise strikes in Hypochondriac passions, such as trepidations, anger, rage, solitude, sleeplessness, and a hatred of all human society and commerce.

What more grave thing shall I add, when we find that by the mediation of this element and the assault of its suffering Water, not only men, but the entire lower region of the universal worldly frame is affected by distress and sickness? For in the air, it is the cause of comets, fiery dragons, burning columns, fire-vomiting flames, and similar meteors; specifically where the active force has greater dominion, but the "patient" <note>The passive element receiving the action, here water</note> is not so abundant. But where its patient (namely water) is equally powerful and strong, there crashes, thunders, and lightnings weigh down the lower region. Yet if the patient be endowed with the highest power and overcomes the fiery faculty, then floods overwhelm the earth, and the middle region of the air grows dark with the covering of thick and gloomy clouds, from which infinite calamities arise. Although (as the proverb has it, "There is no wind that brings no one profit") sometimes a gloomy air presages abundance and fertility of the earth; and also sometimes, led by experience, we observe that the vapors of a cloudy body are consumed and dried up by febrile heat, just as we notice that lightnings (which are the febrile effects of the air) dispel and absorb the morbid exhalations of the air. And so much I have seen fit to declare to you concerning the nature and disposition of the element of fire.

# SECTION I. PORTION III. PART I. BOOK II.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### The final appearance or vision, outlining the nature of the fifth Element, called the quintessence.

Now at last we have overcome the elementary heavens of the sublunary world, and we make our entry into that region which is distinguished by the Alchemists by the name of the **quintessence** <note>literally "fifth essence"</note>, by the philosophers as the **ether** or most simple matter, and by the Poets as heaven, Olympus, or the Elysian fields. Here, however, I would wish you to understand in passing that just as in the structure or composition of any thing we proceed from one to five—which is a round number and the true center of the number ten <note>original: "denarii cētrum"</note> proceeding as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5—so also in the destruction and resolution of a thing back to one, we must proceed from 5 to 4, and so backward even unto unity. This region is therefore called the **quintessence** by the Hermetic philosophers because it stands five degrees distant from the earth. This, I say, is the reason: that the appearance of water follows closest to the earth, which air follows, and then fire follows air; and after fire, that golden moisture of the quintessence ascended—so called from its relation to the true quintessence of the mystical philosophers—which is the final sign of this violent dissolution. For in this element is that true life, by means of which the remaining four elements act in the human body; that is, by the central virtue or internal moving principle through which the entire composite thing subsists.

And just as we see that a man who is forced by compulsion to give something of his own to another usually offers first and before all else that which he himself values least and is of lesser price, thinking he will thus be set free; but perceiving his first offering is by no means enough for the one compelling him, he is then forced to hand over from his treasury something a little more dear and precious to himself, which nevertheless he does not value as much as what seems to him of greater price in his domain; and so he proceeds step by step by bringing forth things of lesser value, until at last he comes to distribute that of the greatest value: namely, the dearest blood of his life. So also the matter stands in this dark **Chaos** or black **Corpse of the earth** <note>original: "terrræ Cadauere"</note>; for when the watery element (which portion is less useful for the preservation of its species) does not suffice for the appetite of the false Alchemist, the earth offers him air as a more precious thing after the water, and so it proceeds in bringing forth the richest dignity of its treasure, until the very **balsam of life** is withdrawn from it by fiery violence, and the mass itself—once raw and undigested—now remains as nothing but a **dead head** <note>term: caput mortuum; the useless residue left after distillation</note> in the ignoble condition of damned earth, deprived of almost all grace.

It remains, therefore, that we finally approach the most precious gem of the vegetable chaos, or the **solar and life-giving balsam** in the wheat, which we have divided from its mass by the highest extremity of the fiery art. Indeed, the earth was so greedy and prone to hide this gem in its lap or center, and to deceitfully withhold it from the Alchemist, that it was a matter of the greatest difficulty and labor to separate this from it—so much so, indeed, that if I had attempted to treat this chaos with greater harshness and violence to obtain its balsamic treasure, I would have extinguished and suffocated this spirit rather than conveniently separating it in its native color and property. Whence it happened that I was frustrated in a great part of my labor; therefore, I attempted a more expeditious way and method to rescue and draw out this golden treasure from its spongy hiding places. To accomplish this, I found it necessary to find a new kind of heat, which exerted its power from one part of the vessel, by means of which I rescued this ethereal moisture—

—and reduced it to the highest purity of splendor by various preceding **rectifications** <note>term: rectification; the process of refining a liquid by repeated distillation</note>. Then indeed, with eyes opened, I perceived a wonderful disposition to be in this balsam; for by even the slightest heat it became liquid and red like blood, filling the entire vessel with atoms, and conversely, by the cold of the air, it immediately hardened into a transparent and clear substance like a precious stone, partly of a bright crystalline color, and partly of a golden Hyacinth tint—that is, like crystalline glass, sown everywhere with shimmering sparks and as if with **little sharp stars** <note>original: "acidulis stellulis"</note>.

But here I strongly warn the reader to observe that I have not in this place brought to light the true and simple quintessence or heaven of the ancient Philosophers in its purified and naked disposition, but only that which, because of its purity, seems to the common person to be distinguished from the 4 other visible elements; which we have therefore named the quintessence because it participates more in the nature of the quintessence or ether than any of the other 4 elements mentioned above.

Here and there, the resolution of these questions or objections occurred to me as I watched more attentively: namely, how the **soul** <note>original: "anima"</note> differs from the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritu"</note>, and how, notwithstanding this, both are sometimes—indeed, very often—taken interchangeably for one and the same thing? And how the spirit is called the "vehicle of the soul" by the **Platonists**, as also: What is the "sphere of equality" in which the soul of the world reigns, of which they made such religious mention in their writings? Furthermore, what did the Platonists understand by *the soul in the spirit, and by the spirit in the body?* And consequently, what does **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Merc. Trism."; the legendary Hellenistic figure and reputed author of the Hermetic Corpus</note> mean when he says, *Mind in reason, reason in soul, soul in spirit, and spirit in body?* What indeed is that thing in this world which attributes life to every creature and nourishes the same? And many more such doubts, by no means to be explained by the common crowd, from which we can easily extricate ourselves by this experiment of common Alchemy, if only we consider this substance of the heavens with due diligence and attention. To the first question, therefore, we say: the vital Soul is a splendid light emanating from God, which in a clear spirit—

<columns>2</columns>

Desire is carried as if by a shining vehicle, by the rowing of whose wings she flies, and by whose presence she sometimes appears to the eyes. Under this form, golden-haired Desire <note>original: "auricomus cupido"</note> was discovered lying in the embrace of beautiful and fair Psyche, as Apuleius devised in his enigmatic fable. In such a hermaphroditic subject, the clear spirit is the female or passive part, while the light, with its rays expanded everywhere within it, is the male or active part. By the power and office of these two gathered into one, all things live. And by this same reasoning, we explain the second doubt: namely, where we affirm that a thin, clear, and transparent matter, similar to bright crystal, is the vehicle of the soul. For we say the soul is the splendid light, and the spirit is the white radiating substance. By these reasons, we can discern how the soul is said to be "all in all," and in any part of any thing. Likewise, the solution to the third question is drawn from the same demonstration, since this very soul is infused into the body within the spirit (which two are often jointly called by the name of "soul" alone). As for the opinion of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurii Trismegisti," the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and hermetic philosophy</note>, we shall explain it in the following chapter. Regarding the opinion of the Platonists, which holds that there is a certain sphere called the "sphere of equality" or of the soul, this very object teaches us that it is that very orb in which the sun revolves. For the very matter which descends downward to vivify animals, vegetables, and minerals teaches us this by its composition; indeed, in it there is held so exact a proportion between spirit and light that light cannot, by any act or violence, hold dominion over the spirit. From this it happens that the whole substance seems to be fixed and converted into a crystalline stone, as if by the mediating power of Medusa's head. Yet, on the other hand, the spirit does not so abound that it obscures the equal splendor of the light with its density, or shadows it with any darkness, or blunts the vivifying power in the light or the action of the celestial fire. For this reason, they are so equally proportioned to one another that neither can be hindered or oppressed by the other; on the contrary, one strengthens and animates the other in a perfect and absolute temperament, so that the spirit nourishes, sustains, and carries the light as if in a chariot, while the light (or its formal part) gives essence, life, and motion to the spiritual part, dispels the darkness of shadows from it, and promotes it first to vivifying, and then to vegetating. This, therefore, is the reason why that place from which this spirit flows is called the sphere of equality or of the soul. This clear composition is nothing other than that central sun of every creature—whether animal, vegetable, or mineral—drawing its origin from that sun which inhabits the middle point of heaven and is continually revolved in the orb or sphere of equality. There, the formal light and the material spirit are weighed in the equal scales of nature, so that each in its kind completely pleases the desire of the other, whereby their action extends perpetually toward life due to the lack of contrariety between them. For because of the equal portion between them, they are reduced to a symphony, which is most aptly delineated and demonstrated by the intersections made by the mutual meeting of the sides of two pyramids of the same dimension. One of these pyramids is formal, the other material. By their contrary positions, I have attempted to delineate and uncover the disposition of the entire worldly nature in the physical history of my Macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the universe as a whole, a central theme in the author's work</note>. For the material pyramid (from which this bright spirit emanates) has its base or foundation in the lowest earth, being the hieroglyphic image of those waters which originally gushed and emanated from the darkness or the abyss, the principal part of which is the receptacle of this celestial light. The formal pyramid, however, has its base or foundation in the highest heaven, and its apex in the center of the earth, bearing the icon of that flame—

—or light, which in the first creation of the world descended from the circumference downward toward the center. Through the material pyramid, with its apex from the earth toward heaven, the water ascending from the earth toward the circumference of heaven is proved to be gradually thinner and thinner. Conversely, the light or fiery form descending from the circumference of heaven toward the earth is, for the same reason, rendered weaker and thinner the more it declines from its source toward the center of the earth—not otherwise than we see in the figure of a geometric pyramid, which abounds more in weight, substance, and strength the more it progresses from its apex toward the base. A demonstration of these two pyramids, disposed in an opposite manner where they intersect each other, follows here. However, I have made more abundant mention of them in our booklet assigned to pyramids and annexed to the end of the technical history of our Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being as a reflection of the universe</note>, to which I would most gladly refer you so that you may more exactly understand what I think about pyramids there. Here I would also wish the reader to be advised that although this "quintessence" <term>Quinta essentia: the "fifth element" or purest essence of a substance</term> of ours is not that true one of the Philosophers in its purity, yet it stands to that one as the human soul stands to its spirit. Whence we say that since the spirit is the image of the soul, so also this quintessence of ours is the image of that invisible and hidden one, and consequently, the latter is indicated by the former through an external demonstration of this kind.

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book II.

<margin>☉ <note>The symbol for the Sun.</note></margin>
Here, **A** denotes the Earth; **b** and **c** represent the base of the *material pyramid*, and **m** its cone <note>the apex</note>. On the other hand, **☉** <note>the Sun</note> and **B** are the sole source of light and smoke; **d** and **e** are the base of the *formal pyramid*, created by the emanation from the source **B**. The cone of this said formal pyramid is **A**. The intersection made by these two, where the portion of one pyramid is equal to that of the other, is marked **f** and **g**; therefore, this orb passing through the heavens is distinguished by the name "Sphere of Equality." From this kind of matter and form, the celestial Sun was procreated, and for this very reason, it is called the "Sphere of the Soul of the World" <note>original: *anima mundi*</note> by the Platonists. Thus, it is clearly declared from the drawing of the pyramids placed here how each pyramid claims dominance for itself in every heaven. For instance, at **K.L.**, the proportion of the formal pyramid is triple to one part of the material pyramid; therefore, it is called the **Empyrean Heaven**, or the **Fiery Heaven**, because the splendor of fire dominates there absolutely. Conversely, in the space **o.n.**, we likewise find three parts of the material pyramid to one of the formal pyramid; for that reason, it is called the **Elementary Heaven**, as it is the place where matter has its dominion. But the **Middle Heaven**, through which the Sphere of Equality passes—where the parts of the said pyramids of light and spirit are found to be equally distributed—is called **Ether** <note>original: *Æther*</note>, as if it were *Aeth-aer*, that is, "fiery air." In this way, it shares an equal naming from the nature of both pyramids, which dominate in equal parts within it.

But if I wished to apply my mind and study to exploring the adaptation of these two pyramids, I swear by God that I could fill an entire volume with the thread of this narration and the explanation of the mysteries contained in this subject of ours. However, because I have already explained those things more extensively in my two-fold *History of Both Worlds* <note>Referring to Fludd's *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*</note>, I thought it sufficient to expose to you in this place the true and natural cause drawn from reason: namely, the reasoning that led me to discover these two pyramids—this equal proportion of spirit and light which concurs in the composition of my **Fifth Essence** <note>original: *quinta essentia*; the "quintessence" or purest element</note> mentioned a little earlier in this chapter.

Now, however, we shall proceed to the final doubt: namely, what is that thing in the world which first imparts, and then through its continuous succession preserves, life in each of these three kingdoms of nature—the animal, vegetable, and mineral? To this I respond: it is that very most subtle and simple Fifth Essence inhabiting this coarse and unpolished Fifth Essence of ours, which we mentioned in this chapter. To confirm this, I will bring forth an experiment from this coarse substance of the Fifth Essence, so that I may make you certain along with me (provided you have faith in the truth) that a life-giving virtue exists exactly within this pure element.

### The first experiment proving that the true agent of life is contained in this fifth element.

When I was occupied one day with the extraction of this **celestial balsam**, prepared in the common chemical manner, I was somewhat frustrated; for, by treating the "earthly chaos" more severely than was right, I burned a portion of this celestial flower, rendering it useless to the senses. I therefore washed the glass vessel in which the failing matter was stored in a larger vat made of thick, square stones, arranged to receive rainwater from the roof-gutters. But behold, after a few days had elapsed, I found the water swarming with worms of a wondrous form and length. They were of unusual length, yet somewhat slender or thin in width, and whitish in color, all of one kind and shape. I immediately observed that they proceeded from this life-giving nature, since before that time not even one such **little animal** <note>original: *animalcula*</note> appeared in this receiving vessel.

From this, it is manifest that the vital nature is one and the same in vegetables and in animals; the only diversity is in the vessel or body containing this celestial virtue. Hence it happens that in plants it is called the **vegetative soul**, but in animals, the **vital soul**. This is indeed confirmed by the fact that bread nourishes the vital soul and converts itself into an animal nature. From this, one can clearly and evidently see the ignorance of some in this world, who attribute nutrition, the preservation of life, the multiplication of blood, and the increase of every humor to the external bread and similar foods; but they are entirely ignorant of the specific parts, their internal workings, or their natural offices. They are no different from the blind commoners of this world who ineptly and ignorantly claim to know a man perfectly, though they have only known his exterior appearance. But how few (good God!) are those who rightly perceive the **internal man**! To understand this well is the principal goal of all human life, toward which one ought primarily to strive: namely, to know and uncover the light in the darkness. For to the "sons of earth," all things are darkness, just as the things appearing sensibly in the world truly are; but conversely, it is given to the "sons of light"

to look into the darkness itself, and to behold with spiritual eyes that hidden light lurking in the center, which is the true and most ancient honor and dignity of every creature, communicated to them by the Creator at creation. And although I by no means profess to have reached the summit of such perfection, I nevertheless rejoice and congratulate myself that at least some spark of that light shines in me—a light which renders any soul secure and immune from the foolish anxieties over earthly things, for which the world burns with greed and desire. I conclude, therefore, that since daily experience (which does not deceive even the peasants) shows us that the presence of the sun is the author of both life and multiplication, it follows that this Fifth Essence of mine is the closest relative to the Sun—or to the true and simple Fifth Essence—and is joined to it by the closest bond of blood; indeed, it is of the very substance of the celestial orb, insofar as it contains such a property of life within itself.

### The second experiment regarding the excellence of this fifth essence in Medicine.

I CONFESS that I have used this natural balsam in the practice of Medicine only once; and even then (as was said before) I experienced its power upon myself. For when I was once afflicted with great trouble and pain in the hump <note>likely referring to the carpus or back of the hand</note> of my hand, and suffered from a weakness of the nerves (which indeed used to happen to me quite often at that time of year when the cold weather, companion to the harsher air, is accustomed to rush in), I took a very small amount of this golden balsam and immediately anointed the affected hand. I solemnly testify that from then until this very day (thanks be to GOD) I have hardly felt any pain or torment. From this it is to be honestly gathered how friendly that substance is to nature, and how greatly it resists its impediments. Something lies hidden here which will not be open to everyone: if, therefore, the internal parts of this essence could be drawn out a little more exactly, with its garments still stripped away, there is no doubt that it could perform far greater things yet.

### The third experiment teaches how this fifth element clearly differs from the remaining four inferior ones by sense or smell.

The EARTH in this Chaos <note>original: "Chaos" — here referring to the primordial, unrefined matter of the experiment</note>, due to the foul disposition caused by the element of fire, breathed out a heavy odor; the Water breathed out an unpleasant aura, proceeding partly from the earth and partly indeed from the air, which smelled only a little of the nature of a fiery odor. But truly, this [the quintessence] was different and much more pleasing than either that of the earth or the fire. The Fire breathed out a most foul stench, affecting the senses suddenly and heavily, by which it sufficiently proved that it was the cause of putrefaction. But the Ether or fifth essence, although it is close to fire in respect to both its composition and its simplicity, was nevertheless sweetly fragrant in its own peculiar and proper nature, and wonderfully pleasant to my sense. It embraced such efficacy and power within itself that if I only touched it, I would still perceive its fragrance two or three days later, so penetrating and effective was it. And certainly (saving the judgment of others), to speak for myself, I prefer the power of this uncooked balsam of life to all other fragrant things that I have ever applied to my senses. From this it seems established that, as far as its substance is concerned, this first essence has a nature far different from that of the four inferior substances which differ from one another.

# CHAPTER IX.

## A certain transcendent inquiry, which can be performed and achieved through the speculation of the higher natures of the human soul, based on the previously observed and established visible foundations.

JUST AS in that half-pyramidal proportion delineated above, which stretches from the sphere of the sun downwards, we find the entire composition of both the external man and the material world in a hieroglyphic manner—inasmuch as its basis is earth, in which the watery moisture visibly dominates, while the airy spirit is invisibly contained, as is the element of fire, and finally that central gift of life or food which is enclosed and hidden within it—so that the external visible circumference of the human world is earth, while water possesses the next sphere, followed by air, and with it fire. To this visible orb, the life-giving ray of the sun or the fifth essence stands as the center or internal principle, to give essence to the others mentioned, not unlike how the celestial sun is accustomed to provide its lucid path to each star of heaven. In the same way, the rays of the sun or the ethereal splendor are the basis or foundation of the internal, spiritual, and invisible man, whose center is GOD himself. For this reason, with premeditated logic, St. John calls Him the light of man; he who has once received this into the innermost chambers of his heart can say with the best right that he not only knows himself, but also understands how to sincerely worship (as becomes an honest and just man) his GOD dwelling within himself. For with this kind of self-knowledge leading the way, it is by no means judged impossible by Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurio Trismegisto"</note> either to know GOD or to revere Him as is fitting for us; for in a certain passage he speaks in these words: *Think that the word of the Lord sees and hears within you.* Whence he also infers elsewhere: *You, moreover, to whom a portion of mind has been granted, recognize your race and consider your immortal nature.* For which reason he designates to us elsewhere, saying: *God is Light and Life, and the Father, from whom man was born; if therefore you comprehend yourself as composed of life and light, you shall transcend back to life and light.* From which the same author elsewhere infers and concludes: *He who knows himself, passes into God, as the word of God has handed down.* And in these things he seems to differ not at all from St. John, who affirms that *God was the Word, and that all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made; in him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.* This, therefore, is the external man, who meets the eyes, whose foundation is earth; for *God had formed man from the dust of the earth* (Genesis 3). GOD created man, whose basis, foundation, or internal principle is the spirit; and this celestial spirit was breathed by GOD himself into the face of the muddy man, according to that text: *And he had breathed into his face the breath of life, and man was made into a living soul* (Genesis, ibid). So we see here the foundation of both the internal and external man, and that the summit or apex of the structure of the external man is the basis of the existence of the internal. And just as we see the sun, filled with that breath of life which GOD breathed on the first day of creation into the universal watery mass of the world so that the world might live by its power, seen magnificently and with a most excellent appearance throughout the whole circle of the lands,

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book II.

Just as the sun is the purest and highest thing in the world that can be discerned by human senses—so much so that it can scarcely be reached by the sharpness of human sight—so too has man placed his internal beginning, or fundamental cornerstone, upon the same spiritual base. Thus, the circumference of the spiritual man’s substance serves to contain the outermost embrace of the internal man, just as the earth performs this same function in the external man. 

The sphere nearest to the spiritual circumference is that light which, flowing in this spirit, imparts life to all creatures, not unlike how water flows nearest to the earth. Then, after that, the rational spirit moves in that sphere, just as air is enclosed in water. Next, within that rational spirit, the spirit of the lucid mind wanders, emanating immediately from the center, in which **GOD** himself resides, clothed in his own glory—yet not by way of confinement, or to speak with <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term><note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus, blending Greek and Egyptian wisdom.</note>: *Inasmuch as he is the divine center of man, whose circumference is nowhere,* that is, whose property it is to be within and outside all things. 

Therefore, emitting the rays of His grace from the center of the internal man, **GOD** either restrains them from the entire bodily composition according to His divine pleasure, according to that word of the royal <term>Psalmist</term><note>Referring to King David; the quote is from Psalm 104:28-29.</note>: *When God gives to the creatures, they gather; when he opens his hand, they are satisfied with good; when he hides his face, they are troubled; when he takes away their breath, they expire and return to their dust.* By these words, the Prophet seems clearly to declare the various actions of **GOD** reigning in the center of the internal man, inclining either toward punishment or toward the benevolence of life. 

We see, therefore, that he approaches somewhat the center of the <term>fifth essence</term><note>The "quintessence" or ether, the purest element beyond the four earthly ones.</note>, in which **GOD** himself primarily acts and presides. Hence it is said, *He set his tabernacle in the Sun,* which the same Hermes Trismegistus tells us, saying: *Mind is in reason, reason in the soul, soul in the spirit, and the spirit with all these in the body.* 

Elsewhere he describes the movement of the spirit in the body thus: *The spirit, diffused through the arteries, veins, and blood, stirs the soul everywhere, and contains and carries the suspended mass of the body.* Thus we see that there is no element in corporeal or visible matter that does not refer to a spiritual substance of the same kind looking back at it. Nor is there any proportion or ratio in the material or formal pyramid beneath the sphere of the sun tending toward the nature of a cubic body, which does not also have that same image or form in the part rising above the sun, according to that word of the Apostle to the Hebrews: *By faith we know that the world was always so constituted by the word of God that from things which could not be seen, those things which can be seen were made.* 

The most wise Rabbis and <term>Cabalists</term><note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, Jewish mystical tradition.</note> also say that all lower things are representative of higher things, and as it is done below, so it is acted above; a sentiment upon which all the sages of both the Hebrews and the Egyptians agree. Truly, the difference (if there be any) consists only in this: that the lower part of the world from the sun is material, while the superior part is spiritual. From this it evidently appears that just as the soul is the spiritual image of the King, so the body is the image of the soul, being a tabernacle or palace ordained to receive it. The only difference between the soul and the body is that the latter is visible and gross, while the former is spiritual, invisible, and subtle. 

Hence Hermes Trismegistus teaches us, *that which is thick is like that very thing which is subtle, and vice versa, that which is subtle is like that which is thick.* And so we have heaven in earth, and vice versa, earth in heaven. In turn, we possess heaven enclosed in earth, and earth in heaven; and by consequence, earth and heaven are but one and the same thing, namely water, as Saint Peter testifies, saying that *of old the heavens and the earth were of water and through water, consisting by the word of God.* 

Therefore, the brightness of the divine word is the base of the formal pyramid, just as water is the base of the material one. Light from the shining word is the life of the waters; the watery mass circles everywhere from the center, according to that word of John: *In him was life, and the life was the light.* 

We conclude, therefore, that the progression from visible thickness to invisible subtlety made through the steps of nature—namely from earth to water, air, fire, and ether—demonstrates to us the progression from the ethereal sphere (the light of equality or the highest point of visibility) upward or inward toward the very point of **Unity**, beyond which no progression is given. 

The ascent from the sun toward **GOD** is of this sort: namely, the ethereal spirit as the receiving base; then the light or soul swimming in that spirit; then the Empyrean or rational spirit included in the soul or vital light; then finally the mind lurking in that intellectual spirit, in whose center is **GOD** himself, the first actor and first mover. Here, the ethereal spirit relates to the soul as the element of air relates to fire;

<columns>
and the soul relates to the Empyrean spirit as the element of fire relates to the ether; and the ethereal spirit relates to the substance of the sun's life as the Empyrean spirit relates to the divine mind; and finally, the living substance of the sun relates to its center or internal actor, as the mind relates to **GOD**. In this way, sub-solar things can be most aptly compared with super-solar things: where the dark earth is the base of the portion of the pyramid tending upward toward the sun, but the solar earth, most rich in light, is the base of the pyramid aspiring from the material to the cone of spiritual things.

But we, in this place—namely, heaven in earth, or the internal in the external—will attempt to explain how it truly exists in nature in the form of a certain solid pyramid. In this pyramid, we have delineated the position of every creature of the element, but especially the grades of the internal man within the external, according to the true opinion of both philosophers and theosophers.

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

Thus we see how we must occupy ourselves and work around the invisible parts of man with the eyes of contemplation alone; for with that alone leading the way, we climb toward the blessed cone of unity through that central and most hidden scale of the pyramid. From this we learn at the same time that all these five particles, or orbs, at the base are reduced to a single point in the cone. This is the unity delineated and extended from the base of the center through its own axis to the cone, where all things coincide into one nature. The scope of this and the remaining pyramidal mysteries is infinite; it will not be difficult to establish the entire structure or fabric of nature, both visible and invisible, upon their bases. But because an exact <term>Epitome</term><note>A summary or condensed abstract of a larger work.</note> of all those things which can be proposed by me concerning these matters is granted to be found in my larger volumes, I will pass over them here with a light step, so that I may bring an end to this book with a description of the earth, as it is the foundation of the visible world, both the macrocosm and the microcosm.

## CHAPTER X.

->*The final appearance concerns the element of earth, which is the basis of all the rest.*<-

In the first place, therefore, before we gird ourselves for the description of the element of earth, it must be known that it may seem likely that the greater spirit of the sun—which began to exercise its kingdom in heaven on the fourth day of creation—was the last of all to have departed and been extracted from the earth. This occurred, surely, after the remaining four elements were segregated from it. For it was said by Moses that the earth was created on the third day, and a proper place was assigned to the sublunary water to contain it, which was given the name "Sea." Consequently, air and fire were finished on that very day and produced out of the dark chaos. Whence it seems probable that, the earth having been first situated and founded, the lucid substance of the sun proceeded from Chaos in order and series after the other three transparent elements. By the virtue of its own light, it was elevated to the center of the middle heaven on the fourth day of creation. In plainly the same way, we perceive in this ocular demonstration of ours that, in imitation of the course of nature, the sun of our central matter emerged from the earth after the separation and disposition of the remaining four sublunary elements. This separation was indeed made by the virtue of that thick and terrestrial fire which receives its action from the God who presides over light and fire, and consequently it must necessarily imitate Him in its action, according to that philosophical axiom: *That which makes a thing such, is itself more so.* Therefore, since by the virtue of that act (which, although it be terrestrial, is nevertheless the true and hidden act of God Himself) a central sun indeed results and emerges manifest from the earth or dark chaos after the appearance of the four elements, it can be seen—according to the probability of nature in producing her actions—that the Sun of the greater world was produced from the mass of terrestrial chaos on the fourth day in plainly the same manner, immediately after the other elements were reduced to order according to the metric and symphonic law of Nature. 

But to return to our purpose: the <term>quintessence</term><note>The "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance, extracted through alchemy.</note> having been separated, we find a dark mass, a <term>caput mortuum</term><note>Latin: "dead head." The useless dregs or residue left after chemical distillation or sublimation.</note>, the earth, which in the opinion of man is condemned as having no effect. For as it was said, the earth before the creation of the greater world was empty, because neither sign nor any effect, nor any vivifying light, was manifest in the darkness before creation. Whence also those darknesses were called <term>Hyle</term><note>A Greek term for "matter" or "raw substance" before it receives form.</note>, which afterwards, by means of the appearance of light and the act existing in it, became Chaos, and was later called Earth. Thus at the end of the creation of the world, these dregs or muds of the waters were converted into fruitful and fertile earth, which, immediately after it was placed in the center of this universe (as we read in Genesis 1), most abundantly brought forth both vegetables and minerals, and finally even animals. 

We assert, therefore, that we have found a certain central heat naturally implanted in this earth of ours, which is the true act and primitive seed of every plant, mineral, and vegetable—namely, a salt fixed in a certain way, participating in those four volatile natures which fled from this terrestrial chaos by the force of fire. And for that reason, in creation, plants and minerals containing the natures of various elements in themselves were produced: the hotter and subtler of which proceeded from the fixed salt of the fiery element; the temperate from the fixed salt of the air; the phlegmatic, cold, and watery from the salty portion of the water; and finally those which were most thick and dry from the earth. Because something of the vivifying moisture of the sun remained in these (which the thick spirits of the earth constrained and embraced so tightly that it could not ascend together with the solar body), it now struggles to ascend, with a desire of seeing its universal nature reigning in heaven and joining itself with it. So much so, that it drags along with it various thick spirits that retain it, and thus they are converted into vegetables, whose roots are fixed to the earth for the reasons demonstrated in the first book. 

I have found all these vivifying but also fixed salts in my terrestrial mass, which, according to their mediocrity or firmness in fixation, produce either vegetables or minerals. For the animal participates in the more volatile substance of the elements, which is therefore not bound or fixed to the earth like the vegetable or mineral, but is mobile from one place to another—namely, on the earth as well as in the water or air. However, the residue of my Chaos, overflowing with condemned darkness and now destitute of almost all virtue, I compare to Lucifer, or the spirit of strife, or the prince of darkness, who, despoiled of his splendor, was cast down headlong toward the darkness, and is an exile from all light and grace. Because of this, it is called by some <term>terra damnata</term><note>Latin: "damned earth." The final, exhausted residue of a substance after all spiritual or medicinal essence has been removed.</note>, devoid of every good quality for preserving its own subsistence. And if the reader has understood me rightly in these things which have now been said, he will perceive that under this figure of my discourse, I have hidden—in a mystical manner—the truly damned earth and the fall of Lucifer, and under a sensible veil, I have explained a matter of great importance.

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book II.

### *The first experiment by which it is proven that the mineral nature can participate with the vegetable.*

I endeavor to prove this by a twofold experiment. For first of all, I cut away a fungus or "wick" <note>original: "lychnum"; likely referring to a specific type of fungal growth used as a lamp wick</note> from this dark and dross-filled earth so that I might burn it with oil. However, I discovered it to be of such great hardness that although it burned continuously, it was not consumed in the manner of other vegetable matter. Thus, it might not undeservedly be called an "incombustible wick" <note>original: "lichnus incombustibilis"</note> and is distinguished by some by such a name. Afterward, having taken pieces of it, I cast them into a glowing fire, and they took on a color entirely similar to live coal; yet later, when withdrawn from the fire and cooled, they turned out similar to steel or iron, assuming a quasi-metallic disposition.

### *The second experiment expressing the internal heat of this earth proceeding from the salt fixed within it.*

After my final distillation, I removed this "dead head" <note>original: "caput mortuum"; a technical term in alchemy for the useless residue left after distillation</note> from the vessel. I found it to be somewhat cold and, as it seemed to me, destitute of the heat of the fire. However, when this dross-filled earth was placed upon wooden boards and drew the air into itself, after five hours had elapsed, it began to burn so freshly that unless it had been discovered and its flame extinguished with watchful care, it would have set fire to the place and the house.

And so I have briefly subjected the anatomy of this most excellent vegetable to your eyes for inspection, with each element elicited from its chaos, comparing them with their likenesses in the greater and lesser world <note>The "Macrocosm" (the universe) and the "Microcosm" (the human being)</note>. And although I could write a full volume concerning the explanation of this subject, I have instead proposed in this treatise of ours to open and explain to you the very base and foundation upon which I have constructed my volumes on the Macrocosm and Microcosm. 

Because of this work, some—either stifled by ignorance or puffed up with envy—think a window has been opened for them to interpret my actions, to judge my religion, and to accuse me of the crime of introducing recent and new opinions. These people condemn my doctrine according to their own whim and say that I foster I know not what sects, and especially that of the **Brothers of the Rosy Cross** <note>original: "fratrum Roseæ crucis"; the Rosicrucians, a mysterious secret society of the era</note>. It seemed to me, therefore, and especially necessary for the sake of my fame and reputation, to declare the unblemished truth to sincere men who, with all prejudice far removed, weigh the matter with an equal balance. This is so that they might not, by perhaps adding faith to the idle and wicked babbling of such men, be circumvented and themselves induced to pluck at my actions. 

But I foster a firm hope that from these things which have been proposed by me in this treatise, they will easily discern the truth and come around to my opinion, having considered the sensible demonstrations brought forward here by me. I adjure and attest, moreover, that if they refuse to give credit to these things I have recited, I will choose four or five men of grave judgment and reputation, in whose sight I will demonstrate anew the things I have committed to writing here. But if any spiritual things lie hidden beneath my corporeal and visible demonstration, they are by no means seen by the ignorant; they condemn not me, but the blindness of their own intellect. Those submerged in earthly darkness cannot judge the colors of heaven; for those things which are spiritual or heavenly are accustomed to be seen by the intuition of the mind and not of the flesh.

Now indeed I shall proceed to the final book of this treatise, in which I have resolved to apply each of these mysteries to the mechanisms of my greater and lesser world, both interior and exterior.

## CHAPTER I.

### *The reason why the Author made mention of Hyle <note>original: "Hyla"; a Greek term for the fundamental "stuff" or raw matter of the universe</note> or the first matter in creation, from which all things were made.*

In the first book of my volume on the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "greater world" or the universe as a whole, as opposed to the "microcosm" of the human being</note>, I made mention of the <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: "materiæ primæ"; the original, unformed substance created by God at the beginning of time</note> from which the world and all things contained within it were created. And although a great distinction has been established between that substance called <term>Hyle</term> and my own <term>Chaos</term> (which I have so often cited in the preceding pages and compared with the greater world), there is a significant difference: for Hyle is nothing other than empty and void darkness, containing not even a spark of light within itself; whereas Chaos is opaque and formless only on the outside, but on the inside it is most full of the actual elements (albeit undisposed and confused). # 44 Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book III.

The eternal form of my chaos is understood as something conceived as being destitute of all action, embracing no actual element within itself; that is, a thing existing simply in potentiality alone, and therefore nothing in actuality. And hence it was that in the third chapter of my first book on the Macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the great world or universe, a central concept in Robert Fludd’s philosophy</note>, I established that this first matter—this *Hyle* <note>original: "Hylam"; from the Greek 'hyle' meaning wood or raw material</note>—was by no means created. Because of this opinion or assertion of ours, I have felt myself unjustly and falsely accused by certain ignorant people or those overwhelmed by envy, without my cause being heard at all. It was as if I had concluded from this that some thing was originally uncreated, and consequently that something was co-eternal with God, even though Scripture nevertheless teaches us that God created all things primordially out of nothing. But truly, such detractors, while they do not understand my meaning, deceive and trick themselves in this censure of theirs; for far be it from me to say that any thing besides God alone is uncreated. Rather, I say that this *Hyle* is my "actual nothing," insofar as it is called "something" only in potentiality and power. Conversely, we find that a thing existing in potentiality or the "power to be" differs greatly from that which exists as a thing in actuality. From this it follows that since first matter is something in potentiality—that is, a thing conceived by the mind in potentiality alone—it is simply and absolutely nothing in actuality.

Now, since every creation is the reduction into act of that thing which never before really existed (for the presence of God gave form to all things which previously were nothing), it is gathered by inevitable consequence that creation is nothing other than the actuation or reduction of a "real nothing"—that is, a thing in potentiality—into something actual. But truly, since *Hyle* or first matter did not exist as such a thing before the Spirit of the Lord shone out of the darkness and moved over the waters, it follows that it was nothing, being devoid of every form and essence by which any individual thing is named. Hence it was that it seemed to Plato that this matter could be compared to no other thing than a phantom exhibited to someone in sleep, which, once he has awakened, is known to have been a mere fantasy; and Saint Augustine compares it to silence, which in respect to speech is mere nothingness.

<margin>Wisdom</margin>
Others truly have estimated it to be so remote from every truly existing thing that they define it as that thing which can scarcely, or not even scarcely, be imagined. Furthermore, to comprehend it in one word: it was a certain imaginative something which in the truth of the matter was nothing, before God, appearing out of the darkness—as one who out of His grace willed to hide Himself no longer—dispelled the dark deformity (which was the form of nothingness) by the power of His splendor, and put on the actual form of the waters as they now appear. Thus He extracted them from the opaque whirlpool of potentiality and brought them forth into that clear splendor of light which informs all things and illuminates all things, by whose power they were cleansed and purified. This also the Sacred Scriptures seem to argue in express words, where according to Pagninus's translation <note>Santes Pagnino (1470–1541), a Dominican friar and leading Hebrew scholar of the Renaissance</note> we read: *The hand of the Almighty made the world out of unformed matter.* According to the exposition of Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a Jewish convert to Christianity and a famous Hebraist</note>: *Thy hand created the world out of unformed matter.* But Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> says: *Thy hand created the orb of the earth out of invisible matter.* From this we conclude, first, that this deformed matter existed before the creation of the world; second, it is clear that it was not "created" [in the formal sense], because it was deformed, whereas all creation is the giving of form <term>information: the act of bestowing a specific shape or essence upon raw matter</term>.

I depicted the type or image of this *Hyle* in the fourth chapter of my first book on the Macrocosm, namely in the form of an infinite mass or thick cloud, black like pitch, without any consideration of a spark of light included in it. However, as pertains to the full resolution of that question—whether first matter or *Hyle* be created or not—I advise those of you who possess a full desire for resolving this doubt to refer to Section 1, Portion 1, Part 2, Book 1, Chapter 5 of the *Preternatural History of Both Worlds*, as in that place you may see the complete opinion of my mind and the authorities firmly establishing it.

## Chapter II.

### The Author's Chaos aptly applied to that of the Greater World.

Immediately after the appearance of God from the darkness, the viscous spirits enclosed in the darkness embraced an infinite number of sparks or rays of light. These rays, penetrating into the dark abyss, changed that mass—whether *Hyle* or first matter—into the obscure Chaos, which is raw and undigested matter. Whence it is said that in its inner recesses or center, the five elements were enclosed in such a confused manner that they struggled and contended among themselves with great impetus; not otherwise than happens in a dark and vast abyss collected in the middle region of the air, where a thundering cloud is observed to resist the action of the most rapacious lightning enclosed in its belly, which indeed does not cease to attack it until it breaks out from its prisons into liberty. To this chaos, therefore, which on the second day of creation fluctuated in the deformed region of the third day, I apply the model of my own chaos, from which I extorted my five elements by the violence of terrestrial fire, in imitation of that Almighty Craftsman who, by His power, primordially extracted those four elements of the world from the universal chaos by means of His celestial fire. Hence it is that in the 10th chapter of the 1st book of the *Physical History of the Macrocosm*, I expressed a double image or figure of chaos, the first of which I formed according to the inten-

### CHAPTER III.

->*Concerning the appearance of the divine spirit which moved upon the waters out of the darkness, and the allusion of our experiment to it, as well as concerning the creation of the first three days.*<-

It is to be gathered from the discourse of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurij Trismeg." Referring to the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note> that when the spirit of the Lord moved upon the waters, those waters were like a gathered or disturbed smoke or vapor; whence he himself calls them a moist nature, agitated by an ineffable countenance. He says that in this moist nature—so disturbed by the sight and aspect of this immense light and splendor of the spirit of God—a terrible shadow or a certain immense darkness fell downward into the moist nature thus disturbed, in a spiral or oblique revolution. Now, indeed, so that we may apply these things in some way not unsuitably to our present work, we find in our first appearance the thick and cloudy appearance just reported by us; and in it, a black and opaque shadow precipitating itself downward toward the bottom of the water or moist nature by the power of fire or a certain reverberating light. This light, in its operation, imitated that divine splendor, inasmuch as its origin proceeded from the word "Let there be" <note>original: "Fiat"</note>, and together with the declining of the darkness, progressed downward toward the center (as seen on page 49 of the same book). And since in the writings of Moses <note>original: "Moysem"</note> mention is made of three days before the creation of the world was completed—on the first of which the highest heaven (namely the fiery or lucid one) was made; on the second, the middle region or ethereal heaven; and on the third, the lowest or elementary heaven—it necessarily follows that since only the first heaven was made on the first day of creation, then indeed the containing cavity of the second or middle heaven was shapeless and still overwhelmed by darkness, and consequently that space of the lowest heaven as well. From this it follows that if the darkness, which before the existence of any things would destroy and deprive the form of the first heaven, was not driven away by the presence of the reflected light moving downward toward the center, then this shadow of darkness thus thrust and depressed downward was mixed with those shadows which denied all form to the middle heaven (or the operation of the second day) through the space of the first day. Thus, the darkness of this middle heaven was now doubled or duplicated; and consequently, for the same reason, the darkness of the lowest region was tripled after the perfection of the second heaven. From this, therefore, arose that chaos <note>The primordial state of matter before it was organized by the Creator.</note> which contained the three elements within itself: namely, the sphere of fire, that of moisture, and the globe of the earth. From this, therefore, proceeds that triple kingdom in the composition of nature: namely, the Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral. And from here proceed those three complete regions in the earth or the kingdom of darkness, each of which has respect to one of these elements. From here (I say) first of all we have the earth, which is cold and dry like a certain thick or cold and dry water, since from it almost all moisture is drawn out. Next to this succeeds the sphere of moisture, which is either cold—commonly called the element of water—or hot and moist, which we commonly call air. Then afterward follows the sphere of fire, which is like a hot and dry water, so that this hot and dry water is nothing else but a certain dross of the spirits of the fiery or empyrean heaven. The sphere of moisture, however, is the thicker portion of the spirits of the ethereal or middle heaven which were enclosed in darkness; and the hot and moist part of this sphere is the basis of the ethereal part which is above the sphere of the sun, and its cold and moist portion is the denser part of the spirit which floats between the sun and the sphere of water. For this reason, therefore, I have expressed the figures related to the creation of the first, second, and third days on pages 55, 88, 63, 66, and 69, from which the degrees of darkness shine forth—namely, to what extent in measure and proportion they descended toward the center of the world, where they were established in that place where they even now remain, on the third day when the name of "earth" was bestowed upon them.

The celestial light, springing immediately from the Spirit of GOD, forged the five elements of the greater world out of a triple chaos by its circulating and reverberating power. However, the manner in which each of these four sublunary elements was separated from the dark mass and from the remaining elements—along with the true method of operation in their partitioning—you will find in the second book of my volume on *Macrocosmic Physics*, chapter 11, page 63. Among these, the element of fire is seen to enjoy the highest place, which nevertheless, beyond all doubt, was the last to flash out and emerge from the black mass of the earth. This has been demonstrated by us both in our experiment of extracting fire from our own chaos <note>The author refers to his laboratory "chaos," likely a starting material in an alchemical work</note>, and also in chapter 12, pages 64 and 66, declaring the position of the dark earth. There, it finally manifested itself in its own proper nature once each of the remaining elements had been divided and extracted from its bulk. Then, chapter 13, pages 66 and 68, describes the method and character of the sphere of moisture, which seems to flow from the deformed mass with a double nature, both joined together: namely, water gushing out first before the air, and afterwards the air mixed with water, followed by fire as was just mentioned.

Thus, this place expresses those elements as somewhat confused, disturbed, and impure in their first appearance; but truly the figure on page 69 depicts the same elements purified and completely distinguished and arranged in their natural seat by means of the bond of the **quintessence** <term>quintessence: the "fifth essence" or ether, a pure substance thought to bind the four physical elements</term>. Furthermore, beyond all these things, just as in our small operation we find the quintessence—or the spark of the grain—leaping out in the last place after everything else from the sphere of our central sun of chaos, so also it is likely and probable that the fiery and spiritual globe of the sun in the greater world finally emerged after the chaos was stabilized in the center of the universal machine or structure, and was sublimated into the heaven. 

Experience in this operation of ours confirms this, in which we find the first element, namely water, was first liberated from the dark prison; afterward the second, which was air; then fire, which was the third; finally the quintessence, the fourth; and at last the earth, which was the external foundation of all the aforesaid. Thus we find that the quintessence or fifth element (whose chief habitation is in the center or heart of the middle heaven) was extracted last from the womb of the great and general chaos. And indeed, if we only note how the Sun of the greater world is assisted by Moses—easily the prince and father of the wise—and is said to have been made after the positioning of the earth and the limitation of the waters, we shall perceive most clearly that this mystery of his tends toward my same goal. For I am compelled to reason thus: Since the creatures of the first heaven were created on the first day, and the creatures of the lowest heaven, such as minerals and vegetables, were made on the third day, what was the reason why the creatures of the middle heaven—namely the sun, moon, and the rest of the stars—were only procreated on the fourth day? I answer: it seemed so to the supernatural GOD, that this terrestrial chaos, according to its natural position, should bring forth or give birth to a "natural GOD," or the splendid light of nature, hidden in the dark chaos to vivify the world in a temporal way and to produce multiplication in sublunary compounds; which light was established in the heaven at the beginning of the fourth day. 

Nor should this seem impossible to us worldly folk, since the supernatural and spiritual GOD himself springs forth from the earth, by whom invisible souls and spirits are preserved in their essence. For in the actual text <note>Isaiah 45:8</note> it is found: 
> The earth shall be opened and bring forth a savior. 
<note>original: "Aperietur terra & pariet saluatorem."</note> 

And here this spiritual and supernatural GOD, the invisible son of GOD the Father (just as the worldly Sun is called the visible son of GOD by Plato), directs and governs from the sun upward, through a spiritual and invisible **Diapason** <term>Diapason: a musical interval of an octave, used here to describe a harmonic resonance between the physical and spiritual worlds</term> harmony, just as the visible sun works downward through a similar visible and material one. He who immerses himself in our worldly harmony in Book 3, Chapter 3 of our *History of Physics* will find things pertaining to this matter. And as for the figure of the formal and material Diapason, see page 90. Furthermore, I have explained this matter more diffusely in the 6th and 7th chapters of my first book of the *Macrocosm*, where sufficiently valid reasons are brought forward with figures confirming the matter. Whence I have proposed to myself to persevere in this mind and opinion until rigid and violent rejectors of such demonstrative opinions bring forward sounder reasons, supported by stronger experience than has been produced by me.

Now, therefore, as far as the body of the Sun of the greater world is concerned, we find it to be nothing other than condensed spirit; whence the philosophers defined it as the denser part of its orb. We all see that it is also illuminated on all sides by lucid flames, whose rays are like agents that generally work in the spirit of this visible world. And because we see that lucid body placed in the very center of the middle heaven, and God himself—the source and origin of all forms—is said by the prophet David to dwell in the highest heaven (that is, in the highest purity), while on the other hand the infected earth (which is a gross and great mass or mother of matter) is placed in the lowest center, so that the source of form differs from that opposition of matter by a diametrical space in the middle of which the sun is established; it follows infallibly, therefore, that the sun participates equally in form and in matter. Namely, it looks downward toward material spirit and gazes upward toward formal light. And this is the reason why the ancient philosophers spoke so many words about the "sphere of equality" in which the sun is driven around, and others about the sphere of the Soul of the World, which I have approved by the reasons of wise philosophers in Book 4, Chapter 10 of the *Macrocosm*, and demonstrated their truth with figures and conclusions explained on pages 81, 89, 90, and 165. 

And this is that which I mentioned regarding my central sun which I elicited from my artificial chaos: For (as I said) I found a pure and limpid spirit, like crystal, totally irradiated with lucid rays, so exquisitely proportioned that the spirit did not exceed the proportion of light, nor did the formal light surpass the measure of the material spirit; but the appetite of the spirit seemed satisfied by the act of the light it required. Whence it happens that such a substance is marked by immortality and contributes to the sustenance of life. From the observation of such a substance, I perceived what the philosophers understand by the "sphere of equality"; which

...investigating the [proportions] of the excellent action and passion <note>In this context, "action" refers to the active, formal force (spirit/light) and "passion" refers to the passive, material capacity to be acted upon.</note> of life. Therefore, by a geometric method of inquiry, I discovered that the earth is the fountain of matter and passion, because I perceived it to be the thickest foundation of material substance. I perceived the truth of this matter all the more clearly because I observed that Water—the element closest to that place and nature—is to that extent lighter and more transparent; then Air is lighter than water, and Fire than air. Finally, by a logical consequence, I gathered that the ether (or the substance of the starry heavens) was thinner than elementary fire by the same proportion. Lastly, I concluded that the intellectual or empyrean heaven <note>The highest heaven in medieval/Renaissance cosmology, believed to be composed of pure light or fire.</note> was the thinnest of all, inasmuch as its substance, due to the immediate presence of GOD, is nothing other than the thinnest spirit of the world turned into fire and light; for in this heaven, light was created on the first day. Now, since no created matter or spirit can exist within GOD, we have freely and sincerely asserted that matter must necessarily cease and be terminated in this place—being contiguous to GOD—as if in a unity or a material point, as if one were to say: *No further.*

Wherefore we perceive that the material progress from the opaque fountain of the earth upward is like a flame of fire, which the higher it ascends, the more it is sharpened and reduced to a point. And this is the reason why we have reduced the entire scope or foundation of matter lying in the earth into the form of a pyramid, whose base is placed in the earth as the thicker portion of matter, while its peak touches the very throne of GOD; and this empty pyramid we call the material, watery, and passive pyramid.

Now, because the seat of GOD is said to be in the heights of the heavens—in the highest heaven or the heaven of heavens, namely where the point of the earth's radius (or the point opposite the center) terminates at the circumference of the world—and perceiving moreover that the act of GOD in creation is proportioned and relates equally to the passion of moist matter, we have fashioned another pyramid contrary in position to that material one. For its base is, as it were, continuous or contiguous to the presence of GOD (namely, at the circumference of the fabric of the world), but its peak points downward toward the base of the material pyramid, or the center and heart of the macrocosmic fabric, just as the material peak reached the formal base above.

And that this is so in reason, I deduced in this manner: because GOD is truly called the fountain of all light; next, the heaven placed nearest to Him, in which He shines immediately by His splendor, is called the Empyrean or Fiery; next, the middle heaven is called Ether, as if "fiery air," because air and fire are equally proportioned; finally, we perceive by experience that the effect of light in the lower heaven is weak, so that the appetite of matter is never satisfied (whence it continually desires to change an old form into a new one, which is the cause of alterations in the lower heaven). Hence we see the power of light gradually and step-by-step remit its virtue in its descent and decrease in its action, and this is due to the dominion of the lower matter, which extinguishes and restrains its force—not unlike how light, the more it raised itself on high, mutilated the thickness and resistance of matter by its own efficacy and the force of its dominion in the upper region.

It follows, therefore, that just as the mass of moist matter can be reduced to a pyramidal form (called the material pyramid), so also the mass of light emanating in the world from the presence of GOD—shining out of darkness or potentiality into act—can be reduced to a formal pyramid. In its descent, this is seen to cut and divide that ascending material pyramid in equal proportion, so that where their meeting and intersection occurs, there appears to be the "sphere of equality," or the seat of the Soul of the Greater World <note>The *Anima Mundi*, the vital force connecting the divine and the material.</note>, in which the sun completes its daily course. The diagrams and reasons for these two pyramids meeting one another, together with their intersections, are vividly expressed in my said book on pages 105, 118, 84, 89, and 90. And how these two pyramids are to be understood not just geometrically but physically is sufficiently declared with reasons and demonstrations on page 76.

And so that I might make this pyramidal doctrine of mine easier for you, I have explained my entire intention regarding them in a special book, which you will find inscribed in the technical history of my microcosm <note>Referring to Fludd's massive work, *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*.</note>, *On the Speculative Metaphysical and Physical Science of Pyramids.* We have gathered this entire doctrine which we found concerning these two pyramids from the contemplation of that middle substance, inasmuch as it is tempered exactly and completely in light and spirit. And just as reason itself dictates to us that no one can imagine a "middle" without having regard for the two extremes—no differently than we see in Arithmetic that the number two cannot exist unless its two extremes (namely unity and three) are weighed—so, finding the mean in the radius of the orb of Nature, I immediately measured its extremes, making the mathematical radius the axis or central line of each of these pyramids of nature, both the material and the formal.

Upon these reasons, therefore, as the most stable and safe foundations, I have placed the structure of my philosophy, to refute those rumors which have spread—following the ignorant custom of the unthinking crowd—that the foundations of my doctrine are erroneous because they are new. But I would urge these insolent censors to put hand to pen and confute what I have proposed, so that all who lean upon the wings of justice may see both them and me for what we are, and thereby learn to judge more rightly of us and our errors.

Lastly, the principle of the growth and multiplication of plants described by me in the first book of my Macrocosm (as also that of the sensible and vital spirits in animals expressed in the next following chapter) is fully demonstrated in the second chapter of the first book of this treatise, and the fourth chapter of the second book, and especially in its third experiment. And thus we have contemplated the entire course of visible nature in the greater world within this small subject of a vegetable creature; wherefore we shall proceed and demonstrate how we have applied this to the use of the microcosm, or our lesser world,

->by demonstration.<-
