## Second Part
## OF THE THIRD BOOK
# CONCERNING THE MICROCOSM
<note>The "Microcosm" or "Little World" is a traditional philosophical term for a human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>

## Chapter I.
### *Concerning Man.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'N' decorated with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>
Now, so that we may apply this experimental conclusion of ours to man and his parts—that is, first to his external and visible parts, and then afterwards to the internal—we say that the human body, which is his external part, is to be compared to the dark and opaque earth. For this part, without the infusion of spiritual parts into it—namely the soul (which derives its origin and essence from heaven)—is of no greater esteem or validity than our lifeless earth mentioned before, namely the "dead head" <note>original: "caput mortuum"; a term used in alchemy to describe the useless residue left after distillation or sublimation</note>, or the dregs of our foul chaos. How this human body may rightly be called "earth," I have shown in the second chapter of my fifth book on the history of the microcosm, page 106, where I proved at the same time that although it is called earth, it nevertheless contains within itself the elements of water, air, and fire, which are entirely necessary for its composition.

Afterwards, just as we asserted in Book 2, Chapter 9 of this very treatise that the Platonists themselves established that the soul is in the spirit, and the spirit is in the body; so also in our "fifth essence" <term>quintessence: the purest, most essential part of a substance</term> we see the manner in which the life-giving rays of light (which is that true soul of which the Platonists understood) are carried into the body by means of a clear and bright spirit, acting as a vehicle or "patient" <note>In this context, a "patient" is the medium that receives or undergoes an action</note> most excellently adapted to it by Nature. And hence the spirit of man was called by the wisest philosophers the "vehicle" or "chariot" of the soul; and because the spirit is bound so closely to the soul by the invisible joints of nature, it is frequently taken for the vital soul itself. Hence it was said by the Apostle: *The sword of God is powerful, an acting sword even unto the division of the soul from the spirit* <note>A reference to Hebrews 4:12</note>, for no one except God alone can separate these two from one another. Regarding this soul and spirit, and their union and division, we have made mention at length in Chapters 1 and 2 of the 13th book of my history of the physics of the macrocosm, as well as in Book 12, Chapter 14, and various other places pertaining to this.

Now, truly, how the spirit works in the body—carrying the vital light within itself like the oil of a lamp carrying its flame—I have sufficiently expressed in Book 8, Chapter 8. There, I demonstrated in the first place that this spirit is the true "radical moisture" <term>humidum radicale: the fundamental fluid or "fuel" believed to sustain life and heat in a living being</term> of every creature, whether animal or vegetable, and that its principal seat is in the heart. For this reason, the heart hangs downward like a formal pyramid because of the shape of the life-giving light working invisibly within. In that same place, I describe the method by which the spirit is conveyed into the body on the authority of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and hermetic philosophy</note>, who speaks in these words: *The spirit, diffused into the veins and arteries and the blood, moves the animal on all sides, and holds the mass of the body suspended, and carries it about; the soul is in the spirit, reason is in the soul, and the mind is in reason.*

Then, we also reported what the life-giving soul is in the very next chapter: namely, a spark, as it were, of celestial light, which is nourished by its own spiritual crystalline liquor. Concerning the operation of this soul and the degrees of its power in the body of every animal creature, we have dealt abundantly in Chapter 5 of the said book, where I indicated that the abundance of vital light in this spirit is the cause of the body's agility. So also in Chapter 3 of the said book, I declared this soul (which I imagined floating in an ethereal spirit, as it were) to be like a "middle soul," or the middle region of the human soul. There, I noted at the same time the reason why an animal is often called immortal, and often in turn called mortal. And finally, as pertains to its property in the human body, you may read it described at greater length, and fully so, in Chapter 1 of the same book. This, therefore, is that act of Nature, that worldly or celestial ray of which I spoke in Chapter 6 of the third book of the same volume, which we asserted to be entirely necessary for the life of both man and other creatures; for it is the highest portion of the essence of the visible world, which is like a part or spark of the most bright, shining solar mass, swimming in a spirit most worthy to receive such a gem. In this mixture conducive to life, just as the light acts benevolently toward life, so the spirit receives its passions sweetly and with a natural embrace.

# On the Exact Anatomy of Bread or Wheat.

## CHAPTER II.

->On the Natural faculty, and that all vegetation proceeds from the Liver,<-
->likewise concerning the seed or the Liver of man.<-

I have told you in my experimental operation—namely in the second book and second chapter of this present treatise—that the principal and immediate cause of vegetation proceeds from the air, where I brought an experiment to light for the sake of proving this very thing. Thus it is also evident that the airy part itself procreates blood within the nourishment, by the virtue of which the entire mass of the body is vegetated and increased; whereas, when that part is lacking, the body wastes away and becomes flaccid. From this it is manifest that the natural faculty is principally cherished and sustained by this element mixed with a portion of the soul’s quintessence <note>The "fifth essence," a celestial substance beyond the four earthly elements.</note>, which I cited above. Concerning this vegetable or airy essence, I have spoken sufficiently in the seventh chapter of the ninth book of my *History of the Macrocosm*, where I aptly applied the airy part of my experiment to this business and clearly explained all actions within this natural faculty. And although it is established by some that the seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> is a foamy and superfluous part of the "third digestion" <note>In medieval physiology, the final stage of nutrition where food becomes part of the tissues.</note>, I am nevertheless certain and instructed by faithful experience that the central and principal part of the spermatic mass is of an ethereal and vital nature. We have spoken of this previously, and what can be said regarding this point of the subject we have discussed more fully and even more clearly in the third, fourth, and fifth chapters of the second book of my *History of the Macrocosm* and in the *Mystical Anatomy*. We conclude, therefore, that this natural faculty is that act within the airy spirit which we mentioned in chapter 7, book 3 of the same *History of the Microcosm*; where, not without just reason, I called it the "elementary ray" and the subject of the sensitive soul, or the base of the entire fabric of the human soul.

It stood firm in our experimental demonstration that we beheld with corporeal eyes the visible portions of the vegetable and animal soul consisting in the subtle substance of that entire spirit which exists between the sun of heaven and the dark earth from which the body is formed. So it is fitting for us to contemplate the spiritual and invisible parts of the soul with the eyes of the intellect; these ascend from the visible body of the sun to the "cone of matter" contiguous with God himself. Therefore, just as the ethereal spirit is carried in the air as if in its vehicle, and the luminous soul is carried in this ethereal spirit as if in a vehicle—the foundation of all of which is the opaque earth—so the soul of man is the base or vehicle of the rational or intellectual spirit, in which the rays of the Mind rejoice to bathe and wash themselves invisibly. It is clear that the essence of God dwells in the center of the Mind. And this is the very thing that Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus," the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and wisdom.</note> inculcates in us with these words:

I described the entire method of this descent into the human body in the third book, eighth chapter of my *History of the Macrocosm*, where these things are contained:
> *By which vehicles or through which media the lights of any heaven flowing together are joined to the human soul and body;*

and in the third chapter of the fourth book of the same, which contains this:
> *By what virtue of mundane harmony is the Mind attracted to its opaque body?*

At the end of that chapter, a hieroglyphic demonstration is also expressed with the harmony of the soul's descent into the body. And in the fourth chapter of the said book, where these things are read:
> *How the mind and intellect, penetrating from above through the whole world toward the lower parts even to the center, may perceive the mysteries of any heaven, and participate in the nature and disposition of any heaven; and is not man rightly called the image of God?*

This, therefore, is that Mind, by the possession of which man is rightly called the image of God, as you find described at greater length in chapter 5 of the third book of my *Macrocosm*. As far as pertains to this excellent "head" of the human soul, we have placed that in the fourth chapter of the third book of the aforementioned history, where I call it the "super-celestial ray" and the "act of God," as also in the whole seventh book of the same subject, and in various places of my *Microcosmic* work, where I demonstrated the mental part to be the unity of the internal man. And although Hermes Trismegistus affirms that the Word <note>original: "Verbum"</note> is in this mental ray, it is nevertheless my opinion that this mental ray is the Word itself, since it is an immediate emanation from the fountain of unity and light. I have proved in the book cited by me above that this can in no way suffer change in itself; and because it is also the first emanation from the Father, I have demonstrated it to be the Messiah or the power of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>, which seems to be confirmed by that saying of St. John:
> *In him was life, and this life was the light of men, and this light shone in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it,*

but this is also more clearly explained in our *Cabalistic History*. I could bring forth and commit to writing infinite things concerning this matter; but this is not the time for my intention, which strives to declare to the world how, raised by the rowing of my own wings, I have reached this point, and what remains in my power for each thing by me in...

# Section I. Portion III. Part I. Book III. On the Extraction of Bread or the Anatomy of Wheat.

The evidence cited in my writings, concerning both the Macrocosm <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole</note> and the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," referring to man as a reflection of the universe</note>, provides experimental testimony; and what is more certain than ocular demonstration? And so I shall bring an end to this brief treatise. Although it may perhaps seem ridiculous to those who understand very little at first glance, or those darkened by ignorance, and even to critics <note>original: "momis," referring to Momus, the Greek god of mockery and censure</note> or certain mercurial wits prone to rash judgment because of the commonness of the subject matter, I nevertheless advise my readers not to pass over obvious and common things with a "light foot" (as they say). For although they are able to recognize and distinguish the external coverings of these things, it will seem very difficult to uncover the treasures hidden within them and to behold them with open eyes. 

This is the reason why the more foolish people turn up their noses at things they have never seen, judging them to be impossible—as if, forsooth, all things were so stretched to the measure of their own capacity that they must, by right, either be made manifest to their own brutish senses or be utterly denied the possibility of existing in the nature of things. Hidden mysteries are suited to the wise alone; manifest and common things are for the foolish as well as those intoxicated by worldly wisdom. The former, since they are truly learned and well-versed in the mysteries of God and the light of nature, are regarded by the world as fools, inasmuch as they do not wish to reveal themselves to the world. The latter, though in truth overwhelmed by mere folly, are falsely held by the common people to be learned and wise; for in a deceptive manner they appear prudent when in truth they are the most dull-witted of all. Thus, in vanity, the glory of the world passes away; for whatever is under the sun, except for the true knowledge of God, is vanity, according to that saying of the wise man: *Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity* <note>A famous quote from Ecclesiastes 1:2</note>.

# P R E F A C E.

## C H A P T E R I.

### *In which the various formulas of speech used by Anatomists, before they arrive at the direct sequence of their practice, are discussed; and also the Author's method in this matter, its reasoning, and its model are explained.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial M featuring a figure standing in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>IT is the custom and quite laudable habit of almost all physicians that, before they enter upon the path of a public anatomy <note>A public dissection performed for students and the public</note>, they deliver a certain oration. This is done both to render the minds of the listeners more attentive and prepared, and so that the subject to be handled by their hands might be made more pleasing by such a refined introductory speech. But truly, the artists differ wonderfully from one another in the subject of their orations; for some turn their speech only to the structure of the human body, others to the praises of the body's perfections and symmetry, others to the antiquity and excellence of the art of <term>Anatomy</term> <note>The art of dissection</note>, and finally others delight in celebrating with elegant words the encomiums of <term>Anatomists</term>, both ancient and modern. 

Yet (as it seems to me), nothing is more suited to the prelude of the anatomical art, and nothing more honorable or glorious can happen to the corpse to be dissected, than that the lineage, essence, governance, or properties of its mistress (namely the soul that once inhabited it) be revealed to the minds and ears of the listeners with the greatest oratorical wit and in words ornately delivered. For who, I ask, well-versed in philosophy, would desire to look upon or affect the effects of a natural thing while remaining ignorant of their intrinsic acting causes? For the former are familiar to the senses and consequently to the beasts, but the latter are subject to the internal intellect, which is the principle of man. And who, passing through some noble palace and admiring its wonderful craftsmanship, would not inquire after the master of such a great building, even if absent, and labor to know his status, condition, and lineage? Therefore, we think it a matter to be chastised with the whip of ignorance if anyone plunges himself into the sea of corporal anatomy—that is, of the external man—rashly, making no mention of the internal man. For the soul alone (by divine will) is the architect of this <term>microcosmic</term> <note>The "little world," a common Renaissance concept of man as a reflection of the universe</note> lodging; by its fingers the organs of such a most noble palace were skillfully fashioned, and this whole visible house was fabricated with admirable art according to the invisible model of its spirit. 

As for the praises of the body and its parts, and their exact and symmetrical proportion, as well as the excellence and dignity of anatomy and anatomists: what need is there, I ask, for commendation in the preface of an anatomy? For the practice itself will clearly exhibit to the spectators the most worthy excellence of the parts of the human body, their admirable joining in the body, their harmonious arrangement and position, and finally their utility in perfecting the functions of the soul, its mistress. Furthermore, through the exquisite skill of the expert anatomist, the science will sufficiently extol itself with praises; the parts of the human body, equally divided and demonstrated, will speak for themselves, as will that anatomical art by whose direction the dissection of such parts is performed. Therefore, the formula of the soul's descent into the muddy body, its conditions while dwelling in that lodging, and finally the reason for its separation and departure from its tabernacle, I have narrated in the sequence of the anatomical oration (performing the office of anatomical lecturer in the London College of Physicians in the year 1620) in the context of a speech of this kind.

## T H E  O R A T I O N.

**J**UST as the insolence of the envious and malevolent is not to be borne—from whose number, may God grant me better than that anyone should have crept today into this solemn congregation of wise men secretly and without our knowledge—so I ask and beseech you (the President, holding the highest rank in the medical magistracy of both dignity and command; Doctors and colleagues most skilled in the art of medicine; Nobles, for whom the foundations of illustrious origin have created glory; and all listeners in general, most adorned with both learning and benevolence) by the common law of humanity, that you remain in the duty of your holy goodness. And although you may rightly feel that I am in no way to be equaled to my predecessors in this art—who, having approached the anatomical mystery with toilsome labor and the daily experience of others preceding them, have diligently cultivated it—nevertheless, that something may be produced today upon this medical stage before you, by which your thirsty ears and eyes, perhaps greedy for novelty, might be in some way soothed, the famous custom of this College (which we celebrate publicly before this most pleasing assembly of Doctors through annual returns) commands and warns me, and your sweet gentleness toward me urges and persuades me.

Behold then, we pray for pardon if, in this administration of anatomy, either through manifest error or...

# Common Anatomy

The traces of limping science <note>original: "scientiæ claudicantis vestigia" — a humble reference to the limitations of human knowledge compared to divine truth</note> might penetrate the keen gaze of any of you, or your finely polished touch. But before we draw back the tragic curtain of this desolate palace (though it be white in color), or fold away the theatrical veil of this masked image, I shall begin by making clear to you the essence of the divine lady <note>The Soul</note> who once inhabited this lineage, the manner of her descent into such a variety of ranks, the laws of economy within her, and finally her flight—the palace now having been violated by the blow of the executioner—offering these as proofs of reason, like untainted truth.

I speak of the Mind, the sacrosanct breath of God, the noble offspring of divine parents, adorned with every beauty, made in the likeness of the Holy Trinity, equal to eternal glory, ordained within itself for blessedness, and the legitimate heir of salvation. This most beautiful of creatures (I say), reclining sweetly upon a bed of thin and dewy spirit above the high peaks of the world, and surrounded by every choir of graces and the service of angels, was gently carried downward by the mild breeze of the softly breathing West Wind <note>Zephyr</note> in its tranquil spirit. Gradually descending through the slopes of the high worldly valley, she lightly glided down and came to rest in the most pleasant little garden of the earthly paradise. In the very center of this, planted with tall and vast trees of wondrous condition, where among other pleasing herbs the virgin Roses flowed with morning dew, this winged child of the eternal Creator—the sweet and honeyed soul of the microcosm <note>The human being as a "little world"</note>—beheld a spring, placid with the crystalline milk of the vital spirit. Near its flow, a certain royal house was built, not by human hands, but by divine arts: I mean a noble palace, made from the precious earth of clay into the human image, which you would say at first sight had been the bright and pleasant lodging of some God. And certainly, by the testimony of Holy Scripture, this was the temple of the Holy Spirit. The admirable arrangement of this earthly Tabernacle greatly pleased the heavenly Soul, and she was immediately captivated by its beautiful appearance.

And now the heaven-dweller confidently entered it, by whose presence even the inner chambers, arranged far and wide—a house precious beyond price—so flash with their own splendor that the house creates its own spiritual day for itself, even if the sun of the macrocosm <note>The physical universe</note> were unwilling. Thus the color of the shining rooms of the dwelling flashes against the life-giving edge of this internal sun; thus the bright clarity of its walls shines forth (with the soul governing within it). Nor do the other parts respond differently to the majesty of this animal house, so that it rightly seems to be an earthly palace built after a heavenly model for the conversation of a divine and incorruptible nature with a corruptible human one, for some great deity. And now the breast yearns to be lifted by the swelling of the clay image, now the healthy vein yearns to pulse, now the body yearns to be filled with spirit. Now the mass is suffused everywhere with a bloody redness and native heat. The face, previously deformed by earthy paleness, now seems to redden with a beautiful habit and a truly virginal modesty, as if out of shame; it is decorated in a wonderful way with flashing eyes, blushing cheeks, and open eyes. The head shines with resisting hair, and the breast is most accurately adorned with white breasts and glowing nipples. And so the entire clay work of the eternal Signifier is converted into a true and complete youth of fair beauty. And now, testing himself, he tries to move his limbs little by little, and at last the first Adam rises, who, snatched up by the contemplation of his own divine form, emerges happy and eager, suffused with the quite deceptive and fragile joy of earthly things.

By this means (I say), the soul—once free and flashing with holy splendor—is now bound to a dark heart, captured by the long-lasting shackles of love. I mean the bright heaven, corrupted by the love of lower things, unexpectedly plunges itself into the opaque prisons of the earth, plucking a taste both sweet and bitter. For by this heavy bond, she herself has obtained an earthly disposition, and thus separated from her heavenly lineage, she has miserably brought upon herself a long-lasting forgetfulness. Indeed, now lulled to sleep by bodily passions and led away from herself through the sensible forms of her palace, she has forgotten what she is or what she was; since she remembers having been nothing else, she believes for certain that she is nothing except what she appears to be.

Therefore, she burns with such a vehement love for her prison that she seems to be sharply afflicted by its pains, she who by herself knows not how to grieve or suffer; she dreads destruction, she who knows not how to perish; she fears deficiency, whose divine nature cannot fail. She feeds on the speculation of the eyes; she is soothed by sonorous hearings; she is delighted by the sweetest odors; she is refreshed by large feasting. And although she herself in no way uses all these things because of the simplicity of her nature, she is nevertheless affected by heavy sadness, and her sorrow is greatly doubled if the necessities of this house of hers are withdrawn. From here, therefore, vices contrary to reason creep in, while the soul, by indulging the delighted body too leniently, is known to give place to sin. But by the secret decree of the immense Creator of things, a fatal commerce was made between these two; He, noticing that the specimen of divine likeness neglected gross things and was least of all inflamed by the desire for earthly things, willed it to be covered with a dark garment or an earthy house. For this reason, He ordained that man, the most noble creature, be fashioned from a heavenly soul and an earthly body—as if from an eternal and a mortal nature—so that the rational animal thus conformed could satisfy both of its origins: to wonder at and pray to heavenly things, and to inhabit and govern earthly things.

And now, for the enclosed soul, the internal image of the external man is rightly defined: for whom supreme wisdom is taste, intelligence is vision, the mind is the eye, reason is the gaze, and reasoning itself is the investigation of the object. There are three powers by which she operates: the **desiring** <note>concupiscibilis</note>, the **irascible** <note>irascebilis</note>, and the **rational**. By the first, she desires and loves; by the middle, she despises and hates; and by the latter, she discerns between the two former. There are four affections, the foundations of every virtue as well as vice: Joy and Hope, which are derived from the desiring power; Grief and Fear from the irascible. Finally, the steps through which she shows herself both upward and downward are her five strengths: for by means of **sense** she observes bodies; by **imagination**, the likenesses of bodies; by **reason**, their natures; by **intellect**, the created spirit; and by **intelligence**, the uncreated one <note>God</note>. For sense informs imagination, and imagination informs reason and creates...

# Preface

knowledge, which is also called prudence; then divine presence instructs the reason and brings forth wisdom. From here, two actions of the soul’s life are recounted: by the virtue of one, it looks back at things falling and transitory, and is inclined toward the flesh by means of the senses; by the effort of the other, it is raised to the heights and flies away on full wings to God, dwelling in and around Him. And this is that divine <term>economy</term><note>original: "oeconomia"; here meaning the internal management or divine arrangement of the soul's functions</note> of the soul governing in its lodging; these are the admirable laws of its <term>polity</term><note>original: "politiae"; the organized "government" of the soul over the body</note> in the human body, by which it expands itself at will to things lower and higher, and is divinely illuminated to know and contemplate God above itself, itself within itself, the Angels beside itself, and whatever is contained within the circuit of heaven beneath itself.

Thus, the soul, having been born and so fortified with all bodily necessities, runs to and fro through the vast ocean of the world (with the soul as mistress and guide). It either completes its journey peacefully on a barely stirred sea and is gently vibrated in a mild wave (a life indeed known to very few), or it is endangered, tossed by various whirlwinds of storms. Indeed, if the guidance of the female governor is lost or at least neglected, the soul itself, thrust to the margin of further unhappiness, is often accustomed to be submerged headlong and overwhelmed by unexpected death; nor can that agile and noble effort of so divine a leader go before the severity of human fortune.

Behold, you have before your eyes the tragic and ghost-like object of such a condition: the former carnal lodging of the soul, in which she long established and administered the laws of her economy. But now, destined at last for the shipwreck of the cross or the gallows by the cruelty of fate, and fixed there by the savage hand of the executioner (placing the noose upon the neck and, with it tightened at the throat, cutting off the duties of the spirit), the soul has emerged by secret paths, leaving its hearth and deprived of all earthly things. In a moment (carried on ethereal wings), flying away on high, it has left this terrestrial palace of its own—destitute of life and action, but not of the perfection of its fabric—in this custody and power of ours.

Behold therefore (most distinguished spectators, who pursue the pleasure of this sufficiently famous spectacle), I, the public minister of this day’s exercise, bring forth this mournful subject, everywhere suffused with a boxwood color <note>pale or yellowish, typical of a corpse</note>, into the middle of the stage like a kind of victim to be offered to your eyes, so that I may satisfy your curious zeal for seeing and my duty toward you in this matter. Behold, I say, the ghost-like image, deformed by the penal fury of death and the squalor of wretched privation; consider with curious, but also pious and Christian eyes, the external Man (I say) by himself alone, the internal and eternal one having been lost and slipped away. While I, the principal—though unwilling—actor of this tragedy, or rather the involuntary author of so great a butchery (not so much inhuman as necessary) now to be performed in this enclosed theater <note>original: "caveae"; referring to the anatomical theater</note>, gird myself to confidently reveal with a dutiful hand this most wretched but admirable example of human frailty, covered in linen cloths. I do this so that, with the knife or scalpel plunged very deep into the corpse even to the pith, you may recognize the secret chambers of the same, which once served the soul inhabiting it, under the judgment of one or two days' light.

### I HAVE SPOKEN.

I have not produced this formula of orating for you in this place for the sake of teaching—as one whose success in Latin elegance was never so great—but to indicate that the subject to be placed before an Anatomical Oration ought to be the internal and spiritual part of man, which is to be dissected by living words rather than by a scalpel, however dexterous or sharp. Consequently, it is to be directed and explained only by the pen of an oration. As the field of this subject is wider and more spacious than others, so also students in Anatomy will never find it sterile but most fruitful, so much so that it is permitted for anyone to bring forth various orations or discourses on this subject in his own manner.

# CHAPTER II.
## *On Human Anatomy in General.*

The more skillful of the Philosophers, and those best versed in medicine, were accustomed to warn their auditors not to place certain faith in books treating of Anatomy, but rather to gaze frequently and diligently upon that [anatomy] inscribed by Nature herself, with eyes governed by reason. By this, they might more rightly judge concerning individual things or members in the human body not well perceived or understood before, and diligently notice their sites and positions.

Moreover, they seem to suggest to us that this observation of human parts is to be explained by a manifold description, explaining their names, origins, substances, compositions, or actions and the diseases commonly happening to them, and even the constellation presiding over each part.

The word "Anatomy" (as we find among some) is derived from *Ana* (which is "equal") and *tomia* (that is, "division"), as if one were to say Anatomy is as it were an "equal division"; whence it is defined by some that Anatomy is the right and equal division especially of the internal and external parts. <note>The author's etymology is folk-linguistic; "Anatomy" actually comes from the Greek 'ana' (up/throughout) and 'temnein' (to cut).</note>

The effect of this kind of operation is employed either in living bodies or in dead corpses; whence Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the influential Roman-era physician</note> himself established several books both on the Anatomy of the living and of the dead.

The ancients were accustomed to divide the practice of this matter into four species, according to the number of the principal members: one of which pertained to the brain, to which the animal virtue is referred; another looked to the heart, which serves the vital virtue; the third embraced the liver, attributed to the natural faculty; and the last looked with strict inquiry at the testicles, which especially regard the generative power. Concerning these, we shall speak (God willing) in their order and methodically.

# Book I of the Lowest Region.

### CHAPTER III.

#### On the general division of man into three regions, corresponding to those of the greater world.

The general relationship between this structure of the Microcosm <note>The "small world," a term used by Renaissance philosophers to describe the human body as a reflection of the universe.</note> and that of the greater world <note>The Macrocosm, or the universe at large.</note> consists either in a mathematical similarity of shapes or in a clearly physical respect for both. And although by Geometric consideration the body may appear irregular, we will very easily perceive that in truth it is spherical and possesses a fixed center no differently than the world does, if we mark out circles with a compass from the point of generation—whether male or female—or the seat of the private parts (with the radii extended equally from there to the head). Indeed, this location corresponds perfectly with the earth of the macrocosm, the mother of the elements, which contains their seeds and the life-giving influences of the higher realms. From this, the error of those who placed the navel as the center of the body is clear, since its radii are unequal, as can be seen by experience and as has been demonstrated elsewhere in the history of my Microcosm. Furthermore, by physical comparison, the head of the Microcosm (being the lodging of the divine mind and reason) regards the intellectual world or the Empyrean Heaven <note>The highest part of heaven, believed by ancient and medieval scholars to be the realm of pure fire or light and the home of the divine.</note>. Likewise, its chest or middle region—from whose center the heart, the greater light of the Microcosm, is accustomed to hurl rays of life to every limb of the entire structure—responds to the starry heaven of the macrocosm, from whose midpoint Apollo <note>A poetic reference to the Sun.</note> disperses and emits the thinnest waves of vital spirits in every direction. Finally, the Choler, blood, phlegm, and melancholy <note>The four humors of ancient medicine: yellow bile, blood, phlegm, and black bile.</note> of this same lowest region are held in close relation to the four elements of fire, air, water, and earth in the sublunary world <note>The realm below the moon, subject to change and decay.</note>.

In the specific description of this body, however, I shall begin my discourse from its lowest region (as it is more liable to putrefaction), and thus step by step and little by little, I will strive toward the higher parts, with God assisting.

### Description of the Lowest Region.

The description of the lowest region or the abdomen is divided into five books, of which:

*   The first two are concerned with *its containing parts*, namely:
    *   Book One, concerning the common parts.
    *   Book Two, concerning the proper parts.
*   The three following books encompass *its contained parts*, for:
    *   Book Three denotes those on its surface.
    *   Book Four describes those appearing in the center.
    *   Book Five explains those hidden in the depths.

# Book I of the Lower Region.

## CHAPTER I.

### Concerning the Epidermis or Little Skin.

We shall begin by descending little by little and step by step from the surface of this lower belly toward its center; and first, we shall treat the cuticle <note>The outermost layer of skin, now commonly called the epidermis.</note> which first presents itself to our eyes.

<margin>This part of the common coverings <note>The "common coverings" or *continentia communia* in Renaissance anatomy referred to the skin, fat, and membranes that wrap the whole body.</note> is the first to meet the eye.</margin>

It is named:
- In Greek, *epidermida* & *epidermis*.
- In Latin, *Cuticula*.
- In English, the scarf skin or chaff skin, by way of similarity.

It appears to have an origin (according to the opinion of almost everyone) that is excrementitious <note>In Galenic medicine, "excrementitious" does not mean waste like feces, but rather a byproduct of nutrition or heat, like hair or nails.</note> and not originating from the seed. Authors vary regarding this, for:
- Some claim it arises from the "efflorescence" or flowering of the blood.
- Others say it is born from the superfluity <note>Excess material.</note> of the true skin.
- My own opinion in this matter is that it is produced by the denser and drier portion of the air drawn in through the pores, adhering to the external surface of the body or the true skin.

It has a substance that is very thin, delicate, and porous.

It possesses a form very similar to a spider's web, or the chaff of wheat (as we have observed): For as the true skin relates to the flesh, so we perceive the bran of the wheat relates to its flour; similarly, the cuticle is observed to adhere to the skin no differently than the husk of wheat adheres to its bran. It is divided from the true skin, and is gradually brought to the eyes or subjected to treatment by blistering medications, or a glowing iron <note>A cautery tool.</note>, or other such means, and is thus lifted away.

It is entirely destitute of sensation, for it falls away without feeling or pain both in those afflicted by sickness and those endowed with health (from whom it is sometimes removed for the sake of beauty by the skillful mystery of decoration <note>Likely a reference to cosmetic peeling or treatments to clear the complexion.</note>).

In temperament, it is cold and dry.

It has a double use:
- First, it defends the true skin (which is very sensitive) from the cold injuries of the external air.
- Secondly, it retains the serous <note>Watery.</note> humors, which without such an obstacle would very easily penetrate through the true skin, as is clearly demonstrated in those who have been flayed.

It is affected by many various diseases, such as Spots, Purple Fever <note>Purpura, or purple spots on the skin.</note>, Morphew <note>A term for scurfy eruptions or skin discolorations.</note>, Jaundice, Dandruff, Pustules, Miliary Herpes <note>A skin eruption resembling millet seeds.</note>, etc.

It has a Saturnine constellation <note>In medical astrology, the skin was often associated with the planet Saturn due to its cold, dry nature and its function as a boundary.</note>.

<header>Concerning the Common Containers.</header>

# CHAPTER II.

## Concerning the True Skin.

<margin>
The second part of these common containers.
</margin>

<image-desc>The following anatomical definitions and descriptions are organized with large curly braces to show sub-categories or multi-part explanations.</image-desc>

The Name
- In Greek, it is *derma* <note>original: "δέρμα"</note>.
- In Latin, *cutis vera*.
- In English, The Hide or skin.

Its Origin is derived from the denser or thicker substance of the seed <note>The author refers to the "spermatic" theory of tissue formation common in early modern medicine</note>, or (as others maintain) from the periosteum <term>periostium: the membrane covering the bones</term> itself.

Its Substance is composed of fibers of all kinds, so that it may expand more easily; fibers of this sort are derived from the thin threads of the nerves, which is why this part claims such exquisite sensation for itself. It is extremely porous, for through those passages, vapors, sweats, and humors are accustomed to flow out.

Its Composition is nervous <note>meaning "full of nerves"</note>, and it acquires for itself tiny little veins and even capillary arteries.

Its Form is likened to the bran in wheat, just as we previously compared its cuticle <note>the epidermis</note> to the chaff.

Its Quantity is so ample and spacious that it envelops the entire body, except only for the perforated places (such as the mouth, ears, etc.). In density, however, it is unequal, as it is thicker on the head than on the face.

An Observation regarding a continuous break <note>a wound</note> is that it does not regenerate, insofar as it is a "spermatic" part <note>Early medicine believed tissues formed from "seed" in the womb could not regrow if destroyed</note>; however, a certain scar, induced either by art or by nature, supplies this defect, by means of which the lips of the wound are glued together.

Its Sensibility is quite apparent because of its nervous composition (as has been said); although Aristotle seems to attribute that property to the flesh rather unwisely.

Its Temperament is cold and dry, as are all other nervous members.

Its Connections are made with the parts lying beneath it, either by:
- The mode of union, as in the head and face.
- Communion, as in the hands, feet, and back.
- Hanging or placement, as in the remaining members. And the instruments by which connections of this sort are made are the nerves, veins, and arteries.

Its Use is twofold, namely for:
- Protecting the fat and flesh against the cold attacks of the external air.
- Receiving and retaining serous vapors, lest they vanish suddenly while exhaling from the center.

The Ailments or diseases most familiar to it are itching, the mange <note>original: "scabies"</note>, ringworm <note>original: "serpigo"</note>, skin eruptions <note>original: "impetigo"</note>, the itch <note>original: "psora"</note>, leprosy, smallpox, and others of this kind.

Its Constellation is Saturn <note>original: "♄"</note>, who has power over hides.

# Book I of the Lowest Region.

### CHAPTER III.
### Concerning Fat.

<note>The following text is organized using large curly braces to show hierarchical relationships between terms and descriptions, stemming from keywords on the left.</note>

It is named { In Latin, { Fat <note>original: "Pinguedo"</note>. Suet or Lard <note>original: "Adeps"</note>. | In English, *fat* or *Greace*.

It has its origin, as some wish to claim, from thick blood; although it seems to me that it is derived as much from the oily vapor of the external air inhaled through the pores as from the fattier juice of nourishment. ### CHAPTER IV.
### Concerning the Fleshy Membrane.
<note>original: "De Panniculo Carnoso"</note>

<note>The following text is organized using large curly braces to show hierarchical relationships between terms and descriptions, stemming from keywords on the left.</note>

It is called { By the ancients, who were mostly occupied with the anatomy of infants and beasts; the Membranous Layer. | By more recent authors; because in adult humans it appears to be such, the Fleshy Layer <note>Panniculus carnosus</note>.

It is said to arise from liquefied fat.
It has a membranous substance in infants and brutes, but in humans it is fleshy (as has been said).
Its composition requires veins and arteries interwoven throughout.

<margin>This part fills the fourth place of the common containing layers</margin>
It is located between the fat and the common sheath of the muscles, to which it strongly adheres; between this membrane and the true skin, superficial veins are observed to be scattered and spread out, except in the head, forehead, scrotum, penis, and similar parts.

It has a shape like the thinnest parchment.
It has its connection with the underlying muscles through fibers, and with the skin through the fat.
It has this use: to defend the muscles and interior veins against external cold, like a skin or tunic.

It has a Constellation, { Common, Saturn ♄. | Specific to this region, { From the planets, Venus ♀. | From the signs, Virgo ♍ and Libra ♎.

## CHAPTER V.

### Concerning the Common Membrane of the Muscles.

<image-desc>A hierarchical diagram with curly brackets classifying the "common membrane of the muscles". The text is listed under categories of Name, Origin, Substance, Composition, Position, and Use.</image-desc>

<margin>Of the last of the common containing parts</margin>

*   The Name is the common membrane <note>Latin: *tunica*</note> of the muscles.
*   The Origin is derived from the periosteum <note>The dense layer of vascular connective tissue enveloping the bones</note> as some wish, or rather (as it seems to me) from the fibers of the muscles.
*   The Substance is nervous and membranous.
*   The Composition: it receives nerves, veins, arteries, and its own appropriate flesh.
*   The Position is between the bare and simple substance of the muscle and the fleshy layer <note>Latin: *panniculum carnosum*</note>.

    *   One is to keep the muscles in their natural site and position.
    *   The other is to preserve them from corruption, as without it, purulent matter from neighboring parts would flow and drip into the empty cavities of the muscles.

### Concerning the muscles in general.

Now at last we proceed quickly to the twofold nature of the proper containing parts of this region—that is, its muscular substance and that subtle membrane which is called the peritoneum. Of these, the muscular substance is divided into ten parts. Lest we proceed blindly to their particular description, I have judged it worthwhile and suitable to our work to first say a few words regarding the general disposition and nature of the muscles.

# Book II of the Lowest Region.

It is named a muscle <note>original: "musculus," literally "little mouse"</note> because when dried, it has a head or beginning, a body or middle, and a tail or end, very similar in its boundaries to a mouse. Yet, nevertheless, we find a clear exception to that general rule in certain types of muscles, as they seem to deviate from that standard description of muscles.

<image-desc>A complex analytical diagram structured with large vertical brackets and branching paths. The diagram categorizes the composition, movement, and governing organs of muscles. The text flows from central primary categories on the left into detailed sub-categories and descriptions to the right.</image-desc>

<margin>This is an organic part of the body which (according to Galen in Book I of *On the Movement of Muscles*) is the instrument of that movement which occurs according to impulse.</margin>

It is composed of parts:

Similar parts <note>In Galenic anatomy, "similar" parts are uniform tissues like bone or fiber, while "dissimilar" parts are complex organs made of multiple tissues.</note>, which are five:
* Fibrous flesh, which is formed most aptly to receive the influence of the motor faculty.
* Nerve, which exists as the instrument of movement itself, by which it directs the muscle in its action like a hand directs a pen.
* Tendon or ligament, by whose service strength or power is usually conferred to the muscle.
* Vein and artery, whose role is to nourish that muscular substance and preserve it in its natural condition.
* The common sheath of the muscles, which we mentioned above.

Dissimilar parts, which are three:
* The head or beginning, which is usually composed of ligaments originating from the bones, and these are for the most part nervous <note>meaning composed of sinewy or nerve-like fibers</note>.
* The belly or middle, which is always fleshy, except in the diaphragm.
* The tail or end, which is a nerve or tendon constituted of many fibers of membranous substance; however, these ends or tails are not always tendinous, but only in those muscles which are naturally disposed to move the bones.

It is moved by a twofold motion, namely:

Voluntary, by the animal faculty <note>The "animal faculty" refers to the power of the soul/mind (anima) to control movement and sensation.</note> as its internal principle or agent, and is of this kind:
* Simple, which is performed in six ways, namely:
  * Upward.
  * Downward.
  * To the right.
  * To the left.
  * Forward.
  * Backward.
* Composite, which is performed in only one way, namely in a circle.

Involuntary, which is of a violent and forced nature.

By means of a threefold organ, namely:
* The brain, which commands like a king in his kingdom; for its duty is to judge the desired object—namely, is it useful? Is it to be pursued with hatred? Or the opposite—by means of reason, as if in a theater with a raised judicial bench, acting as a judge. From here, therefore, arises the principle of voluntary motion.
* The nerve, which like a messenger or immediate minister, hastens to carry the commands of the brain downward; this organ operates by the power of the animal spirits <note>The "animal spirits" were believed to be a subtle fluid or gas that traveled through hollow nerves to trigger movement.</note>, which usually communicate the brain's commands to the muscle.
* The muscle, which, illuminated by the animal spirits like divine rays, contracts itself and moves in various ways according to the requirement of the matter to fulfill the commands of its king. Thus the judge gives the sentence of death, the intermediate minister leads the condemned criminal to the cross, and the executioner, in the final place, carries out the judge's sentence.

I believe I have said enough regarding these matters; therefore, I shall descend briefly, and with a light leap, to the particular description of the five pairs of abdominal muscles.

# Concerning the Proper Containing Parts of the Abdomen.
<note>original: "De Continentibus Propriis Abdominis." This refers to the layers of the body that enclose the abdominal cavity, such as the skin, fat, and muscle.</note>

I have deemed it worthwhile and not at all inconvenient to inform you that you find these anatomical figures expressed in this work of mine not by my own choice, but through the prayers and insistence of Johann Theodor de Bry, our engraver <note>original: "calcographi," literally a writer in copper or engraver</note>. Indeed, I wish you to know this was carried out against my own desire. He has twice explained the reasoning for his request in his letters: first, that by this service of mine I might spare him the expense and the loss of wasted labor; and second, that by reducing such expenses, he might be able to sell this work of ours at a cheaper price, more affordable for scholars. Moved by this consideration, I was forced to constrain myself to those figures of the most renowned Caspar Bauhin <note>A famous Swiss botanist and anatomist (1560–1624)</note>, even though it went against the goal of my own invention and the inclination of my will. These plates were engraved in copper at the expense of the said Theodor de Bry in the year 1605, and have been kept ready at his disposal without further cost or weariness to him.

# CHAPTER II.

## Concerning the Muscles of the Abdomen, and first concerning those two that descend obliquely.

<margin>
These muscles
</margin>
*   Are ten in number.
*   In appearance, there are only five; for they are divided into pairs, which differ neither in nature, nor shape, nor substance, but are distinguished only by their position on the right or left side.

---

In the obliquely descending muscle <note>original: "musculo oblique descendente"; today known as the external oblique muscle</note>, the following aspects are considered:

*   **The Name, which arises**
    *   From its downward movement.
    *   Because its flesh is constructed from fibers stretching downward. *See Table 2.1.*
*   **The Substance, which is**
    *   Nervous <note>In early modern anatomy, "nervous" often referred to sinewy or ligamentous tissue rather than nerves in the modern sense.</note> at the beginning or head.
    *   Fleshy in the middle or belly.
    *   Tendinous at the end or tail.
*   **The Shape, which tends toward a triangular likeness.**
*   **The Quantity, which is very ample and wide.**
*   **The Number, for there are two: a right and a left.**
*   **The Connections, for**
    *   Above, its binding is to the sixth, seventh, and eighth ribs by a certain finger-like embrace in this manner. *For this, see A. CC. Table 2.*
    
    <image-desc>Two small woodcut diagrams. The one on the left depicts a jagged zig-zag line representing the serrated or "digital" attachment of the muscle to the ribs. The one on the right is a diamond-shaped figure containing internal diagonal hatching, illustrating the direction of the muscle fibers or the area of attachment.</image-desc>
    
    *   Below, it is bound to the pubic bone and the outer Ilium <note>The upper part of the hip bone.</note>. *As may be seen in Table 2 by the letters B. CC.*
    *   At the sides, it is attached to the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae. *As is clearly seen in Table 2 without letters.*
    *   Then its tendinous tail is inserted into the white line <note>original: "lineæ albæ"; the fibrous structure that runs down the midline of the abdomen.</note>. *See Table 2, letters CC.*
*   **The Use, which is twofold. For**
    *   It extends itself to both the dilation and contraction of the Thorax <note>The chest cavity.</note>.
    *   It defends the parts contained within from the external injury of cold: and it is observed to preserve internal heat.
*   **The Fixed Constellation, which is Virgo ♍.**

## Concerning the obliquely ascending muscles.

<margin>
The obliquely ascending muscle possesses
</margin>

- A Name, derived both
    - From its motion, which is carried upwards.
    - Because its flesh is composed of oblique fibers stretching upwards, as demonstrated in Table 2 by the letters H H.
- A Substance that is partly nervous <note>In this period, "nervous" often referred to sinewy or ligamentous tissue</note>, partly fleshy, and partly tendinous, as has just been stated.
- A Quantity that is sufficiently large and spacious.
- A Figure defined by the position of its fibers which, in relation to those of the obliquely descending muscle, mimic this intersection. For this, observe the X in Table 2 at fiber I, intersecting fiber H, so that the fibers appear to cross one another at a center point. And indeed, if we explore the matter a little more accurately, we find that all the fibers of all these four muscles coincide in the same center, as if Nature herself wished to contract the entire power of these muscles into a single point, so that the forces thus united might perform the function destined by Nature for this part more expeditiously and powerfully. Therefore, the position of the fibers of the four muscles intersecting themselves in the center is of this kind:

# Book II of the Lowest Region.

## CHAPTER IV.
### Concerning the Straight Muscle. <note>Latin: Musculus Rectus; today commonly known as the rectus abdominis or "six-pack" muscle.</note>

**To which belongs**
*   **The Name, with respect to**
    *   Its position.
    *   The path of the straight fibers that make up its flesh, as explained in Table 2 by the letters EEE.
*   **The Substance,** which is nervous, fleshy, and tendinous; it is divided into three portions by three tendinous intersections, which it seems to claim for itself for the sake of greater strength.
    *   In Table 2, the figures 1, 2, and 3 denote these tendinous intersections.
*   **The Shape,**
    *   At the beginning (which is located at the pubic bone), it is forked, and one prong of its fork is usually nervous <note>meaning fibrous or sinewy</note> while the other is fleshy. However, the head of this muscle is sometimes found undivided, which in such a form is always observed to be fleshy. This is indicated in Table 2.
    *   At its end or "tail," terminating around the breastbone, it is broad and membrane-like, as appears by the letter F in Table 2. <note>original: "os sternon"</note>
*   **The Size,** quite long, extending all the way from the pubic bone to the breastbone. Its dimension is noted by EEE in Table 2.
*   **The Connection,** which occurs:
    *   At the head, to the outer part of the pubic bone.
    *   At the broad tail, to the lower ribs.
*   **The Use,**
    *   Manifest <note>obvious or visible function</note>, for:
        *   Drawing the chest downward.
        *   Making the belly spherical.
    *   Hidden <note>internal or subtle function</note>, for compressing the belly toward the center.
*   **The Fixed Constellation,** Sun in Leo <note>original: $\odot$ imp. $\cdot \Omega$</note> according to the position of its parts. <note>The author links anatomical parts to astrological influences; Leo traditionally rules the heart and upper back, but here is associated with the central strength of the abdomen.</note>

**The Transverse Muscles**
*   **The Name, arises**
    *   From its transverse <note>horizontal</note> path or position.
    *   From the appearance or movement of the fibers from which its fleshy part is composed. The path of its fibers is expressed by the letter K in Table 2.
*   **The Substance:** the head is nervous, the belly is fleshy, and the tail is tendinous.

    *   At its beginning, it adheres to the processes of the lumbar vertebrae.

    *   Compressing the intestines for the sake of easier excretion.

    *   Lending aid to the voice. <note>By providing abdominal pressure for breath control.</note>
*   **The Constellation,** is Virgo. <note>original: $\mathbb{m}$</note>

# On the Proper Containing Parts.

## CHAPTER VI.
### On the Pyramidal muscles, and on those which are called the cremasters.

<margin>The pyramidal muscle</margin>
- *It is said to take its **name** from its likeness, since it displays the shape of a pyramid.*
- *It has a fleshy **substance**, and in this it seems to differ from the property and definition of a true muscle (according to the opinion of Colombo <note>Realdo Colombo (1516–1559), a famous Italian anatomist</note>).*
- *They are **numbered** as right and left.*
- *It has its **position** above the pubic bone, where its fleshy base takes its beginning, but its peak rises directly into the hollow of the straight muscle <note>The rectus abdominis</note>. As is indicated by the letter F. in the following Table 2.*
- *Its base is **connected** to the pubic bone, upon which it is supported as if on its own foundation; however, its peak, stretching into the hollow of the straight muscle, is also attached there by a more tendinous flesh. As indicated by F. in Table 2.*
- *It is **useful** (contrary to the opinion of Colombo, who denies that a part of this kind has either the definition or property of a muscle) for perfecting the erection of the penis, as seems probable from its location.*
- *It has a fixed **constellation**, which is Libra ♎ according to the opinion of the Astrologers.*

Now, as pertains to those muscles which are called the **Cremasters** <term>Cremaster: from the Greek 'to hang', these muscles support the testicles</term> and the suspenders (inasmuch as the testicles of both man and woman <note>In early modern anatomy, ovaries were often referred to as female testicles</note> are suspended in them), they are not usually numbered properly among those of the abdomen, as they belong to that region only improperly, although Cabrollius <note>Barthélemy Cabrol (1529–1603), royal anatomist at Montpellier</note> seems to support this opinion.

---

## CHAPTER VII.
### On the White Line.

<margin>Of which the</margin>
- ***Name*** *is attributed to it from its likeness, since it displays the image of a white and somewhat broad line.* <note>The Linea Alba</note>
- ***Substance*** *is tendinous or membranous.*
- ***Composition*** *is made from the meeting of the tendinous extremities of the eight aforementioned muscles of the abdomen into a unity of essence.*
- ***Quantity*** *is unequal, inasmuch as it is larger and wider above the navel, but below it, it is much narrower and tighter.*
- ***Figure*** *is compared to the Milky Way in the sky in respect to its color; but in respect to its straight passage, it can best be compared in the Microcosm <note>The human body</note> to the meridian circle of the Macrocosmic sky. For since the belly is round, it can be compared with the hemisphere of the world, of which we imagine the navel to be the arctic pole, through which this meridian of ours seems to pass, just as the cosmic one passes through the polar star of the world.*
- ***Position*** *is in the middle of the belly, which it intersects into two equal parts, like the artificial meridian of the world's hemisphere. This is delineated by ddd. in Table 2.*
- ***Action and use*** *is that by the gathering of the said extremities into one line, both the Peritoneum itself and the umbilical vessels are strengthened by it.*
- ***Constellation***
    - *From the **Planets**, it is referred to Saturn ♄ and Venus ♀.*
    - *From the **fixed stars**, it has regard to those looking upon the peculiar members of this region.*

### CONCLUSION.

The diseases of these muscles are wounds, bruises, abscesses, inflammations, gangrenes, tumors, and others of this kind.

# CHAPTER I.

->Concerning the Peritoneum.<-

In the preceding portion of this second section regarding the parts contained within this region, we have methodically, and in proper succession, stripped away first the double-layered cloak—namely the skin with the cuticle; then their "double-plate" <note>original: "diploide," referring here to the layer of fat</note>, that is the fat; and finally their many-layered undergarment composed of the muscles. Now, indeed, we have arrived at its final and most internal garment, or thin chemise: that is, the membrane called the **peritoneum**, which immediately encompasses beneath itself and wraps within itself all the parts or members included in this region. We shall, therefore, speak of it in this place, so that once its history and description are thus completed, we may proceed slowly to the revelation and explanation of the parts contained under it.

<margin>It is called</margin>
> In Greek, *peritonaion* <note>original: περιτόναιον</note>, because it stretches around the internal organs on all sides, and seems to float, as it were, both above and below them.
> In Arabic, *Syphach*.
> In Latin, the membrane containing the internal organs.

---

<margin>The membrane immediately encompassing the internal organs</margin>
*It originates, according to the opinion of Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medical science for centuries.</note>, from the extremities of the transverse muscles; specifically in that very place where they meet with the fleshy portion of the Diaphragm—that is, around its circumference—namely around AA. and KK. in Plate 3.*
*It has a "spermatic" substance <note>In early modern medicine, "spermatic" referred to tissues believed to originate from the primary reproductive fluid, characterized by being white, cold, and dry, such as membranes or bones.</note>, which in its nature is simple and thin, yet also quite firm and sinewy, the better to retain the natural heat within the center.*
*It appears to be composed of two coats (although Galen attributes only one to it). Furthermore, nerves, fibrous membranes, as well as small veins and some small arteries, concur in its composition. For the Arteries and veins, see II. and KK. in Plate 3.*
*It enjoys a quantity so ample and spacious that it extends itself over all the vessels of nutrition: for it embraces all those parts which are contained between the diaphragm and the legs themselves, and it even folds in upon itself internally near the loins, in which part it is also observed to be thickest. Its extension is demonstrated by the letters AA. B.C.D. in Plate 3.*
*It possesses a nearly oval shape if it is extended entirely as it is, and in its form it imitates that sack in which the oil of almonds or olives is usually pressed out. On the outside, it is observed to be rough, so that it may adhere better and more firmly to the muscles; but on the inside, it is quite smooth and free from roughness, lest it bring any discomfort by its unevenness to the intestines situated beneath it.*
*It is found perforated in many places, yet these are not useless holes; rather, each of them is destined for its own use and function. Its openings are marked in Plate 3 by the \*\* signs.*
*It claims its position immediately beneath the transverse muscles: and the "white line" <note><term>linea alba</term>: the fibrous structure that runs down the midline of the abdomen.</note> passes through its middle, as seen by EE. in Plate 3. It lies over the <term>omentum</term> <note>a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines</note>: see Plate 4. aa. BB. and Plate 5. BB. where it is divided.*
*It is connected to the transverse muscles by their tendons; and also to all the common parts, insofar as it is observed to attribute a common coat to them; and above, it is attached to the <term>mucronate cartilage</term> <note>the xiphoid process at the base of the breastbone</note> F. in Plate 3: and in Plate 4. a. 1. its connection to the base of the bladder is indicated.*

---

<margin>It has a manifold use, for</margin>
> It gives a common coat to all the contained members of this region, namely those pertaining to nutrition and generation as well as to excretion. As is shown by A A. B. C. D. in Plate 3.
> It contributes to the excretory faculty of the intestines. How it brings forth the intestines can be seen from Plate 3 by its position.
> It secures the intestines in their natural position. As is explained by the same plate.
> It preserves the stomach and stands in place of a defense for it, lest it be suffocated by flatulent vapors.
> It retains the innate heat in its center, for it protects it from escaping or flying away: and it is seen to perform this because of its firm compaction. For this, see Plate 3.

# On the Peritoneum and the Parts Contained Immediately Beneath It.

<margin>It is affected by particular diseases, such as</margin>

That rupture, which is therefore called a Rupture of the *Syphac* <note>original: "Ruptura Syphac"; Syphac is an Arabic-derived term for the peritoneum</note>, which usually occurs around the ** signs in Table 3.

Relaxation, which occurs mostly from excessive humidity, from which diseases of this kind arise.

> Intestinal hernia <note>original: "Enterocele"</note> involving the intestines
> Omental hernia <note>original: "Epiplocele"</note> involving the omentum <note>The fatty apron covering the bowels</note>
> Mixed hernia <note>original: "Enteroepiplocele"</note> involving both together
> Watery hernia <note>original: "Hydrocele"</note> involving water

It descends to the lower base of the intestines; this descent occurs through that passage which reaches from the Peritoneum to the testicles, concerning which see Galen <note>A famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> in *On the Causes of Diseases* chapter 10 and *On the Differences of Diseases* chapter 10. See the signs ** in Table 3.

For these types of diseases, I have known craftsmen highly skilled in surgery to use an incision both in the lower <term>Mirach</term> <note>An Arabic term for the abdominal wall</note> or part of the Abdomen, as well as toward its upper part, in safer locations removed from the membranes of the muscles. At the same time, I saw them employing a variety of ligatures, sometimes made of hemp thread, silk, and occasionally of pure gold (which they praised above all others), but I confess with varying success.

Dropsy <note>original: "Hydropisis"; an old term for swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, which is accustomed to gather around that membrane; and this is the reason why Paul of Aegina <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note> quite aptly taught that the incision for Dropsy should be made a little above the navel, namely toward the side opposite to the side in which the principal organ is affected. For example, if the cause of the dropsy lies in a poor disposition of the liver, let the incision or perforation be made toward the left; if from that of the Spleen, toward the right. Nevertheless, more recent authors, taught indeed by daily experience, were accustomed to perforate the navel itself for this ailment, a practice which I myself observed many times. Here, however, it should be noted in passing that I am not referring to two types of Dropsy, namely <term>Anasarca</term> <note>General swelling of the whole body</note> and <term>Tympanites</term> <note>Swelling caused by gas</note>, but to <term>Ascites</term> <note>Fluid buildup in the abdomen</note> and its treatment in this place.

# Book III of the Lower Region.

## CHAPTER III.
### Concerning the Omentum.
<note>The omentum is a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines like an apron.</note>

The name, according to:
- The Greeks: *epiploon*, as if "floating upon the intestines."
- The Arabs: *Girbe* or *Zirbus*.
- The Latins: *Omentum*, and by Aristotle it is called the "membranous or fatty skin."
- The English: The caul or coif. <note>A "coif" was a close-fitting cap; the omentum resembles a lacy covering.</note>

**Origin:** partly from the peritoneum, and partly from oily blood.
**Substance:** spermatic <note>In early medicine, "spermatic" referred to white, fibrous tissues like membranes or tendons.</note> or membranous, interspersed with fat.
**Composition:** made of a double membrane interwoven with fat, which also requires for its completion veins, arteries, and nerves springing from the sixth conjugation <note>The sixth pair of cranial nerves in the old system, now understood as the Vagus nerve.</note>. For this, see Table a. 4. Q Q Q Q. and Table b. 4. l. mm. and Table b 4. fig. 2. C. where a notable vein is shown. And B. C. D. And g. fig. 1.
**Quantity:** larger and deeper in women, on account of their childbirths, than in men.
**Shape:** like a pouch or a knapsack. See Table b. 4. a a a a. b b b b. And I. I. where the shape is indicated.
**Position:** it is above the intestines. See Tables 4. K K K K. And Table b 4. HHH. And CCC.
**Temperament:** with respect to the nature of the membrane, it is earthy or cold and dry; but truly, insofar as it is mixed with fat, it seems to claim an airy, or hot and moist quality.
**Connection:** with the Colon intestine, for the Omentum is present at this intestine in place of the Mesentery. Regarding which, see Table b. 4. G. G. It is also bound to the vessels of the spleen as in Table b. 13. B B C C.

**Use:** so that it may contribute:
- To the digestion of the stomach and the small intestines, inasmuch as it is retained internally, and for that reason it preserves the natural heat, by means of which digestion is perfected. See Table b. 4. G. G. where it is shown to pass through the bottom of the stomach.
- To support the branch of the portal vein coming out of the liver and tending toward the spleen, as in g. Table b. 4.
- To defend the intestines from external cold, for its fat, together with the veins and arteries, warms the belly and also the stomach. See Table a. 4. K K K K. for it covers the intestines.

<margin>
To which belong:
</margin>
<margin>
The more common diseases:
</margin>
- That rupture called an *Epiplocele*, which occurs when the omentum descends into the lower tunics of the testicles. <note>An omental hernia.</note>
- Precipitation, namely when the substance of the omentum falls into the bottom of the belly. I knew a certain "Golden Knight" <note>A knight of a specific order or a titled gentleman.</note> nearly 80 years of age affected by a disease of this kind, who, on account of the resulting defect of the Omentum, was oppressed by a sensible coldness of the intestines. From this it also happened that he used to suffer from frequent looseness of the belly and a catarrh descending from the head. To counter these evils, he was compelled night and day to fortify his viscera against the attacks of external cold with the skins of dogs and foxes; nevertheless, a certain monthly matter used to sweat out and spring forth in the region of the groin and the pubic bone; its color tending toward yellow, which I judged to have come from the fatty matter of the fallen substance, which can be felt and discerned by the hands from the outside.
- Consumption <note>Wasting away.</note>. For I saw a boy suffering from this evil, in whom, once this member was consumed, a rebellious catarrh with a vehement cough came upon him, so that a no small thinness soon occupied his whole body. I judged him to be affected by Wasting and Phthisis <note>Tuberculosis or general lung decay.</note>, not indeed without the agreement of others. But truly, when this patient of ours died, and the corpse was more curiously examined internally by a skilled surgeon, we found the omentum destroyed, the intestines as if frozen by cold, and the brain filled with a phlegmatic and icy humor, which used to drip steadily and copiously into the lungs. The lungs were healthy enough beyond expectation, except that their convex surface had taken on a somewhat bluish color on account of the abundance of catarrh. The small veins appearing on the surface of the heart were swollen; the blood contained in them was frozen by the copious catarrh and defluxion into fixed branches of a leaden color. Finally, I concluded the cause of the disease was the failure of the Omentum, by which the intestines, serving digestion, were weakened by cold and could not perform their duty for lack of native heat. The liver, however, for lack of the juice of chyle <note>The milky fluid taken from food during digestion.</note>, which the mesenteric veins ought to supply to it steadily, began to burn with an unnatural heat because of the lack of the usual humor. It greedily raised the spirit of the raw chyle into the region of the brain, which in that region was frozen into water or rheum, and steadily cast itself downward into the cavity of the lungs, excited a vehement cough, and at length, the life-giving spirits being suffocated by the abundance of watery matter and the blood being frozen, and thus deprived of natural motion, I perceived it necessary that the sick man should exchange life for death, even while his lungs remained whole.

**Constellation**, from:
- The Planets: Venus.
- The Signs of the Zodiac: Virgo.
