# Concerning the Parts Contained Within It

This noble organ <note>The heart (Latin: *cor*)</note>

* Is positioned, with respect to:
    * The **Base**, in the middle or center of the **Thorax** <note>The chest cavity</note>. For this, see C.D. Table 5.
    * The **Apex** or cone, turning toward the left side, and also inclining more toward the interior. For its point, see E. figure 2, Table 5.
* Varies in quantity or size, for in:
    * Bold and courageous men, it is observed to be narrower and more compressed.
    * Fearful and small-souled men, it is usually more swollen and large.
* Has a connection with:
    * The **Brain**, via the nerve of the sixth conjugation <note>The vagus nerve, which early anatomists numbered as the sixth pair of cranial nerves</note>.
    * The **Liver**, via the *vena cava*. See A. figure 1, Table 5.
    * The **Lungs**, via:
        * The **Arterial vein** <note>The pulmonary artery</note>. See F.G. figure 2, Table 5.
        * The **Venous artery** <note>The pulmonary vein</note>. See H. figure 2, Table 5.
    * <margin>How it adheres to the heart, see L.M.N.O. Table 5, figure 1.</margin>
    * The **Pericardium** <note>The protective sac surrounding the heart</note>, via its base. As in B. figure 1, Table 5. And the **Diaphragm** <note>original: *Septo transuerso*</note>. See Table 5, figure 1, F.G. and H.I.
* Is useful in every way for the existence of man, for according to the opinion of:
    * Almost all **Physicians**, it is believed to be the home of the vital faculty, the origin of life, the fount of innate heat, and the source of the arteries.
    * **Zeno** <note>The Stoic philosopher</note>, it is said to be the receptacle of the natural fire.
    * **Prometheus**, it is called the vessel of celestial fire, which fire he is said to have stolen from heaven for the purpose of enriching man with life; for it is the fuel of life, growth, and generation, without which an animal cannot endure for even a moment of time.
* Is prone to fall ill, for it is affected by many diseases, such as:
    * Tremor of the heart, palpitations, cardiac passion, fainting <note>original: *Syncopis*</note>, and the collapse of strength.
    * **Abscess** <note>original: *Apostema*</note>: I saw a titled knight named **James Cromer** <note>likely Sir James Cromer/Crowmer, a Kentish landowner</note> severely and fatally affected by this disease (as was said). After his death, when he was opened, I observed the pericardium was entirely consumed, so that not even a sign of it remained. The heart was everywhere abscessed and so foul that it was hardly recognized by the surgeon. When the surgeon touched that putrid substance with his fingers, I saw them penetrate into it as easily as if it were composed of the softest mud or butter. Immediately, I noticed putrid and poisonous matter flow out. But what was even more wonderful (as it seemed to me) was that I saw the sick man himself, four days or thereabouts before his death, playing cards at a table with other nobles. Nevertheless, for six weeks before his death, I noticed him affected by palpitations of the heart and a pulse that was sometimes intermittent, sometimes failing and vibrating. During that time, the entire cavity of the Thorax was filled with thick and fetid water, like thick urine or lye. Consequently, in the middle of his illness, there was a gathering and consultation of many learned physicians, who all (contrary to what I felt, who said he labored from an abscess in the thoracic cavity with a quantity of water) unanimously felt that his disease was composed of flatulent matter enclosed in the venous artery or the arterial vein. But the outcome of the matter proved their consensus to be false.
* Has a constellation <note>Astrological correspondence</note> from:
    * The **Planets**:
        * The **Sun** ☉.
        * With the signs of the Zodiac, { Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, Mars ♂, Venus ♀, Mercury ☿ } in { Aries ♈, Cancer ♋, Leo ♌, Virgo ♍, Libra ♎, Scorpio ♏ }.
    * The **Signs of the Zodiac**: **Leo** ♌.

The organic parts of the heart are examined within the chambers of the heart, either in the:

# Book IV of the Middle Region

The organic parts of the heart are examined within the chambers of the heart, either in the:

**Right Chamber**, which is called the "sanguineous" <note>original: *sanguineus*; meaning full of blood</note> because it contributes to the purification and thinning of the blood. In this chamber, we observe four things, namely:
- **One auricle**, which serves to retain the blood and prevent it from flowing from the *vena cava* <note>The "hollow vein," the main vein returning blood to the heart</note> into this right chamber in too great a quantity. See Image I, Figure 1, Table 5.
- **The vena cava**, which transfers blood from the liver into the right chamber of the heart, so that there, by a "third cooking" <note>The Renaissance theory that digestion happened in three stages: in the stomach, the liver, and finally the organs/heart</note>, it may be better prepared and purified according to the needs of the nourished organ, which is the lung. The substance of the lung is lighter and more airy than other parts of the body; for if it were nourished by the same blood as the other parts, it would be less fit to perform its required duty, which consists of continuous motion. Thus, a light substance requires light nourishment, since we are taught that "like is most aptly nourished by its like," and nature rejoices in its own likeness. See A, Figure 1, Table 5.
- **The arterial vein** <note>original: *venam arteriosam*; today known as the pulmonary artery</note>, which pours the blood—purified and thinned in the heart—through infinite branches and small shoots to the lungs, so that they may be nourished by it. For this vein, see F. G., Figure 2, Table 5, and Figure 1, Table 7, Chapter 1.
- **Six valves or small membranes**, namely:
    - **Three in the opening of the vena cava**, open toward the outside but closed toward the inside. These are called "sagittal" <note>arrow-shaped</note> by some, as they are similar to the tips of arrows; their use is to prevent the blood introduced from the vena cava into the right ventricle of the heart from flowing back into that vein again. For these, see Bauhin’s <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624), a famous Swiss botanist and anatomist</note> Table 10, Book 2.
    - **Three in the opening of the arterial vein**, open toward the inside and closed toward the outside, so that blood does not return into the heart. These are called "semilunar" <note>half-moon shaped</note> due to their appearance. Through these, the nourishment elaborated in the heart enters the lungs. For these, see Bauhin in the place mentioned before.

**Left Chamber**, which is called the "spirituous and spiritual" chamber, inasmuch as the vital spirits <note>In early medicine, "vital spirits" were believed to be a refined substance in the blood that provided life and heat</note> are generated within it. Here we observe:
- **One auricle**, which serves both for the attraction of air into the left chamber of the heart and the expulsion of its waste, as well as for conducting the "fifth essence" of life <note>The *quinta essentia* or most purified spirit</note>—separated and collected from the waste of the air—into the great arterial vessel called the **Aorta**, as a place adapted and destined for receiving the vital spirits. See K, Figure 2, Table 5, for its location.
- **Seven more internal parts**, namely:
    - **Two vessels**, specifically:
        - **The great artery** <note>The Aorta</note>, through which the vital spirits are carried from the heart, as if from a fountain, to all parts of the body. See a, Figure 1, Table 5.
        - **The venal or venous artery** <note>original: *arteriam venalem*; today known as the pulmonary vein</note>, through which air is introduced by inhalation to the left ventricle of the heart, both for the sustenance of life and for the cooling of the heart and arterial blood; its waste part is expelled again through exhalation. For this, see Figure 2, Table 5, H, and Figure 1, Table 7, D.
    - **Five valves** inserted into the said vessels, of which:
        - **Three** are arranged in the opening of the great artery facing the chamber of the heart; they are open toward the inside but closed toward the outside, and by reason of their similarity, they are called "semilunar," for they do not differ in form and figure from those three found in the opening of the arterial vein. These are ordained by nature so that the vital spirits, forged in the left laboratory of the heart and placed into the great artery (destined to receive them), should not return again into the laboratory. For these, see Bauhin in the place cited before.
        - **Two** are inserted into the opening of the venal artery, open toward the outside and closed toward the inside; these are therefore called **Mitral** valves, as they are very similar to the mitres <note>The tall, cleft hats</note> of Bishops. The duty of these is both to receive the air introduced by inhalation and to emit the useless part of it.

## CHAPTER IV.
### Concerning the Great Artery.

<image-desc>A complex hierarchical diagram (synoptic table) classifying the anatomy, nomenclature, and function of the aorta (arteria magna). <margin>
In which five things are to be observed, namely its:
</margin>

*   **Difference, specifically between it and a vein, for**
    *   A vein has only a single coat <note>tunica</note>, and that one is thin and porous, composed of straight fibers and some moderately slanted ones.
    *   An artery is provided with a double coat, of which:
        *   The outer is very similar to that of a vein, being of the same substance and composed of the same or similar fibers.
        *   The inner is five times denser or thicker in proportion, and woven from transverse fibers: the better to contain the subtle spirits of life.
*   **Name, and it is**
    *   Called *Aortes* in Greek, and commonly *aorta*.
    *   The *Great Artery* in Latin.
*   **Origin, which is from the left ventricle of the heart.** For this, see *a.* in Plate 6. a. and *A.* in Plate 6. b. And *A.* in figure 2 of Plate 8 denotes its opening <note>orificium</note> where it is cut away from the heart.
*   **Offshoots, which are observed either in**
    *   **Small Shoots <note>surculis</note> such as the Arteries:**
        *   Coronary, proceeding from the aorta before its trunk exits the left cavity of the heart. This circular cluster of small arteries is intended for the preservation of the heart, just as the coronal veins are for its nourishment. For these, see *B. B.* Plate 6. b. and *aa.* fig. 2. Plate 8.
        *   Intercostal, produced from the *Azygos* <note>The "unpaired" vein of the thorax</note>, whose duty is to assign vital power to the muscles of that place. For these, see *I.* Plate 6. b. and *H.*
        *   Phrenic, dispersed through the entire Diaphragm, concerning which see *K.* Plate 6. b.
        *   Mammary, concerning which see *LL.* Plate 6. b.
        *   Epigastric, to which the mammary arteries are joined. See *ee.* and *vv.* Plate 6. b.
        *   Celiac, which is larger than the other branches. This creeps toward the stomach, and also liberally imparts vital spirits to the Liver, Spleen, and Omentum <note>epiploo</note>. For this, see *P.* Plate 6. b.
        *   Mesenteric <note>original: messeraica seu messenterica</note>, is that branch which waters the *mesaraon*—that part of the mesentery pertaining to the small intestines—with vital blood. And concerning this, see *X. Y.* Plate 6. b.
        *   Renal, passing to the kidneys, called the "Emulgents" <note>term: Emulgentes (from 'to milk out'), an old term for renal vessels thought to strain impurities from the blood</note>. See *f.* Plate 6. a. and *v. s.* Plate 6. b.
        *   Spermatic, such as those two arterial vessels dedicated to generation. For which see *t. t. u u.* Plate 6. b.
        *   Lumbar, which descend to the loins. For these, see *y y y.* Plate 6. b.
    *   **Branches, and these are either**
        *   **Ascending, such as:**
            *   Carotids. (**Right.** / **Left.**) *X. Y.* Plate 6. b.
            *   Cervical, and they are denoted by *MM. NN.* Plate 6. b.

            *   Sacral, see *ε.* Plate 6. b.

            *   Crural <note>leg</note>, concerning which see *π π.* Plate 6. b.
*   **Utility and property, which is to perpetually pour out the vital spirits—expanded within the arterial blood as if in their own proper vehicle—throughout the entire body.**

# CHAPTER V.
## Concerning the Lungs.

Before we arrive at the description of the lungs, it must be known that there are three kinds of respiratory organs; for some are {
- Moving, such as the 65 muscles of the Chest <note>Latin: Thoracis</note>.
- Carrying air to the lungs and to the left chamber of the heart, such as the windpipe <note>Latin: aspera arteria</note> and the Larynx.
- Receiving, and of this kind are the lungs, which we shall treat here.
}

The Lungs' {
- **Name**, {
    - In Latin, — { By the philosophers, it is the *fan of the heart*.
    -             { By *Avicenna* <note>A famous 11th-century Persian physician</note>, the *cushion of the heart*.
    -             { By physicians in general, *pulmo*.
    - In English, it is *The Lungs*.
}
- **Substance**, is soft, rare, and spongy.
- **Composition**, is made from {
    - Its own flesh, which is called *Parenchyma* <note>The functional tissue of an organ</note>.
    - Nerves descending from the sixth pair <note>The vagus nerve, classified as the 6th pair in older anatomy</note>.
    - The *arterial vein* <note>The pulmonary artery</note>, concerning which see fig. 2, Table 7.
    - The *venous arteries* <note>The pulmonary veins</note>, concerning which see fig. 4, Table 7. } Small branches. Concerning these, see C. & D. fig. 1, Table 7, and figures 3 and 4 in abundance.
    - A single coat <note>membrane</note>, which it receives from the *Pleura* <note>The lining of the chest cavity</note>.
    - The *Trachea Artery* <note>The windpipe</note>, whose bifurcated trunk plunges into the substance of the lungs, as in Table 9.
}
- **Quantity**, it fills the cavity of the Chest.
- **Shape**, it is likened to an ox's foot. As appears in figure 2, Table 7.
- **Temperament**, is more hot than cold by reason of its airy and light flesh; for this reason nature formed it light and spongy, so that it might be more easily lifted upward, and perform its natural duty with less labor. And for this cause, nature prepared for them a more pure and thin nourishment in the right chamber of the heart, elaborated from thick blood, as was declared above.
- **Number**, it is estimated to be two-fold, whence they are called "lungs" <note>plural</note>, since that entire mass is divided into a right and left part by the mediastinum, as in fig. 2, Table 7. Each of these is observed to have its own lobes, but in truth their substance is continuous, wherefore they are usually called both "the lung" and "the lungs." For the upper and lower lobe, see P. Q. Table 4, and N. O. in Table 5. L. M. N. O. are its 4 lobes, which are more clearly indicated by E. F. G. H. in fig. 1 and 2, Table 7.
- **Position**, is in the middle of the chest, where they also surround the pericardium <note>the sac around the heart</note>. Their front face is denoted by Table 7, fig. 1; the back by fig. 2.
- **Connections** are made with the {
    - Heart, by the arterial vein and the venous artery: which is indicated by A. B. of figures 3 and 4, Table 7.
    - Brain, by the nerve from the sixth pair. See q q. Table 8.
    - Vertebrae and ribs, by membranes from the *Pleura*.
    - Rough or *Trachea artery* <note>the windpipe</note>, by a strong union. As is indicated by B. Table 7, fig. 1.
}
- **Use** is, that it be an organ for {
    - Respiration and voice, and also fashioned for the cooling of the heart.
    - Not absolutely necessary for life, seeing as some animals such as fish and reptiles can and usually do live without it.
}
- **Diseases** are —————— {
    - *Dyspnea* or difficulty breathing.
    - *Asthma*.
    - *Cough* <note>Latin: Tussis</note>.
    - *Damaged voice or hoarseness*.
    - *Pleuritis* <note>Pleurisy</note>.
    - *Empyema, the spitting of blood with a cough*.
    - *Phthisis* <note>Tuberculosis or wasting</note>.
    - *Peripneumonia* <note>Pneumonia</note>.
}
- **Constellation**, from ———— {
    - The Planets, ————— { Of the Sun, ☉
    -             ————— { Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, Mars ♂, Venus ♀, Mercury ☿, Moon ☾
    - With the signs ————— { Aries ♈︎, Taurus ♉︎, Gemini  Gemini ♊︎, Cancer ♋︎, Leo ♌︎, Virgo ♍︎, Libra ♎︎, Scorpio ♏︎, Sagittarius ♐︎, Capricorn ♑︎, Aquarius ♒︎ } In { [Diagrammed signs] }
    - Celestial sign. Pisces ♓︎
}
}

# Concerning the Parts Contained Therein.

## CHAPTER VI.
### Concerning the Recurrent Nerves.
<note>The recurrent laryngeal nerves, so named because they "loop back" up toward the throat after descending into the chest.</note>

{ They received their name from their flexible, looping motion.
{ They arise from the sixth conjugation of nerves <note>original: "sexta neruorum coniugatione"; in older anatomical systems, the Vagus nerve was often classified as the sixth pair.</note>. As appears by *ee.* fig. 1. Plate 8.
{ It has a motion,
> { Downward, together with the carotid arteries (by which they are supported and braced) through the neck into the cavity of the Chest. For this see *OO.* fig. 2. Plate 8. and *HH.* indicating the carotids and *GG.*
> { Upward, while a branch of each of them returns again from the depths of the chest by the same path it previously descended; and in its return or retreat, each of them adhering to the windpipe <term>Aspera Arteria: an old term for the trachea</term> along the way, seeks those six muscles by which the larynx is usually opened and closed. And these nerves are connected to those muscles for the sake of producing the voice. For this observe the adherence of *OO. HH.* and *GG.* to the windpipe, fig. 2. Plate 8. For the location of the revolution of the right branch see *P.* fig. 2. Plate 8. as also *R.* for that of the left; but the right ascending part is *QQ.* fig. 2. and the left ascending part is *SS.*

{ They obtain a varied position or site after their descent, for
> { The Right one, under the collarbone, is reflected around the branch of the great artery <note>the subclavian artery</note> which is carried to the right armpit, wound about it like a pulley, and runs back upward until it is dispersed into the three muscles of the right part of the larynx. For this see *P.* fig. 2. Plate 8. for the place of reflection and *S. N.* and *M.* for the location of the larynx.
> { The Left one, submerged much further and more deeply, is wound around the greatest artery <note>the Aorta</note> near the heart, especially at that part where, emerging mostly from the [front] part, it reflects itself toward the spine, and then afterwards returns to the larynx, and is distributed into the remaining three muscles of the left part of the larynx, the tongue, and the hyoid bone, as shown by *π.* fig. 1. ->Concerning the<-
# ROUGH ARTERY AND THE
## PARTS OUTSIDE THE THORAX
### CONNECTED TO IT.

## CHAPTER I.
## Concerning the Rough Artery <note>original: "Aspera Arteria"; this is the historical term for the trachea or windpipe, so named because of its bumpy, cartilaginous rings.</note>.

<image-desc>The following text is structured as a large analytical diagram. A vertical brace on the left labeled "Whose" connects to several defining categories for the trachea.</image-desc>

Whose:
<image-desc>Branch 1: Nomenclature. A brace groups "Trachea" and "Rough" as types of "Artery."</image-desc>
*Name, is the* { Trachea / Rough } Artery.

*Substance, is cartilaginous, so that it may be more suitable for producing the voice; for by a composition of this kind, it is itself moderately disposed between hard and soft.*

*Composition, is firm, to which the veins arising from the external jugulars, the carotid arteries, the recurrent nerves from the sixth conjugation <note>The "sixth conjugation" refers to the vagus nerve in the numbering system of Galen, common in the Renaissance.</note>, and a double membrane all converge.*

*Quantity, is spacious and ample enough for the measure of respiration or the proportion necessary for the body.*

*Figure, is round and ringed with joints and imperfect circles, especially in the back part which presses against the Esophagus; this was indeed so ordained by nature so that it would not hinder the passage of food to the stomach. For the front of this, see Table 9, figure 1. For the back, figure 2.*

*Site, begins immediately below the larynx and extends all the way to the lungs, and in its extension, it passes over the gullet. After it has reached the lungs, it divides into two branches, namely the right and the left, and each of them is subdivided into several others. For the division, see fig. 2; for the rings or semi-circular cartilages, see dd. fig. 2. Table 8. C.D. and bb. fig. 1. Table 9. For its subdivision into branches, see CCC. fig. 1. Table 9. For the pipe, see aa. fig. 1. Table 9. Furthermore, for the cartilages of the larynx, see mm. and nn. fig. 2. Table 9.*

*Temperament, is cold and dry, inasmuch as it is a spermatic part <note>In early modern medicine, "spermatic parts" were tissues believed to originate from the primary reproductive fluid, such as bone, cartilage, and nerve, characterized by being cold and dry.</note>.*

*Connection, is with the aforementioned extreme parts, namely the Larynx and the lungs; with the Larynx specifically at kk. fig. 1. and mm. nn. fig. 2. Table 9.*

<image-desc>Branch 9: Use. A bracket lists two primary functions.</image-desc>
*Use, is twofold, namely:*
> To conduct Air into the lungs and the left chamber of the heart, and also to expel its smoky wastes <note>original: "excrementa fuliginosa"; refers to the ancient belief that the heart produced "sooty" vapors that needed to be exhaled.</note>.
> That it may be the proper and principal organ of the voice.

<image-desc>Branch 10: Diseases. A bracket lists four pathological conditions.</image-desc>
*Diseases, are:*
> Strangulation from food.
> Retention or sticking of a bone <note>original: "spinae"; literally a thorn or fishbone.</note> or some such thing.
> Entry of a leech through the mouth.
> Quinsy or Dog-strangle <note>original: "Angina seu Cynanche"; severe throat inflammation or swelling.</note>.

<image-desc>Branch 11: Constellation. An astrological section linking the organ to planets and signs.</image-desc>
*Constellation, from:*
> The Planets { With the signs [Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon] In [Gemini, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Capricorn, Aquarius] }
> The Sign is Taurus.

# Book V of the Middle Region.

## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the Larynx.

<image-desc>A text-based hierarchical diagram using large curly braces to classify the characteristics of the larynx (Larynx).</image-desc>

Regarding its:
- **Name, Larynx:** For a detailed description of this part along with its appendages, see Table 10, the second Table after 10, and Table 3 after [10].
- **Substance or composition is made of three large cartilages, of which:**
    - **The first (Anterior)**, is the largest in size; it is convex on the outside but hollowed out on the inside in the shape of a shield, which is why it is called the *thyreoid* <note>original: θυρεοιδὴς; from the Greek 'thyreos' meaning shield-shaped. Today known as the thyroid cartilage.</note>. For this, see F. fig. 2. 3. and aa. fig. 1. Table 10, and n. in the second Table fig. 3, and n. n. fig. 4, and n. n. fig. 5.
    - **The second**, is smaller than the first and larger than the third; it is positioned toward the esophagus and is called the *cricoid* <note>original: κρυκοειδὴς; meaning ring-shaped.</note>. See fig. 2. Table 9. n. n.
    - **The third**, is the smallest and ends in a very narrow point; this is called the *arytenoid* <note>original: ἀρυταινοειδὴς; meaning ladle-shaped.</note>, named after the shape of a vessel. See c. c. fig. 1. Table 10, and c. c. fig. 5. of the second Table.
- **Muscles serving it, are 20 in number, of which:**
    - **Twelve are intrinsic to it.** <note>original: proprij; muscles that belong specifically to the organ itself.</note>
    - **Eight are shared.** <note>original: communes; muscles shared with surrounding structures.</note>
    -> For several of these, see fig. 1. e. e. & fig. 2. f. g. & l. & m. & e. f. g. fig. 3. of the second Table, and f. fig. 5. & g. & l. fig. 7. <-
- **Location**, is at the very top of the rough artery <note>term: aspera arteria; the historical name for the trachea or windpipe.</note>. As seen in fig. 1. 2. Table 9, and k. fig. 4. of the second Table, and fig. 6. And 2. Table 3 after 10.
- **Nerves**, proceed from the sixth pair <note>The author refers to the historical numbering of cranial nerves; these are the vagus nerves.</note> and especially those called the *recurrent* nerves. See m. fig. 3. of the second Table after 10.
- **Use and action**, is to form the voice; for it is greatly dilated and compressed, opened and closed.
- **Diseases**, are those attributed to the Artery, since the larynx is the summit of the rough artery.
- **Astrological Influence**,
    - **From the Planets:** of the ☉ Sun and
    - **From the Signs:** ♌ Leo
    -> Along with the planets, those listed for the rough artery. <-

## CHAPTER III.

### Concerning the Epiglottis.

<image-desc>A text-based hierarchical diagram using large curly braces to classify the characteristics of the epiglottis (Epiglottis).</image-desc>

Regarding its:
- **Name,**
    - Greek, *Epiglottis*.
    - Latin, *Lingua laringis* <note>Literally: "The tongue of the larynx."</note>.
- **Substance**, is membranous, and like a thin, fatty cartilage: it pertains to the esophagus and adheres to the root of the tongue and the cartilage of the larynx. For this, see fig. 2. Table 10.
- **Shape**, is in the form or likeness of the reed of a pipe <note>original: fistulæ; referring to a musical pipe or flute.</note>, namely round and slightly larger in size. For this, see b. fig. 4. 5. & 6. of the second and third Tables after 10, and fig. 1. Table 10, and κ. λ. fig. 10. Table 3 after 10; N. and n. describe its base and apex.
- **Location**, is opposite the arytenoid cartilage and originates from the root of the tongue, as Galen teaches us in *On the Use of the Parts*. See b. fig. 1. Table 10, and O. fig. 1. & 2. Table 9, and b. second Table fig. 4, and fig. 5. 6. & 7.
- **Temperament**, is clearly moist and viscous.
- **Connection**, is made to the root of the tongue and is continuous with the shield-shaped cartilage. See Table 3 after 10, fig. 10. θ. N. and b. fig. 4. second Table after 10, where * explains its beginning.
- **Use**, is to serve as a lid or a plug for the opening of the larynx; specifically, so that when any nourishment is swallowed through the esophagus, none of it accidentally and suddenly falls or creeps into the rough artery. For this organ is raised during the interval of breathing, but during swallowing, it falls and is pressed downward, covering the passage leading to the lungs through the trachea artery—that is, the passage through which we draw in the airy spirit.

## CHAPTER II.
### Concerning the Larynx.

<image-desc>A schematic diagram summarizing the anatomy and characteristics of the Larynx. A large bracket on the left groups several categories under the word "Whose." These categories branch out into further details using smaller brackets.</image-desc>

**Whose**
- **Name, Larynx**: For a detailed description of this part along with its appendages, see Table 10, the second Table after 10, and Table 3 after.
- **Substance or composition**, is made of three large cartilages, of which:
    - The first (Anterior), is the largest in size; it is convex on the outside and hollowed out on the inside in the shape of a shield, which is why it is called *thyroid* <note>original: θυρεοιδὴς (thyreoeidēs), meaning shield-shaped</note>. For this, see F. fig. 2. 3. and aa. fig. 1. Table 10, and n. second Table fig. 3, and n.n. fig. 4, and n.n. fig. 5.
    - The second, is smaller than the first and larger than the third, having its position toward the Esophagus <note>The food pipe</note> and is called *cricoid* <note>original: κρυκοιδὴς (krykoeidēs), meaning ring-shaped</note>. See fig. 2. Table 9. n.n.
    - The third, is the smallest and tapers into a very narrow point; this is called *arytenoid* <note>original: ἀρυταινοιδὴς (arytainoeidēs)</note>, from the shape of a vessel <note>specifically a ladle or pitcher</note>. See c.c. fig. 1. Table 10, and c.c. fig. 5. second Table.
- **Muscles serving it**, are 20 in number, of which:
    - Twelve are proper to it <note>intrinsic muscles</note>.
    - Eight are common to it <note>extrinsic muscles shared with other structures</note>.
    - <note>Note on the right of the two lines above:</note> For some of these, see fig. 1. e.e. and fig. 2. f. & g. & l. & m. and e. f. g. fig. 3. second Table, and f. fig. 5. and g. & l. fig. 7.
- **Position**, is in the highest part of the rough artery <note><term>rough artery: the trachea or windpipe</term></note>. As shown in fig. 1. 2. Table 9, and k. fig. 4. second Table, and fig. 6. And 2. Table 3 after 10.
- **Nerves**, proceed from the sixth conjugation <note>The 6th pair of cranial nerves in the system of the time, likely referring to the Vagus nerve</note> and especially those called the *recurrent* nerves. See m. fig. 3. second Table after 10.
- **Use and action**, is to form the voice; for it is greatly dilated and compressed, opened and closed.
- **Diseases**, are attributed to those of the Artery <note>the trachea</note>, since the larynx is the summit of the rough artery.
- **Constellation**,
    - From the Planets: **The Sun ☉**
    - From the Signs: **Aries ♈** Along with the planets, as recited in the section on the rough artery.

## CHAPTER III.
### Concerning the Epiglottis.

<image-desc>A second schematic diagram summarizing the anatomy and characteristics of the Epiglottis. A large bracket on the left groups several anatomical categories under the word "Of this."</image-desc>

**Of this**
- **Name**,
    - Greek, Epiglottis.
    - Latin, *Lingua laringis* <note>The tongue of the larynx</note>.
- **Substance**, is membranous, and like a thin and fatty cartilage: it pertains to the Esophagus, and adheres to the root of the tongue and the cartilage of the larynx. For this, see fig. 2. Table 10.
- **Shape**, is in the form or likeness of the tongue of a certain pipe <note>referring to a reed in a musical instrument</note>, namely round and a little larger in size. For this, see b. fig. 4. 5. and 6. second and third Table after 10, and fig. 1. Table 10, and κ.λ. fig. 10. Table 3 after 10; N. and n. describe its base and apex.
- **Position**, is opposite the Arytenoid cartilage, and originates from the root of the tongue, as Galen teaches us in *On the Use of the Parts*. See b. fig. 1. Table 10, and O. fig. 1. and 2. Table 9, and b. second Table fig. 4, and fig. 5. 6. and 7.
- **Temperament**, is clearly moist and viscous.
- **Connection**, is made to the root of the tongue, and it is continuous with the shield-shaped <note>thyroid</note> cartilage. See Table 3 after 10, fig. 10. θ. N. and b. fig. 4. second Table after 10, where * explains its beginning.
- **Use**, is to serve as a lid or a plug for the orifice of the larynx; namely, so that when any nourishment is swallowed through the Esophagus, nothing of it may accidentally and suddenly fall or creep into the rough artery. For this organ is raised during the interval of breathing, but in swallowing it falls and is pressed downward, covering the passage leading to the lungs through the trachea artery—that is, the passage through which we draw in the airy spirit.

## CHAPTER IV.
### Concerning the Tonsils.

## CHAPTER VII.
### On the Teeth.

-> These members are defined by: <-

*   **Name**: In Greek, they are called *odontes* <note>original: ὀδόντες</note>. In Latin, *Dentes*.
*   **Substance**: Which is bony.
*   **Number**: There are 32 in total, namely:
    *   Eight anterior <note>front</note> teeth: Four in the upper part and four in the lower.
    *   Canines: Specifically, two upper and just as many <note>two</note> lower.
    *   Molars <note>original: "Maxillares"</note>: 20 in total, of which there are ten upper and ten lower.
*   **Nerves**: These proceed from the third conjugation <note>the third pair of cranial nerves in the system used by the author</note> and are inserted into the roots; hence their capacity for sensation is so prompt and easy.
*   **Primary Use**: To prepare the nourishment to be sent into the stomach so that it may be more easily digested.
*   **Diseases**: There are not a few when they are afflicted by:
    *   Difficulty in their emergence <note>teething</note>.
    *   Pain <note>toothache</note>.
    *   Decay and perforation <note>cavities</note>.
    *   Worms <note>a common medieval belief that "tooth worms" caused decay</note>.
    *   Loosening <note>original: "Commotione"</note>.
    *   Numbness from cold <note>original: "Congelatione"</note>.
    *   Change of color.
    *   Grinding at night.

## CHAPTER VIII.
### On the Lips.

-> These members are defined by: <-

*   **Called**: In Greek, *cheile* <note>original: χείλη</note>. In Latin, *labia*.
*   **Substance**: They have a muscular substance, for they consist of four muscles, as we shall immediately declare.
*   **Movement**: They are moved by voluntary motion.
*   **Muscles**: They have various muscles, in which one must observe their:
    *   **Number**: Which is 4. Two proceed from the furthest edge of the lower cheek, and two rise slightly below the cheeks.
    *   **Motion**: Which is eightfold, namely:
        *   Oblique: There are four; two are present for each lip, one tending to the right, the other to the left.
        *   Straight: Just as many <note>four</note>; two of these are entirely straight, and of the remaining two, one pulls the upper lip downward, and the other carries the lower lip upward.
*   **Composition**: Which embraces, besides the muscles, the veins, arteries, and nerves.
*   **Utility**: They are useful both for:
    *   Retaining food until it is well prepared by the teeth.
    *   The ornament and decoration of the countenance or face.
*   **Diseases**: They are afflicted by various diseases, such as:
    *   Fissures <note>cracks</note>.
    *   Tumors and abscesses <note>original: "apostemata"</note>.
    *   Ulcers.
    *   Trembling.

-> Concerning all these matters, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the influential Persian physician</note> treats them in Book 3, Fen 3, Chapters 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15. <-

# THE THIRD REGION.

## A description of the REGION OF THE HEAD, OR THE SUMMIT OF THE MICROCOSM <note>The "microcosm" refers to the Renaissance belief that the human body is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>, distributed into four books.

*   In the highest region of the microcosm, the following are considered:
    *   Its position and name
        *   The name, which is the head, acting as the beginning and the summit of the entire human structure.
        *   The front portion, devoid of hair, is named the forehead.
        *   The upper-front part is the *synciput* <note>The front part of the skull.</note>.
        *   The summit between the *synciput* and the *occiput* is called the *vertex* <note>The crown of the head</note>, named as if from the center of a circle.
        *   The back part is called the *occiput*.
        *   The temples are those spaces found between each eye and ear.
        *   The face is everything that extends from the whole forehead down to the chin.
    *   The parts, which are either:
        *   Containing parts, and these are:
            *   Common parts, which are:
                *   The epidermis <note>The outermost layer of skin.</note>.
                *   The true skin.
                *   The fat.
                *   The fleshy membrane <note>original: "panniculus carnosus," a layer of muscle/tissue under the skin.</note>.
                *   The hair.
            *   Specific parts, such as:
                *   The *pericranium* <note>The membrane covering the skull.</note>.
                *   The skull <term>cranium</term>.
                *   The two *meninges* <note>Membranes enveloping the brain.</note>, namely:
                    *   The *dura mater* <note>The "tough mother," the outer membrane.</note>.
                    *   The *pia mater* <note>The "tender mother," the inner membrane.</note>.
        *   Contained parts, which are:
            *   The brain <term>cerebrum</term>.
            *   The little brain <term>cerebellum</term>.
            *   The seven pairs of nerves.
            *   The eye and its parts:
                *   Membranous parts.
                *   Humoral parts <note>The fluids or "humors" within the eye.</note>.
    *   The use, which is to contain the animal spirits and to serve their faculties.
    *   Disease, which is either:
        *   Of the whole, called *Cephalea* <note>A chronic, severe headache.</note>.
        *   Of a part, called *Hemicranea* <note>A migraine affecting one side of the head.</note>.
    *   The Constellation <note>The astrological influences governing the head.</note>
        *   From the Planets alone:
            *   The Sun claims for itself the brain and the right eye in a man, but the left in a woman.
            *   Mercury possesses the tongue, memory, and thought.
            *   The Moon also commands the brain, and the left eye in a man, but the right in a woman.
        *   From the Signs alone: Aries ♈.
        *   From the planets together with the signs:
            *   In the Planets (Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, Mars ♂, Sun ☉, Venus ♀, Mercury ☿, Moon ☽) and the Signs (Aries ♈, Taurus ♉, Gemini ♊, Cancer ♋, Leo ♌, Virgo ♍, Libra ♎, Scorpio ♏, Sagittarius ♐, Capricorn ♑, Aquarius ♒, Pisces ♓).

## THE HIGHEST REGION OF THE MICROCOSM
### BOOK ONE.
->Concerning<-
# ITS OWN PROPER
# CONTAINING PARTS.
### CHAPTER I.
#### Concerning the Hair.

**Regarding which:**
- **The Name is**: Tresses, Head-hair, or Body-hair. <note>original: "Crines, Capilli, Pili"</note>
- **Origin**: It arises from the smoky and earthy excrement <note>In early modern medicine, "excrement" refers to any byproduct of the body's metabolic processes, not just waste.</note> of the third digestion. <term>Third Digestion: The final stage of nutrition occurring within the individual tissues and organs.</term>
- **Location**: For the most part, these are the more moist and soft places of the body; the skin to which they adhere is usually thick and sufficiently hard, such as that of the cranium or head.
- **The Use is for**: 
    - Covering parts for the sake of ornament.
    - Consuming thick waste products.
    - Defending and protecting the skin and flesh against external cold.
- **Diseases are**: 
    - *Rhopalosis*, or the indivisible matting of the hair. <note>Likely referring to Plica Polonica.</note>
    - *Dichophyia*, or the splitting of the hair into two.
    - *Quassatio*, that is, the uneven falling out of the hair.
    - *Atrophy*, or their excessive thinness.
    - *Aridias* <note>Dryness or brittleness.</note>
    - *Canities*, or the changing into white.
    - *Fluxio*, or the shedding of them.
    - *Alopecia* <note>Patchy hair loss.</note>
    - Depravity of color.
    - Excessive thickness, etc.

->On the Specific Containing Parts.<-

# CHAPTER II.
## Concerning the Pericranium.

<image-desc>A hierarchical diagram using brackets to classify the anatomical definition, origins, and properties of the Pericranium.</image-desc>

This is understood either:
- **Specifically**, as that membrane which wraps the skull beneath the skin of the head, and in this sense:
    - **It is called**,
        - **Pericranium** <note>original: "Pericranium"; from Greek meaning "around the skull"</note>.
        - **Periosteum** <note>original: "Periostium"; meaning "around the bone"</note>.
    - **It originates** from thin fibers arising from the *dura mater* <note>The "tough mother," the outermost thick membrane surrounding the brain</note>, emerging from the hollow of the skull outward through the sutures; in this emergence, the said fibers are formed into the membrane called the periosteum. For its appearance, see Table 2, Figure 1, marked N; M represents the skull.
    - **It is connected** with the *dura mater* by means of the fibers beneath the skull. See GGG in Table 2, Figure 1, and HH, II.
    - **It is useful** for investing <note>covering or wrapping</note> the skull and for containment, so that the animal spirits and also vapors do not escape in too great a quantity through the cracks of the sutures.
- **Generally**, and in this way every membrane or tunic immediately investing all bones is called a periosteum; for these also are derived from the *dura mater* or the "thick membrane" <note>original: "crassa meninge"</note>.
- **And of this part**:
    - **The diseases** are fracture, incision, and bruising <note>original: "confusio"</note>.
    - **The constellation** is Aries ♈; among the planets, it is Saturn ♄.

---

# CHAPTER III.
## Concerning the Skull.

<image-desc>A complex branching diagram detailing the nomenclature, sutures (true and false), bones, function, and pathologies of the skull (Cranium).</image-desc>

Regarding which:
- **The Name**, it is called:
    - In Greek, *Cranion* (κρανίον).
    - In Latin,
        - *Calvaria* <note>The dome of the skull</note>.
        - *Cranium*.
- **There are five sutures**, of which some are:
    - **True**, in which we consider two things, namely their:
        - **Number**, for there are three; and of these:
            - **Two are transverse** <note>crossing side-to-side</note>, namely:
                - The **Coronal**, so named from the crown of kings; see A. B. Table 1.
                - The **Lambdoid**, from its likeness to the Greek letter Lambda (λ); see C. D. Table 1.
            - **One is direct**, the **Sagittal**, named from its arrow-like shape; see E. Table 1.
        - **Various functions**, for:
            - The **Coronal**'s function is to distinguish the "bone of the prow" <note>the frontal bone</note> from the others.
            - The **Lambdoid** divides the "bone of the box," "bone of praise," or "bone of memory" <note>the occipital bone at the back of the head</note> from the others.
            - The **Sagittal** separates the two parietal bones from one another.
    - **False or spurious**, of which there are two:
        - **Names**:
            - **Squamous**, so called from their likeness <note>to fish scales</note>.
            - **Mendose** <note>meaning "false" or "deceptive"</note>, by the common folk.
            - **Temporal**, by Galen <note>A famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note>. For these, see F. G. H. Table 1.
        - **Use or function**, that they may distinguish the petrous <note>stony/hard</note> bones, and that they may release vapors laterally from the brain.
- **The specific bones are four**, namely:
    - **Two of the temples**, which the sagittal suture divides, and they are called the **parietal** bones. See N. in the following Table 1; and for the bones of the vertex <note>top of the head</note>, see I. K. Table 1.
    - **One of the forehead**, divided from the others by the coronal suture; and this is called the **bone of the prow**, the **coronal bone**, and the **bone of common sense**. See L. Table 1.
    - **One of the back of the head** <note>occiput</note>, and it is divided from the others by the Lambdoid suture; this is called the **bone of the box** or the **bone of memory**. See M. Table 1.
- **The function or use** is to fortify both "mothers" of the brain—namely the *dura mater* and the *pia mater*—and also the brain itself against accidents and external injuries, defending them like a helmet.
- **Diseases** are:
    - Fracture.
    - Fissure.
    - Incision.
    - Decay <note>original: "Caries"</note>.
- **The constellation** is commonly Aries ♈.

# Concerning the Proper Containing Parts.

### CHAPTER IV.
#### Concerning the Membranes of the Brain

<margin>In which eight things are especially to be observed, namely their:</margin>

*   **Names, either**
    *   General, which are—Membranes <note>original: "Meninges"</note>, Envelopes, Webs, or Mothers <note>The term "Matres" (Mothers) refers to the medieval belief that these membranes gave birth to all other membranes in the body.</note>.
    *   Specific, namely—
        *   One is the *Hard Mother* <note>original: "Dura mater"</note>, or the thick membrane.
        *   The other is the *Pious Mother* <note>original: "Pia mater"</note>, or the thin membrane.
*   **Substance, which is varied, for that of the**
    *   *Hard Mother*, is thick, and double in its composition: and this is observed especially in the center of the brain, into which it is seen to penetrate like a sickle or the arc of a circle. See HHH. fig. 1. Plate 2. for this reflected downwards. And GG. & PP. fig. 1. Plate 3. it is situated beneath the thin OO. And VV. fig. 2. Plate 5.
    *   *Pious Mother*, is thin and simple, woven in the form of a spider's web or a net. As indicated in EEE. fig. 2. Plate 2. And OO. fig. 1. Plate 3. where it is shown divided from the brain.
*   **Figure**, for that of the pious mother is like the uterine membrane called the *Chorion* or the afterbirth, which is fashioned from a varied texture of veins and arteries. Whence, by the Greeks, it is also called "choroid" from this similarity. That of the Hard Mother is like a thick membrane. See EE. fig. 2. Plate 2. For the texture of the Pious Mother itself made of veins and arteries, see FFF. fig. 2. Plate 2.
*   **Folds or three-fold entanglements**, which they make, by which three cells are distinguished from one another with wonderful skill, in which nothing exists without a miracle. Whence by some they are not inaptly called "sacred," since they are the secret chambers of the temple of the soul: But indeed, more recent Anatomists have established four such cells, as we shall say below.
*   **Connection, namely**
    *   Of the *Hard Mother* with the skull through fibers. See GGG. Plate 2. fig. 1. And HH. And II. similarly ZZ. fig. 2. Plate 5.
    *   Of both, namely the hard as well as the pious, with the brain, whose soft mildness and delicate tenderness—impatient of hardness beyond measure—they defend against the roughness of the skull and bones.
*   **Use or office, for**
    *   The *Hard Mother's* role is to distinguish the ventricles of the brain, and to defend the pious mother from injuries.

# SECOND BOOK. Regarding
## THE BRAIN AND ITS ORGANS.
### CHAPTER I.
#### Concerning the Brain in general.

<image-desc>A large analytical table or synoptic chart defining the characteristics of the brain (Cerebrum). It uses a hierarchy of braces to categorize aspects such as its origin, substance, quantity, division, figure, temperament, motion, color, location, use, diseases, and astrological associations.</image-desc>

Regarding its:
- **Origin**, it is from the seed <note>original: "spermate"</note>, which is why it is white.
- **Substance**, it is soft, liquid, and similar to marrow, so that it may better receive impressions and sensible properties while the soul is at work.
- **Quantity**, it is larger in humans than in beasts of the same mass or dimension; this was fulfilled by nature so that it might contain more duties, and consequently, more "workshops" <note>The author views different parts of the brain as specialized workshops or *officinas* for processing thought and sensation.</note>.
- **Division** occurs either:
    - **Into parts**, namely:
        - The **Anterior** part, called the *cerebrum* <note>The main forebrain</note>, which is softer, whiter, and larger than the posterior; see C.N.B. Table 3. fig. 1.
        - The **Posterior** part, which is called the *cerebellum* <note>The "little brain" at the back of the skull</note>, and this is smaller and harder than the anterior one; see A.H.D.E. Fig. 1. Table 3.
    - **Along the middle** descending, a partition made by the *falx* <note>The falx cerebri, a sickle-shaped fold of membrane</note>, though this division does not go to the full depth. For this division see A.A.B.B. fig. †. Table 3.
- **Figure**, —
    - **External or Geometric**, it is round so that it might be more capacious in quantity and more mobile in its action, as may be seen through both figures in Table 3.
    - **Internal**, and unique to itself: which
        - **On the outside** resembles intestines, for it is twisted with various gyri and convolutions; this is not for the purpose of understanding (according to the opinion of Erasistratus <note>A Greek anatomist/physician, 3rd century BCE</note>), for if so, even a donkey would understand, as its brain is fashioned with such entanglements. Rather, these gyri are impressed in the brain so that the *pia mater* <note>The delicate innermost membrane surrounding the brain</note> (which is woven from veins and arteries) may penetrate deeper into its substance for the sake of both nourishment and vitalization. For the gyri or windings of the brain, see CC. Table 3. fig. 1. and AAA. BB. fig. 2. Table 3. And DDD. indicates the divisions.
        - **On the inside**, it represents fresh cheese.
- **Temperament**, is cold and dry; hence Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> maintains that the brain is the seat of the cold and the glutinous.
- **Motion**, is voluntary and not involuntary or forced; it enjoys *Systole* and *Diastole* <note>Contraction and expansion</note> no differently than the heart itself. In *Diastole* it draws both vital and natural spirits from the *rete mirabile* <note>term: "wonderful net" - a complex of blood vessels at the base of the brain once thought to refine spirits</note>, and air from the nostrils; in *Systole* it compresses the internal sinuses and pours the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>The refined essence responsible for sensation and movement</note> from the upper ventricle into the third and fourth, and also into the organs of the senses.
- **Color**
    - **Outside**, it is ash-colored.
    - **Inside** truly, it is white, so that the soul itself may better perceive all colors by means of this color—since white is susceptible to all other colors, yet has none of its own.
- **Location**, is in the most eminent place so that it might be safe as if in a citadel; for this reason, it is fortified and surrounded on all sides by very firm bones. The brain in its position is indicated by A A. as is the cerebellum by BB. fig. 1. & 2. Table 8.
- **Use**,
    - It is **not** that which Aristotle mentions (namely, for the cooling of the heart), but rather as Galen <note>Prominent Roman physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> teaches in Book 8 of *On the Use of the Parts*, it is for the generation of animal spirits and the execution of animal functions.
- **Diseases**
    - **Universal**, such as Apoplexy, etc.
    - **Particular**, concerning which see below.
- **Constellation** <note>Astrological correspondences</note>, from
    - **The Planets**

<margin>Here however</margin>
*   **It is called**, { Commonly the choroid, choriform, and reticular plexus. / By André du Laurens <note>original: "Andrea Laurentio," a famous French anatomist</note> it is called the "wonderful net" <note>original: "rete admirabile"</note>.

### Chapter X.

| | |

| **Quantity** | Its dimension in length is somewhat long and straight, and it stretches from the lower to the posterior part of the brain; for this reason, it is very easy to send the **animal spirits** <note>In early medicine, these were subtle fluids believed to transmit sensation and motion</note>, now fully refined, from this ventricle into the fourth, which are afterwards carried to the nerves and the spinal marrow. For the union of the third ventricle to the fourth with the "buttocks" <note>nates</note>, see I. K. fig. 2. Plate 6. |

This passage is clothed in a thin membrane; it is wider at first, then gradually slopes into a narrow space like a funnel, and for this reason it is called both the *infundibulum* <term>infundibulum: Latin for funnel</term> and the *pelvis* <term>pelvis: Latin for basin</term> by Anatomists. # ON THE CEREBELLUM AND THE SEVEN
### Pairs of Nerves.

## CHAPTER I.
### Regarding Nerves in general.

<image-desc>A hierarchical bracketed diagram (ramified tree) outlining the properties, divisions, and pathologies of nerves.</image-desc>

In the Nerve, generally considered:
* *The Substance is soft and porous so that the animal spirits <note>In early medicine, "animal spirits" were thought to be subtle fluids that traveled through nerves to cause movement and sensation.</note> may more easily pass through and penetrate it.*
* *The Composition is provided with both a thin and a thick membrane, so that its substance might be safer and more secure from external injuries.*
* *The Origin, according to the opinion of more recent Anatomists, is from the base of the Brain, and this near the third ventricle; this is contrary to the opinion of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his views were being challenged by Renaissance dissections.</note> who (as has been said) assigns their origin to the cerebellum.*
* *The Division is into pairs or "conjugations" which are:*
    * *By Position:*
        * *To the right.*
        * *To the left.*
    * *By Number: they are seven.*
* *The Use is to be the organ through which the spirits—both of sensation and of motion—are carried to every member of the body: From which it elegantly follows that he who lacks nerves is deprived of both sense and motion.*
* *The Diseases:*
    * *Spasm or convulsion*
        * *From:*
            * *Inanition <note>Emptying or exhaustion of fluids.</note>.*
            * *Repletion <note>Over-fullness or excess of fluids.</note>.*
        * *Through sympathy <note>original: "per colligantiam" - referring to a condition where one part of the body affects another through their connection.</note>.*
    * *Paralysis.*
    * *Tetanus <note>A state of rigid muscle contraction.</note>.*
    * *Twisting of the mouth, or "canine convulsion" <note>likely referring to Bell's Palsy or similar facial spasms.</note>.*
    * *Tremor.*
    * *Stupor <note>Numbness or loss of sensation.</note>.*
    * *Twitching <note>original: "saltus" - literally a leap or jump of the muscle.</note>.*
* *The Astrological Association:*
    * *With the Planets: The Moon ☽.*
    * *With the Signs: Aries ♈.*

# Book III of the Highest Region

### CHAPTER II.
### Concerning the seven pairs of nerves, and first, concerning the first pair.

<margin>The first pair or conjugation is attributed to the eyes, and of these nerves:</margin>
{ *The name is "optic," as if to say "pertaining to sight."* <note>original: "optici quasi visorii"</note>
{ *The origin occurs at the anterior base of the brain. For these, see figure 1 and 2, Table 8, and the letter 'o' in figure 7, Table 13.*
{ *The substance is thick and the softest of all, and more spongy than the others, though without visible pores. For its proportions, see A.B. in figure 3, Table 6.*
{ *The size is the largest of all.*
{ *The union or intersection occurs above the "saddle" of the sphenoid bone* <note>The sella turcica, a saddle-shaped depression in the skull base.</note> *or beneath the clinoid process; then afterwards, the said union is divided again and separated, and each member of that division extends itself to each eye, so that the union appears to be like the center of a cross, and the nerve is shaped into a cross in this manner. For the meeting of the intersection, see H. in figure 1, Table 8. For this, see also R. in figure 6 of the same.*

<image-desc>A small anatomical diagram showing the optic chiasm, where two optic nerves cross each other in an X-shape, ending in two circular eye-like structures at the top.</image-desc>

{ *The covering is the membrane* <note>original: "meninx," referring to the meninges or protective layers of the brain.</note> *both the thin one, concerning which see p. in figure 7, Table 13, and the thick one, which q. indicates. And see QQ. in figure 6. And p. q. in figure 1; and see a. in figures 2, 4, and 8 of Table 15 for the nerve, and b. c. for the coverings.*
{ *The reasoning, namely why these nerves tend toward a cross—that is, why a union is made from a duality, and then finally a duality from the union—is so that a single and same thing does not appear as two. This ensures that the double image of one object, penetrating to the center of each eye and meeting in a union of this kind, appears not as two things, but only as the single thing which it truly is.*
{ *The use is for the sake of vision, of which the optic nerve is the primary instrument. The exit from the brain is through the sphenoid bone, as indicated by p. in figure 6, Table 6.*

---

### CHAPTER III.
### Concerning the second pair.

<margin>The second pair regards the muscles of the eyes, and of this:</margin>
{ *The substance is quite hard.*
{ *The size is the smallest.*
{ *The movement starts from the base of the brain, through its own specific openings, and thus through the fissure of the orbit to the five muscles (as Columbus* <note>Realdo Colombo (c. 1515–1559), a famous Italian anatomist.</note> *claims) or (according to others) to the 6 muscles serving the eye. For the proportions of this nerve, see G G. in figure 3, Table 6. It is clearly indicated by KK. in figures 1 and 2, Table 8.*
{ *The division is into 7 small branches, of which:*
{ *Five are destined for the five muscles administering to the eye.*
{ *Two pass to the two muscles opening the eyelid, and a branch turns toward the lining of the nostrils. See O. in figure 2, Table 8.*
{ *And also a small shoot of these branches tends toward the temporal muscle and is inserted into it; from which it happens that when the temporal muscle is injured, the eye is observed to be greatly offended and to suffer. For this, see N. in figure 2, Table 8, and Q.*
{ *The use is observed to contribute primarily to the movement of the eye muscles as well as to the sensation of the same.*

# On the Cerebellum and the Seven Pairs of Nerves.
<note>The "seven pairs" refers to the classical Galenic classification of cranial nerves, whereas modern medicine identifies twelve pairs.</note>

### CHAPTER IV.
### On the third pair of nerves.

<image-desc>A complex analytical diagram using nested curly braces to categorize the origin, quantity, motion, division, and use of the third pair of nerves.</image-desc>

Of this pair {
* The **Origin** occurs further back and to the side in the depths or base of the brain.
* The **Quantity** <note>meaning the size or thickness</note> is very small.
* The **Path** <note>original: "Motus"</note> penetrates downward in its progress and passes through the skull via a certain opening <term>foramen|a natural hole or passage in bone</term> shared with the fourth pair. For this, see LL. figures 1 and 2, Table 8.
* The **Division** or distribution varies into shoots and branches, of which {
    * A single one passes through as far as the temporal muscle.
    * Another, piercing the eye socket <note>original: "orbitam oculi"</note> and passing through the eyebrow, proceeds to the {
        * Forehead.
        * Muscle that constricts the eyelid.
        * Muscle that dilates the nose.
        * The nose itself.
    } And here it disperses into many small branches.
    * A third, penetrating through the eye socket, passes through the third [opening] of the upper jaw <note>original: "maxillæ superioris"</note> and is then distributed into many small nerves which are spread through the {
        * Upper lip.
        * Muscle called the masseter <note>the primary muscle used for chewing</note>.
        * Muscles of the cheek.
        * Cavity of the nose.
    }
    * A fourth extends to the root of the upper teeth.
    * A fifth descends to the lowest jaw, a portion of which is also designated for the sensation of the lower teeth.
    * What remains extends toward the chin; its duty is to provide sensation to the lower lip.
}
* The **Use** is explained by the aforementioned: namely, for constricting the eyelids and providing them with sensation; likewise, it contributes to the dilation of the nose, and to the movement and sensation of the mouth, lips, and teeth.
}

---

### CHAPTER V.
### On the fourth conjugation or pair of nerves.

<image-desc>A nested brace diagram describing the fourth pair of nerves.</image-desc>

Of this pair or conjugation {
* The **Quantity** is smaller than the third. For this, see ZZ. figure 2, Table 8.
* The **Path** is almost the same as the third, as it descends with the third toward the bone; for through the openings of the fifth bone of the upper jaw, four of its branches penetrate to the teeth and gums, and then they pass through the membrane of the palate toward the front; and two others tend downward toward the root of the tongue. For the position of this, see M. figures 1 and 2, Table 8. And S. figure 2, and T. and V. and XX.
* The **Division** occurs {
    * First into 4 small branches which are carried downward by the route related above in its path.
    * Then into two other small branches which, by descending downward, seek the root of the tongue (as was said), through the upper membrane of which they are spread. For this, see R. figure 2, Table 8. For its absorption into the membrane of the tongue, see YY. figure 2, Table 8.
}
* The **Principal Use** is to serve the sense of taste, and to bring sensation to the teeth and gums, as does pair 7.
}

---

### CHAPTER VI.
### On the fifth pair.

<image-desc>A nested brace diagram describing the fifth pair of nerves.</image-desc>

This pair {
* **Arises** from the base of the brain, namely at the side and around the middle of it. It is indicated by M. N. figure 1, Table 6.
* **Moves** through the "blind passage" <note>original: "foramen cæcum"</note> and tends toward the "workshop of the ears" <note>the internal structures of the ear</note>; and when it reaches the eardrum <term>tympanum|the membrane or cavity of the middle ear</term>, it divides into two branches, of which {
    * The larger appears to serve the sense of hearing. See a. figures 1 and 2, Table 8, and Φ.
    * The smaller extends to the larynx; and from this, the reason is readily apparent why, when the eardrum is touched with an instrument, the patient is provoked to cough. <note>This describes the "Arnold's nerve reflex," where stimulating the ear canal can trigger a cough.</note> See a. b. c. d. Table 8.
}
* It has its **Principal Use** or duty designated for the sense of hearing.
}

# Book III of the Highest Region.

### CHAPTER VII.
### Concerning the sixth pair of Nerves.

<image-desc>A bracketed diagram outlining the origin, division, and use of the sixth pair of nerves. The text is organized with curly brackets to show hierarchical relationships.</image-desc>

> <margin>Its origin</margin> The origin is from the posterior part of the base of the brain, and this pair is to be seen at the back with various small shoots or roots. This pair is indicated by *e* in figures 1 and 2 of Table 8.
> The movement <note>The path or course</note> occurs from its source through that opening which is situated between the back of the head <note>the occiput</note> and the temporal bone, specifically in that place where the internal jugular vein ascends to the skull. This pair is indicated by *M. N.* in figure 1 of Table 6.
> The division after its descent occurs into a { Right / Left } branch. And each of these is subdivided into three branches, one of which is the { Costal <note>relating to the ribs/chest</note> / Stomachic / Recurrent, concerning which we have treated abundantly above in its proper place, and it is called the cervical nerve. See *f.* in figures 1 and 2 of Table 8, and *g.* indicates its insertion into the larynx.
> The use is to convey sensation and motion to all the organs <term>viscera: the internal organs of the body</term> of the chest and the abdomen.

---

### CHAPTER VIII.
### Concerning the seventh pair or conjugation of nerves.

> <margin>This seventh pair</margin> Takes its origin toward the back of the head, where it is filled with various tiny roots. This is indicated by *h.* in figures 1 and 2 of Table 8.
> It moves from its source through an opening proper to itself situated in the back of the head, which is oblique; and after it has exited from the skull through that opening, it tends primarily toward the front, then is distinguished into various small branches which are scattered into the muscles of the tongue, the hyoid bone, and the larynx. The larger of these, however, passes under the lower jaw and also under the tongue; it runs from the root of the tongue all the way to the tip, providing it with sensation and motion, just as it was explained that it drew the faculty of tasting from the fourth pair. Moreover, it is joined with the sixth pair, as seen through *1.* in figures 1 and 2 of Table 8; see also *l.* and *m.* in the same place.
> It is useful for attributing the faculty of moving and feeling to the muscles of the tongue, and it also seems to contribute in some way to the muscles of the larynx in their motion and sensation.

<margin>The order and use of the 7 pairs of nerves is thus described in a few words:</margin> { The first, the Optic, sees; the second moves; the third tastes; / The fourth and fifth hear; the sixth is the wanderer <note>the vagus nerve</note>; the seventh is for the tongue.

---

### CHAPTER IX.
### Concerning the eighth and ninth pair discovered by Vesalius and Columbus.

Columbus <note>Matteo Realdo Colombo, a 16th-century anatomist</note> seems to recognize two other pairs beyond those seven, one of which—namely the eighth—he admits was detected by Vesalius <note>Andreas Vesalius, the famous author of 'De humani corporis fabrica'</note>; the other, namely the ninth, he seems to boast was first revealed by himself. However, as far as that eighth pair is concerned, it seems likely, according to the opinion of Vesalius, that it is a root of the fifth pair, or at least a shoot of it. But the ninth discovered by Columbus is (as he himself testifies) a slender pair of nerves, taking its origin from those processes of the brain which are called the "buttocks" <note>original: "nates," now known as the corpora quadrigemina</note>. They move toward the front, as they tend toward the face, and are observed to pass near the second and third pair, and finally are inserted into the third muscle of the eyelid. Furthermore, a small branch of this is conveyed to the fifth muscle of the eye. As for my own opinion in this matter, I think these "discovered" pairs are rather roots or shoots springing from some of the roots of the 7 pairs, rather than existing as such by themselves; moreover, no certain and distinct use or office can be assigned to these pairs. Columbus.

### Chapter X.
### Concerning the Cerebellum.

<margin>Because</margin>
> { It has such a name because it is a "little brain," yet smaller than the supreme brain <note>The cerebrum</note>.
> Its substance is harder than the Brain, as Galen <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> maintains; but in truth, experience teaches us that there is no great difference between this and the brain regarding touch. It is united to the spinal marrow as indicated in GG. Table 9 and H. For the cerebellum covered by the thin membrane <note>The pia mater</note>, see XX. fig. 2. Table 5. and RR fig. 2.
> In quantity, it is twice as large as that <note>referring to specific sections</note> of the brain: how it appears in a man standing upright is indicated by B. fig. 2. Table 8, just as fig. 1 teaches its position conversely.
> It possesses a shape filled with winding coils, but they are superficial; for these types of coils are not as deep as those of the Brain, and these coils end in two processes similar to those white worms <note>The "vermis" of the cerebellum</note> which are usually bred in hazelnuts or rotten wood. And these processes are called <term>testicularia</term> <note>Testicular-shaped; likely referring to the colliculi or the rounded lobes of the cerebellum</note> by some from their similarity. Their chief use is to support the posterior portion of the brain as if with columns, lest the fourth and last ventricle be crushed by its mass. For the "winepress" <note>The "torcular Herophili," the confluence of the venous sinuses</note> where the progress of the 4 sinuses occurs, and for the parts of the cerebellum, see B.C.D. Table 6. fig. 1. Its processes are indicated by E. fig. 1. Table 6. For its vessels, K.L.
> It has its site in the lowest part of the Skull <note>Original: "Caluaria"</note>, which is circumscribed by the two pits of the occiput. See B.D. fig. 1. Table 6 for its site. See P.Q.R. fig. 1. Table 6. For its right and left parts see A.B. Table 9; for its front and back see C.D.; for the worm-like processes <note>The vermis</note> E. and I.K.
> It is useful, insofar as according to Galen's opinion it is the beginning of the nerves; but truly the moderns deny that the origin of the nerves is in the Cerebellum, but attribute it to the brain. Taught by experience, they do not blush to defend this, whence indeed its use seems to be hidden, or at least not commonly known, and conjectured only from mere supposition—except that it is, as it were, the cushion and base of the brain.
> Its constellation <note>In a medical-astrological sense, its governing influence or temperament</note> is the same as the Brain.

# Book III of the Highest Region.

### Chapter XI.

#### Concerning the Nape of the Back or the Spinal Medulla. <note>The term "Nape" (Nuca) was historically used to refer to the spinal cord itself, not just the back of the neck.</note>

<image-desc>The text on this page is organized using a series of large curly braces (brackets) to categorize anatomical descriptions and logical divisions regarding the spinal medulla.</image-desc>

It arises behind the skull, and its beginning is twofold. Namely, either:
*   **The Greater**, which emanates from the Brain <note>original: "Cerebro"</note>; when it is derived from there, it is a single unit and is observed to gush forth from the base of the Brain. This origin seems to stand a short distance from the origin of the optic nerves. How it begins within the skull is indicated by A. fig. 2. Plate 10. and B. fig. 2.
*   **The Lesser**, which proceeds from the Cerebellum; it is bifurcated, for it is distinguished into a right and left side. See B. C. D. fig. 1. Plate 6.

It possesses the same substance as that of the Brain, for the spinal medulla seems to be nothing other than a portion of the brain drawn out lengthwise through the vertebrae and the sacred bone <note>The "os sacrum" or sacrum at the base of the spine.</note>. This, divided from the brain, is indicated by AA. fig. 2. Plate 6; and for where it is attached to the brain, see B. C. in the same place. It is moreover clothed in a membrane indicated by N. O.

The Spinal Medulla { Nevertheless, it differs from the brain itself in two ways:
1. The Brain is observed to move by contraction and expansion <note>original: "Systolem & Diastolem"</note> like the heart, which motion is certainly not attributed to the spinal medulla.
2. The bones containing the brain are immobile, whereas conversely, those of the spinal medulla are observed to be mobile. It is divided into the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar portions, and that pertaining to the sacred bone.

It enjoys a double wrapping; for when { it exits the skull, it is surrounded by both the "pious mother" and the "hard mother" <note>The Pia Mater and Dura Mater, the protective membranes of the central nervous system.</note>. For this location, see P. fig. 2. Plate 6. and D. E. fig. 1. & 2. Plate 8.
As it is carried through the bones of the vertebrae, it puts on another membrane, lest it be injured by the hardness of the bone.

It claims for itself an unequal dimension, for { while it exits through the opening of the occiput into the cavity of the vertebrae, it is observed to be somewhat thicker than elsewhere. For its beginning, see F. G. H. fig. 1. Plate 6, where 5 pairs are dedicated to the brain, concerning which see 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. fig. 2. Plate 10.
From the top of the chest all the way to the sacred bone, it is equal in its dimension.
Only in the sacred bone does it become more slender and pass into filaments, which again meet in nodes. See C. & MM. fig. 1. Plate 10. For the end of the spinal medulla, see H. fig. 2. Plate 10.

It has a **Figure** { Geometrically similar to an oblong triangle: see Plate 10.
An essential figure that is twofold, for { from its origin to the end of the chest, it is medullary <note>Pulp-like or marrow-like.</note>.
In its progress downward from the end of the chest, it becomes more nervous <note>Fibrous or stringy.</note> and like little cords.

It possesses the same **Temperament** as the Brain, namely cold, although in this we contradict Aristotle and the rest of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, who asserted quite thoughtlessly that this medulla was hot.

Its **Position** or seat is seen to be in the cavity of the back vertebrae, beginning after the skull and ending in the sacred bone.

It is **Connected** { To the Brain through continuous unity.
To the bones and muscles through nerves.
To the fourth ventricle of the brain through a kind of natural glue, as it were.

It is **Useful** for the procreation of nerves, which are destined both for movement and for carrying sensation to the remaining parts of the body, which the seven aforementioned pairs of brain nerves cannot reach. And concerning these parts of the nerves arising from the nape, we shall make mention in the following chapter.

# Book III of the Highest Region.

### Chapter XII.

#### Concerning the pairs of nerves derived from the spinal medulla <note>The spinal cord</note> in general.

<image-desc>A bracketed logical diagram (tree structure) outlining the origins and divisions of spinal nerves.</image-desc>

> The origin is from the spinal medulla. For this, see A. Table 10. fig. 1. Immediately around the end of the medulla, filaments arise, concerning which see I. LL. fig. 1. Table 8. Then nodes <note>ganglia</note> arise from the meeting of the filaments, as marked M M.
> The substance is the same as those produced in the brain.

<margin>Of the pairs of nerves of the back</margin>
* The division is into pairs assigned to the vertebrae, either:
    * Of the neck <note>Cervical</note>, which are five in number.
    * Of the chest <note>Thoracic</note>, which are eleven in number, as Columbus <note>Realdo Colombo, a 16th-century anatomist</note> maintains.
    * Of the loins <note>Lumbar</note>, which are five in number.
    * Of the sacred bone <note>The sacrum</note>, concerning which see below.

> The use is to bring motion and sensation to those muscles which cannot participate in the 7 pairs of cranial nerves. Therefore, we shall deal with them particularly as follows.

---

### Chapter XIII.

#### Concerning the particular pairs of nerves gushing forth from the vertebrae of the neck or throat.

<image-desc>A complex hierarchical bracketed diagram detailing the first four pairs of cervical nerves, their origins, motions, divisions, and uses.</image-desc>

* The First
    * The origin is the summit of the spinal medulla.
    * The movement occurs between the back of the head <note>occiput</note> and the first vertebra of the neck, between which it is sent out in a marvelous way, lest it be injured by the movement of the head.
    * The division after its exit is made into very small little nerves, for its trunk is but tiny. See F. Table 11. and G. & H.
    * The use is so that the branches, scattered into that series of small muscles serving the head, may serve their sensation and motion.

* The Second is distinguished by two principles, of which:
    * The Larger
        * The movement is through the back parts of the vertebrae, from which it is transferred here and there through the sides of the second vertebra.
        * The division after its exit is made immediately into several shoots which are carried upward to the skin, the ears, and some muscles. See I. K. Table 11.
        * The use is to provide motion and sensation to the parts to which its branches are carried.
    * The Smaller
        * The movement occurs through the front parts of the vertebrae, namely between the first and second vertebra.
        * The use is to be distributed to the fifth muscle common to the larynx and the esophagus.

<margin>Of these nerves there are five according to Columbus: although by others 7 are counted: see Table 10. fig. 1. D. & D. fig. 2. but of those five</margin>
* The Third
    * The movement occurs through the opening <note>foramen</note> common to the second and third vertebrae; namely, exiting from their sides.
    * The division immediately after its exit is made into four shoots, each of which is again subdivided into many more branches which are inserted into the parts named below. See L. Table 11.
    * The use is that, for the sake of both sensation and motion, its branches are carried to:
        * Some muscles of the head.
        * That oblong quadrangular muscle which pulls the lip obliquely downward.
        * That muscle which carries the shoulder blade <note>scapula</note> upward.
        * The skin of the neck.

* The Fourth
    * It moves from the substance of the spinal cord <note>original: "nucæ"</note> between the fourth and third vertebrae through a certain opening familiar to both.
    * It is divided into many shoots, some of which:
        * Descend.
        * Ascend.
        * Penetrate through the back parts.
    * It has various utility according to the variety of places to which its branches are led, since:
        * Some are carried to the muscles serving the neck, giving them motion and sensation.
        * Others extend themselves to the muscle called the "Hood-like" <note>original: "Cucularem," referring to the trapezius</note>. And from the front ones, some penetrate the muscles situated beneath the stomach.
