# On the Cerebellum and the Seven Pairs of Nerves.

<image-desc>A bracketed diagram showing the divisions and functions of the fifth pair of nerves (Quintum). The text branches from a central point into various anatomical destinations.</image-desc>

<margin>The Fifth Pair <note>original: "Quintum". This refers to the fifth cervical nerve pair, not the fifth cranial nerve.</note></margin>
* It has its exit between the fourth and fifth vertebrae.
* It is divided into many nerves, of which some are:
    * **Anterior**, which are more conspicuous, and
        * By their motion, they descend to the side of the **Esophagus** <note>The gullet or food pipe.</note> through the front parts of the neck, and they descend as far as the part of the **transverse septum** <note>The diaphragm.</note> where they terminate.
        * In use, they are chiefly dedicated to the transverse septum.
    * **Posterior**, of which:
        * One branch descends to the sides of the neck.
        * Others tend toward the shoulder.
        * Others to the **square muscle** <note>The platysma or similar muscle of the neck/jaw.</note> which pulls the lips obliquely downward; and also to the 4th muscle of the **hyoid** <note>The U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue.</note>.
        * Others are carried to the cavity of the **scapula** <note>The shoulder blade.</note>.

---

### CHAPTER XIV.
### On the pairs of vertebral nerves directed to the hand.

<margin>Pairs of nerves of the hand</margin>
* The **origin** is from the **spinal medulla** <note>The spinal cord.</note>.
* The **motion** occurs through the common openings of the subsequent vertebrae of the neck and from the first of the **thorax** <note>The chest/upper back.</note>.
* The **union**: for after their exit, they are so united that we can scarcely distinguish them, but when an exquisite anatomy is performed, they will appear in the likeness of a certain net <note>A reference to the brachial plexus.</note>.
* The **number** is fivefold, for there are five pairs for the hand.
* The **use** is for complete sensation: for nature sends out these five pairs of nerves: namely, three to the tips of the fingers, and two as far as the end of the hand, seeing as the sharpest and most acute faculty of the sense of touch is required for the duty of that member.

---

### CHAPTER XV.
### On the nerves springing from the vertebrae of the thorax.

<margin>Pairs springing from the thoracic vertebrae</margin>
* They **arise** from the spinal medulla.
* They have a **division** after their exit from the openings of the vertebrae, for you will see those nerves divided in two, but not by an equal division, since one sprout is seen to be larger than the other, or reflected more forward or backward.
* (Of these nerves, however:)
    * The **anterior** ones proceed under the ribs, through the lower part.
    * The **posterior** ones tend toward the lower parts.
* In **number** they are eleven. See figure 1, Table 10, from a. 7 to 19, or from a. D to E. And E. figure 2, where he counts 12 pairs.
* They are **useful** for conducting the **animal spirits** <note>In early modern medicine, these were subtle fluids believed to transmit sensation and motion through the nerves.</note> to those muscles which are adapted to them, and to which the seven pairs of cerebral nerves have brought no benefit.

---

### CHAPTER XVI.
### On the pairs of nerves springing from the vertebrae of the loins.

* They **arise** from the spinal medulla like the others.
* In **magnitude** they are larger than those of the thorax. For this, see B. figure 1, Table 10.
* In **number** they are five. See Table 10 from E. to F. or from 19 to 24. And F. figure 2, Table 10.
* They **exit** through only four openings, although there are five pairs, for between the last vertebrae of the thorax and the first of the **loins** <note>The lumbar region.</note>, the first pair of nerves passes, whence this pair can also be referred to the thoracic vertebrae.
* They are **divided** into small branches or filaments: See C. figure 1, Table 10.
<margin>Pairs of nerves of this kind</margin>
* They are **connected** to one another; for a pair is bound:
    * The first to the second.
    * The second to the third.
    * The third to the fourth.
    * The fourth to the fifth.

->They are moved<-

Book III of the Highest Region.

<image-desc>A complex analytical diagram using curly braces to categorize the origins and functions of nerves. The text is structured in a hierarchical tree format, branching from left to right.</image-desc>

<margin>They move in various ways, for</margin>
* The first emerges through the common opening located between the 12th vertebra and the first lumbar vertebra, and then passes beneath the Peritoneum <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity</note>. It then splits into two branches, one of which is larger and the other smaller.
* The second exits between the first and second lumbar vertebrae and proceeds beneath the peritoneum.
* The third emerges between the second and third vertebrae and is carried beneath the peritoneum.
* The fourth arises between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae; this nerve is the largest of all the lumbar nerves.
* The fifth is drawn out between the fourth and fifth vertebrae and migrates beneath the peritoneum toward the front.

<margin>The first is split into two branches after its exit, of which</margin>
* The larger is the origin of the transverse septum <note>The diaphragm</note> in which it first produces small branches; it also passes to the lumbar muscle and to those of the abdomen.
* The smaller migrates to the muscles of the back, giving them sensation and motion.

<margin>They are useful for bringing sensation and motion to the parts designated for them, for</margin>
* The second gives motion and sensation to the first muscles of the thigh and the sixth of the shin <note>tibia</note>; another branch of this performs the same for the sixth muscle of the thigh, while another small branch accompanies the seminal vessels.
* The third gives the power of feeling and motion to the dorsal muscles.
* The fourth regards the fifth muscle of the thigh, and the branches springing from it contribute to both the penis and the scrotum, but these are superficial and cutaneous <note>skin-level</note> and do not penetrate deeply; furthermore, its other branches are distributed to the anterior muscles which serve partly the shin and partly the thigh.
* The fifth is extended to the ninth and tenth muscles of the thigh, and its other branches to the 7th and 8th muscles of the same; others extend to the penis, others to the bladder, and even to the uterus in women. Another part of this nerve reflects behind the dorsal muscles and to the skin.

---

### Chapter XV.
### Concerning the Nerves springing from the Sacred Bone <note>original: "osse sacro"; the sacrum</note>, from whose union the principal nerve of the foot arises.

* The origin is the innermost marrow <note>spinal cord</note> of the sacrum.
* The exit occurs between the last lumbar vertebrae and the top of the sacrum, and also from the first, second, and third openings of the sacrum.
* The union is made of four; as soon as the beginnings have exited the said openings, they are united together into a single nerve and constitute the largest nerve of the whole body <note>The sciatic nerve</note>.
* The number before they run together into one is four. Furthermore, from the posterior part of the sacrum, small and short nerves arise which extend to the dorsal muscles, the buttocks, and the outer skin. There are therefore six in total, concerning which see G. figure 2, Table 10.
* The movement from the said openings after their union occurs beneath the peritoneum from the internal part of the abdomen toward the external buttocks; this nerve, arisen from the thickening of many, passes between the hip-bone <note>coxendix</note> and the tailbone <note>Corcygem/coccyx</note> above that 4th muscle by which the thigh is rotated, and is divided there, as will be said below.

<margin>Of these nerves</margin>
* Some [go] to the three muscles arising from the hip-bone, whose office is to flex the shin.
* Others to the eighth muscle, called the Livid <note>original: "Liuidum"; likely the pectineus or a specific gluteal muscle described by its color in dissection</note> muscle.

<margin>The division after its descent to the thigh into various sprouts</margin>
* Finally, it proceeds directly through the back of the thigh between the 4th and 5th muscles of the shin, where it sends out two notable unequal branches, of which
    * The larger occupies the posterior part of the shin and sends small branches under the bend of the knee to the first muscles of the end of the foot. But first it is subdivided into other nerves, one branch of which tends under the two muscles of the first foot, the other sends sprouts to the fourth muscle, which is the larger among the posterior muscles of the shin.
    * The smaller possesses the anterior [part], from which a small nerve arises that is attached to the muscle hiding under the knee-pit <note>popliteus</note>, and also extends another into the third muscle arising from the outer head of the thigh.

<margin>The use is to bring motion and sensation to the said muscles to which they are adapted.</margin>

# Book III of the Highest Region.

### TABLE XII.

->Here follows the Universal Mirror <note>original: "Catoptrum"; a common Renaissance term for a comprehensive visual overview or "looking glass"</note> or demonstration of the nerves, both of the brain and of the spinal medulla <note>the spinal cord</note>, as they emerge outside their own bones, explained through both numbers and letters so that those things described above may be more clearly understood.<-

1. *A filament of the first branch of the third pair <note>original: "coniugationis"</note> of cranial nerves, tending toward the forehead and eyelids.*
2. *A filament of the second branch of the same pair, descending to the nostrils and lips.*
3. *The opening <note>the foramen</note> through which the nerves of the sixth pair emerge and tend downward toward the chest and internal organs, from which the recurrent nerves are formed.*
4. *A portion of the third branch of the third pair, inserted into the lower jaw. It emerges through the opening described in the jawbone held in the hand, so that it may be more easily demonstrated to you.*
5. *The offshoots of the branch of the sixth pair turning toward the right side, following the path of the recurrent nerve.*
6. *The remainder of the nerve of the sixth pair, appearing at the location of the second lumbar vertebra, where it returns to the mediastinum <note>the central compartment of the chest cavity</note>.*
7. *The return of the nerve of the sixth pair <note>the recurrent laryngeal nerve</note> which occurs around the fourth true rib.*
8. *Another notation of the return of the said nerve toward the left side.*

A. This is the first junction of the nerves originating from the third, fourth, and fifth cervical vertebrae, and also the first of the back <note>thoracic</note>; this junction is later divided into two large branches. The higher one includes the nerves of the third and fourth cervical vertebrae, while the younger <note>lower</note> one unites and joins the branches springing from the fifth and sixth cervical vertebrae and also from the first of the back. Nevertheless, from this demonstration, one may see that these two branches unite again at the end.
B. The branch which creates the fusion of the offshoots springing from the cervical vertebrae and the first of the back; here it tends lengthwise through the dimension of the arm, then divides and separates in various ways through the substance of the muscles.
C. This is another branch generated from the fusion of the said small branches, which divides itself into two unequal parts. The smaller part is scattered and ends through the substance of the muscles of the posterior portion of the arm; the larger passes to the interior of the arm and is distributed with the muscles of that part; it descends as far as the fist <note>the wrist/hand</note>, and then afterward to two fingers to which it sends small branches, namely the thumb, the index, and the middle finger.
D. This is the third branch which is seen to accompany the aforementioned branch in its movement; it turns more toward the lower part of the arm and mixes with the internal muscles until it reaches the fist, where it divides into two portions. The smaller of these passes to the extremities of the fingers, namely the middle, index, and pinky, under the mark K; then some of its small branches migrate to the outer portion of the hand, to which they give sensation.
E. This is the fourth branch of the said cervical junction, which passes through the internal part of the arm following the path of the internal vein, which they call the Basilic; in its movement, it throws out branches laterally to the internal muscles; and finally reaches the fist, where it meets with the aforementioned ones under that ligament which, at the extremity of the fist and around the place of the pulse, divides into six small branches that move to the places assigned in the figure or model.
F. This is the fifth branch of that production, which is distributed to the muscles of the arm, but this one hardly extends to the fist.
G. This is the sixth branch of the same, which passes with the higher ones to the outer part of the arm, where it provides sensation and motion to the muscles belonging to this part, as it desires to impart a small branch to each of them; similarly, it proceeds to the skin and fat of this region. Its length does not exceed half of the arm.
H. In the palm of the hand is seen the fourth small part of the third branch, where it mixes with the sixth.
I. Some thin portions of the nerves placed outside their usual locations, so they would not impede the demonstrations of those nerves which have their origin from the vertebrae of the neck, and principally from the seventh vertebra, extending as far as the Diaphragm.
K. The nerve of the sixth pair of the "nucha" <note>the spinal cord at the neck</note> passing to the sides through the membrane of the heart <note>the pericardium</note> to reach the Diaphragm.
L. The nerves of the thoracic vertebrae coming to the muscles which are between the ribs, and especially the internal ones; these, passing over the ribs, reach the sternum.
M. Nerves springing from the tenth thoracic vertebra near the Diaphragm, which are finally inserted into the straight <note>rectus abdominis</note> and descending oblique muscles of the abdomen.

N. The nerves of the twelfth vertebra of the back <note>the T12 thoracic vertebra</note>, which are very short or brief; they are carried to the upper part of the transverse muscles of the lower belly <note>the transversus abdominis</note> and continue toward the muscles behind the loins.

O. These denote the nerves of the first lumbar vertebrae <unclear>——</unclear> passing through the transverse muscle of the abdomen; they are dedicated to the parts adjacent to the said members, so that they are imbued with the fat of that region.

P. These are the nerves of the second lumbar vertebra, which are very large and long; for they extend from each side all the way to the legs, and from there they ascend to those muscles of the abdomen which are called the "obliquely ascending" <note>the internal oblique muscles</note>.

Q. This mixture of nerves passes with its branches to the muscles of the hip, and likewise to the bladder, the womb <note>original: "matricem"</note>, and the anus, and the internal parts neighboring them. Furthermore, another branch goes to the thighs, the shins, and to the membranes of the muscles and to the skin.

R. This is the division whose branches are transported to the anterior muscles of the thigh.

S. A confusion of nerves which appear as if they were only one, yet in truth they are several covered by a common membrane. This confusion divides itself into several branches, some of which are marked by the figures O and R; they are sent out to the muscles of their region even to the skin, so that nothing in the whole thigh, shin, or foot, even to the tips of the toes, can lack sensation by reason of the presence of this confused—or rather, composite—nerve <note>likely referring to the sciatic nerve</note>.

T. Small branches produced from the nerve or pair which lead to the private parts <note>original: "pudenda"</note>.

V. The extremities of the division declared by the letter R, which appears toward the middle of the thigh.

X. The manner by which the nerves of the aforementioned mixture are sent out both to the neck of the foot <note>the ankle</note> and to the tips of its toes, and also to the entire skin of that member.

->Concerning<-
# THE ANATOMY OF THE EYE.
### CHAPTER I.
### Concerning the Eye in general.

The Eye
* *Is endowed with immense dignity, insofar as it exists as an organ created with the greatest craftsmanship and wisdom of the Creator. Indeed, there is nothing in the human body that so represents the two great lights of heaven as the two eyes; for the right eye is not inaptly compared to the sun, and the left to the moon.* <note>The author draws on the common Renaissance "microcosm" theory, where the human body reflects the celestial universe.</note>
* *Derives its origin from the Brain.*
* *Has a composition consisting of parts*
    * *Essential, of a twofold nature, namely:*
        * *Six Tunics <term>Tunics: the layers or membranes of the eye</term>.*
        * *Three Humors <term>Humors: the fluids within the eyeball</term>.*
    * *Attached externally to its globe, namely:*
        * *The Caruncle <note>The small, pinkish nodule at the inner corner of the eye</note>. See r. figures 7 & 8, Plate 13.*
        * *7 Muscles.*
        * *Nerves, see S. figure 6, Plate 13.*
        * *Small veins.*
        * *Small arteries.*
        * *Glands.*
        * *Fat poured out all around. See T. figure 6, Plate 13.*
* *Claims for itself an exactly spherical shape, in which it differs from that of other animals, which seem to deviate somewhat from the laws of a circle. For the tunic of the eye upon which the visual ray is expanded <note>The retina</note>, see II. Plate 8, figures 1 & 2.*
* *Has its site in a sufficiently safe seat; for it is arranged in two well-fortified cavities of the upper jaw: Furthermore, the eyes are raised in a more eminent place of the body, so that, like the faithful guards and scouts of a well-governed city, they occupy the higher place of a citadel or watchtower by virtue of their office, from which they can look out further. For the position, see A, B, & C, figure 1, Plate 13.*
* *Is protected*
    * *Above by the frontal bone and the eyebrows. See A. figure 1, Plate 13.*
    * *Below by*
        * *The Bone*
            * *The first of the upper jaw. See B. figure 1, Plate 13.*
            * *The second, the cheekbones.*
            * *Finally, by the zygomatic bone. As shown by c. figure 1, Plate 13.*
        * *The Nostrils. See D. figure 1, Plate 13.*
        * *The cartilaginous Eyelids. See FF. figure 1, Plate 13.*
        * *The muscles that constrict the eyelids.*
* *Is useful for granting man the faculty of seeing visible objects, by the mediation of the visual spirits <note>In early modern medicine, "animal spirits" were thought to be subtle fluids that carried sensory information</note> brought from the brain through the optic nerves.*

The author emphasizes the eye's role as a "watchtower" for the body, powered by visual spirits from the brain.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV.
#### In which the six tunics <term>tunic: a layer or membrane covering an organ</term> or membranes of the eye are treated.

### The first membrane of the eye, or tunic, or skin, or covering.

<margin>Of the first tunic of the eye</margin>
> *The name is the* { *Adnata <note>The conjunctiva</note>.* / *White.* / *Adherent.* / *Joined.* } *Tunic.*
> *The origin is from the pericranium <note>The membrane covering the skull</note>.*
> *The substance is subtle and thin.*
> *The color is bright white.*
> *The position ends at the larger circle of the Iris. See e. fig. 2. 5. 6. 7. & 8. Table 13. And V. fig. 6. 7. 8. And d. fig. 1. Table 15.*
> *The use is to veil and cover the entire eye from the outside.*

---

### The second tunic of the eye.

<margin>Of the second</margin>
> *The discoverer was Columbus <note>Matteo Realdo Colombo (c. 1516–1559), a famous Italian anatomist</note>, as he himself seems to boast.*
> *It has received no name from its discoverer as of yet, whence it is "innominable" <note>unnamed</note>.*
> *The origin is observed to come from the thin extensions of the nerves of the eye muscles.*
> *The boundary is found under the adnata membrane near the iris.*
> *The utility and function seem to be unknown by the discoverer himself, inasmuch as he makes no mention of it.*

---

### The third tunic of the eye.

<margin>Of the third tunic</margin>
> *The name is the Cornea, from its similarity [to horn], which expresses the horns of an ox both in its substance, transparency, and color.*
> *The origin is from the thick membrane or "dura mater" <note>The tough outermost membrane enveloping the brain and spinal cord</note>.*
> *The substance is more solid than the others, hard and thick, so that, since it is closest to external things, it may better resist external injuries.*
> *The division is into its* { *Anterior part, which they properly call the cornea, because it shines through like horn. For this see m. fig. 1. Table 15.* / *Posterior part, which they call the Sclerotica. This portion is indicated by d. fig. 8. Table 15.*
> *The quantity <note>extent</note> encloses all the humors <note>fluids</note> of the eye, and also the other membranes. Furthermore, its anterior portion is thinner than the posterior, which is more thick and solid: Whence it is ordained by Nature to be transparent for the reason that the pupil is located directly in its middle.*
> *The shape is peripheral <note>spherical/circular</note>, and in its cavity the three humors and also the other coverings of the eye are contained: For the cornea rolled back or removed, see K. fig. 6. Table 15.*
> *The site is around the iris and the pupil: See I. fig. 2. Table 13. and see e. fig. 1. Table 15.*
> *The color is of no effect, insofar as it is clear and transparent: and this tunic was so ordained, namely to be of no color at all, so that in this way it might better receive the objects and colors of all things.*
> *The use is to complete the substance of the whole eye into a round shape according to the form of this covering: Furthermore, it also stabilizes the eye and leads it around: and it also invests <note>clothes/covers</note> both the optic nerve and the eye itself.*

# Book IV of the Highest Region.

### The fourth tunic of the eye.

<image-desc>A bracketed analytical chart (tree diagram) describing the fourth tunic of the eye, with various branches detailing its name, origin, site, color, connection, and use.</image-desc>

<margin>Of the fourth tunic</margin>
* **The Name is** { *Rhagoides* <note>original: "Ragoides"; from the Greek 'rhax', meaning grape-berry.</note> / *Uvea, because of its resemblance to a grape skin.* / *Chorion, that is, the secundine <note>The vascular membrane or afterbirth.</note> and choriform.*
* **The Origin proceeds** from the thin membrane of the brain, that is, from the *pia mater*. See for its shape, P. fig. 17. Plate 15.
* **The Site and movement are of this sort.** { *First, it clothes the optic nerve.* / *Then it is dilated under the cornea and extends toward the anterior part. How the uvea is pressed, where it recedes from the cornea, is indicated by m. m. fig. 4. & 5. Plate 15.* / *Finally, it circles the entire inner eye, except in that single anterior part where it is perforated in a circular fashion; indeed, we call that opening the pupil of the eye, from which it reflects back again to the beginning of the iris, and there it is made double. For its site, see f. fig. 1. Plate 15. It is described by i. fig. 3. & 6. Plate 15. And the seat where the uvea floats in the aqueous humor is indicated by α. fig. 10. & 16. Plate 15.*
* **The Color is varied, for in it there is a great variety of colors; for in it there is** { *Black.* / *Scarlet.* / *Sky-blue.* / *Ruddy.* / *Green is also attributed to it by some, although Bauhin <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624), a famous Swiss botanist and anatomist.</note> seems to give that cyan color to the eye of an ox, not a human.* / *It must be noted, however, that the uvea tunic is not of the same color in everyone, since in one it is blacker, in another more white, and in another it appears blue or variegated.*
* **The Connection is made** through filaments or fibers to the cornea. See LL. fig. 3. & 4. Plate 15.
* **The Use is varied, for** { *By the variety of color, weary eyes and their spirits are refreshed at the same time.* / *Through its subtle vessels, vital spirits are scattered everywhere through the eye.* / *And it should be observed that nature placed the uvea especially near the vitreous humor so that it might carry nourishment to it.*

### The fifth tunic of the eye.

<image-desc>A bracketed analytical chart describing the fifth tunic of the eye.</image-desc>

<margin>Of the fifth tunic</margin>

### The sixth tunic of the eye.

<image-desc>A bracketed analytical chart describing the sixth tunic of the eye.</image-desc>

<margin>Of the sixth tunic</margin>
* **The Name** { *In Greek is arachnoides.* / *In Latin is Aranea <note>Spider-web.</note>, as it is very similar to a spider's web.*
* **The Origin** is drawn from the thin membrane <note>The pia mater.</note>.
* **The Substance is** very thin and transparent.
* **The Shape is** like a spider's web, or very similar to those skins found between the layers of onions; its anterior part is circular, sprinkled everywhere with straight rays like hairs, and this meeting of rays is called the ciliary processes. For this, see KK. fig. 1. Plate 15. And o. o. fig. 7. & p. fig. 17. Plate 15.

* **The Use is** to divide the two aforementioned humors from the aqueous humor, and to protect them from confusion <note>In the sense of mixing or blurring together.</note>.

# ON THE ANATOMY OF THE EYE.

## CHAPTER V.
### On the Iris.

<margin>Concerning its:</margin>
> { **Name:** Derived from its resemblance to the heavenly rainbow <note>original: "iridem cælestem"</note>.
> { **Origin:** It emanates from the coloring of the *uvea* tunic <note>The uvea is the vascular middle layer of the eye; the author views the iris as an extension of this layer</note>.
> { **Existence:** It is a circle in the eye surrounding the pupil, imbued with various colors, which we have said are derived from the uvea membrane. For this, see letter **f** in figures 7 & 8, Table 13. It is indicated by letter **f** in figures 2 & 3, Table 15.
> { **Use:** To hedge in the pupil on all sides, and to decorate the rays of sight—both those sent outward and those received inward—with colors matching the object, according to the object's own coloration.

---

## CHAPTER VI.
### On the Pupil of the Eye.

{ It is **named** the pupil <note>Latin: "pupilla"</note> because of its roundness.
{ It **originates** from the uvea tunic, inasmuch as that tunic forms and shapes it both by its colors and by the circular boundary of its substance.

<margin>It has color</margin>
> { **In appearance:** It seems jet black because of the cone of the "visual pyramid" <note>An early optical theory suggesting sight travels in a pyramid shape</note> which is deep within the eye—namely, in the center of the crystalline humor <note>The lens</note>—and because of the color of the uvea tunic reflected into it.
> { **In reality:** It is colorless, since neither the pupil itself nor anything beneath it appears black (as it is transparent). However, it is shaded by the reflection of the colors of the uvea membrane (wherefore the pupil is nothing other than a perforation of the uvea membrane), so that visible species <note>Images or sensory impressions</note> may be received in it, or in its center, or at the cone (which is in the center of the Crystalline humor).

<margin>The pupil of the eye</margin>
> { It has its **site or position** in the center of the anterior part of the eye, where it holds the place of the "Arctic Pole" <note>A metaphorical reference to the central axis or "North Star" of the eye's globe</note>. Three reasons teach us that this pupil is situated in the middle of the uvea membrane:
> { For its position, see letter **g** in figures 2 & 3, Table 15, and letter **n** in figures 4, 6, and 7.
>> { **First:** Because it comforts the visual spirit <note>The "spiritus visiuus" was believed to be a subtle fluid that enabled sight</note> with the green or reddish color of the uvea tunic (as these are intermediate between extreme colors).
>> { **Second:** Because if the uvea membrane with its intermediate colors were not there, the visual spirit would be very easily dissolved by external light. Nature has therefore wisely observed that this opening of the uvea tunic, called the pupil, should be placed in a seat directly opposite the crystalline humor. This is also proven by the fact that the more nature dilates this opening, the more the faculty of seeing is hindered; consequently, the more it is constricted to its natural measure, the more it contributes to the duty of seeing.
>> { **Third:** Because all species of a seen thing are emitted from the eye to the object in a pyramidal form, the base of which is on the object seen, while the cone or point penetrating through the pupil ends in the center of the crystalline humor. It follows, therefore, that this opening must be narrow, just as the start of a pyramid's cone must be, which terminates immediately in an angular unity. Its site is denoted by letter **g** in figures 7 & 8, Table 13.

It has a **primary utility**, which is that we may see by means of it: for this opening is made through the anterior part of the uvea tunic where the cornea is more transparent, lest the shadow and thickness of the uvea should hinder the passage of visible species to the center of the crystalline humor.

### In passing, on Cataract, Hypochyma, or Suffusion of the Eye.

We think it not irrelevant to say a few words in this place concerning Cataract or "suffusion" <note>original: "suffusione," an old term for cataracts, thought to be a "pouring down" of fluid</note> of the eye. Since this disease is the chief impediment to the operation of the eye or the sense of sight, and is created in front of the face of the pupil in the vitreous humor, we have proposed—not without deliberation—to explain its cause, its seat, and the method of its cure in this place.

<summary>This page describes the anatomy and function of the iris and pupil, defining the pupil as a functional opening in the uvea that regulates light and focuses the "visual pyramid" onto the lens. It also introduces the topic of cataracts as a primary obstruction of sight located behind the pupil.</summary>
<keywords>iris, pupil, uvea, crystalline humor, lens, visual spirit, cataract, hypochyma, optics, anatomy of the eye</keywords>

--- Page 202 ---
<meta>This page continues the anatomical and pathological study of the eye from the previous section, specifically focusing on the nature of cataracts before transitioning to the three primary humors of the eye.</meta>

# Book IV of the Highest Region.

**Of this Disease**
- **The Name is**
    - **Cataract.** <note>original: "Cataracta"</note>
    - **Suffusion.** <note>original: "Suffusio"</note>
    - **Hypochima.** <note>A Greek-derived term for a fluid "pouring under" the lens.</note>
- **The Origin is** primarily in the stomach, from which a vapor of this kind tends upward to the brain; then from the brain, as if from the nearest source, it moves to that space which lies between the pupil and the vitreous humor.
- **The Substance** in the beginning is a vapor tending toward thickness; in the end, this vapor is condensed into a thick and minimally transparent water.
- **The Seat** is directly in front of the pupil, namely between the pupil and the crystalline humor <note>The lens</note>, that is, in the aqueous or "egg-white" humor; and it is here that, by its thickness, it prevents the reception of visible rays.
- **The Division** is into a cataract that is either:
    - **Unconfirmed** <note>Incomplete or early stage</note>, and its substance is nothing other than a vapor, either thinner or thicker, which is:
        - **Mobile**, and by grace of its mobility and motion, it represents various appearances; and it is from this that the motive faculty judges that shapes—sometimes like flies, ants, gnats, or other such things—appear before the sight.
        - **Colored in itself**, whence it imprints its own color upon the Crystalline lens, and thus deceives; since it is not yet dense enough, it only completely removes the faculty of seeing when it reaches its full thickness.
    - **Confirmed**, which occurs through the reduction of that vapor into an opaque and dense water; and a cataract of this kind:
        - **Covers the entire pupil**, and by this, it removes sight entirely.
        - **Occupies only a part of the pupil**, namely its:
            - **Sides or circular margin**, and a humor disposed in this way makes the thing seen appear smaller than it truly is.
            - **Middle**, and in this case, the thing seen will appear as if perforated; for the middle portion of the object, which cannot be seen, will be imagined as a dark hole.
- **The Harm**, or the effect contrary to nature, is to hinder the reception of external images through the pupil.
- **The Cure** is usually performed either by:
    - **Repression of the humor**, that is, the thrusting of it further downward, which is done by means of a certain skillful needle, inserted deeply enough through the corneal tunic by an oblique passage into the humor, and extended until it reaches directly against the pupil. Then the sharp edge of the instrument is led to the site of the Cataract, by which that preternatural humor is thrust further downward, and the entire spot is submerged into the bottom of the natural humor, directing it more laterally from the pupil toward the Crystalline humor. <note>This describes "couching," an ancient surgical technique where the opaque lens was pushed out of the field of vision.</note>
    - **Extraction of that humor**, or rather the offending vapor, which is also accomplished by a similar preceding manual operation; but before it can be extracted, it is necessary that the entire aqueous humor be drained subtly and with great ingenuity, which is usually performed with the aforementioned instrument. But it must be noted that in this attempt, it is required that the vapor has not yet been "confirmed" into a solid humor; for it is impossible for a dense humor to be drawn out through such a small opening.

---

### Chapter VII.
->Concerning the three humors of the eye.<-

**I**t is right to observe three humors in the eye, differing from one another in substance, color, and arrangement, by means of which natural vision occurs, and without which the sense of sight cannot be perfected. Indeed, if any of these are injured or ill-disposed, the power of seeing will be hindered. It is necessary, therefore, both that they be arranged in the eye according to the proportion of Nature (namely, that the Crystalline holds the middle, the Aqueous the front part, and the Vitreous the rear) and that they be healthy and well-disposed in their substances. Their order, beginning from the front, is as follows.

# On the Anatomy of the Eye.

### The first or anterior humor of the eye.

It is called | **Aqueous** <note>Watery</note> | or | **Albugineous** <note>Like egg white</note> | from its resemblance to water or the white of eggs.

This humor:
| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Its Substance** | Is thinner than the others. |
| **Its Quantity** | Is quite small compared to the others that follow. Its extent is indicated by *y* in figures 10, 15, and 19 of Plate 15. |
| **Its Regeneration** | It is multiplied from an external source; for it has been gathered by observation that if this humor is drained, whether by a wound or during the cure of a Cataract, it is nevertheless regenerated again within a few days. It receives its nourishment from the Vitreous source, as we shall declare below, and it is regarded as that serous and excrementitious <note>In early medicine, "excrementitious" referred to a byproduct of nutrition, not necessarily waste</note> fluid which remains from the nourishment of the Crystalline humor. Its cavity is indicated by $\delta$ in fig. 19, Plate 15. |
| **Its Position** | It is situated in the anterior part of the eye, namely between the Uvea membrane (by which this humor is contained) and the Cornea. From this it follows that cataracts are produced within it. For this, see *c* in fig. 1, Plate 15. The seat where the vitreous is distinguished from the aqueous by the intervention of the hyaloid <note>The glassy membrane</note> is indicated by *2* in fig. 10, Plate 15. |

It has a twofold utility:
| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **First** | It distends the Cornea and causes it to swell out, and by this means it is made to stand apart from the Crystalline humor; for in this way the pupil always remains in its natural dilation, without which vision would be hindered. |
| **Second** | It serves as an internal medium fit for receiving visible species <note>The "images" or "forms" of objects traveling through the air</note>. Hence it happens that in those approaching death, the cornea falls and becomes flaccid due to the drying up of this humor; and then a "web" <note>original: *tela*</note> seems to appear before the eyes of the sick. Because of the lack of this humor, the visible species cannot be received by the Crystalline due to the excessive constriction of the pupil; the cause of this deficiency is the consumption of the animal spirits <note>The subtle fluids believed to carry sensation through the nerves</note> brought about by disease. |

---

### The second or middle humor.

It is named the | **Crystalloid** | or | **Crystalline** | humor, because it shines like Crystal.

This very soft humor:
| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Its Substance** | Enjoys a somewhat hard substance, not unlike that of Camphor. |
| **Its Shape** | It has a somewhat spherical shape, but yet: |
| | **In the Anterior part**, where it faces the aqueous humor or the pupil, it is more depressed and tends somewhat toward flatness. For this, see *u* in fig. 11, 14, and 20, Plate 15. |
| | **In the Posterior part**, where it looks toward the [vitreous] humor, it is observed to bear the likeness of a lens. For this, see *4* in fig. 12, 13, 14, and 16, Plate 15. |
| | **Its Color** is whitish and transparent like Crystal; and if it is removed from its seat and applied over written letters in the manner of a lens <note>original: *specilli*, here referring to a magnifying glass</note>, it will show them far larger than they truly are. And from this, without a doubt, those lenses appropriate for the elderly <note>spectacles</note> were invented. |
| **Its Position** | It is situated toward the front and almost in the center of the eye, so that the vitreous humor embraces its posterior part; but its anterior front is covered by the *Aranea* <note>Spider-web-like</note> membrane. For this, see *a* in fig. 1, Plate 15. For the width of the Crystalloid, see *5* in fig. 12 and 15, Plate 15. |
| **Its Uses** | It has most eminent and excellent uses in the optical faculty, whence: |
| | 1. It is esteemed the principal organ of the faculty of seeing. |
| | 2. It is not inaptly called the "idol" and "image" of vision. |
| | 3. It can be called the great light of the visible world, no differently than the Sun of the greater world, or the heart of the human world. |

# Book IV of the Highest Region.

### The third or final humor.

<note>The "Highest Region" refers to the head in the traditional division of the body into three regions.</note>

<image-desc>A bracketed diagram defining the third humor of the eye.</image-desc>

It is called the { Hyaloid <note>original: "Hialoides," from the Greek word for glass</note> / Vitreous } humor. Inasmuch as it resembles molten glass.

<image-desc>A large curly bracket grouping the following five descriptive paragraphs.</image-desc>

*Its substance is not as firm or clear as that of the Crystalline humor.*
*It is nourished by the retina <note>original: "tela retiua," the net-like web</note>, next to which it has its site and position.*
*In quantity, it is by far the largest of the other two, since it is seen to claim for itself three out of the four parts of the eye's cavity. And from this it is quite clear that it contains the greater part of the Crystalline humor within its own cavity. The Hyaloid indicates the pocket receiving the Crystalline at 'r' in figure 9, Table 15. Its size is indicated by 'x' in figures 10 and 20, Table 15, and by 'β' in figure 18.*
<margin>Which</margin> *It has its site toward the posterior part of the eye; indeed, this humor is so large that it even extends toward the anterior portion of the eye. Moreover, this humor, together with the Crystalline, is contained and wrapped by the spider-web tunic <note>original: "tunica aranea," now known as the lens capsule or hyaloid membrane</note>. For this, see 'b' in figure 1, Table 15.*
*It has a brilliant and pleasant appearance to behold, inasmuch as it is the nourishment for the most bright and clear Crystalline (as has been said); and in comparison to other things, it is not inaptly compared to molten glass, both in respect to its color and its viscous tenacity.*
*It is considered most useful to the visual faculty, insofar as it is observed to provide food and nourishment to the Crystalline humor; and in this kind of nutrition or feeding, this fir-like <note>original: "abigineus," likely referring to the resinous consistency</note> humor is believed or imagined to be produced in the manner of a superfluous and serous excrement <note>In early modern medicine, "excrement" referred to any byproduct of nutrition, not necessarily waste.</note>.*

### CONCERNING THE HIDDEN PERFECTION OF MAN, AND
#### his admirable properties, and the cause of his exaltation and depression.

<margin>Archangelus</margin>
<note>Referring to Archangelus of Borgonovo, a Franciscan Cabalist.</note>
So admirable is the nature of man, that he is called the knot <note>original: "nodus"</note> not only of earthly things, but even of celestial ones; wherefore Pico della Mirandola rightly says, *that earthly things are subject to man, and celestial things favor him, inasmuch as his soul is heaven itself, his body is the earth, and the bond joining these two together is the intermediary spirit:* And from this, the said Pico judged that whatever was said by Moses in the first chapter of Genesis concerning the Macrocosm <note>The Great World/Universe</note>, this can also be understood concerning man himself, who for this reason is not unwisely called the Microcosm <note>The Little World</note> and "every creature." Moreover, God—the better nature—composed him from the mud of the earth and the breath of life, so that he might look toward the earth for the health of the body, and toward heaven for the salvation of the soul: for by the secret decree of the immense Creator of things, such a commerce was ordained between these two extremes, that the specimen of divine likeness (which by its own nature used to neglect gross things and was least of all inflamed by the desire for earthly things) was thus covered with a dark garment or earthly house by means of the mediating spirit, so as to fashion man, that most noble creature. Thus, he was made into a rational animal from an eternal and mortal nature, so that he might satisfy both of his origins: to wonder at and pray to celestial things, and to inhabit and govern earthly things. And by grace of this immortal and celestial gift, Archangelus, in his Cabalistic commentaries, recognizes that a divine race indeed exists in men—nay, rather that the soul is like the seed of God infused within us. He seems to have received this doctrine from Saint Paul, who confidently proclaims *the external man to be the temple of the Holy Spirit.* Hence it was that the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note> affirmed *that man was created by God a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor, having dominion over the works of His hands, putting all things under his feet: namely flocks and herds, the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea.* Nay, even his steps are established by Jehovah,

<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>Psalm 8:5</margin>

Thus, by deceiving the soul with flattery and shrouding it in clouds of darkness, the body easily seduces it from the nature of a "good spirit" <note>original: "boni dæmonis"</note> to the disposition of an "evil spirit" <note>original: "cacodæmonis"</note>. In this way, man—who by the power of the presiding mind ought to be placed above every creature—is rendered equal to the beast, or rather, viler than the brute itself, as he is now imbued and contaminated with the filth and pollution of sin.

Hence it has happened that this creature, most eminent in respect to the breath of God-like life, has now become rotten and most vile by reason of the body. Job seems to acknowledge this in his sequence of words: *Man decays like a rotten thing, like a garment eaten by moths; man born of woman is of few days and full of trouble—that is, filled with many miseries.* Similarly, in respect to the body, man is called *flesh, a wind that passes away and does not return.* Hence he is also called by Job *rottenness and a mortal, and his son a worm or an earthworm.*

Job 26</margin>

Yet God made both the internal and external man upright and most temperate; for He *did not place death and transgression upon the earth, nor does He delight in the destruction of the living; for He created all things that they might exist, and made the nations of the world healthy.* But *injustice, or sin, is the acquisition of death: for justice (which is always with God) is immortal.* By this justice, God fashioned man immortal *and in the image of His own likeness; but through the envy of the Devil, Death entered into the world.*

Therefore, human unhappiness was introduced by the Devil, the presiding officer of darkness; just as supreme and eternal blessedness was brought to man by God, the fountain of light and Commander of justice, through the gift of the mind—and through the blood of Christ, a complete washing from the filth of sin. By Divine blessing, such was the dignity of Adam in the state of innocence, and so exalted was his honor, that he stood immortal; indeed, he was equal to the angels themselves. Even after his fall, an angel reminded him of this nobility when he refused to allow man to offer him reverence or adoration, as is declared in the *Book of Revelation*.

### CHAPTER I.
->*Concerning the four cardinal corners of the Microcosm, concerning its poles: and how, and how aptly, it is adapted to the Macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the great world or the universe at large.</note> in its position.*<-

<margin>
Pythagoras.
Plato.
Aristotle.
Empedocles.
</margin>
Various are the opinions of Philosophers, both Pagan and Christian, concerning the position of the Macrocosm, which the Microcosm is observed to imitate no differently than a son imitates his father; for the Microcosm (according to the testimony of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurio Trismeg." — a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and philosophy.</note>) is the son of the Macrocosm, just as the latter is the offspring of God himself. Hence it is impossible to investigate the hinges and corners of the Microcosm or man, and especially his poles, except through an apt application of the same to his father, namely the greater world. However, to find the exact location of the World’s right and left sides is a matter not so easy, since in this inquiry the industry of the sharpest Philosophers has not only been inconsistent, but even their minds remain uncertain and wavering on this matter to this very day. For Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle placed the right side of the world at the East, because (they say) the motion of the world begins from that quarter. But Empedocles, by no means adhering to this opinion of theirs, extends the right hand of the world toward the summer solstice, that is, toward the Tropic of Cancer, and consequently extends its left toward the winter solstice; and by this reasoning, comparing the world with man, it is necessary that his face look toward the western quarter of the world: just as according to the assertion of the aforementioned [philosophers], he would look toward the North. What then is to be done in such a great controversy, except to flee to the sacred and truthful oracle of God, and elicit the truth of this matter from its response? In many places of the Holy Scriptures, therefore, we find that in the prayers of the prophets and patriarchs, and in the formula of praying, the face of the one praying was always arranged toward the East. And in Matthew we read that the lightning comes from the east and tends toward the west; and elsewhere we have: "Measure also toward the Eastern quarter, and toward the Southern quarter, and toward the Western quarter, and toward the Northern quarter." As if he had said, measure toward the front, the right, the left, and the back. Furthermore, this place is confirmed by Job in that passage where the inquiry into the place or seat of Jehovah is discussed, which is thus interpreted by Pagninus <note>Santes Pagninus (1470–1541), a Dominican monk and leading Hebrew scholar.</note>: *Behold, I will go to the East, and he will not be there; and to the West, and I shall not perceive him; or to the North while he works, and I shall not see him; he hides himself in the south and I shall not see him.* But Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> interprets it thus: *If I go to the East, he appears not; if to the West, I shall not understand; if to the left, what shall I do? I shall not apprehend him; if I turn myself to the right, I shall not see him.* Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a Jewish convert and prominent Hebraist.</note> translates that passage in this sense: *If I go forward, he will not be present; if backward, I shall not notice him; when he acts on the left, yet I shall not see; he will cover the right quarter, yet I shall not look.* Therefore, what Pagninus makes the Eastern corner of the world, Tremellius makes the front part; what the former makes the Western quarter, the latter makes the back; what the former calls the North, the latter calls the left hand of the world, just as the former called the right region of this [man] the South. From which (as it seems to me) this appears without any controversy: that the correct arrangement of man according to the position of the world is with his face disposed toward the eastern quarter, whence the eyes are placed in the front part of man and all other creatures (namely, the face), so that they might salute the rising sun as it visits the dark earth with its golden and lucid aspect after the long night and darkness, banishing the gloom of night into exile; as a type of the invisible Sun, whom the Holy Bible predicted would come from that part of the world on the last day for the renewal of the world. Hence therefore...

# On Mystical Anatomy.

Therefore, it follows that his right hand or side faces the South, just as the left faces the North, and consequently his posterior part must look toward the West. Since this is the case, it is necessary that we seek that Arctic pole in the left region of man, or the Microcosm, from which the North Wind <note>original: *Boreas*</note> sends forth its cold and earthy blasts into the microcosm. And likewise, we must investigate the pole opposite to it, namely the Antarctic, which is necessarily found in his right region. The Eastern quarter of man is the anterior portion of the Chest, toward which the point of the heart (which is the Sun of the microcosm) inclines, just as his western region is in the posterior part, where the seminal vessels, kidneys, and bladder are submerged in the middle of the "earth," namely the mass of the intestines.

### CHAPTER II.

#### On the investigation of the two poles of the Microcosm, and that they are the Spleen and the Liver.

Since, therefore, the disposition of man is found to be such in relation to the disposition of the world—that his left part corresponds to the northern region in the Macrocosm—we must discern through diligent inquiry which portion in the northern region of the microcosm is endowed with such properties that it agrees in almost all respects with the Arctic or northern pole of the greater world. As for the nature of the Macrocosmic north, the effects of the wind blowing from it denote that it is the coldest and driest quarter of the world; its nature is to freeze and harden both earth and water with its coldness and dryness, and to procreate ice, snow, and hail. Furthermore, by its cold and dryness, it thins, constricts, contracts, and makes things wrinkled or produces roughness; it takes away action and stupefies, corrupts fruits and flowers, and dries up herbs; it affects humors both internal and external, and performs other such things which it usually accomplishes by means of its Northern blast. 

In the left axis of man, however, we find nothing of significance except the Spleen <note>original: *Lien*</note>, whose nature we shall perceive does not differ much from that of the polar star if we explore the matter a little more accurately. For since its nature is earthy, it is the coldest and driest portion of the entire lower region, which sends forth cold and dry winds into the universal region of the microcosm no differently than the North does from its quarters. Similarly, with its blasts, it freezes and hardens humors, produces glassy and thick phlegm, procreates icy viscosities, constricts dreggy matter, and disperses melancholy everywhere—which is nothing other than earthy matter, cold and dry. It freezes this into hardness, just as the North Wind by its blast thickens the thin airy humor into snow and hail; it thins by its corporeal dryness, just as the Northern cold constricts and contracts the soft earth; it brings forth stupors and paralysis; and, to put it briefly, it is that member of the body which brings greater harm to human life than any other of the whole body, inasmuch as it participates in the nature of Saturn. This is the "greater misfortune," for it is opposed to life in every way, being most contrary to the innate heat by its extreme cold, and to the radical moisture by its dryness. Furthermore, the agreement between this member and the polar star is declared in this: that both claim Saturn for their constellation, from whom they have their styptic <note>contracting or astringent</note> virtues. But truly, because man is called the son of the world, the North Wind received that power from the Angel presiding over it (in whose care is also the sphere of Saturn), and the spleen of the microcosm likewise drew its power from the North Wind; hence both produce the same effects.

By a similar reasoning, just as the Cardinal wind opposite to the northern one—called the South Wind <note>original: *Auster*</note>—breathes out moist and warm blasts from the southern pole, it is observed in the greater world to make the air gross and thick with its spirit, sometimes to procreate lightnings, and for the most part to bring and multiply rains. And (as our Hippocrates also confesses) that very wind opens the pores of the body, hinders the power of sensation, and creates heaviness in the body; it diminishes hearing and makes it difficult, affects the head with pain, dissolves the humors of the body and moves them from the interior to the exterior parts; indeed, it induces torpor in the senses and even corrupts, destroys, and generates diseases such as gout <note>original: *podagra*</note>, Epilepsy, itching, and fevers. Nevertheless, its natural virtue is healthy enough insofar as it makes hard things soft; it is also sometimes the author of benevolent dew and moderate rain, by which it softens and opens the pores of the earth and makes it fruitful, whence it brings forth, nourishes, and causes to grow fruits, herbs, grasses, and seeds. It dissolves thick and cold humors and causes vapors and superfluous humors to flow out through sweat, both from the bodies of vegetables and of living creatures. 

So also we must seek and explore in that part of the human body opposite to the Spleen by a direct axis, something which can be compared in all things to this southern quarter, from which the microcosmic South Wind is accustomed to blow, either with a preternatural effect or a natural and expected success. By due inquiry, we shall find the Liver <note>original: *Hepar*</note> itself to be such a thing in the right region of the microcosm, which is most aptly compared with the southern quarter not only in position but also in property. For first, the axis of this region—namely, the liver—tends directly to the center of the Spleen, just as the axis of the antarctic pole tends to that of the arctic or northern pole. Secondly, the liver in its nature is warm and moist, and it emits such blasts into the microcosm as the South Wind does from the southern region of the Macrocosm. Furthermore, it reduces the air into healthy dewy and bloody clouds, by which the whole human earth is irrigated, every member of the same is nourished, and generation and vegetation are completed. Humors condensed and congealed by the cold of the Northern wind (or the Spleen) are dissipated and expelled through the pores in sweat (by means of its benevolent heat); and thus, in the manner of a well-disposed macrocosmic South Wind, all things are ordered for life according to the laws of nature. At that time, Jupiter is present with the macrocosmic South Wind as a benevolent and favoring foster-father. But truly, if Mars mixes himself with its temperament, whether in the macro- or microcosm, then preternatural blasts of this kind follow: thick clouds will be raised upward by the intemperance of heat, and they will be turned into catarrhs and defluxions in the manner of worldly rain and flooding; heaviness of the head will be generated, along with stupor of the senses and other infirmities which the worldly South Wind is accustomed to bring forth, namely gout, Epilepsy, and itching; indeed, if the influence of Mars predominates over it a little more—

### Chapter III.
### *Concerning the specific meteors arising from the Spleen, their comparison with those blown forth by the Macrocosmic North Wind. Concerning the primary cause of the Northern wind in the Macrocosm, from which the Spleen receives its power.*

<margin>Job 37:9. Proverbs 25:23</margin>
In the aforementioned series of words, it has been declared clearly enough that the Spleen, by its position in the human body, corresponds to the Northern Quarter of the world. Whether indeed, by its disposition and property, it also agrees with that region, shall be explained from what follows. The Northern part is indeed very cold and dry in its quality, whence it is observed to produce such winds or blasts, according to that passage of Holy Scripture: *The Northern winds produce cold.* <note>original: "Venti Aquilonares producunt frigus"</note> But truly, that such a wind is most dry is explained therein, *because it is handed down by Solomon himself that it chases away and dissipates rains*, which it would by no means accomplish unless it were most opposed to the moisture of the rains. Therefore, just as the Northern Angle of the world is a Cardinal wind, and its receptacle is cold and dry, so also is the Spleen—or the "North" of man—of such a quality, since it is the seat of melancholy, which enjoys a terrestrial disposition, that is, cold and dry. Wherefore also from this kind of cardinal point of the microcosm <note>The "microcosm" refers to the human body as a miniature reflection of the universe.</note>, Northern blasts—namely cold and dry ones—are emitted, exciting unnatural passions in the lesser world no differently than the North wind, or *Boreas*, or the Arctic wind does in the greater world. For as the North sometimes emits snows and hailstones by itself, and produces frost, and is sometimes fortified with tremendous thunder, so also sometimes by raw blasts prone to acidity, inducing a viscous and glassy phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note>, and freezing it into a mucous substance, cachexia <note>A state of ill health and wasting.</note> and other evil habits of the body are produced. Numbness and torpor are effected in the whole fabric; Paralysis, Apoplexy, and other such things are procreated from the condensations of humors and vapors. Similarly, two aquatic species of dropsy <note>Edema or swelling.</note> arise, which is most clearly declared in the scorbutic disposition <note>Scurvy-like symptoms.</note> and the "virgin's disease" <note>Likely referring to chlorosis or "green sickness," an anemic condition.</note>, where the blasts or winds springing from this region are accustomed to freeze the humors into an icy substance, and the frozen humors to block the passages, and the blocked passages to procreate evil dispositions of the body. And often these kinds of Northern windinesses occur in the microcosm with thunder or murmuring and rumbling, inasmuch as spirits are within them (according to the nature of those who inhabit the clouds driven by the violence of the winds from the world's North), which accompany those men whose melancholy for the most part arises from burnt phlegm. This is clearly noticed in hypochondriacs and those afflicted with *tympanites* <note>Abdominal swelling due to gas.</note>, or they occur without thunder or evident belching, and then the phlegmatic humor is made more acid and glassy, and this humor is likened to the snows and frost procreated by the Northern winds in winter time, which intense coldness accompanies. And this is that humor, thus thickened by the cold and dry Spleen-winds, which frequently produces numbness, torpor, and Epileptic passions, inasmuch as in that humor malignant spirits rejoice to hide, who are of the nature of those who flee the light, and who stiffen greatly with terrestrial cold and dryness. Such also are those Northern spirits which, driven from the North wind toward the South, by their terrestrial cold constrain the condensed air into snows and hailstones, and congeal the terrestrial waters into frost. But truly, the blasts arising from the scraping mass of Melancholy in man are likened to those observed to blow from the Northern region of the world in summer time, carrying with them hailstorm-clouds and dry clouds, most full of lightning in a certain fiery spectacle, which bring damage and fears and ineffable sorrows as much to the earth and its fruits as to animals. Hence it happens that men oppressed by this kind of melancholy blast fall into Frenzy, Lycanthropy <note>The delusion of being a wolf.</note>, and infinite other furious vexations of melancholy. It must be understood, therefore, first of all, that there is a twofold beginning of unnatural melancholy: namely, either excessive burning—just as wood is first turned into coals by a fiery nature and afterwards reduced to the disposition of ashes—so bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> is reduced into black bile or a coaly and ashy nature, and this species is that which accompanies the lightning-bolt, which converts fiery substance into ashes and salts, as may be seen in the "thunder-stone" <note>original: "lapis fulminaris"; prehistoric stone tools once believed to be the physical remains of lightning strikes.</note>. So also this melancholy, with inflammation preceding it, is cleansed in the spleen, and the brain is damaged by its terrestrial exhalation mixed with fire, the imagination is deceived, and reason itself is alienated; and this by evil spirits carried in that sweltering cloud, who [drive] men with insane <margin>Finit med. 12.</margin> delirium. But in truth, this species of melancholy never happens from the Spleen by itself, except where there are confluences of evil spirits leaping out from the Liver (which labors from a hot and sweltering intemperance) together with a most dry blast tending toward heat, which is ejected from the spleen. The second principle of melancholy is mortification or freezing, and the beginning of this is not inflammation or burning, but conversely coldness, rawness, and an extreme lack of heat. And this species is attributed to that Northern part of the world which ends in clouds of hail and snow endowed with extreme cold, with no fiery meteor mixing in. And from this kind of imbalance follows a quartan fever <note>A fever where paroxysms occur every fourth day, historically associated with "black bile" and the spleen.</note>, involving a humor with which malignant spirits of that same condition mix. These things (I say) are to be understood concerning the Spleen and its winds when they are poorly and unnaturally disposed—either by themselves or by reason of some contrary malevolent wind—having strayed and changed from their natural state into the opposite. For just as the North wind of the world is observed to bring many benefits to the air and is healthy in itself—since, when well-disposed, it renders the air clear and pure by its breath, dissipates southern clouds, and consequently opposes the plague that arises from the South—so also we see that the wind emitted gently and sweetly from the Spleen, and the humor carried by it into the parts of the body, usually brings more health than disease. From this it arises that it dries up superfluous humors in the body, opposes putrefaction, and dissipates and dissolves vapors unnaturally raised from the "Hepatic South" <note>The Liver, associated here with the warm, moist South.</note>, mitigating unnatural heats by its breath and creating a fit temperament. Hence it is said that a well-disposed Spleen is the source of joy and laughter, according to that line of the Poet: *the spleen makes one laugh, etc.* Furthermore, its sour vapor is the author of appetite and of the retentive or restrictive faculty, as the fathers of both Physicians and Philosophers testify. Regarding the collateral winds of the North, such as the *Aquilo* or *Boreas* <note>North and North-East winds.</note>, which are observed to blow from the Polar axis toward the East, these are compared to the wind blowing from the upper region of the Spleen's cavity; likewise concerning the wind called *Corus* <note>The North-West wind.</note> in the macrocosm, which in man usually blows from the hump of the Spleen and tends to inflate that region (namely from the left hypochondrium), I have proposed to discuss this openly and fully elsewhere in the second section, where supernatural causes of diseases will be treated; and in the following chapter we shall speak of it, albeit briefly. It remains in this place, however, for us to draw out the primary causes of these winds, first in the world, and then afterwards in man.

We Christians therefore say, contrary to the doctrine of Hippocrates, Avicenna, and the rest of the Heathens, that the cause of this or that disease is God. This has indeed been abundantly explained in *Part 1, Book 3, Chapters 1, 2, and 3 of this first section, regarding supersubstantial principles.* For hence it is said, *Good things and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from God* <margin>Ecclesiasticus 11:14</margin>, and elsewhere, *The Lord has power over life and death, who leads down to the gates of death and brings back again:* <margin>Wisdom 16:13</margin> And Moses testifies to this same thing in these words, <margin>Deuteronomy 28:21</margin> *Jehovah shall make the pestilence cleave to thee until he has consumed thee; Jehovah shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with the botch of Egypt, and with emerods, and with the scab, and with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed.* Similarly we receive from Job, <margin>Job 33</margin> *That Jehovah chastens by pain upon the bed.* And among us it is familiar that God brings this or that evil upon us for our sins. We must therefore ask with diligent insight: how does God usually afflict sinners with diseases and plague? Is it directly, or through the mediation of His other creatures? In David we read, *Angels of God, mighty in strength, performing His word, listening to the voice of His word, His armies and ministers, doing His pleasure:* <margin>Psalm 103:20; 104:4</margin> And elsewhere these angels are called the winds or spirits of God, whence it is read, *Who makest thy angels spirits* (as Jerome interprets it) *or winds* (as Tremellius prefers) *and thy ministers a flaming fire:* From this it is clear that when God is said to do this or that, it is done by primary ordination and not by immediate execution; for whatever is ordained by God, whether for bestowing good or for infesting with punishment or plague, is all usually executed by angels as ministers. Hence it is said, the angels of God shall give charge over the just. And Josephus says, *May that Angel who redeemed me from all evil bless these boys.* But on the contrary side it is said, *The Angel would have slain Balaam with a sword, had his donkey not turned away from his sight:* <margin>Psalm 91:11; Genesis 48:15; Numbers 22</margin> Similarly, *David saw the Angel of God devastating with pestilence and afflicting with deadly disease*; furthermore, *it was the Devil who, by the ordination of God, inflicted the plague upon Job.* From these things it is evident that God acts by ordination, and Angels by execution upon these lower things, whether for life and health, or for death and disease; and consequently it is clear that angels and demons, ordained under their command, are the mediating agents between God and lower things, not otherwise than the spirit <note>The "medical spirit" or pneuma that links soul to body.</note> is the glue and bond between the soul and the body. Whence the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> acknowledge, and the Cabalists agree with them, that *an assisting intelligence, beyond its essential form, is attributed to every heaven as the mover of its sphere, which is called an Angel; as one sent by office, it fulfills the commands of the Creator; for an Angel is like a mediating power between God and nature, from which operations in natural things arise.* Thus far their view. And from this it follows that Astrologers, looking more to the exterior than the interior, maintain that God acts continually according to ordination, and the stars according to execution upon these lower things—where they name visible creatures in place of the invisible intelligences who preside over the stars and their infinite legions, about which there is much in the second section here. But let us see at last by what means these spirits, both benevolent and malevolent, strive to perfect the commands of their Creator in the sublunary world. That Angels are winds and spirits, we understand from the place cited before. Furthermore, the royal Psalmist teaches us that God brings forth the wind out of His treasuries; and elsewhere it is said by the same prophet, *That God blows His wind, sending forth His word.* And elsewhere: *A wind went forth from Jehovah and brought quails, etc.* And elsewhere: *Stormy wind fulfilling God's word.* <margin>Reuchlin on the Cabala</margin> <margin>Psalm 135:7; 147:18; Numbers 11:31; Psalm 148</margin> But in truth, we must agree with the philosophers in this: namely, that wind is nothing other than a fluctuating motion of the air; but that this struggle and commotion of the air arises from a hot-dry quality fighting against the middle region of the air, this we utterly deny and hold as ridiculous. Instead, we say the wind is *formal* <note>Relating to the "Form" or soul/essence of the thing rather than its physical matter.</note>, which is an angelic spirit sent by God, which so disturbs the air; the philosophers, looking at the exterior and by no means reaching the interior, called the air thus moved "wind," and therefore unwisely feigned its material cause to be a breath rising from the earth. We acknowledge, I say, that the matter of perceptible wind is fluctuating air, but the cause acting in this noise is the company of lower demons, who by their power drive the air (otherwise quiet) either gently or violently, so that by means of the air thus driven, the will of God may be perfected by His [ministers].
