Furthermore, also that the Liver is hot and moist, contrary to the nature of the Eastern quarter which is hot, dry, and fiery: For if these things are granted, a great discrepancy will occur among the opinions of the philosophers; wherefore I shall gird myself for my preceding intention, and restrain myself until a clearer reason presents itself to me, or a more probable demonstration calls me away from it. For however the matter stands, this is certain and to be denied by no one: that winds or blasts of various conditions are excited in the microcosmic world <note>the human body</note>, which participate in and arise from the nature of those in the greater world <note>the universe</note>. But to rightly adapt any wind of the microcosm to any windy spirit of the macrocosm, and to justly ascribe any region of the one to that of the other—this indeed is the labor, this is the work. This has been attempted by us in every way, as we who see with open eyes that almost all diseases, both of the greater and lesser world, take their origin from the winds. Truly, in this place, we shall here abruptly conclude this little book of ours concerning the mysteries of the Spleen and Liver.

### EPILOGUE OR CONCLUSION.

The air or mundane spirit is indeed an admirable thing, and hidden beyond human grasp; although the philosophers placed it as the middle of the Elements, yet the Hebrew doctors (highly skilled in formal mysteries) refused to number air among the Elements, since they wished it to be something in the nature of things greater and more secret than an element, inasmuch as it is like a medium and glue, connecting the superior forms with the inferior matters—that is, heaven with earth, or the soul with the body. Whence they also made the spirit of the world a resounding instrument, since it receives all the mysteries of the super-celestial region and the influences of the celestials, like the bosom or common womb of the entire sublunary nature, and hastens to impart portions of the same to the other elements and things composed of elements. It is also that most polished mirror in which the wise have looked upon the divine image of creating nature, and the substances of angels and demons, and all things hidden in nature; indeed, through it, the spirits of men dwelling in far distant places can confer with each other and converse in spiritual speech. For the spirit of living things joins itself most easily with it, since they previously emanated from its fountain, and differ from it in substance no differently than a drop of water from its mass. In this kind of spirit, therefore, or spiritual sea of the world, Angels, demons, and spirits both malignant and benevolent swim, no differently than little fish visible in the material sea, who by their violent motion disturb and agitate this invisible sea while they swim constantly from one or another quarter of the world; and this motion of the air is called wind, so that the first agent in the winds is an angel, a prince and leader, having dominion over this or that quarter of the world, who (to speak with the poets) opening that quarter of Aeolus's prison, sends out the spirits retained in it to execute the will of God, by whose motion the air is violently impelled toward the opposite part of the world. Whence a noise is emitted, either greater or lesser according to the violence of the motion, as is permitted to observe in the precipice of a river. So also in the motion of a multitude of herring or other fish in the sea, waves arise, and the agitation of the water is excited in that part of the sea. Moreover, just as the celestial Mercury is observed by Astrologers to be versatile and of a changeable nature, whence he is ready to appropriate to himself the nature of whichever planet he is joined with or regards, so indeed is this air of ours, which truly ought to be called our sublunary Mercury, which changes its nature according to the disposition of the planet or intelligence predominating in heaven. Whence sometimes it grows hot and adheres to the fiery element—indeed, being itself inflamed, it is nothing other than fire or the fiery element—and then it draws this kind of property from the Eastern demon. Sometimes it is air, and then it remains in its spiritual nature, which it draws from the apothecary-shop <note>original: "myrotecio"</note> of Raphael in the West; sometimes it turns itself into a watery nature, nevertheless minutely laying aside its fiery heat, and thus condenses itself into clouds, and thins and consumes itself into rains and tears, namely when Uriel breathes from the South and the raging Metiri <note>a stormy or measuring spirit</note>, that tumultuous demon, emits fiery sighs from his moist breast and gives forth a thundering voice, in which case it participates with two natures, namely the Martial and the Lunar. Furthermore, when Saturn reigns with the Moon, or Gabriel blows from the North, it is converted into earthy, hard, and dry matter, whence it turns its substance into ice, hail, snow, and frost. From which things it is permitted to see that the air with its demons turns itself to the pleasure of the stars, and the stars with their angels are subjected to the commands of the Archangels who stand before God, whose part it is to perfect or execute nothing in this world which is not first ordained by God the supreme creator, the act of acts, and the beginning of motion and life; who, as he is the prince of spirits, so it is said that *the spirit blows where it wills, and you hear its voice but you do not know whence it comes or where it goes* <margin>*John 4* <note>Actually John 3:8</note></margin>; for as we have elsewhere, the winds are brought forth from the treasuries of God <margin>*Job*</margin>. It follows, therefore, that insofar as the natural and vital spirit of animals mixed with the blood is from the aerial fountain, and is no otherwise continuous with it than a ray is to the Sun, or the spirit of God filling the orb of the earth is to its fountain, to that extent it is also moved to the motion of the mundane air, as a part by its whole; and consequently, that the spirits in man respond to the poles and quarters of the world, no differently than a piece of a magnet to the quarters of the world—indeed, no differently than the mere contact of a whole magnet, or the smallest portion of a mass of magnet, is not denied to look toward the poles of this world by natural instinct, as is seen in a mariner's instrument <note>a compass</note>. What then, I pray, is more assimilated to the heart than the sun in the east? What is more similar to it in the west than its descent through the aorta into the terrestrial mass of the viscera, in the bottom of which the seminal vessels prepare themselves to bring forth a new birth, no differently than grains of wheat...

Furthermore, just as we observe the Southern wind to be hot and moist, ready to emit such natural breaths, so also we observe the **Liver** to be hot and moist in its nature and in its temperament. It is also ready to participate in the healthy nature of Jupiter (which produces growth for the entire body and, through the natural blood, shining and ruddy clouds) as well as in the morbid and supernatural disposition of Mercury and Mars. For just as there is no quarter in the air of the macrocosm that is more sufficient for intemperance—both watery and fiery—and for contagious seeds, so also no region is found in the microcosm that brings more diseases to the human body than the **Liver**. Indeed, the faults of the stomach, spleen, abdomen, chest, and even the brain—nay, the very wasting of the entire body and supernatural heats—flow from this kind of source. Is it not common for the South wind (or the Meridian) to mix unnatural heat or the fiery spirits of Mars with its moisture? And does the Liver not have the gallbladder (or the bilious Element) as a joined companion, causing inconveniences to the vital and natural spirit? Does the South wind produce supernatural rains by which the fruits and animals of the earth receive harm, and the earth itself is corrupted by floods? So too the Liver produces its own "Dropsies" <note>Edema or fluid retention</note>, and infests the human body with fluxes and catarrhs. Does the South wind breathe out burning and lightning-filled sighs, mixed with rains from its quarter? So the Liver, by its intemperance—a fiery demon secretly mixing itself with the natural spirit—excites malignant and putrid fevers in the body, in which phlegm and choler reign. Yet we do not say that phlegm or choler is the *cause* of those diseases, but rather evil spirits, perverting the natural spirit into a supernatural disposition; by their action, these kinds of humors are accumulated in the human body as being more suited to their own property, and perhaps these wicked spirits are nourished and refreshed by such humors. Finally, the southern wind is accustomed to produce the refreshment of the lower world by its benevolent breath and its timely rains, by which plants are refreshed, herbs grow, and seeds are multiplied by a natural progress. And the liver itself, when well and naturally affected—that is, guided by its natural genius <note>original: "dæmone," here meaning a guiding spirit or functional force</note> and not seduced by an alien spirit opposed to it beyond the laws and limits of nature—is accustomed to perform this same thing: namely, it transforms chyle <note>digested food fluid</note> into good blood, fit and convenient for the nutrition of the whole. This blood is then disseminated by the liver through the entire "human earth" by means of the veins, where, through application, union, and assimilation, it is converted into flesh, and thus the external man is sustained and continued in his being.

Finally, what part in man is more similar to the Northern part of the world than the **Spleen** itself? For just as that Northern region is cold and dry, earthy, constricting, and full of raw things, so also the Spleen is observed to be the earthiest part of the viscera, cold and dry in complexion, the seat of melancholy, and the receptacle of a thick and muddy substance. Furthermore, we see that the North wind (or the polar wind) emits cold and dry blasts, by which the vapors collected from the South are dissipated, and watery substance is reduced into ice, snow, and hail. In plainly the same way, the spleen excites and breathes those vapors or earthy and melancholic breaths which, on account of their dryness, produce hypochondriac winds. By their violence, like northern winds pressing upon the middle region of the air, they distend the diaphragm in a painful manner and disturb the microcosmic heaven, as if earthy "demons" were conspiring against the God of the Heavens and his creatures in the likeness of the Titans. And by such breathings, the thin wateriness of the stomach is frozen and contracted into a viscous and glassy matter. Furthermore, just as the North wind is accustomed to stir up dark and dense clouds in which fiery demons mix themselves and are perceived to excite horrendous thunders, so also sometimes the winds emitted from the Spleen are mixed with a fiery and burning heat. From this follow burning hypochondriac passions with intense central heat, the effects of which are Mania, Lycanthropy <note>The delusion of being a wolf</note>, and fiery and melancholic furies, accompanied by roaring, murmuring, and continuous belching. This was the case with that demoniac whom Christ finally liberated by casting out that raging demon, of whom it is written: *there met him two possessed with devils, coming out of the tombs, exceeding fierce, so that no man might pass by that way.*
<margin>Matthew 8</margin>

From these things it is manifest that in every disease, from whatever element it may be, and consequently from whatever wind, it is excited by the demon or evil spirit of that wind. Whether mixing with the spirit of the blood through food or through breathing (for the soul or life is in the blood, as the sacred scriptures testify), this spirit alienates the blood from its natural obedience and office. It leads it against the motion of its natural Genius, deceives it with its illusions, and bends it toward its own malevolent appetite adverse to life. It sows its contagious seeds in it, from which nothing but supernatural fruit and corrupted effects are harvested, unless its insults are repelled by a stronger spirit, and this natural spirit, thus seduced, is brought back to its pristine temperament by the virtue of a contrary wind. From this, therefore, it is clear how far the common crowd wanders from the truth, who teach that the cause of disease is phlegm, choler, melancholy, or corrupt blood—judging the abundant matter to be the "sinning form." Thus they propose the unknown to us through the even more unknown, as if a small portion of air or water or earth could perpetrate anything good or evil unless it were impelled to this or that by an occult agent lurking within. Thus indeed it is improperly said that "the mud blocked this or that hole" so that no place for breathing is left in the vessel, rather than the *man* himself doing the blocking. Whence, even if that mud is taken away and the path is opened to the hole, it is in the power of the blocker to block it again without impediment. It happens no differently in diseases arising from obstructions and excited by burnt bile, where the "blocker" is an evil spirit, supernaturally preparing the matter of water or phlegm by thickening it, so that it may better block the passages with its viscosity and density, unless the natural spirits are returned to their pristine obedience. # Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book I.

It happens that when that obstructing phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note> is removed by purges or emetic medicines, and the mesenteric passages <note>the channels of the digestive system</note> are opened, the patient immediately seems to feel better for a short while. However, because the primary agent is not ejected, but the poisonous spider (so to speak) remains untouched, the web—which is hostile to the fly, that is, the natural spirit—is woven again by the spider. This means the passages are blocked once more by the malignant demon using phlegmatic filth, whereby the spirit enclosed in the liver and veins is more easily infected by its poisonous breath.

For we see that even when a person remains in a better state of health, the phlegm, as well as the choler <note>yellow bile</note> and melancholy <note>black bile</note>, are subject to the natural spirit or "Genius" <note>a guardian spirit or life-force</note> joined to the person's life from birth. Indeed, the person would remain in that state perpetually, were they not led astray by an alien spirit or demon that is hostile to the Genius of their birth.

The nature and property of this evil demon <note>original: "cacodæmon"</note> is recognized by the fact that it directs the disposition of its actions more toward the element of fire, air, water, or earth; from these, it is also possible to determine the nature of the wind that produced it. For the East emits fiery spirits, the West airy ones, the North earthy ones, and the South watery ones, which the humors—Choler, Blood, Melancholy, and Phlegm—obey.

But if the humor predominating in the disease is observed to participate in a double nature, it must be believed that the spirit causing the affliction comes from some collateral wind, or one positioned between the cardinal points. For example:
* If from burnt phlegm and choler: from the **South-East wind** <note>original: "Euro-austro"</note>.
* If from raw but thick phlegm and burnt choler: from the **East-North-East wind** <note>original: "Vulturnio"</note>, which contains a part of the North wind's blast (which is cold) and another of the East wind (which is hot).
* If raw but not thick phlegm with a little unnatural heat: from the **South-West wind** <note>original: "Affrico"</note>, which participates in the blast of the South and the West <note>original: "Fauonii"</note>.
* Furthermore, if melancholy is joined with phlegm, we attribute it to the **North-West wind** <note>original: "Coro"</note>.

Thus we see that the harming spirit appears to participate in a double nature. Finally, we must observe here that the nature of these malignant spirits is to reduce all the juice of nourishment—both liquid and solid—into humors more suited to their own nature. This can be seen and noticed in putrid fevers, epilepsy, and other such diseases. From this arises the phenomenon where, if a portion of the burdensome or "sinning" matter is removed today by medicines, we will nevertheless find the stomach and hidden passages overflowing with that same humor tomorrow, as if no part of it had been diminished the day before.

But we shall speak of these things more freely and fully in their proper place.

### Anatomy of the blood is proposed.

### CHAPTER I.
#### *Concerning the Anatomy of the world-spirit, and that the mystical nature of the blood—as much the natural and vital as the animal—is drawn forth from the aerial spirit.*

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'O' featuring intricate floral and vine patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

ALTHOUGH it is a well-worn and proven saying, poured forth not without wisdom from the mouth of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurii Trismeg." - A legendary Hellenistic figure often cited in alchemy and hermetic philosophy as the author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note>: namely, that Man is the son of the world, just as the world is the offspring of God; it follows quite logically that man himself is procreated from the spermatic parts of the world, or from its purest elements mixed together. We believe it escapes no one, however foolish, that a son draws his origin from the seed or sperm of the parents. Now, elsewhere it has been said—and by God's will we shall announce it in a broader discourse below—that this sperm (which is the more visible part of the seed) is nothing other than purified venous blood, and that the seed (which is the more invisible part of the sperm, related to the sperm as the soul is to the body) is originally poured forth from the arterial blood. And since the simplest humor, blood, is nothing other than the element of air in the greater world <note>The Macrocosm</note> transmuted into animal blood through various "concoctions" <note>A term in pre-modern medicine referring to the "cooking" or refining of substances by the body's heat.</note>, we believe it will be worth the effort to speak on the secret disposition of the world's air, and to establish a verbal Anatomy of its secrets part by part. In this way, by knowing the principle, we may arrive at a better understanding of that which originates from it. Concerning the air and the origin of the other elements, and how they were produced in their being by means of the Divine Word, I judge that enough and more has been explained in our history of the macrocosm; likewise, we have made quite a copious mention of the difference between sperm and seed, their origin, and their action in generation, in our treatise on the microcosm <note>The human being viewed as a miniature map of the universe.</note>. However, I will add something in this place pertaining to our current purpose, and especially necessary, so that the origin of the blood, its secret nature, and the admirable mysteries contained within it may be better drawn out.

We say, therefore, that there is a very strict relationship between the air of the macrocosm and the venous or "natural" blood, since both are elements contained within the sublunary region <note>The realm below the moon, subject to change and decay.</note> of each, and insofar as the blood is produced from the air no differently than a son from a father, as we shall declare below. We say also that the same regard exists between the arterial or "vital" blood, inasmuch as both belong to the middle or celestial region of each world, and also insofar as the father of that blood is the ethereal spirit, just as the father of the lower blood was the aerial spirit. The certainty of this our opinion is confirmed both by our doctrine on the Element of air and by the "fifth essence" <note>The quintessence; the purest, most spiritualized form of a substance.</note> in bread or wheat, as is clear from those things which we have sufficiently explained in the third book, *On the Anatomy of the Nourishment of Bread*. And certainly, if you investigate the matter a little more accurately, you will find that the air itself, or the sublunary heaven, differs from the ether or the sublunary heaven in nothing at all except in thickness or thinness, or in mixture and purity; for the universal world-spirit is the same in essence, but truly divided in itself as far as we are concerned, or in what we perceive, because it is observed to be thicker in one place and thinner and purer in another. This is indeed said to proceed from the fact—and has been confirmed by us elsewhere—that the presence (of which...

# Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book II.

The right is to give form to the waters or the worldly spirits <note>original: *spiritus mundanos*</note>) is found more in one place than in another. Now, the powers of light are three: namely, the first resides in its center, and this force is that original power by whose effect light first shone out of the darkness. This power is, therefore, that spirit which was carried over the waters, imparting to them a certain fiery force—indeed, even the anatomy by which like is procreated by like. In the center of light, therefore, is that divine spirit, **Elohim**, winged above the waters, acting upon all things, or that wondrous **Word** creating all things, according to the words of St. Peter:
<margin>2 Peter 3:5</margin>
> *That the heavens were of old, and the earth consisting of water and through water by the word of God; and in verse 7: But the heavens and the earth which are now, by the same word are kept in store.*

Its secondary power is motion. For light is more mobile than any other thing and swifter in its motion, inasmuch as in its center the Holy Spirit of Wisdom, or the Word, reigns forever and ever. According to this:
<margin>Wisdom 7:24</margin>
Wisdom chapter 7:24: *Wisdom is more mobile than all mobile things, for she reaches everywhere because of her purity.* And this point is urgent against the opinion of those who have posited either that the sun is immobile or that the substance of the Empyrean heaven is fixed. The third power is the effect of the light-bearing motion itself, which is heat. Its property is to divide and distinguish the waters—which are dispersed everywhere through the vast cavity of the world—into portions equal in thinness and thickness. Thus, from the beginning, the distinct elements of the world were procreated; thus the various and differing dispositions of the heavens or the spheres of the celestial world are ordered. For the universal light of the world itself, which is the purest essence, does not differ from the presence of the Creator, insofar as it is a most pure emanation from the divine majesty, present everywhere and always, according to the words of the wise man:
<margin>Wisdom 7:25</margin>
*Wisdom is a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; she has every sincere power, overseeing all things, and reaching everywhere by reason of her power.* This emanation of God into the spirit of the world is called **Light**, which is nothing other than a primordial mixture of the God-like **Form** and the informed **Matter** of the waters, in which both divine and uncreated nature, as well as natural and created nature, concur. But truly, because this kind of action abounds more in some places than in others, a lesser effect of the same is observed in one place than in another—more sparingly, I say, in the sublunary heaven of the world than in the other two more eminent ones. Whence, on account of the poverty of light and its effect, the elementary things of this world are more subject to changes. Hence, in my *Worldly Harmony* <note>A reference to Fludd's earlier work on the musical proportions of the universe.</note>, I compared this region of the world to the **Diatessaron** <term>a musical fourth</term> consonance, which is an imperfect consonance. By a clearly similar reasoning, the ethereal or middle heaven is coarser than the Empyrean, inasmuch as it enjoys the benefit of light less than the Empyrean; for its substance has as much of the matter of the waters as it seems to claim of light for itself, since it is fashioned from an equal part of the aquatic nature of the sublunary heaven and the fiery substance of the super-celestial. But this region, in respect to the lowest, is called perfect, and for this reason we have referred it to the **Diapente** <term>a musical fifth</term> consonance, which is a less perfect consonance in respect to the **Diapason** <term>an octave</term>, which is related to the Empyrean heaven in respect to its perfection. This, therefore, is the reason why the lowest part of the world, nearest to the terrestrial center, is observed to be denser and thicker than the middle; and again, the order and disposition of natural things (which are accustomed to be weighed in the just scales of nature) proves that the middle differs from the highest by the same proportion.

These things being known, it must be observed, and that diligently, that **Air** is a spirit of the same nature as the **Ether**, and the ether again in its substance and essence is one with the **Empyrean** or fiery spirit. I say they do not differ in substance, but they appear to differ in their luminous form. Whence the lowest matter of the spirit is denser than its superior, darker, and more subject to cold; because the further light is distant, the less its effects abound—and its effects are motion and heat. Truly, inferior things move more slowly than superior things because they appear thicker, and they exist thicker because they possess a smaller quantity of heat, whose nature is to thin the thick and to lead the impure back to perfect purity. Therefore, Air (which does not differ from the ether or Empyrean spirit except in that it does not abound so much in gold or divine splendor) provides the same thing to the earth that the ether provides to the stars (both wandering and fixed) and the Empyrean or intellectual Spirit provides to angels and souls. Therefore, the life-giving soul of the Air is a **sesquitertia** <note>A ratio of 4:3, corresponding to the musical fourth.</note> portion of divine light, which is observed to lead primarily to vegetation by its original nature. But the portions of ether flowing into it and swimming in it as if in a denser vehicle, are accustomed to minister life to creatures; not otherwise than angels and souls, exulting in the empyrean spirit and descending downward by the divine will, made the ethereal spirit their nearest vehicle—just as the ethereal spirit, full of the influence of both the angelic and the starry heaven, made the air its receptacle.

When these things have been weighed with due contemplation, we shall see that the air not only abounds with the intellectual spirits of the first heaven (namely angels and souls surrounding the center of the spirit of any divine word as their seat and living in a portion of the empyrean heaven), but also that the ethereal portion is burdened with the influences of the stars and the demons of fate; and finally, that the air itself and the sublunary parts swell with the inferior demons, or the companions of **Lucifer**, frequenting them by the will of God. In this way, I say, we see that the air is a receptacle, first of all, of the divine spirit contracting itself in the center of nature, which is the uncreated principle—that is, the means by which the Elements were first informed and are continued in their being to this day. Without its presence, all things would be reduced from act to potency, from light to darkness, from existing things to nothingness and deformity, according to the words of the Prophet:
<margin>Psalm 104:29</margin>
> *When God hides his face, the creatures are troubled; when he takes away their spirit, they expire; when he sends forth his spirit, they are recreated.*

Then it receives the intelligences of the Empyrean heaven, with a portion of the spirit of that heaven, by means of which God, moving from the center, is the cause that those intelligences impart intellect and reason to men. Then afterwards, it is capable of the celestial influences swimming in the portion of the ethereal spirit and of the life of spirits; and then afterwards, it receives its own proper soul from all these, by means of the Word reigning in the midst of the air, in its circular sphere—

From a small portion of the intellectual spirit, therefore, reason is established in the highest region of man himself; from that portion of the ether proceeds the virtue of his life situated in the Thorax; and finally, from that sublunary spirit, the natural faculty of the vegetative soul has its beginning. ### Chapter II.

#### Whether it is likely that the substance of thick air is flowed into the venous blood, the substance of ether with air into the arterial blood, and that of the intellectual spirit with a portion of ether into the [animal] spirits, and how this may be performed.

<margin>Exodus 7. Psalm 104:29.</margin>
That the transmutation of air (through condensation) into blood is possible in the nature of things is evident from the fact that we have accounts from trustworthy authors of blood being poured down from the middle region of the air in the manner of rain, and of waters being transformed into blood; this same thing is also witnessed in the Holy Scriptures, from which it is clear that it is within the power of nature to bring this very thing to its peak and conclusion. But what is more evident in this matter than our daily experience, by which we are taught that the very effect of the first digestion—namely the <term>chyle</term> <note>The milky fluid produced in the intestines during digestion</note>—is changed into blood by the mystical and hidden property of the Liver. Furthermore, by that same observation, we observe that the air drawn into the left chamber of the heart leaves there the specific nature of the ethereal heaven and the most subtle portion of the aerial spirit, which the heart endeavors to attract to itself with its organs, and it expels the useless and watery smoke of the air as a superfluity through expiration. This ethereal nature (I say), which is so necessary for the life of the creature, the heart desires and entices to itself every moment, without which neither man nor any other animal can endure for a moment of time. And Zeno did not hesitate to call that ethereal substance or food of life "natural fire," for which he made the heart the receptacle; for this reason, Prometheus called it the vessel of celestial fire, which fire he is imagined to have stolen from the heavens so that he might enrich man with long-lasting life. For this matter is the food of the vital soul, and since the heart is its common receptacle, it is therefore called by Plato the seat of the soul. This, I say, is that nature which is the invisible fire, present everywhere in the world, from which Zoroaster taught that all things were begotten, with whom Heraclitus of Ephesus seems to agree. And since by the virtue of this fiery <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth element," a pure, celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements</note> Democritus, Orpheus, and many of the Pythagoreans observed a certain soul to preside over every creature, they therefore confidently affirmed that all things are full of Gods, to whom they established divine honors and dedicated prayers and sacrifices. But truly, considering the matter again and again among themselves, they reduced all these souls to the single soul of the world, or referred those Gods back to the one Jupiter. By Jupiter, therefore, they seem to imply the Word or the emanation of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note>, which is the fountain of man; and by the Gods or souls, they understood divine rays, expanded everywhere into the worldly spirit, offering life to every creature, which are no differently separated from the uncreated Word than the rays of the sun are from the sun: but we shall deal with these things more extensively in the treatise on the heart. Finally, that the intellectual spirit indeed dwells in the center of that celestial fire, and how that happens, has been said in the preceding pages, so that this spirit, carrying itself upward through the trunk of the Aorta and leaping out through the narrow orifices of the <term>choroid plexuses</term> <note>A network of blood vessels in the brain that produces cerebrospinal fluid</note>, mixes itself with the sensitive spirits made from the venous blood; and from this it happens that the rational soul, by the mediation of the internal senses, operates with the intellect in the human race. But let us return to the reasoning by which air is reduced into natural, vital, and animal blood, and see how nature can perform this transmutatory work: First, therefore, we wish it to be observed that just as there are two parts of the human composition, namely body and spirit, so also there is a twofold method of nourishing each of them. For since like is usually nourished by its like, it must be considered necessary that the invisible man be nourished immediately by the spirit of the thinner blood—namely the arterial (which is the vehicle of the vital spirits)—just as that spirit is refreshed and multiplied by the ethereal spirit of the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The "great world" or universe, as opposed to the "microcosm" of man</note> through the successive motion of expiration and inspiration. But it is certain that the external and visible man (being composed of thickened elements) is preserved and continued in his being by the successive administration and application of such things, in a remote manner, and immediately from the venous and thick blood [derived] from the juice of nutrients. Now, nutrients exist in various kinds according to the diversity of the kingdoms of composite things (which are mineral, vegetable, and animal), and from these kingdoms, the vegetable and animal contribute chiefly to human nourishment, and not the mineral (as its parts are so compact and difficult to digest that they hardly obey the violence of fire, much less human heat). Of the preceding two, the flesh of animals is more familiar to human action and digestion and easier to digest, since it most easily [returns] into that which it was before, into chyle

# Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book II.

...namely, it is resolved. Bread is the prince of vegetables, both because it is reduced into a chylous pulp <note>A milky fluid of digested food</note> quickly and without any labor of nature, and also because it is exceedingly rich in an airy nature and most full of natural vegetation. It was presented by God to our ancient parents as the primary and royal nourishment, whence God said: <margin>Genesis 3:19</margin> *In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.* Therefore, whether the matter of nourishment be animal or vegetable, it is reduced into chyle by the chemistry of nature—as if in Nature’s own bath. Once the subtle part of all the elements is separated from the gross dregs through the filtration of the mesenteric veins, it is cooked in the concave region of the Liver. In this digestion, the less thin earth, or melancholy <note>Black bile, associated with the element of earth</note>, which is least fit for nutrition, is divided from the airy mass by a second separation and transferred through the splenic branch into the spleen. The superfluous fiery matter, useless for nourishing, is poured into the gallbladder. The phlegm, or element of water (compared to marine humor), is sent downward through the kidneys into the sea of the bladder. 

The element or airy humor is contained in the vessels or the trunk of the *Vena Cava* and *Porta* <note>The main veins of the torso</note>. However, we do not say this is absolutely airy, since it still possesses within itself the subtle part of every element—namely fire, water, and earth. (In the composition of the body, these elements belong to their own members: the office of the more earthy part is to look after the bones, cartilages, membranes, and ligaments; the aquatic part procreates fat; while fire and air are occupied with the generation of flesh.) But it is referred to as "air" because air has the predominance in its mass. 

And here, in passing, a question may arise that is not easily discussed, in the resolution of which even many of the most learned have hesitated: namely, from where does that blood-making virtue arise, by which the somewhat pale chyle, <margin>Whence the red tincture of the blood.</margin> or that verging on whiteness, is so promptly reduced into a red tincture <note>Color or essence</note>? Some wish this multiplying power of staining to proceed from the nature of the Liver (inasmuch as its substance is intensely red), as if the redness of the liver were so infinite that it could stain an infinite proportion of airy chyle without any decrease of its own redness. Furthermore, if this were granted, it would not be considered absurd if we consequently inquired: from where did the liver receive this red tincture adorned with such multiplying virtue? Since it is certain and proven that even the substance of the liver took its origin from the blood. Whence it is clear that the thing created cannot have that innate quality which its principle <note>Its source or origin</note> is said to lack; yet blood is not observed to be so abundant in multiplication within itself that it could attribute an infinite tincture to its like. Others say this property of nature is "occult" <note>Hidden or secret</note>, by which response we gather the unknown through the more unknown, and thus remain utterly ignorant of the essence of the matter. 

To this question, we, taught by better experience, respond: that this faculty of staining consists neither in the liver nor in any part of the human body, but hides itself in the center or "occult" of the air, introduced into the body either through inspiration <note>Breathing</note> or by means of the juice of nourishment. For in Book 2 of the *Anatomy of Bread*, the reason for the vegetation and multiplication of the Plant is most clearly explained: namely, because its airy part—which seems to be nothing other than a certain volatile salt—is manifestly white and clear in its liquid substance, even though in its "occult" it is strongly stained with redness. Indeed, by a certain magnetic virtue born within it centrally, this substance is ready to attract to itself the solar form hiding invisibly everywhere in the vast spirit of the world, and to gather it into itself, as if it were a certain female matter in nature which greedily desires the form of light and rapidly entices it to itself. 

An experiment of this matter was demonstrated in the place cited above, where we declared that the clear and airy matter of wheat or bread itself, exposed to the sun in its white nature, was converted in the space of a few hours into a sufficiently intense redness. Whence I gathered that the property of multiplication and vegetation, both in the vegetable and the animal, flows from this kind of airy substance—not, I say, from its own virtue (as it is not infinite or more-than-perfect), but from its internal magnetic disposition. By this, it successively and gradually contracts to itself the formal rays from the Soul of the World <note>Latin: *Anima Mundi*</note> present everywhere, and the radical moisture from its like expanded everywhere in the world. 

In no other way do we say that this air, formerly hiding in the chyle but now stripped of heterogeneous nature and purged in the liver, does not cease to attract to itself the rays of the microcosmic sun or the life-giving soul of the microcosm <note>The human body as a "little world" reflecting the universe</note>. It could not have performed this in its chylous nature, insofar as its magnetic force, partly submerged in the aquatic or phlegmatic nature and partly hindered by gross and earthy dregs, could not prevail. But truly, partly by the virtue of the mesenterics and partly by the virtue of the liver, having cast off these impediments of foreign elements, it enters vividly upon that work of transmutation and is observed to bring it to a happy conclusion. 

And certainly, examining this matter a little more accurately with the "glowing knife of fire," I perceived that this matter, by slow heat—indeed, by the dew of the bath itself—was sublimated into the head of the alembic <note>A distilling apparatus</note> in the form of the whitest snow or hail. When a glowing coal was applied to it, I saw the matter suddenly melted like honey or butter and changed into a golden or hyacinth color, denoting to us that although the manifest and external part of this airy substance is white, its occult and internal part is marked with the tincture of blood.

As for the arterial blood, the reason for its tincture is the same as that of the gross and venous blood, except that the airy substance of that blood is far thinner and more subtle than the venous or natural blood. Thus, there is as much difference between the substance of one and the other as there is between the lowest and highest regions of the air. For as the lowest region of the air participates more in earth and water, and consequently is more thick and less hot than the highest (which participates in ethereal fire), so also the blood of the lowest region of the body is denser and colder than that of the vital region, which is exceedingly thin and abounds in heat. And this is indeed confirmed by many reasons, the first of which is because the origin...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Blood.

It has its origin from the heart, which according to the witness of Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism, who taught that the soul is a "fiery breath."</note> is the *receptacle of natural fire*, or as Prometheus would have it, the *vessel of celestial fire*. Second, because that heat is more effective and natural in its operation, which is naturally present in the more subtle and pure spirit; for celestial heat is far stronger and more powerful in its action than any elemental heat, since the former is the fountain and origin of the latter. Third, because the heart is recognized by the most excellent of philosophers to be the origin of the blood, inasmuch as the beginning of life is drawn from it. Therefore, the substance of arterial or vital blood is thinner and more spiritual than that of the venous or natural blood, and it stands in relation to it as the visible and purest spirit of wine <note>original: "spiritus vini"; an early term for concentrated alcohol or ethanol.</note> relates to the water of life <note>original: "aquam vitæ"; here referring to a less refined aqueous solution.</note>, in which the other elements are mixed with the true spirit. Just as animal blood relates to vital blood, so the spirit of wine, on account of its purity, vanishes into the air and renders itself invisible; for it is fitting for invisible spirits to be nourished by things like themselves. We say, therefore, that the most subtle air is the vehicle of the invisible substance of the ether, which, containing the food of life, is introduced with its contents into the left chamber of the heart. From there, once the thicker substance of the air (participating in exotic and foreign elements) has been expelled by the action of the heart and the internal attraction of the air's own purity (which arises from celestial virtue), it partly reveals its own internal tincture, and partly collects and contracts the rays of the internal microcosm <note>The "microcosm" refers to the human body as a miniature reflection of the universe (the macrocosm).</note> for its spirit, and thus drinks in a full portion of the blood-red tincture. However, in what manner, or by what art or industry, nature is accustomed to perfect her dissolutions, her separations of the pure from the impure, from form to form, from color to color, and the transmutations from a liquid and thick substance into one more liquid and thin, within this human house, or temple, or rather Laboratory and workshop, you shall have demonstrated in the following chapter.

### CHAPTER III.

->*Concerning the wonderful nature of Alchemy in the human body, the arrangement of its laboratory, the vessels differing from one another, and finally concerning the remarkable method of its working, purifying, refining, and moving toward perfection in this its laboratory.*<-

How empty in mind and void of reason are those men—and with what indignity should they be rejected by Nature herself—who deride, despise, and hold in hatred the chemical art, whether applied to medicine or to the transmutation of one metal into another! The industry of Nature herself, wise and most skilled in her actions, her constant practice in purifying and her virtue occupied night and day in the preservation of the human body, seems to testify and declare this clearly. For what invention (I ask you) is there in the common art of chemistry for distilling, or preparing, or separating the subtle from the gross and thick by any method—whether it be in the skill of circulating and digesting, or the artifice of distilling by descent, ascent, filtration, to the side, or through a sieve—which Nature has not already tasted? And this she did before any science reigned among men, before Adam or any of his successors devised any art. If, therefore, we wish to explore the matter a little more accurately, we shall perceive with open eyes that man himself has stolen the entire science of Alchemy from Nature herself, whose laboratory or distillery is the human body. The vessels contained within it and required for such an operation are the organic members contained there, among which four are more eminent, which we call the "principals": namely, the liver, the seminal vessels, the Heart, and the Brain. The Alchemist, therefore, is adorned and equipped in his laboratory with Alembics, Retorts, Receivers, Baths of Mary <note>original: "balneis Mariæ"; a water bath used for gentle heating, named after Mary the Jewess.</note>, wind furnaces, reverberatory furnaces, baths of Sand, of Ashes, of Antenor, and others of this kind; he has them ready in every business, so that he might better lead the matter to be distilled, little by little and step by step, toward exact purification—that is, from a bodily nature toward a spiritual one. Does not Nature seem to provide this same thing in her operations, by which she is constantly observed to hasten toward the limit of perfection? Let us proceed, therefore, in the exploration of the mysteries of nature’s laboratory, and see if the Alchemist, however skilled and distinguished in his art, can do anything that Nature does not seem to know, or for which she has not first provided him the models of her own craftsmanship.

The Alchemist, therefore, wishing to bring a thing or matter to the perfect goal of subtlety and thinness, first desires to handle it with his hands into smaller parts, whether by pulverizing, or by dividing it into small portions by cutting, or by grinding it into filings; and then afterward, such a preparation having been made, he is accustomed (in imitation of nature) to commit it to a certain suitable menstruum <note>A solvent, often used in alchemy to dissolve solids.</note>, by the virtue of which he makes the first entry or penetration into the body to be dissolved. And so that this work may be performed better, more effectively, and more quickly, he attempts to place that circulatory vessel with its solvent and the subject to be dissolved into a Bath of Mary, or a "horse's belly" (which he also calls the heat of horse dung). Has not the Alchemist, in the beginning of this operation, imitated nature? For she first approaches the preparation of coarse food by the grinding of the teeth, and then thrusts it, thus broken and ground, downward through the long neck of her circulatory vessel (namely, the Esophagus).

...into the stomach, just as a skilled chemist, following nature’s example, introduces his material into the belly of a long-necked <term>matrass</term><note>A long-necked glass flask used for distillation or digestion.</note> through its neck (after first breaking and grinding it) to be refined. Then, nature’s intention—for the better completion of its first operation—is to visit and penetrate the center of the prepared material and make the body porous, so that the subtler spirits trapped within may flow out more easily. To achieve this, it is necessary that a certain liquid be mixed with it, whereby nature becomes moist and makes the eater crave drink, so that a better entry into the dry subject is made, the dry melts in the moist, and thus the first stage of dissolution is perfected. And so that this operation may be done more expeditiously, nature seems to close this first circulatory vessel both above and below, lest the spirits exhaling from the center of the matter break out of their vessel and fly away in vain. Thus, the stomach is said to be closed during the time of the first <term>concoction</term><note>The "cooking" or digestion of food by internal heat.</note>; then, with the fire of the liver and the viscera surrounding it on all sides with moist heat, it intends to circulate it in its own time, namely until the whole matter with its liquid is reduced to a pulp or <term>chyle</term><note>The milky fluid into which food is converted by digestion.</note>. In exactly the same way, the Alchemist, always imitating nature in his operations, firmly plugs his matrass—or his "brachial pipes," or his <term>pelican</term><note>A circulatory distillation vessel with two side-arms that return condensed liquid to the body.</note>—during the time of digestion and circulation of the matter, lest the spirits evaporate and vanish; he delights in adapting it to horse dung or a <term>bain-marie</term><note>A water bath used for gentle heating.</note> (that is, a hot and moist fire), so that by this operation his first intention of dissolution is fulfilled. And thus the coarse medicine, now subject to putrefaction and dissolution, is ready to receive a new form; or the "lead of the philosophers," casting off its filth—by which I mean the pale chyle turning away from useless dregs as if from its own leprosy—is now in a way disposed toward a true transmutation into gold.

Therefore, we must inquire further into the laboratory of both the Alchemist and Nature, and hasten to the second stage of the operation. We see, then, that nature itself—once the time of circulation or concoction is complete and the lower orifice of the stomach is now dilated and opened—pours all that dissolved matter (the useful with the useless, the chyle mixed with the dregs) by a second kind of distillation (which is usually done by descent) into the receiving vessels, namely the slender intestines: the Duodenum, Jejunum, and Ileum. There, she busies herself with distinguishing the coarse from the subtle, the useful from the useless, the necessary from the superfluous, and the pure from the impure. In this operation, the Alchemist, following nature’s pattern, either pours off the dissolved matter by tilting the vessel (shaking the pure with the impure) or, by skillfully opening an orifice made in the bottom of the matrass, allows the digested matter to flow into another vessel placed beneath it, by which means the subtle is distinguished from the thick, and the pure from the impure. Here, then, we arrive at the third type of distilling, namely that which is called "by filter." For the artist of Chemistry perceives that nature herself, by the power of the <term>mesenteric veins</term><note>Veins that drain blood from the intestines.</note> with which the thin intestines are most copiously filled, attracts and raises the thinner portion of the first concoction (that is, the matter circulated in the stomach) upward toward the region of the Liver. By this path, she separates the subtle from the thick—that is, the pure, whitening chyle from its coarse dregs—and the more earthy part or dregs remaining in the bottom of these intestines are cast out into another more ignoble vessel, namely the colon. In the colon, they are reserved so that by the heat of the place, spirits that are still more fixed and participating in the dregs might be drawn out and raised on high through certain filaments of that same "filter" to the region of the Liver. Here, I say, the Alchemist—that "ape of nature"—endeavors to undertake this same thing in his artificial operations. In place of the mesenteric veins inserted everywhere into the intestinal vessels, he chooses either a cloth made of wool or cotton, or instead of that, a piece of thick and porous paper, and divides and cuts it into various sections in a manner well known to chemists. Each of these is intended to correspond to a mesenteric vein. He then immerses this cloth, thus divided into small portions, into the receptacle of that matter circulated in the Bath, so that in the manner of the mesenterics, it might separate the subtle from the thick and raise it on high to another clean vessel, so that in it, it may be led to the third scale of perfection. And this mode of distilling is called "filtration" by the Alchemists.

But now at last we come to that organ in nature’s laboratory, or the furnace of digestion, in which she works upon the pure matter prepared in the first digestion, now rectified and accustomed by further distillation. In an operation of this kind, the pale and weak chylous nourishment is transmuted by a miraculous power into red blood. The "animal lead," I say, somewhat pale and now cleansed of its leprosy, is now transmuted into true gold, or a golden nature and disposition. Here, therefore, we have the first order of circulation and cooking in <insert>Antenor</insert><note>Likely a reference to a specific alchemical vessel or stage named after the Trojan hero, or a typographical error for a chemical term.</note> in which coarse gold is melted down through the first degree of Alchemy. How coarse, then, are those men, and how submerged in ignorance, or how overwhelmed and rebellious in their vain opinions, who believe that a transmutation from one species to another cannot be made? And yet, in this place, one may behold the whitening chyle itself being converted into the reddest blood by the industry of nature. Nor certainly (if we look at the matter with just eyes) shall we perceive that raw lead and imperfect metal differ more in substance and nature from gold than do chyle and blood. For as the beginning or principle of blood was nothing but chylous water—that is, an aqueous humor, imperfect and raw in its chylous nature—so indeed it is reduced to mature perfection in its bloody form. So also gold in the beginning was Mercury, or a coarse, immature, and raw water, whose first degree toward concoction is lead itself, but the last, and the goal of its perfection, is gold. Is this to be believed impossible, when we see even greater miracles in nature? Namely, we may observe vegetable nature itself converted into animal nature, as in the flesh and blood of creatures, in which herbs, grasses, and nutritious fruits are transformed into substance. And yet, that these effects of nature happen daily is evident even to the senses of fools...

it is clearly declared and demonstrated; moreover, that the substance of an irrational animal migrates into that of a rational one, and vice versa, I know to be a fact hidden from no one and doubted by none, since it is a thing known to all and proven by experience. From this, therefore, the foundations of most excellent contemplations can be drawn, and very difficult questions and doubts produced: namely, whether the substance of a beast (and indeed even that of plants) can be converted into human body and substance? Whether there shall be a future resurrection of the beastly or vegetable body on the last day? Since by the operation of nature they now become the same—namely, the same flesh and bones—as the human body, for which there will certainly be a resurrection from death to eternal life. If that follows, it is asked: is it within the power of nature to so prepare irrational animals, and indeed even plants themselves, so that through their conversion into the human body they might be able to live forever through the resurrection? 

This is against the opinion of those who, with a hard mouth and full of lies, exclude God from the works of nature, and say that operations of this kind exist outside the power of nature; as if God worked outside of nature in this world, when He is essentially here and everywhere; as if (I say) the internal soul of passive nature, dwelling in its most exact center, could be distinguished from the substance of God himself. Therefore, let those scoundrels be relegated to eternal exile, who with unheard-of audacity do not hesitate to pronounce that Physicians are for the most part Atheists, as those who contemplate nature so deeply that they are accustomed to utterly reject God himself and His worship, nor wish to acknowledge any God besides nature. 

To whom I indeed do not doubt to respond with a serene brow and full of confidence, that he is rather the Atheist—indeed, he should be held as an irrational brute—who seeks and endeavors to find God outside of nature, and who is ignorant that God is found and exists within the hiding places of nature. For insofar as He is outside of all things, which of mortals can find Him, or comprehend Him with the thinnest eyes of the intellect? Hence it is said that *Moses saw the back parts of God, and not the front* <note>Exodus 33:23</note>, that is, not God in His essence, but clothed in the garments of nature, that is, in His creatures, in whose center He is said to be moved by the spirit. For *in the word (according to that of Saint John) was life*, and the Psalm says, *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the spirit from his mouth*. From which it is clear that the power of any creature (which consists in the power of the soul) proceeds immediately from the spirit. 

Furthermore, it is said that *God is clothed with light*, which light is indeed the thinnest of His natural garments; then *God placed his tabernacle in the sun*. Afterward He is adorned with a still thicker and denser garment, whence it is said, *A thick cloud is his pavilion*, and elsewhere, *You are the temple of the Holy Spirit*, and elsewhere, *The earth shall bring forth the Savior*. From which it is clear that God is in passive nature like an agent in a patient, or a soul in a body, or rather, the Divine Mind in the soul itself, for the mind is the center of the soul. And this agrees with that definition of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Merc. Trismegist."</note>: *God is a circle, whose center is everywhere, but whose circumference is nowhere.* 

We conclude, therefore, this collateral discourse of ours against such adversaries and despisers of nature, by affirming that Nature itself is God—I do not say the passive and numbered or created nature, or the universal waters, but the active numbering or creating nature, or the virtual active nature, informing the shapeless universal waters, and emanating immediately from the Throne and being of creation. Therefore, let the fools be silent if they cannot comprehend these things, since they are agreeable not only to the opinion of divine philosophers, but also of the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles, among whom Saint Peter fell into this kind of opinion, namely, that *the heaven and the earth were established through the waters, and in the waters by means of the word*. 

Let such men know, then—and let this not be said by us unadvisedly—that whoever cannot look into the mysteries of nature with "Lynx-like" eyes <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for keen, piercing sight</note>, and knows not how to penetrate into its deep storehouse of perfumes <term>myrothecium: a cabinet for ointments or medicines, here used metaphorically for nature's secrets</term>, it is certain that they wander as far from the knowledge of God and true Theology as darkness from the height of light, the Devil from God, or truth from falsehood. And these are the kind who occupy themselves in the letter, or the exterior bark, or the surface, which are said to kill; they reject the living spirit and the creating light dwelling in the center, where life is present, so that they tread the broad road leading to perdition, while few acknowledge and enter the path of God and nature. But concerning these things it has been disputed more widely elsewhere; wherefore I shall turn the thread of my discourse back to our purpose, and I will now say what further is done in the laboratory of nature.

The furnace (I say) of Antenor <note>A chemical/alchemical term for a specific type of furnace or heat</note> or the secret furnace of the first grade or operation, in this laboratory of nature, is the **Liver**, whose task it is to smelt the animal gold of the first order, namely the thicker and elementary blood, as that in which the four elements are still mixed together in a confused manner—I mean the four humors corresponding to the four elements. For although this secret furnace, by means of its airy heat, strives as much as it can toward the separation of superfluous elements (which it indeed attacks by a triple purification: namely, partly through a distillation of the fifth kind which is called "to the side," by which action it divides the earthy or melancholic dregs from the blood mass, and pours and instills them laterally through the splenic branch into the spleen; partly through a light descent, by which way the yellow bile or fiery superfluity is sent into the gallbladder; and partly through a deeper descent, by which distillation the matter of salty phlegm <note>original: "pituitæ"</note> is sent into the sea of the bladder through the kidneys and ureters), nevertheless it cannot so purify its golden and ruddy matter but that it is still somewhat contaminated by some useless dregs of the elements, so that this mass is most rightly likened to the air of the sublunary world, which on account of its impurity seems to claim for itself the title of imperfection. Whence it happens that as elementary air is subject to changes, so also this blood mass, and the solid and fleshy parts which arise from it and are nourished by it, are subject to diseases and changes. Therefore, the property of this secret vessel corresponds to the nature of the sublunary world, as it is ordained for nourishing and sustaining the elementary parts of the body; wherefore this animal gold, although it be coarse and of the first order, nevertheless seems to suffice for cherishing the unworthier and coarser parts of the body. Here, therefore, we have the principal actor of the sublunary or Elementary world, whose

# Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book II.

The passive, still imperfect substance—if it is treated again in a more noble **Antenor** <note>A technical term used here for a chemical furnace or digesting vessel, named after the Trojan hero; here it represents an organ of the body.</note>, and is digested by its heat which is of the second degree—is accustomed to consist of a Blood or "gold" inclined toward a heavenly disposition, and far purer and more subtle than the first. This is destined by nature for the restoration of the lighter and more worthy members with nourishment. Nature, therefore, takes a portion of that blood perfected by heat in the first Antenor (namely, the Liver), and through ascent (which is the sixth species of distillation) sublimates it from the bottom of the **cucurbit** <note>A gourd-shaped chemical vessel; here the cavity of the liver</note> (that is, the cavity of the liver) through its narrow neck (which is the **vena cava**) to the right chamber of the heart, as if into an **alembic** or "head." Once its joints and openings are well sealed, this bloody matter is reduced by circulation into a substance far purer than the before.

But this secret furnace of nature is an Antenor of the second order, whose heat is very temperate and is likened to the celestial sun. Moreover, the arrangement of this furnace is wonderful, since in it not only elementary gold but even that celestial gold is digested. For since this vessel is double and its cavity binary, the right side is adapted for the elementary blood sublimated from the Liver through the vena cava; this circulates and is digested therein until it is reduced to the nature of the highest region of the air, so that it is now made into food ready to nourish the light substance of the lungs.

The left side, however, is in its nature so subtle and of such mystical property, that it is accustomed not only to constantly steal away celestial fire like **Prometheus** himself, but even further—once digestion is performed and the pure separated from the impure—it dispenses this fire of life through the universal body by means of the arteries. It is seen to impart innate heat to every member of the body; for the office of this smooth, double-ventricled furnace is to attract to itself the hidden rays of the sun and heaven, or the invisible fire of **Zoroaster and Heraclitus** <note>Ancient philosophers associated with the primacy of fire as a cosmic element</note>, to prepare what is attracted by the separation of pure from impure and useful from useless, and finally to administer the separated part to the whole body; for fire of this kind is the food of the **radical moisture** <note>The essential life-fluid or "fuel" of the body in medieval medicine</note>.

In this fire, therefore, gold—both elementary and corporeal (or earthly and passive) as well as that celestial, subtle, ignited, and active gold—is purified. The former is effective for the nourishment and preservation of the body, while the latter is ordained for the rectification and continuation of the spirit, both **animal** <note>From 'anima' (soul/breath); the spirit responsible for sensation and movement</note> and **vital**. Therefore, this heat of the Antenor or secret furnace is the second degree in the purification of the blood (or Elementary gold), but it is truly the first in the digestion and preparation of the celestial blood or gold.

From this, therefore, we see as if wine were first circulated in the stomach, then its tartaric dregs are separated through the **meseraic veins** <note>Mesenteric veins</note> as if by a filter from the pure or more liquid part; then afterwards the **aqua vitae** <note>Water of life; concentrated spirit</note> with the other Elements is elicited in the liver or another vessel. Then it becomes a pure but visible spirit of wine, and finally the last degree of subtilization occurs in the ventricles of the brain, where those spirits are so exactly subtilized and rectified that they invisibly pass into a spiritual smoke, which on account of its purity is made fit to receive the impressions of reason itself, and indeed of the intellect.

We shall proceed, therefore, to the final degree of the digestion of blood, which occurs in the **animal Antenor** (that is, the brain), just as the middle degree was completed in that **vital** one (namely, the heart). This degree of animal fire in the brain—which we have compared to the super-celestial fire, just as we compared the middle or vital fire in the heart to the celestial fire, and the first or natural degree in the liver to the elementary fire—is perfected in a vessel adorned with a triple ventricle. In the first two of these, certain organs woven from little veins and arteries in a **Daedalian** or Labyrinthine fashion, called the **choroid plexus**, convert the humor in the veins into a smoke or most subtle air by secret digestion. This is the subject of the **phantasy** <note>The faculty of imagination or mental imaging</note>, into which the impressions of the rational soul are inserted. It changes that which is contained in the tiny arteries into an invisible spirit and a light of intellectual nature lurking in such a spirit; this acts upon the airy or "fantastic" smoke no differently than the soul acts upon the body, or heaven upon the earth, or the sun's rays upon the air.

But the vehicle of that acting divine light is that vital or arterial spirit, which these choroid plexuses are accustomed to render invisible by an admirable art or property, so that it is now as fit in such a subtle and invisible form to perform the duties of the rational soul as it was in its visible form (when it was arterial blood) to perform the duties of the vital soul. Thus we also see that the spirit of wine or its **quintessence** (which we can compare to arterial blood) is rendered invisible by repeated rectifications, so that the whole is accustomed to be converted into an airy or invisible spirit and vanish into the air.

In this manner, therefore, these spirits—both venous and arterial—existing in the first two ventricles are prepared, cooked, and thinned; they are still coarse animal spirits like smokes before they come to the natural sense. The perfection of this whole work is finished in the third ventricle of the brain (or the Antenor of the third degree), and then these spirits, having been made invisible, migrate into the fourth ventricle, where they set about to fulfill the will of reason—both invisibly through sense and imagination, and visibly through motion.

Therefore, the first Antenor, namely the **Liver**, administers the elementary region in the microcosm, and consequently corresponds to the sublunary heaven of the macrocosm, in which action is taken toward vegetation and generation. The second, namely the **Heart**, is related to the Sun in the celestial macrocosm. The third regards the **Empyrean** or intellectual heaven. I am silent in this place concerning the wonderful artifice of natural chemistry which is perfected in the seminal vessels, as I have proposed to make mention of that elsewhere.

From these things, therefore, one may see how many mysteries of natural chemistry are observed in the various dispositions and operations of the human body, and how subtly and sagaciously nature is accustomed to lead its affairs to a conclusion in the Microcosm. Consequently, how worthy of hatred and contempt are those men who are accustomed to hold Alchemists in derision! For the true chemist attempts to undertake nothing which nature has not delineated in the human body. For example, in the composition and preparation of medicines, nature teaches him first of all to dissolve them in a certain proper **menstruum** <note>A solvent</note>. Then, to separate the impure dregs from the pure juice: then afterwards, by the nature of the Liver through the first degree of digestion...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of Blood.

### CHAPTER IV.
### *On the Anatomy of human blood, dissected by artificial chemistry.*

Having now completed the description of natural chemistry and the power of blood through its various preparations, we shall proceed quickly to its artificial explanation, by which the elements of the blood are distinguished from one another, so that we may then move on to the wonderful mysteries of the blood brought to light by art.

Indeed, I have seen many chemical operations on human blood in my time, and I have been an eyewitness to their effects; yet I truly confess that I have held only one in high esteem, which was put into use and practice by a certain German most skilled in common chemistry and very familiar to me, named La Pierre <note>Jean de la Pierre, a 17th-century apothecary and chemist</note>, who performed this kind of experiment many times in Paris. He said that he himself received this secret from the Bishop of Noyon through the mediation of a certain nobleman called Menanton; and he said, or certainly believed, its purpose was that, by a preceding philosophical cooking <note>original: "coctione philosophica"</note>, he might finally arrive at the Philosopher's Stone (so long sought by sophists and spurious philosophers, but never found). I will say nothing of the hoped-for effect of such a secret, nor is it truly in my mind to give any credit to it. My intention in this place is to declare how to divide the elements of blood in the common manner, and to explain the mysteries of some of them in medicine; and so that I may accomplish this more clearly, I shall follow the experiment of my friend regarding this matter.

He chose blood extracted from men between 25 and 30 years of age, healthy in body and robust in habit; he rendered it putrid in horse dung or some other warm place. He covered an excellent retort on every side with well-tempered clay <note>luting: a clay paste used to seal and protect glassware from direct flame</note> so that it might better withstand the violence of the fire (except at its summit, where a certain circular spot was left uncovered for the sake of looking inside). He poured as much of the aforementioned material, prepared by putrefaction, into that vessel as could fill it up to the middle. The figure of the clay-covered retort is this, lest this seem difficult to understand for beginners in the chemical art.

Then he adapted the retort, protected in this way, to a certain furnace commonly called an Athanor <note>original: "Antenori," likely a variant or error for Athanor, a furnace designed to provide steady heat</note>, specifically so that only half of the vessel remained in the power or contact of the fire. When it was well-fixed to the furnace, he applied to its orifice a certain receiving vessel, sufficiently vast and ample, in which the spirits leaping upward from the material might play and circulate well. He stopped up the joints with papers soaked in a glue made from flour and egg whites; and when these were well-dried, he covered them a second time with the same papers smeared with the same glue, and indeed even a third time. # Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book II.

He finally proceeded to the formula for distilling, which (by gradually increasing the fire) he extended over a period of 8 days, or a full week, as if he were imitating the action or operation of Nature itself in this matter. Thus, up to the fourth day, he administered a heat very similar to the heat of the Sun in the month of June, so that each drop followed the next only every quarter of an hour; for this kind of operation, the first two degrees of fire were required, during which time the element of Water was accustomed to reveal itself as <term>phlegm</term> <note>In alchemy, "phlegm" refers to the tasteless, watery distillate that comes over first.</note>. Then, he stirred a somewhat stronger fire by the power of the third degree of fire, by whose action a certain cloudy Air began to ascend into the receiving vessel. When this had entirely breathed out from the <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation.</note> and was collected in the receiving vessel, he proceeded to the fourth degree of fire. Finally, by its impulse, the Element of Fire came forth, first in a yellow form, and then afterwards tinted with a dark redness. It was observed that this element, on account of its worthiness alongside the celestial spirit, participated in some way in the **Fifth Essence** <note>The "Quinta Essentia" or Quintessence: the purest, most spiritualized form of matter.</note> itself, which he affirmed—when well rectified—participated in the nature of true **potable gold**.

But truly, it must be noted in this place that (since that fifth essence is only drawn out at the very last) the fire should be increased in every way on the final day, and even lit beneath the grate itself; for that glutinous matter (as was said regarding the fifth essence of bread) does not come out except by the violence of fire, and is thus raised from the earth. And when it is noticed that nothing more distills, the fire should be extinguished, and once the furnace has cooled, the retort should be removed. Furthermore, regarding the investigation of the fourth element, namely **Earth**, he affirmed it was to be drawn from the <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>Latin for "dead head"; the useless solid residue remaining after distillation.</note> residing in the bottom of the retort. Concerning this sediment of matter, he related a truly admirable story to me, which I intend to declare to you in the following pages, since we have now decided to treat the common and non-miraculous operations of nature. And so the first chemical preparation of this matter was completed, in which he himself observed, through a hole left in the top of the retort, various colors appearing in the cavity of the glass. He said that in the final degree he covered this hole with ashes, so that the heat of the fire might be more effective in its operation. We proceed thus to the second preparation or purification of this mystery.

All that which flowed out from the Retort into the receiving vessel in this first operation must be taken: and let it be placed back into a Retort similar to the first (but not coated with <term>lute</term> <note>A clay or cement used to seal alchemical vessels.</note>). It should be placed in a pot filled with sifted ashes well-fitted to the aforementioned furnace, and the beak of the same shall be connected to the glass <term>vesica</term> <note>A bladder-shaped glass vessel used as an intermediate connector.</note> described below, whose other orifice must enter the mouth of the receiving vessel. Let small pieces of paper be soaked with the lute or glue described above, and with these let the joints be well sealed, lest the subtle matter escape. The order and shape for joining the vessels to one another follows here:
