Therefore, through the first degree of fire, the phlegm or element of water is very easily drawn out, but this degree must be very slow, lest the cloudy air be sucked out together with the water. Once the water or phlegm is extracted (which you will perceive from the fact that, when that work is complete, cloudy air will gradually appear in the receiver), the receiving vessel must be changed. Then we will perceive a certain matter or air, almost invisible, ascending, which by gradually thickening itself, will be converted into a substance or murky and somewhat whitening smoke, and in the end will be transmuted into a lemon-yellow liquor and condensed; when the smoke ceases, the receiver must again be changed immediately.

In the third place, you will await the element of fire, which will acquire a ruddy color for itself, and that redness will be dark.

Finally, the **fifth essence**, or the fifth element, rises with difficulty and diligent observation, for otherwise it will suffocate itself in the neck of the Retort and be burned.

It should be noted that for the production of each element, the space of one day is required, for this operation must be done slowly and step by step.

As for the element of earth of the blood itself, it is to be drawn from the *caput mortuum* after the breaking of the Retort in this manner (in which our author first saw wonders, as we shall declare below): This must be taken not only from the first Retort, but also from that of the second distillation or operation, and reduced into a powder, then [placed] in a vessel...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of Blood.

It should be entrusted to an earthenware vessel, which must be very well sealed with its own lid. This lid ought to have a hole at its summit, through which the vapor rising from the material to be calcined may exit most easily. Let it be exposed to a violent fire for a space of 8 or 10 hours, until it is perfectly calcined <note>Reduced to a powder by heat</note>. Then, once the fire is extinguished and the vessel cooled, the calcined material should be extracted, reduced to an *alcohol* or fine powder, and reserved for the process described below.

We now arrive at the third operation, which is nothing other than the rectification <note>purification by repeated distillation</note> of the elements previously separated. First, therefore, the **phlegm** <note>the watery element</note> must be rectified, and this by a gentle heat using a *Bain-Marie* <note>a water bath for even heating</note>; you shall keep that part aside.

Next, you shall also purge the **air** in the *Bain-Marie*, and separate it from both its watery and fiery additions. But our author himself distilled that material through oiled paper and reduced it into a substance like snow or the purest manna; this material must also be kept for its use.

After these things, the **oil** (referred to the fire) is to be rectified seven times in small retorts until it acquires the color of a hyacinth <note>a reddish-orange gemstone</note>. With this, he also joined the essence which he called the **fifth** <note>the Quintessence</note>, and this material, thus mixed and so many times rectified, he called his **potable gold** <note>Latin: *aurum potabile*, a legendary alchemical medicine</note>. He said that this, when applied or administered for dangerous diseases, would bring about stupendous benefit. Whether his assertion be true or false is not for me to dispute in this place; I only wished to relate to you what I have found to be true and proven by experience regarding the chemical anatomy of human blood and its dissection into its elements.

Finally, I took the calcined **earth**, placed it into a sufficiently large alembic <note>a distilling flask</note>, poured over it at least a large portion of the rectified phlegm, put on its head, and macerated it in a gentle *Bain-Marie* or in moderately warm ashes. In this kind of maceration or infusion, a receiving vessel should be applied to the beak of the alembic's head, and if anything distills into it during the maceration, it must be poured back over the whole. This infusion is to be continued for three whole days, and in the interval, the material must be moved and shaken many times. Finally, this work being completed, this macerated material is to be poured into a clean vessel, and its clearer part, separated from the turbulent dregs by way of filtration, is to be extracted in a *Bain-Marie*. Thus I found a whitening **salt** at the bottom of the alembic, which I rendered white and clear like crystal by dissolving it in the recently extracted liquor, and by triple filtration and distillation.

That author of ours thought to produce an extraordinary medicine by the admixture of some of these elements, once a "philosophical decoction" had been performed. By this, he did not doubt he could cleanse even impure metals, and truly refresh and restore a human body languishing with sickness. Therefore, he mixed one portion of that with three parts of his potable gold and two of air, and treated this composition for a long time with the heat of a lamp in the manner of common alchemy. I do not believe the effect of this operation differed much from that of the "spurious" chemists, who, leaving the right path, dream of distorting and violently forcing the efforts of nature to fit their own fantastic conceptions and inventions. As for me, I hope I have performed my duty toward you (Excellent Readers) skillfully and abundantly, in that I have produced for your eyes the anatomical division of the elements of human blood, performed by the ministry of the chemical art.

And although it might perhaps be objected by some against my assertions that, through this demonstration of mine, only a tiny portion of blood is found to participate in the element of air: nevertheless, I would wish such people to remember that I did not say the entire mass of blood was simply "airy," but that the mass was compacted from the more subtle portions of the elements remaining after the separation of the dregs of the first digestion. For what physician or philosopher is ignorant of this? That the *vena cava* <note>the main vein to the heart</note> is never destitute of bloody serosity (which is water), or that the blood itself naturally lacks its fibers, or is entirely immune from its bilious or oily matter? Indeed, we read quite easily of blood itself being converted into fat; for if it is cooked, tallow or <margin>*Aristotle, Book 3 on the Soul*</margin> fat can be made from it. That blood is also endowed with its own dregs escapes no one of wisdom. But blood is called "air" because it participates more in air than in any other element; nor is it unknown to physicians and philosophers versed in nature that blood is purer in some and more impure in others, which happens according to a person's complexion <note>temperament/constitution</note> as well as their age. Whence the author of the aforementioned secret seems to have regard for age; there is also a certain time in life in which the "balanced temperament" is said to reign, in which without doubt the blood (*which, by the testimony of the Holy Scriptures, is the seat of life and the soul*) is most temperate and pure in the human body.

But now, lest you object that this experiment of ours brings you no utility beyond the anatomization of the mass itself (which alone pertains to our purpose), I desire to set forth some of the uses of its elements in medicine.

Its **phlegm** is said to contribute wonderfully to itching and the scabies, and for this it has indeed been tested.

The element of **air** and also of **fire** is accustomed to mitigate—wonderfully, and indeed in the very moment—the pains of gout, knee-pain, sciatica, and hand-gout.

Also, its **salt** dissolved into a liquor is observed to restrain all pains and to provide many other things which have not yet been tested by us; but for the pains of gout, I have tested it many times.

And so you have blood divided into its elementary parts by the chemical art. Now, however, I shall gird myself to recite to you an admirable history, proven by the testimonies of many, concerning a certain notable accident that came upon this author of ours during his first operation. But before [I come] to the declaration of the same...

### CHAPTER V.

#### *Concerning the mystical and hidden disposition of the air, and that it is the vehicle and receptacle of souls, demons, Angels, and many other invisible mysteries; likewise, that by condensation it is converted into blood.*

<margin>Tobit 12:15.
Psalm 103:20.</margin>
As the Empyrean spirit <note>The highest, most refined celestial fire or light.</note> is said to be the medium between God and the celestial bodies (whence also the Angels inhabiting that spirit *are said to stand before the face of God*, and elsewhere: *Ministers of God, most mighty in strength, performing his word, hearkening to the voice of his command*), that is, they are mediators between God and the celestial creatures; so also the aerial spirit of the world is the medium between the celestial soul and the body. From which it is clear that God and the angels, by means of the Empyrean spirit, are in the celestial soul, just as the celestial soul, by means of the sublunary spirit, is in the body. From these things it is clear that by means of the aerial spirit, God, the intellectual spirit, and the celestial soul are present in us, that is, in our external man or body. This indeed seems to be confirmed by Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings on philosophy and magic.</note> with words of this sort: *The soul of man* (he says) *is carried in this manner: the Mind in the reason, the reason in the soul, the soul in the spirit, and the spirit in the body.* And elsewhere he says that *the garment of the Mind is the soul, but the garment of the soul is the spirit itself.* And elsewhere he recognizes the ethereal spirit to be the vehicle of the divine mind. To which also Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> seems to agree with these words: *The soul, in descending, is clothed in various ways, and finally prepared.* And Hermes Trismegistus seems to explain the reason for joining these contraries—namely the divine mind with the body—clearly in a discourse of this kind: *The divine mind cannot exist in an earthy mass, nor was the earthy dregs able to receive so divine a mind, or sustain such a great divinity. Hence (he says) it is that the mind takes the soul as if for a cloak, because the divine soul uses the spirit as a vehicle.* But lest these things should be rejected by certain profane people as if they were not at all approved by the sacred scriptures, I shall not cease to bring forward one or two passages from them, by which I shall show that the divine philosophers do not at all disagree with the word of God. In the Royal Psalmist <note>King David.</note> we find that God is the enlightener of the lamp of man. Whence we can directly infer that, since by the lamp of man he understands his soul, it is necessary that all light of the spirit or soul proceeds from the life-giving ray of the face of God, without which the soul is dark, and not a soul, but nothingness. And hence immediately after, the prophet adds: *For God makes the darkness of the shining one.* Whence it is clear that the splendor of God, which is the divine mind, is accustomed to illuminate the candle of man or the soul, without which the soul is no more bright than a candle without a flame. From which it is quite clearly established that the life of the soul is the divine mind, and consequently the divine mind, by means of the Empyrean spirit, is present in the ethereal soul or vital spirit. But this is also better confirmed from Job, who says to God: *Thou hast exercised life and kindness toward me, and thy visitation has preserved my spirit*, by which he seems to argue that by the presence of the face of Jehovah <note>The Hebrew name for God.</note> the vital spirit is preserved in man, and consequently, that life remains in the power, or rather in God himself. And that the life-giving splendor of God is the true actor in the celestial spirit for this temporary life, and in the super-celestial spirit for eternal life, since from these is the fountain of life and the living water mentioned by Christ and John in Revelation. Is it not also said elsewhere by the Psalmist, *that Jehovah is a sun giving life and glory?* In John also we read that he is the true life, and that in life is the light of men; for he does not say in that place that life is the light of men, but *in life*, that is, in the vital spirit *is the sun giving life and glory*. By life he understands temporary life, and by light or glory, eternal life; the vehicle of the former or momentary life is the intermediate spirit, participating in the darkness of the lower world, but the vehicle of eternal life, where the Lord of Hosts <note>original: "Sabaoth"</note> reigns forever and ever, is the Empyrean spirit adhering to the eternal light. But this is also explained in many other places; for example, it is said by David that life is the benevolence of Jehovah; and elsewhere, *The fountain of life is with God*; and elsewhere, *Jehovah is the restorer of life*; and elsewhere, *The strong God of my life*. But that passage is the most open of all regarding this matter: *When God hides his face, the creatures are troubled; when he takes back their spirit, they expire; when he sends forth his spirit, they are recreated, etc.* By these things, therefore, it is manifestly declared that this sublunary or aerial spirit is the receptacle of God, since his tabernacle and vehicle is a thick cloud, since he himself walks upon the wings of the wind, and yet his nearest vehicle or garment is the Empyrean light, as that which is present everywhere in the world; for he sits upon the heaven of the ancient heavens, whence also it is said, *Jehovah, who is esteemed equal in the higher cloud.* And yet he is present everywhere and always; oh, how admirable and hidden is the spiritual sense of the sacred letters! How deeply its letter wounds! This spirit is also the vehicle of the angels of the higher heaven, whence it is said, *Who makest thy angels winds, and thy ministers a burning fire*; and elsewhere, *Angels are the ministers of God doing his pleasure*. In which sense both the angels who avenge and pursue with evil, as well as those who affect men with divine kindness, are understood; for as Job testifies, both good and evil angels stand before Jehovah. Thus, God sends an angel before the righteous in their affairs. Thus also an evil angel afflicted Job, and struck the firstborn of the Egyptians with death. And David, with eyes lifted up, saw the angel of Jehovah standing between heaven and earth with his sword drawn, extended in his hand against Jerusalem, devastating the people and seizing them with pestilence, so that David was deterred by fear. Thus also Jehovah sent his angel who cut down every man of mighty strength, and the leader and prince in the camp of the King of the Assyrians. Furthermore, that the air is the common receptacle of celestial souls, of the ethereal spirit inclining downwards, of the influences of the stars both fixed and wandering, and that (I say) of wonderful actions and se—

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Blood.

...and that it is a sanctuary and a vessel of precious ointments <note>original: *myrothecium*</note> for great secrets of both the heavens and the earth; that it is one spirit and a single essence, covering the entire globe of the earth and the mass of the waters, which also reaches from the earth all the way to the highest concealed heaven, and even ascends above it. For the ether is nothing other than moderately thin air, which is led and moved by the Word of God (reigning in its center and outside its periphery), and by whose power it shall remain until it finally perishes. It embraces within itself the hidden mysteries of winds, lightning, and thunder, as well as comets, rain, snow, and hail. It is the worldly sea in which the specific forms of all lower things and the radical moisture <note>The "radical moisture" was believed by medieval physicians to be the fundamental fluid that sustained life and determined its span.</note> of every living thing swim. It is that common space into which the souls or spirits of the deceased return; finally, I believe it is hidden from no one moderately versed in philosophy that this is that spirit which mixes itself with all sublunary things, acting as the vehicle for spirits or forms—both health-giving and malignant—and those composed of poison.

Hence, air is defined by some as the vital spirit which penetrates all things that exist and connects them to one another; it fills everything and moves everything by the power of its soul. For this reason, by some Hebrew Doctors <note>Referring to Kabbalistic or Rabbinic scholars.</note>, this spirit is not counted among the elements, but they esteem it as a glue joining the elements and the things composed of elements together. They call it the "Resounding Spirit of the World," receiving all influences and spirits into itself. This, therefore, is that spirit which transforms itself into human blood by the aid of Nature, like another Proteus <note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will.</note>; in which visible species it nevertheless encompasses its invisible mysteries, such as the divine mind. (And hence man is called the temple of the Holy Spirit). It also contains good Angels, such as the one of whom the prophet Zechariah speaks: <margin>Zechariah 2:3</margin> *Behold, the Angel who spoke in me went forth, etc.* And Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on theurgy and the soul.</note> describes his office thus: *This angel (he says) reconciles the soul to the body, communicates with it, directs the life proper to the soul, etc.* That it is also capable of containing wicked spirits and demons is taught to us not only by the testimony of the sacred scriptures but also by daily experience in the case of the demoniacs and those possessed by diabolical spirits; for it is granted to wicked spirits to inhabit the lowest spirit of the world, since they cannot inhabit the ethereal or Empyrean spirit due to their impurity.

Furthermore, the air contracted into blood is the seat of the soul, in whose center (as was declared above) the divine mind has its seat in its Empyrean spirit. This is confirmed by many passages of the sacred scriptures. For hence God said, <margin>Genesis 9:4</margin> *you shall not eat flesh with the blood; for I will require the blood of your souls from the hand of all beasts, and from the hand of man, and from the hand of his brother I will require the soul of man; whoever sheds human blood, let his blood be shed, for man was made in the image of God.* And hence it is said in Job 24:12 *that the soul of the wounded or slain cries out, and God does not allow it to go unavenged.* It is as if he were saying: the Soul cries out for the violation of itself and the pouring out of its tabernacle, etc. From which it is clear, first, that the soul or life is in the blood; second, that the likeness of God is in the blood, inasmuch as it is established by the Word in which there is life. For this reason, the severest punishment is ordained for those who attempt to violate the temple of nature and the sanctuary of the soul. For although blood is visible air, yet invisible species seem to inhabit it, such as the mind, the Angel, the soul, and the invisible spirit. The immediate receptacle of all these is the air, and as blood is procreated from air, it is their remote and outer vehicle.

But that the soul is in the blood is evident from this passage of the sacred letters, where it is said, <margin>Leviticus 17:10</margin> *Whoever eats blood, I will set my face against that soul, and will destroy him from among his people, because the soul of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you so that you may make atonement for your souls upon the altar, and blood is for the soul as an expiation; therefore I said to the children of Israel, no soul among you shall eat blood: if therefore anyone in hunting or fowling takes a wild beast or bird which it is lawful to eat, let him pour out its blood and cover it with earth, for the soul of all flesh is in the blood.*

But let us hear (I pray) what the ancient philosophers, distinguished by the title of divinity, say on this matter. Some maintain that the vigor of life consists chiefly in the humors of choler <note>Yellow bile, one of the four classical humors.</note> and blood: in the blood, I say, so that it may be dispersed through the whole body, and in choler so that it may be rendered more lively in its action. Hermes Trismegistus says *that blood is the course of life or the soul, so that when life moves, the vehicle is also driven to its motion; but he says that fluid blood deprived of this life becomes coagulated and frozen and exists as if dead.* Empedocles placed the chief force of life or the soul in the heart, and this by way of the blood. But the Epicureans deny this, because they observed that when the heart was extracted from crocodiles, life nevertheless remained in them for a long time. The Stoics acknowledge that life is in the heart, but they entirely deny that it is present in the heart by reason of the blood, but rather by the power of the spirit; and Chrysippus seems to demonstrate this clearly. Others, agreeing with Moses in this, affirm it was forbidden and prohibited by the Oracles to eat the blood of a creature, as being that in which its soul resides.

But in my opinion, it is very easy to produce peace and concord among all these philosophers and to reconcile them with one another. For he who said the soul is in the heart by means of the blood spoke the truth; nor did he lie who asserted it is in the heart by reason of the spirit. Because just as a portion of the ethereal spirit or the celestial soul is in the worldly spirit, so also that spirit is in the blood, whose vessels are the heart and the liver. Nor does the reasoning of the Epicureans follow—that because the animal dies immediately when the crocodile's heart is removed—since the force of life is diffused through the veins and arteries into the whole body. For it does not follow that a green tree dies immediately because it is deprived of its root; for as long as blood is perceived to move in the parts of the animal, so long is life said to remain in it. We conclude, therefore, from these things which have been said, that the Word is the center of every thing, without which it cannot endure; and that the divine mind in man is in the angelic spirit, and that intellectual spirit is in the celestial soul, and the celestial soul is in the invisible air, and the invisible air is in the visible air, which is the blood.

<summary>This page argues that blood is the visible form of air and the physical vehicle for the soul, angels, and the divine mind. It reconciles various ancient philosophical views (Stoic, Epicurean, Hermetic) by explaining how the spiritual hierarchy descends from the Divine Word into the physical blood.</summary>

# Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book II.

And blood is in the heart and liver, and by this reasoning the soul can be said to be in the heart as much by reason of the blood in which it exists mediately <note>indirectly</note>, as by reason of the spirit in which it exists immediately <note>directly</note>. Thus also God can be said to be within the human spirit, the blood, and the heart, and consequently to be everywhere in the Microcosm <note>the human being as a "little world"</note> as much as in the Macrocosm <note>the universe</note>. Hence, the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> quite deliberately called man the Temple of the Holy Spirit.

These things being so, it is evident that the soul—without its ethereal spirit (which is, as it were, the radical moisture of life), and that spirit, unless in its own course, which is the worldly air, and that air without its vehicle, which is the visibly condensed Human [substance], which is the blood—can neither enter into the body, nor move within it, nor finally depart from it by the violence of death. This is because the blood is bound to the air, the air to the ether, and the ether to the radiant or vital soul by the bonds of nature in such a way that one cannot move in this elementary region without the other. Indeed, every part of the blood has such a relationship to its whole while the soul acts in the body, that it is also regarded by its whole; for the airy spirit can no more be divided from its like (as is clearly declared in the effect of the "weapon salve" <note>original: "unguenti armarii," a sympathetic medicine believed to heal a wound by treating the weapon that caused it</note>, of which more below) than a part of the soul from its whole. Hence, when it is said that the soul of the slain cries out, it is not understood as a partial soul, but a whole one, with its invisible vehicles both airy and superlunary <note>beyond the moon/celestial</note>, which are indeed bound by a wonderful bond to their final vehicle, namely the blood.

<margin>Job 24:12</margin>
And from this it follows that if anyone passes through a place where a man has been killed, or where the corpse of a dead or slain man is newly hidden, he is sometimes affected by stupor and fear. This is because in the air, which is now the final vehicle in which the soul of the slain is carried, it is disturbed by such a slaughter and is surrounded on all sides by horrible and terrifying specters. Thus, joining itself with the internal spirit of the person passing by, it affects him with similar invisible figures, from which fear is struck. For the spirit of nature is so tender that it most easily receives external impressions, even invisible ones. From this it arises that if the sense of vision of the spirit becomes weak due to long illness, and the air is dense enough to serve as a mirror for it, one may perceive the image of one's own face in it; this is not only written by Aristotle and Albertus <note>Albert the Great</note>, but was also found to be true by myself when laboring under a certain dangerous fever. From these things it is clearly evident that the air, which is the seat and chariot of the slain person's soul, has an inseparable connection to the blood still remaining in the body of the deceased. Is this not clearly shown in the case of the accused? For in the presence of those conscious of the murder, the corpse is often known to emit fresh blood; but if they are not at all guilty, no blood will issue from the corpse. Indeed, unless the airy spirit, the receptacle of the soul, had such a relation to the corpse, this would never happen; for this spirit, not yet totally separated from the blood of the corpse, is moved as if struck by fear, and by such sudden motion liquefies the clotted blood by the heat of its movement. Furthermore, there is a struggle and contention, as it were, between the spirits of the slain and the slayer, such as there was between the spirits of Eteocles and Polynices <note>Brothers in Greek mythology who killed each other; legend says the flames of their funeral pyre split in two</note>; when they killed each other in battle, even the flame of their funeral fire allowed their spirits to be distinguished, flame from flame. For without doubt, the soul of the dead is accustomed to dwell in the airy spirit as its vehicle, even when separated from the corpse. Hence, it is affected by similar passions after its separation from the body, since the passions of man do not come from the body, which is immobile by itself, but from the sublunary spirit, by which it is moved turbidly and perversely by the soul as if pushed by an agent, and in its motion it stirs up passions governed by fatal influences. For the soul exists so pure in itself that unless it is affected by such a rebellious spirit, it acts sweetly and kindly; for it is the sublunary spirit, and not the ethereal one, which is ready to receive spirits both malignant and benevolent, by which the soul is either disturbed or pacified. For the heaven is not naturally subject to changes, because it acts mercifully in its spirit, but where its actions are poorly received, their effects will be perverse. But to proceed further in this inquiry of ours, Hermes Trismegistus says that when the soul recurs into itself, the spirit is contracted into the blood and the soul into the spirit.

<margin>Pimander 10</margin>
Furthermore, he says that the soul is the receptacle of the mind, and that the spirit is the garment of the soul, but he makes the blood the receptacle of the spirits; for the spirit, by means of its internal essences, acts upon the blood no differently than the soul upon the body, or heaven upon the earth. A similar respect is held between the soul and the spirit, and between the mind and the soul. Whence he concludes that the spirit, diffused through the body via the veins and arteries and the blood, moves the animal <note>the living being</note> everywhere, and sustains and carries the suspended mass of the body. And elsewhere he concludes that just as the soul could not penetrate the body except by the mediation of the spirit, so also it cannot exit the body except by the mediation of the same spiritual vehicle; nor can that spirit be so separated from the blood that it does not have a relation to the blood, since it is its vehicle, which will also be converted into its invisible and spiritual nature by dissolution. And this is the reason that the souls of the dead sometimes appear to men, and again vanish from sight as if they were food for the eyes; for just as a visible cloud is nothing other than condensed and contracted air, which when dilated again is converted into its invisible being (even dissolved with no rain appearing), so also this spirit, the vehicle of the soul, joined with the spirit of the blood (already thinned by prior putrefaction and reduced to invisible air), swimming here and there in the mundane spirit in the vast cavity of the world, is accustomed to contract itself suddenly, and by that contraction appear visibly to men in the same form and likeness that the body had while it enjoyed the "feeding breeze" <note>original: "vescali aura," the breath of life</note>. For it is certain and proved by philosophers that there is no figure in corporeal things which was not first in spiritual things, nor is there any likeness of a creature here on earth which was not first formed in the heavens. Thus also the spirit of Samuel appeared to King Saul, real and not a deception, namely by the condensation of his invisible spirit into a visible species, which suddenly became invisible again through dilation. Thus also Elijah, made spiritual by transfiguration, appeared with Moses to Christ and the Apostles on Mount Tabor. And also that...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of Blood.

That appearance of Christ after the resurrection in the midst of the Apostles occurred by contracting his subtle form and rendering it visible through condensation; but when they wished to vanish, they did so by a sudden expansion and thinning. For according to Saint Paul, *they rose from corruption to incorruption, from a corporeal state to an incorporeal and spiritual one.* <note>original: "à corruptione surrexerunt ad incorruptionem..." Reference to 1 Corinthians 15.</note> From this, therefore, it happens that the spirits of the dead—when their corpses are deprived of the proper funeral ceremonies, or when their blood is treated in an immoderate and violent fashion—are sometimes observed to appear visibly. We could cite innumerable examples of such apparitions in this place, but because other matters call me away, I shall reveal to you this single history of a similar event which happened to our aforementioned author while he was formerly working on the secret described before.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### ->Concerning the wonderful history demonstrating the mystical connection of the blood after someone's death with their spirit and soul.<-

Whether a certain celestial constellation, or a varying method of working, or the hour chosen at the beginning of the work, or the reason for the death of some of those from whom the blood was first extracted, or the long putrefaction <term>putrefaction: a chemical process of breaking down organic matter to release its "spirit"</term> of the blood-matter was the cause of this thing now to be recounted, the craftsman himself, and I, and many other eye and ear witnesses are entirely ignorant. But that author of ours cited before, in the city of Paris <note>original: "Lutetia"</note> near that place called The Temple, at the urging of many of his friends, steadily undertook this work, or the chemical anatomy of human blood. He therefore received blood from his friend, which had undergone putrefaction for two years in a well-sealed jar; and that blood had been let and extracted from the arms of various persons. He thus made the beginning of this work of his on a certain Saturday, around the ninth hour, as that is the time for celebrating the common Mass. For an entire week, by observing various degrees of fire (as declared above), he pursued this intention with a continuous fire.

In the meantime, on the following Friday, around midnight, while our craftsman was lying in bed in his chamber adjacent to his laboratory, between sleep and wakefulness—while meanwhile the splendor of the full moon illuminated the room, which was in the upper part of the house—behold! Suddenly a horrible lowing arose, like the lowing of oxen or the roaring of a lion. Having heard this, the craftsman was struck with astonishment and stupor, and flowing everywhere with cold sweat, he kept himself quiet and motionless in bed. When that sound in the laboratory ended, he suddenly perceived between himself and the window a certain cloud condensed in an oval shape, which seemed gradually to take on a complete human likeness, and making another sharp cry, it suddenly vanished.

And certainly, although this may seem incredible to some, nevertheless not only the noblemen in the next rooms, but even the host himself with his wife, lying in the lowest part of the house, and even the neighbors living on the opposite side of the street, distinctly heard both the roar and the voice, and some of them were even awakened by its vehemence. But the craftsman said he found solace in this: that the Bishop from whom he had received this prepared blood, as well as the secret of the same, had forewarned him that if any of those from whom the blood was extracted should die during the time of putrefaction, their spirit would often appear in the craftsman's object with great disturbance.

Furthermore, on the next day, namely the following Saturday, he removed the Retort <term>Retort: a glass vessel with a long neck used for distillation</term> from his furnace, broke it with a light strike of a key, and found in it the "dead head" <term>dead head: (caput mortuum) the useless residue left after distillation, but here used as a pun on a literal head</term> of the blood. A head, I say, not unfitly called "dead," since in every feature—namely in the face, eyes, nostrils, mouth, and hair, which was somewhat thin and of a golden color—it represented a human head. And of this matter there are very many eyewitnesses, namely my dearest friend and a nobleman most worthy of trust, Lord de Bourdalone, first secretary to the Duke of Guise. He, by sending me letters about this matter to England, was the reason that I set out for Paris—partly to learn the certainty of this matter and partly moved by other private business—where I heard this history corroborated and confirmed by grave and honest men: namely by Master Menanton, living in that house at that time, by a certain Doctor of Medicine, by his host, and many others. From this it is clear that the entire spirit of that dead man regarded the spirit of that small amount of blood extracted during his life with an indivisible relation; so that when a portion of his blood was tortured by fire, his spirit, exhaled from the body, was also disturbed and vexed because of the symphonic continuation of the one to the other. But this is also best explained by the following experiments.

### Chapter VIII.

#### Concerning a certain Experiment depending on the occult sympathy of blood with its own kind, by means of which the senses of two men distant from each other by a long interval can be very easily discerned (without any letters or messengers mediating).

The preceding experiment (as I said) was the foundation for this following one. For when some of the sharper-witted men perceived such a great sympathy between the flesh of one man and that of another (the origin and nourishment of which was blood), they noticed that this proceeded from the hidden spirit of the blood of both. For if the seat of the soul is the spirit, and the seat or vehicle of the spirit is the blood, it is necessary that this kind of sympathy in nature proceeds primarily from the First Actor or Agent, whose carriage and mediated receptacle is the blood, and whose immediate receptacle is the spirit wandering invisibly through the mass of the blood.

Hence, they approach the matter in this way: they either wound the arm or some other place with an incision, or pierce it by cauterization. Once the wound is well cleansed of its own blood or mucous matter and begins to form new flesh, the companion of that wounded man must extract some drops of blood, either from a finger or some other place by incision or puncture, and pour them into the other's wound. Thus, with the opening closed by some plaster, this infused blood can ferment and finally unite with the blood of the wounded man. But if anyone should object that the infused blood, being outside its own proper place, would become rotten, we acknowledge that the substance of the blood can contribute nothing to this sympathetic work of ours, but only the hidden spirit within that blood, by means of which the soul of one seems to communicate with the soul of the other. For spirit is very easily joined to spirit by the glue of nature, since nature rejoices and delights in nature—just as we see in a drop of water or grains of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, which are accustomed to be inseparably joined to their whole. Therefore, once the wound is healed in the usual manner, they say the secret lies in this: namely, that if the scar of the wound is pricked with a needle or a small pin, the place or part of the other person from whom the blood was extracted (however far distant from the wounded one) will immediately feel the same puncture by a wonderful sympathy of spirits. Since this is so, they conclude it is a very easy thing, by means of a certain Alphabet, to communicate anything of whatever nature or condition between themselves. For example, for the letter A, a single puncture is to be made; for B, two; for C, three; and so on for the rest. Indeed, I have heard that the consensus and bond of such blood is so strong by the power of this communication between the spirit of one and that of the other, that when the man from whom the blood was extracted dies, it is necessary that the nature of the infused blood in the wound also be rooted out by incision, lest the place rot; and then afterwards the wound must be healed in the former manner. Finally, this kind of consensus of blood with blood is wonderfully explained in that cure of a wound by the Magnetic Ointment, which (God willing) we shall treat sufficiently in the following chapter. Furthermore, the probability of this kind of sympathetic operation is confirmed by that well-tested conclusion regarding the Magnet stone <note>lodestone</note>, so loudly proclaimed by some, by virtue of which communication has been made between friends living in distant places. The hollow basins are to be divided through the bottom by two diameters, distinguishing them into four parts or quarters. The ends of these diameters, extending over the hollows, are accustomed to indicate the four cardinal points or parts of the world: namely, the East, West, North, and South, which are usually marked on the edge of the hollow by N. S. E. W. <note>original: "Orientem, Occidentem, Aquilonem, Meridiem"</note> Then, above the hollow on each side of the diameter's end in the eastern corner marked by E, let four primary letters be expressed: namely, *a. b.* on one side and *c. d.* on the other. Furthermore, a diligent little bell <term>tintinabulum: a small signaling bell</term> is to be adapted to the hollow in such a way that the forward part of the needle, striking against it, may warn one or another friend of the time for conversation. This being done, two iron instruments must be kept ready, made of iron smelted seven or more times, the dimension of which ought to be the size of a thumb in roundness. To one end of each, you shall apply a certain wooden handle <term>manubrium</term>, so that you may hold it when heated in the fire without injury to the hand. The other end, however, must be reduced to the shape of a Rhombus or a square Diamond; above the quarters of that Rhombus, write according to the position of the world: N. S. E. W., that is, North, South, East, and West. Therefore, let these rhomboidal or diamond-shaped ends be held in the fire for a long time, almost to the melting of the metal. Then, extracting the iron from the fire and holding the rhomboidal end downward, let its South quarter (S) be turned directly to the south; and let it be rubbed or touched strongly with a most powerful magnet. Then, rub its Northern part, placed directly toward the North, with that species of magnet called *Theamedes* <note>A legendary stone mentioned by Pliny the Elder, said to have the opposite property of a magnet: it repels rather than attracts. Here, the author suggests it draws "air from the North."</note>. After these things are applied, as before, let the South (S) be raised to the South, and the East quarter of the Rhombus (E) be stroked with a Diamond. Then, according to the same station (namely, with S looking toward the South), turn the West quarter (W) toward the west, and let it be rubbed in the aforesaid manner. This being done, let those two iron instruments be hung up with the rhomboidal ends looking downward until they cool completely. ### CHAPTER IX.

#### *Concerning the various compositions of the Armary or Magnetic Ointment, its property, and its sympathetic operation through the blood.*

Exquisite is the sympathy between things of the same nature, just as the antipathy of contrary dispositions between them is admirable—which would indeed seem impossible at first glance to men overwhelmed by ignorance, unless the infallible properties of such natures in diverse things had been confirmed by ocular experience. Nor indeed is anything found outside of human nature that more clearly proves the sympathy of things than the very strong relationship of the magnet itself to iron, and its affection for the polar star. Nor certainly (to come to the kingdom of man) is there anything that more clearly demonstrates the sympathy and compassion between him and the parts appropriated to his vital disposition than that manifest relationship observed between the ointment compounded from blood and other human parts and the wound, and between the gore shed by the wounded man and the mass of blood still reserved in the injured body; whence, by way of comparison made between the effects of the magnet and those of this kind of ointment (inasmuch as they are very similar), this is called the **magnetic ointment**.

First, therefore, we shall explain to you the ingredients of its composition and their measures, and we shall describe those effects which practice and experience—the teacher even of fools—has produced, so that you may more easily judge the human parts entering into it. Then, let it be permitted for me to draw forth the natural reasons for this occult and sympathetic work from the sanctuary or <term>perfume-cabinet</term><note>original: "myrothecio." A metaphorical storehouse of remedies or secrets.</note> of my intellect, such as it may be, in which I will briefly show you what truly is my mind's sentiment and opinion on this matter.

->*The composition is as follows.*<-

> Take: Moss <insert>or Vine</insert> growing from the skull of a man long hanged, or in the absence of the same, from the bones of one hanged and choked by a noose, long exposed to the air and hardened, together with human fat, 2 ounces each. <term>Mummy</term><note>In 17th-century medicine, "mumia" referred to prepared human remains used as a drug.</note>, human blood, <term>Armenian Bole</term><note>A medicinal red clay from Armenia.</note>, 1 ounce each. Linseed oil, 2 ounces. Let them all be ground in a mortar until they are reduced to a fine ointment, which is to be placed in a small box and wisely reserved for use.

We see, therefore, in a composition of this kind, that this ointment is fashioned from things best suited to human nature, and consequently, that it has a great regard for its health and existence, since blood—in which the force of life is situated—occurs in the first place in its composition. Here (I say) are present the bones of man and their essence in the form of the moss or vine growing there; here is his flesh, namely in the Mummy made from flesh and balsam; here the fat of the human body agrees with the rest for the perfection of such an ointment; and with all these, the blood (as was said) is mixed, which was the origin and nourishment of all the aforesaid, as that in which the spirit of life, and with it the bright soul itself, is accustomed to lurk and act in an occult manner. So it is that the entire perfection of the human body seems to concur in the making of this precious ointment. And it is from this that such a great regard is created between this ointment and the blood of the wounded body: for it is necessary that some of the wounded blood be drawn even from the depth of the wound, as is clearly explained in what follows.

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Blood.

When, therefore, a wound is inflicted on someone, one must either recover the weapon that caused the wound, smeared with gore, or, if that is lacking, a piece of sharp wood must be thrust into the deep opening where the wound gapes so that it may be stained with blood. That instrument—whether it be a sword, a knife, an axe, or finally a piece of wood thus infected with blood—must be brought back to the location of the box <note>The container for the sympathetic ointment</note>, however far removed from the patient it may be. Then, it should be immersed in the ointment and left there until the healing is complete. In the meantime, every morning, the wound ought to be bound with a fresh linen cloth soaked in the patient's own urine. And so (God willing) it will be healed without a plaster. This has been proven in the case of wounded men who were 10 or 20 German miles distant from the ointment itself. It is also beneficial for other pains, such as those of the teeth and the like, which are observed to proceed from a corrupt disposition of the blood. Likewise, if a horse's foot is wounded by a nail, either through the negligence of a blacksmith or by some other accident, it has been found that by plunging a piece of wood into the bottom of the wound and placing it in the box or small chest, the wound is healed within a few days.

First and foremost, however, one thing must be noted in passing regarding this cure: a supreme and constant regimen must be observed. For if this ointment is kept too warm, the wound will be affected by excessive heat; or if it stiffens with cold, the wound will also taste of that same indisposition. And now, from my own experience and knowledge, allow me to recite a story to you. A certain nobleman and knight of the golden grade, named Sir Nicholas Gilbourne—my brother-in-law, as he married my eldest sister—a man, in my opinion, second to none among the nobility of England in learning and philosophy, held a royal office concerning the ships of the King, having the naval apparatus of England in his care. This man (I say), keeping a box full of this ointment with him, heard that a certain carpenter hired to repair the ships had been severely wounded by an axe. Upon this news, he ordered the axe, whose edge was smeared with the blood of the wounded man, to be brought to him immediately. Rubbing the bloody edge of the axe with his ointment and protecting it from the cold with linen cloths, he hung it on a certain nail in his chamber and departed, closing the door. Suddenly, the wounded man confessed that he felt relief and proceeded to recover more and more every day. But truly, on a certain day, he complained greatly of his wound and of the pain and its intemperance; all those standing by wondered why, with no evident cause given, he was afflicted with such sudden restlessness. They immediately fled to my brother, who hurried to his chamber and found that the axe had by chance fallen to the ground, stripped of its linen coverings, and the anointed part was exposed to the inclemency of the air. Therefore, a second time, he smeared the edge of the instrument with the ointment and clothed it in linen coverings; immediately the pain of the wound was mitigated, and it was restored to its former temperament, and thus he soon recovered.

Now, indeed, we shall proceed to the natural demonstration of this sympathetic cure, so that we may speak not only with the mouth of experience (as is the manner and custom of mechanics), but that we may clearly depict the mystery of this action in the manner of philosophers, using reasons drawn from the hidden bosom or storehouse of nature.

Since air (as was said before) is the vehicle or carriage of the spirit of any thing, which is also called the chariot of the soul itself, or of celestial light, or of the primary agent; and furthermore, since blood is the receptacle of all these, it follows therefrom that the motion of the blood in the vein or artery is from the impulse of the spirit itself, just as that spirit is again agitated by the light or soul within it, like a direct wind. This, by a similar reason in man, is incited by the intellectual spirit dwelling in the center of the soul, in the midst of which resides the Divine Mind as prince, commander, and first internal agent—which is the principle of the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or universe, as opposed to the "Microcosm" of man</note> made before all things (according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus: *Wisdom was created before all things*). This Mind, therefore, was the first blower into the mundane spirit in its organ, the first striker of the string of the mundane <term>Monochord</term> <note>A single-stringed instrument used to illustrate the harmonic proportions of the universe</note>, always moving in the lucid or Empyrean spirit, just as that spirit moves in the celestial light or soul, which also, with its spirit, is carried in the aerial spirit no differently <margin>Chapter 1.</margin> than the soul is carried in the blood. This, therefore, is the reason that blood is linked to the visible air by a bond of nature, just as the element of water is to the earth; and again, the air of the visible blood is linked to the invisible air implanted in it, just as the element of water is to that of air. And also the lucid soul with its lucid vehicle is linked to the air (in which it is carried) as the element of air is to fire. Furthermore, the intellectual spirit relates to the soul as the celestial or ethereal substance relates to the Empyrean, or the intellectual spirit as God relates to the spirit of an angel, with which He is everywhere surrounded (according to the words of the Royal Psalmist): *God is clothed with light, that is, with a fiery spirit*. From these things it is manifest that Blood and life are primarily moved by the Mind, but secondarily by the soul, by whose impulse the spirit is provoked, at whose nod the blood is moved in its vein; which also <margin>Psalm 104:2</margin> Hermes Trismegistus confirms with a discourse of this kind: *The human soul is carried in this manner: the Mind in reason, reason in the soul, the soul in the spirit, and the spirit in the body; and finally the spirit, diffused through the veins, arteries, and blood, moves the living creature everywhere, and sustains and carries about the mass of the body.* <margin>Pymander 10.</margin>

From these things, therefore, it is clear that insofar as the substance of the blood is joined to its spirit by an inseparable bond, and its spirit is nothing other than air in which the celestial soul resides—and this by a continuous connection, no differently than the ether to the air—it follows that the relationship between the blood and its spirit is wonderful and firm. Similarly, since its spirit is nothing other than air enclosed in the blood, it adheres to the air in the macrocosm as a part to its whole, or as a drop of water is united with its whole in an inseparable way. But truly, insofar as this spirit is enclosed in the blood and adheres to it, no differently than air to water, and insofar as it has been made the guardian of the specific soul of this or that man, to that extent it participates in the nature of that individual, just as, for example...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of Blood.

It has been explained by the testimony of those living in England: I say, so great is the harmony and **sympathy** <note>A Greek-derived term meaning "feeling together" or natural resonance.</note> between the spirit of one blood and its like, that even if a single drop of blood, or something originating from it, is treated poorly or well by a magus in distant places, the other person will either be tormented or affected by joy and health. By these means, it is best perceived how great a compassion <note>In the literal sense of "suffering with."</note> exists between the blood of one and the blood of another, even in places far distant from each other. This occurs because of the hidden spirit enclosed within them, whose action is a ray of the soul. 

But someone might perhaps reply that an invisible line of this kind, stretched through the air from the wounded person to the seat of the ointment box, could be broken and divided into parts by the movement of men or animals; and that it would follow from this that the power of the ointment would work in vain, since its conducting spirit is interrupted, and for this reason, it cannot lead the healing power to the desired port. To this we answer: the logic is the same for the division of air as it is for water. For if a portion of water in a river is colored in a long line, and a boat passing through its middle divides that colored line, its parts are nevertheless perceived to rejoin each other in the blink of an eye; nor does it follow that air divided into two parts by a sword does not return to the unity of its substance.

We conclude, therefore, that the effects of the invisible spirit hidden in the substance of human blood are admirable and stupendous, both **sympathetic** and **antipathetic**. We have already spoken of the former above; we shall deal briefly with the latter below. And for this reason **Arbatel** <note>Refers to the *Arbatel de Magia Veterum*, a famous 16th-century manual of spiritual magic.</note> (a man highly versed in supernatural mysteries) established an entire treatise on **Microcosmic Magic**, in which he denotes what the **microcosm** <note>The "little world," i.e., the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note> has performed through its spirit and the geniuses <note>Attendant spirits or guardian angels believed to be assigned to a person at birth.</note> added to it from birth, magically—that is, by spiritual wisdom—and how: and through that wisdom, the teacher of all things, the mind is carried in the human soul by means of its intellectual spirit, as we understand the soul to be within the human spirit.

### CHAPTER X.

->*On the logic of antipathy, both Macrocosmic and Microcosmic, and how the internal spirit of both is sometimes alienated from the soul inhabiting it, and is usurped by evil spirits.*<-

Concerning the sympathy of blood through its aerial spirit with its like, even when placed in a distant location—and much more so when running in the same vein by which healthy life or health and balance are acquired by man—enough has been treated in the preceding sections. Now, however, our discourse will be established in this place briefly concerning the **antipathy** <note>Natural aversion or opposition.</note> between the living soul and that evil, corrupting one—that is, one opposite to it in disposition—mediated by the same spirit: and how this spirit, the vehicle of its own soul, may be alienated from its mistress and her care.

Just as it is impossible for any sympathetic harmony or symphonic society to exist where the aerial spirit is diverse from its soul or contrary in disposition (according to that saying of the Savior Jesus Christ: *A kingdom divided by opposition cannot long endure*), so also it is necessary that this alienation in the sublunary spirit proceeds from a demon of nature, contrary to the life-giving soul. For the air itself is of a moist and passive nature, and is led either by an internal agent naturally implanted in it from birth—by which it is made regular in the faculty of living—or by one coming upon it preternaturally, by which it is turned against its natural and ordinary course. Thus it is made rebellious to the living soul, and in the manner of **Phaethon’s** chariot <note>In Greek myth, Phaethon lost control of the sun-chariot, nearly destroying the earth.</note>, carried outside the path of nature, it attempts to destroy the "lesser world" (the human) either by fire or to submerge it in a deadly cold and moist flood like that of **Deucalion** <note>The Greek equivalent of the Noah figure who survived a Great Flood.</note>, headlong and in an insane manner, like those swine who, driven by evil spirits, cast themselves headlong into the sea. 

This inferior spirit, I say, is so fragile and so liable to defilements that, in the manner of celestial Mercury, it is fit for the disposition of any demon or evil and foreign soul, however much it may be contrary to its own mistress, the soul of life. And this is the reason why the sublunary spirit, both in the **Macrocosm** <note>The universe or "great world."</note> and the **Microcosm**, is imbued with such great changes and inconstancy. Whence it happens that it hungers with a constant appetite for new forms, and uses "privation" <note>A philosophical term for the absence of a quality that should be present.</note> as a go-between, by means of which it constantly procures new loves for itself. Hence comes such great uncertainty in the sublunary world; hence the origin of the unhappiness of the human race and the beginning of sin. For (as I said before) although the air suffers in its moist nature, the influences of the celestial bodies flowing into it serve as agents or souls. But truly, insofar as we see that the influences are diverse, according to the varying logic of the planets predominating in the heavens, so far do we observe diverse impressions and alterations produced in the air and inferior things, flowing from a variety of causes. For example, meteors are sometimes ignited, sometimes watery, and even windy, according to the diverse condition of the celestial influences in this or that region of the air. 

From this, moreover, it is right to draw out the variety—nay, even the contrariety—of the influences of heaven: namely, because the aspect of **Jupiter** is favorable and propitious to the nature of human life, while that of **Saturn** is perceived to be greatly opposed to it by a certain antipathy ordained by the Creator. For certain Saturnine aspects are most hostile to life and the human race, being cold and consequently contrary to the human heat, and dry, which therefore [attacks] the radical moisture in every way...

So also hypochondriac winds <note>Refers to "vapors" or gases believed to be produced in the lower abdomen (hypochondrium) that affected the mind and spirit.</note> are agitated by a malignant spirit and driven with such fury that he may cause the visible temple of man itself to be shaken and sometimes to collapse. Albotali <note>Likely a reference to an Arabic medical or astrological authority.</note> seems to affirm this same thing: that *melancholy is from a demon, and that he has seen those affected by the demon in every age of the world*. The Holy Scriptures also make mention of these things, whence we also find *that the aerial spirit of the swine, by the permission of Christ, was made the vehicle of Cacodaemons <note>Evil spirits or "bad demons."</note>, by which, being violently agitated by the malignant spirits, those swine were suddenly drowned in the sea*. Furthermore, as was said in Job, *by the malice of the Devil, fire fell from heaven and consumed the cows, sheep, and boys*. In that act it is certain that the malignant spirit himself was present, namely in the ignited air. So 

<margin>Clar. maior. ch. 4</margin>
also (according to Artelius) the Devil joins himself to human infirmities arising from Choler <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors, associated with fire and anger.</note>, as we shall declare more widely in what follows. From which it is clearly taught that the human soul, sailing in its lowest spirit, is afflicted through the antipathy of natures by a daemon or foreign spirit hostile to the man's genius. Indeed, through the possession of this lowest spirit, man is deceived by false prestiges and delusions, afflicted with bodily diseases, driven by fury, imagines false things for true, and is affected by fear and sadness without cause.

But observe, I pray, the mystery of this matter, as I prepare to touch upon it with a needle <note>A metaphor for precision or "hitting the mark."</note>, so that you may more easily understand how God or the Mind, how one's own soul, and the vital daemon or foreign soul, are said to inhabit the human spirit. For as the seat of the Mind is the Empyrean or intellectual spirit, in which neither a daemon nor a soul of the lowest order can ever dwell, so the proper place for the vital soul is the ethereal spirit, to which the soul is so joined as form is to matter. To the first place, on account of its singular purity, the malignant spirit cannot penetrate, being banished from the throne and presence of God into dark exile from the beginning of the world, and overwhelmed with darkness on account of his disobedience. But this Empyrean spirit or air is the seat of the good angels, who are indeed before God. Also, malignant spirits of this kind cannot reach the ethereal spirit because, on account of their imperfection and impurity, they cannot approach a place so pure, perfect, and lucid, unless God so wills it, insofar as they are called "shunners of light" and "haters of light." And hence it is that they have no power over human life—that is, over his ethereal spirit—without the special permission of God. 

<margin>Job 2:6</margin>
Whence God said to the Devil, *Behold, he is in your hand, but save his soul*, that is, do not touch his ethereal part. But truly, harmful spirits or angels who deceive men with delusions are familiar with the spirit of the sublunary world, since this lowest portion of the world, namely the sublunary, was destined for them as a habitation in the beginning after the fall of Lucifer. Hence in the Apocalypse we find: *I saw four angels standing upon the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, that they should not blow upon the earth, nor the sea, nor any tree; and I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God, and he cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, saying: Do not harm the earth, nor the sea, nor the trees, until we have sealed the servants of God in their foreheads*. By which it is clear that harmful angels have power over the air or winds, over the earth, and over the sea; but when they proceed to execute their malice, they are accustomed to move through the winds or the aerial spirit. For "spirit" is 

<margin>Wisdom 7:20</margin>
taken for air and wind, in which the Wise Man <note>Referring to Solomon, the traditional author of the Book of Wisdom.</note> seems to recognize the whole force of inferior things to be; whence by John, in the place cited before, angels of this kind are said to preside over the winds. Similarly, from the preceding passage, it is evident that the angels of the superior heavens command those of the sublunary world. For superior things always rule inferior things; thus, as the heaven sends its influences into the air, it is observed to move that air and the spirits enclosed in it. So also the angels flow their virtues or the force of life from the Empyrean heaven through the <term>Sephyrotae</term><note>The Sephirot, the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> into the ethereal heaven, which also successively flows those acts into the sublunary world. And God, by a similar reason as the prime agent, rains down from His uncreated spirit or lucid fountain all the virtues of the Empyrean heaven, with which angelic creatures being filled, they are accustomed to pour them liberally from their lucid spheres into the lower ethereal and aerial regions, as has been sufficiently declared in our Kabbalistic physiology. By these things, therefore, it seems to be declared that it will be very easy for a malignant spirit to penetrate into the air of the microcosm or the subtle part of the blood, since the air and elements or sublunary spirit were destined by God for wicked and harmful daemons as their natural seat. # On the Mystical Anatomy of the Blood.

<margin>1 Chronicles 21:1</margin> even into the external spirit of the elect, [the devil] sometimes creeps by divine permission, whence it is said: *And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel.* <note>original: "Surrexit autem Satan contra Israel. & incitauit Dauid vt numeraret Israel."</note> But in truth, he was unable to reach his ethereal or vital spirit, much less that intellectual spirit against which the Devil has never dared to attempt anything, seeing as it is the seat of God and his angels, from which he was expelled from the beginning through his disobedience. So also the Devil *put betrayal into the heart of Judas*, <margin>John 13:2</margin> into his heart, I say, because it is there that air is drawn in by inspiration, and with the air or wind, malignant spirits are sometimes introduced into the heart; and so that deceived spirit proceeds to the agitation of that introduced spirit, as if it were by the instinct of its own soul granted to it from birth. Thus, in such a delusion of a foreign demon, the sick sometimes think they see, touch, and taste things which in reality are not there, and sometimes even believe themselves to fly or swim, when nevertheless it is not in their power either to fly or swim. Others again believe themselves to have been turned into a donkey or a horse. Others think they ride upon beasts and offer sacrifices or victims to Diana by the shining Moon, and yet meanwhile they are observed to sleep securely. Some falsely think they have a fox's tail growing in their anus, others a truly enormous nose, others snakes living in their stomach; and with infinite vanities of this kind, that spirit, led without reason, deceives the man. And yet the spirit of celestial life is not affected in these people, because the demon is not permitted to touch the soul. 

But indeed, sometimes they do touch the soul by permission, but they are not permitted to extinguish it totally, according to that saying of Augustine: <margin>Book on the Divination of Demons, ch. 5</margin> *Evil angels often receive the power both to inflict diseases and to make the air morbid by corrupting it, and to persuade the perverse to evil deeds.* And elsewhere he says: *That it happens by the ineffable power of God that evil angels can do what they do, if they are permitted;* <margin>On the Trinity, Book 3</margin> but they cannot do it precisely because they are not permitted. For that spirit, which reigns on its empyrean <note>The "Empyrean" refers to the highest heaven, associated with pure fire and light, the dwelling place of God.</note> throne in the center of the air of both the macrocosm <note>The universe</note> and the microcosm <note>The human being</note>, either by contracting itself into itself permits demons to approach the aerial margins of the soul itself, or by extending itself, puts to flight the light-fleeing and wicked demons from the outer soul by the light of its countenance, according to that saying of the Prophet alleged above: *When God hides his face, the creatures are troubled; when he sends forth his spirit, they are recreated.* <margin>Psalm 104:29</margin> For it was by the mediation of the lucid spirit of God that *Christ cast out unclean spirits.* <margin>Matthew 12:28</margin> Wherefore it is necessary that the human soul, floating in the middle between the divine or empyrean spirit and the mundane or aerial spirit, should adhere to Christ or the Word reigning in the intellectual or highest heaven, if it wishes to be secure from the insults of wicked demons. For if, by neglecting higher things, it tends toward lower or sublunary <note>Things beneath the moon; i.e., the earthly, changing world.</note> mundane things—that is, if it fixes its gaze upon the Elements or things made of elements—it cannot be immune from the tyranny of Devils; indeed, it is very much obnoxious <note>In the Latin sense of "vulnerable" or "subject" to.</note> to them. Whence David prayed that <margin>Psalm 143</margin> *God by his good spirit would lead him into a level path,* that is, into the path of truth, which is the spirit of perfection, just as the way of falsehood is that aerial spirit subject to demons; for *the Devil is called the father of lies, because there is no truth in him.* <margin>John 8:44</margin> Hence Augustine says *that the cause of all evils is sin, which is the disorder and distemper of the soul.* And elsewhere the same Augustine says: *What shall we say of the delusions of demons, except that we must flee from the midst of Babylon? For the more power we see them have in this lowest realm, the more tenaciously we must adhere to the Mediator, through whom we ascend from the lowest to the highest.* <margin>Augustine, City of God, Book 18</margin> 

Therefore, the actions of demons which are performed in the nobler spirit of both the macro- and microcosm are for that reason illusory and lying, and deceivers of the sight and human senses, both because they happen in the air, over which the malignant angels of God preside, and because the Devil (who is their father) is a deceiver and a liar from the beginning of the world. Whence it happened that the Egyptian sorcerers or enchanters presented their deceptive miracles and illusory visions to the senses of Pharaoh, seeing as they acted sophistically both in the mundane middle air full of inconstancy, and in that of the soul of Pharaoh and those standing by; so that by their fantasies there seemed to be no difference between their diabolical miracles and the divine miracles of Moses. But indeed, when they came to the creation and appearance of gnats, <margin>Exodus 8</margin> they who had previously made frogs and serpents could not produce gnats, because the greater dominion of the prohibiting God was present through the Holy Spirit, which even the magi confessed, saying: *This is the finger of God.* For they placed the foundations of their art in the sophistical and deceptive air by the mediation of the appearances of demons; but he [Moses] planted the bases of his wisdom and operation in the divine and Empyrean spirit, where no deceptions are found, where truth alone reigns, where all things exist infallibly and permanently, with the good angels assisting. 

And hence it happens that the impious man is said *to turn his spirit against God,* that is, to alienate it from God, which happens when the soul, more prone to the flesh and the external spirit of the blood than to the mind, subjects itself to the power of demons. Thus also an antipathy was made between the spirits of two people, whence Job spoke in this sense: *My spirit has become a stranger to my wife;* <margin>Job 19</margin> for the soul of Job, adhering firmly to the divine mind, kept his lowest spirit in its natural laws and in obedience to God, whence also this spirit was alienated from that of his wife, because her soul, looking toward lower things, permitted her spirit to be deceived by the Devil and to become rebellious to the divine mind. Whence there was as great a difference between the spirit of Job and that of his wife as there is between God and the Devil, which Job also seems to declare directly where he says: *The spirit from my understanding made me answer,* <margin>Job 20:3</margin> that is, the intellectual or Empyrean spirit, by the mediation of divine wisdom: for his soul adhered firmly to it even until the final temptation. For the soul adhering to the aerial spirit does not differ from that of a beast; for it is human to adhere to that spirit by which it was primordially created. But in the same author we read that <margin>Job 33:4</margin> *the strong spirit of God made man, and it is said by the wise man, that Jehovah weighs the spirit of a man.* <margin>Proverbs 16:2</margin> And elsewhere: *The spirit of Jehovah weighs all the ways of man.* And elsewhere: *My spirit shall not remain in man forever;* <margin>Genesis 6:3</margin> by which spirit he understands that which, reigning in the soul of man, administers his life, and is called that Empyrean spirit; for with respect to the lowest or aerial or impure spirit, this indeed seems to differ very little from that of beasts.
