And this seems to be clearly confirmed by the Wise Man <note>Referring to Solomon in the book of Ecclesiastes</note> in these words: *One generation (he says) passes away, and another comes, though the earth remains forever; the sun rises and after the sun has set, it pants again toward its place, where it may rise,* <margin>Ecclesiastes 1:4</margin> by which he seems to imply that generation and corruption have a relationship to the rising and setting of the sun. Therefore, from the rising of the sun—or the worldly heart—life follows the life of man, inasmuch as he is the son of the world. And as in the beginning of the world the Sun is said by Astrologers to have made its motion from the east, as if from a starting point (just as the spiritual Sun is said to be coming at the last dawn of day), so also it is probable that human life had its origin from the Eastern region of the microcosm <note>the human body</note> in imitation of the beginning of macrocosmic life, which begins from the Eastern angle; and consequently, that the heart is that Eastern angle or hinge, since from it the light of life first shone forth in the embryo.

### CHAPTER III.

### *That the breath of life proceeds from the east both in the macrocosm and microcosm, and concerning the metaphysical reason of the life and souls of both worlds.*

Since, therefore, the heart is the eastern region of the microcosm, no differently than the place of the sun's rising, the eastern angle, called the *horoscope* <note>The ascendant point in astrology</note>, it follows that a similar wind blows from such a hinge in man. And this wind blows for the entire human spirit of animated life, no differently than that macrocosmic wind of life is said to give motion to the spirit, or the air, or the human wind. Whence the Wise Man says, *that after the sun has set, it pants again toward its place where it may rise, hastens to the south, and circles the North.* From these words it is clear that the Sun—in which (according to the Platonists) the soul of the world is located (and as the Psalmist says, *God has placed his Tabernacle in the Sun*)—is the principal mover and inciter of the winds. And hence the Wise Man proceeds by connecting this discourse to the preceding: *The air (or, as Jerome interprets it, the spirit) hastens, circling in its conversion, and according to its circuits the air returns; which Pagninus interprets thus: by continually circling the wind proceeds, and to its circuits the wind returns.* Jerome says: *The spirit proceeds, illuminating in its circuit, and returns into its circles.* By which speech the Wise Man argues clearly enough that the disposition of the air depends on the solar motion, as its rays are like a soul to it. Whence the air is moved naturally in no other way than by the motion of the sun, by whose action it is agitated in a circular motion. Hence it is that the winds are called the children of Titan, Astraea, and Aurora, insofar as they are generated from the heat of the Sun, as Aristotle says, which renders the air subtle and rare, and this especially at Dawn. But they are said to obey the commands of Juno insofar as they do not blow except in the air, which is called Juno <note>In alchemy and mythology, Juno often represents the element of Air</note>. By equal reasoning, we see the spirit of life blow from the east of the microcosm, that is, from the Chamber of the heart as if from the chest of a microcosmic Aeolus <note>The ruler of the winds in Greek myth</note>, and by its inspiration it sweeps all the airy spirit of the blood with it into a sort of gyre. By means of its life-giving rays of spirit and life-giving motion, the winds—both northern and southern (that is, the splenic and hepatic <note>relating to the spleen and liver</note>) as well as western—are excited in the microcosm. For as was said in the previous discourse of the Wise Man: *The rising of the life-giving sun or vital heat, after it has set into the spermatic vessels, and then afterwards descended below into the womb or the south of the earth, it pants again toward a new rising, and hastens through the branches of the aorta to the hepatic south and the splenic north, and excites various breaths in them.* For since the flame of the heart is the offspring of the sun and its true son (whence it is said *the heart is the seat of the human soul, as the Sun is the seat of the world soul*, and that soul is called by Zeno *natural fire*, and by Prometheus *heavenly fire, enriching man with life*), it follows that it is moved according to the motion of the sun, inasmuch as it is a ray of the same, which cannot be separated from it. Whence it happens that as from the center of the whole world the seeds of life and life-giving light are ejaculated into the mundane spirit (which are also drawn in by the heart by means of inhalation), so also from the center of the microcosm's sun, or the soul of the heart, vital heat is disseminated and dispersed everywhere in the microcosmic spirit (which is also derived from the worldly air). This the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note> also confesses in express words in this manner: *Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it proceed the actions of life.* <margin>Ecclesiastes 1:4</margin> <margin>Psalms 4:23 <note>Actually Proverbs 4:23</note></margin>

But to approach the internal or metaphysical soul of the Eastern wind of both the macrocosm and microcosm, and its nature both in the sun and in the heart: we have said that God originally inspired life into his creatures through his spirit, and this by means of his angels, who are his fiery ministers, whose exterior or manifest part is air or wind, but the interior is divine fire. Whence it is written, *the name of Jehovah was in the angel whom God sent before the Israelites.* <margin>Exodus 23</margin> Hence therefore (says David) *Who makes your angels winds, and your ministers a burning fire, doing your pleasure.* <margin>Psalms 103:4</margin> We have also declared elsewhere that some angels have care of life, others of the body, etc. But because it is known to all that the sun of the world is the fount and origin of life, let us see, I pray, which angel presides over it, what his nature may be, and whether he is a Prince spirit having dominion over the breaths, or of life...

Pico della Mirandola says: <margin>Pico della Mirandola, *On the Archon*, book 4, ch. 4.</margin> *Human affairs are not ordered by the mystery of bodies but of angels, who are by nature and dignity intermediate between us and God; therefore, when you descend from God to the earth, descend through heaven; when you descend from God to men, descend through angels.* And all the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, and indeed even the Rabbis most skilled in the Kabbalah <note>original: "Caballa"; Jewish mystical tradition.</note>, acknowledge *that an angel is <margin>Reuchlin, *On the Kabbalah*.</margin> like an intermediate power between God and nature, from which operations in lower things are produced.* And elsewhere they affirm that all lower things are representative of higher things, and *as it is below, so also it is acted upon above*, and in this all Kabbalists agree. And the more secret theologians have affirmed that this is the Archangel Michael, inasmuch as the presidency of the Sun is assigned to him, which is the fountain of life and of living souls. And hence it is that all Platonists have said *the soul of the world was in the Sun*, and the Holy Scriptures say that GOD (who is the fountain of life and light) placed his Tabernacle in the Sun, and that in the *Messiah or Word* (which is the light of the world) there was life. Michael, therefore, or Metattron (that is, the soul of the world) is the intelligence or internal soul (in which, as it is written, the name of God is) moving, governing, and presiding over the Sun, whence it happens that the lives of the world and its creatures are assigned to him. Hence, therefore, the wise, agreeing with the Holy Scriptures, have said: <margin>Archangelus [of Borgonovo], *On the Kabbalah*.</margin> that Michael with his angels and ministers fought for the souls of all against the ancient serpent: And elsewhere it is said that he is the high priest in heaven, offering rational souls to God, and again; *he is handed down as the prince of the host of Christ, appointed over all souls to be received; he weighs them, not with physical scales or balances, but with a balance having a symbol with measure.* This, therefore, is that Michael who (according to Archangelus in his *Kabbalah*) holds the primacy among the angels standing before the tribunal of divine justice: For as there are four evil angels who carry the widest sails of the avenger in the army of Satan, namely Samael, Azazel, Azael, and Mahazael, so also there are four <margin>Reuchlin, *On the Kabbalah*.</margin> standard-bearers in the army of God, namely Michael, Gabriel, Uriel, and Raphael, of whom Michael is the Prince, whence Gabriel said to Daniel, *Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me.* <margin>Daniel.</margin> The more secret ones in Theology also made him the angel of Christ. Whence it is written that this is that angel who appeared to John, *whose eyes were like a flame of fire, and his voice like the voice of many waters, who had in his right hand seven stars, and his face shone like the Sun in its strength.* <margin>Revelation 1.</margin> And from this it is declared that this is the internal spirit of the sun in which consists the life and light of the seven planets, which are signified by the seven stars in his hand, whence it is said *that he stood in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks*, denoting here that he is that spirit in which the name of God is written, who placed his tabernacle in the center of the sun, that is, in the middle of the planets. Hence, therefore, we say with the wise that the Angel's internal fiery word or name of Jehovah was that holy emanation or fiery power of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note> which first shone out of the darkness—that is, that wisdom created before all things, which has power over all other angels, from which light and life were first imparted to the worldly spirit. This is that highest Archangel whom the spirits or angels who preside over the winds obey, no differently than the remaining stars are subjected to the command of the Sun's glory and exuberant excellence. Whence it is written of him in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> thus: *I saw four angels standing on the four corners of the earth, holding the winds of the earth so that they should not blow on the earth, nor on the sea, nor on any tree; and I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the Sun, having the seal of the living God, and he cried with a loud voice to the four angels of the earth, to whom it was given to hurt the earth and the sea, saying: Do not hurt the earth or the sea, nor the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God in their foreheads.* <margin>Revelation 7:1.</margin> Whence it is clear that this was the Prince of the angels, insofar as he commanded them, and they in turn obeyed him. Furthermore, he seems to be that Archangel Michael who has dominion over the Solar body, or rather is as it were its soul, whence John said: *His face shone like the Sun in its strength:* <margin>Revelation 1:16.</margin> and this all the more because he is said to have ascended from the rising of the sun, in which corner or hinge of the world Michael has his empire. Finally, from this place we can conclude that it is in his power to permit the malignant angels, by means of the winds, to bring harm to the earth and to men, and again at his pleasure to send forth or recall and restrain the powers of those angels for the preservation and natural health of the air, the earth, and its creatures. Hence those more skilled in the secrets of Theology maintain that Michael is that great priest of heaven, sacrificing in the upper world, and that he presents the stainless souls <note>original: "animal" used here in the sense of the "animated part" or soul.</note> of men to blessed God, but subjects those that are unclean and burdened with vices to the devil: according to whose pattern, the high priest in the lower world (as we have in Leviticus) is commanded to offer clean and innocent animals to God, but to deliver those burdened with crimes and a mass of guilt to Satan; for thus the prince, although he is most greatly inclined toward doing good and mercy, is nevertheless declared by God himself to punish sins in a discourse of this kind: *Behold, I send an angel before you to keep you in this way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared. Beware of him and listen to his voice; do not provoke him, for he will not bear your rebellion, because my name is in him.* <margin>Exodus 23:20.</margin> Moreover, the Kabbalists affirm this Angel to be the tutor of Moses, and they assertively conclude that he is Metattron or Michael. By the power of his voice, the wicked angels desist from their evil breaths or winds, with which they infect the air to the ruin and destruction of lives, as is declared from the passage cited above from the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. But if it be the pleasure of the Supreme Spirit to chastise a creature in His wrath for sins, then this good angel desists from his benevolent breaths and gives place to the avengers. These, dispersing themselves in the air, infect it, and either by striking the trees or fruits and cattle they bring on famine, or by corrupting the air, the cattle, or the nourishment, they disseminate pestilence everywhere, or they destroy those abandoned to them by horrendous tempests both on land and sea. But truly Michael, in whom is the name of God, and to whom the seal of the living God is committed, cries out to these infesting demons (as is declared in the passage alleged above from the Apocalypse): *Do not harm the earth, nor the sea, nor the trees, until we have marked the servants of our God on their foreheads.* Hence it happens that in a plague not all are destined for death and destruction, and Lot with his faithful ones was preserved from the sulfurous tempest among the others of Sodom and Gomorrah.

We conclude, therefore, that the Sun is the region of the Oriental microcosm because it is under the care and protection of the Archangel Michael; and it is in his protection because it is the sanctuary of the microcosmic life which rains down from the Sun. Its act and soul is the World Soul inhabiting the Sun, which flows into the seeds of life, and to which (as is declared) the eastern region and its wind are subject. Whence, as a great consensus is observed to exist between the heart and the Sun—inasmuch as both are fountains of life and receptacles of the souls of both worlds (but that of the microcosm arises from that of the macrocosm, since the microcosm is the son of the macrocosm)—it is necessary that the fiery spirit which inhabits the heart should spring from the breathing of Michael. For he is the fountain of worldly life, in whom the Word of God is inscribed, which is the true light of the world, first shining forth from the Father lurking in darkness, and informing all things by the benefit of life; concerning which we have dealt abundantly in our metaphysical and cabalistic discourse.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*Concerning the matter or substance of human life: what it is, whence it arises, and how it is continually introduced into the left chamber of the heart for the sustenance of life, and there worked upon by natural chemistry.*<-

<margin>Aristotle, Physics, Book 2.
Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2.
The Art of Chemistry, Ch. 4.</margin>
Now indeed, after we have spoken of the metaphysical act or first origin of the vivifying substance, it remains for us to delineate the essence of life itself and its hidden substance, insofar as it exists in the universe of things. That is, we must demonstrate the subject of that occult and invisible nature, which is the beginning and food of the life of creatures, by whose succession and fulfillment the life of any living thing is contained. Aristotle calls this kind of nature *the principle and cause of motion and rest in a natural thing, in which it exists primarily and per se, that is, not by accident.* But Cicero defines it as *a certain force of motion necessarily rousng bodies.* Others have called it *a certain hidden force, perceptible not indeed by sense but by intellect, so instilled by God that it supplies essence and any natural powers to every natural thing—namely element, animal, vegetable, and mineral.* But truly the Philosophers, more certain in the mystical Anatomy of natural things, are accustomed to express the nature of this vivifying substance with a loftier and clearer style, writing that it is a certain infinite force, procreating like from like, generating, increasing, and nourishing all things. It is the bond of the elements, the power of mixing, by which it effects the mixtures of elements in any thing of this sublunary world and imprints the form suitable to its species, through which one thing in the kingdoms of nature is distinguished and segregated from another; wherefore it is said to have the names of all things in itself. It is of no color, and yet is a participant and effecter of all colors; of no weight or quality, yet the fertile mother of all qualities and things. Indeed, this nature is so wonderful that the ancients hesitated whether Nature be God, or God be Nature. Whence they concluded: God is *natura naturans* <note>Nurturing or creative nature.</note>, that is, uncreated light in which is life; and nature is not God, which they therefore called *natura naturata* <note>Nature that has been created or "natured."</note> or created, by which they understood the moist spirit which exists by means of His uncreated light. Just as, therefore, we said in our preceding treatise on sperm, that it is created from seed as a celestial form and from sperm as an elementary substance, so also we say that the internal part of the vivifying nature is pure celestial fire, which is the throne of uncreated light; its external part is the ethereal spirit, which is the dwelling of the uncreated spirit; and the sublunary air is the common vehicle of both. Hence it was that the ancients said, *Nature is God, and God is Nature, namely because God* <margin>Pimander 3.
Pimander 1.</margin> *is in the moist nature, in which He inserted Himself in place of life*; whence Hermes Trismegistus affirmed *Nature to consist in divinity itself.* And elsewhere he says *that the moist nature cherished the Word.* Which indeed seems to differ very little from the sense of Holy Scripture, in which we find...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Heart.
## Z 3

*That the heavens were established by the word of God (that is, the fabric of the moist spirit) and all their powers by the spirit from his mouth.* From which it is clear enough that every form and every soul is derived from the Holy Spirit. Is it not also said in the creation of the world that *the spirit of God was carried over the waters*, (that is, the moist spirit, imparting fiery vigor to it,) whence we see that the form of the primordial worldly spirit flows from the radiation of the divine spirit, by whose presence it was created. And thus the moist nature is called a creature, but the first informing form is the luminous power of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>, which the Cabalists and the Doctors of the Hebrews called the angel Metattron <note>Metatron, often identified in mystical texts as the celestial mediator or the "Lesser YHWH."</note> (whom they called the soul of the world) in whom the name of Jehovah exists, that is his word, which is uncreated light. And hence <margin>Exodus 23.</margin> it is that we see in many places of the Holy Bible, the angel is sometimes called Jehovah, namely in respect to his uncreated form, and sometimes called by the name of an angel, in respect to his external part, which is a created spirit; For this reason, therefore, the Cabalists called all forms floating in the air "mouths," inasmuch as they receive luminous life immediately from God in the manner of angels, but contract their external part from the moist celestial nature: Hence it was that the philosophers established two species of nature, namely: the material, which they call the passive principle of motion, since it allows itself to be informed, and this is what Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg."</note> understands by the moist nature; and the formal, which nature they recognize to be more noble, inasmuch as it informs the passive nature. Whence they called it the active principle, and this is the same thing that Hermes Trismegistus understood by the "word standing by the moist nature," which cherished that passive nature. Is this not the same thing that St. Peter seems to suggest in 2 and 3 <note>2 Peter 3:5</note> where he says, *that heaven and earth were made out of water and through water by means of the Word*, and St. John <margin>Through John 1.</margin> in that passage *all things were made and without him nothing was made that was made*. In this active principle, therefore, is the presence of the word or divine spirit, which we signified above through the internal aspect of the angel Michael or Metattron. Hence Hermes <margin>Pimander 1. John 4. Pimander 12.</margin> Trismegistus says *the Father of all, being Mind, Life, and Radiance, procreated a Man similar to himself*, and we receive from St. John *that Life is from Christ*. And the same Hermes says, *the Soul is in the body, the Mind in the soul, and in the mind the Word. Indeed, he asserted God to be their father*. Whence he concludes, *that the Word is the image of God, the mind of the Word, the soul of the mind, the spirit of the soul, and the body of the spirit itself*, it follows therefore *that the purest portion of matter is air, of air the soul, of the soul the mind, and finally of the mind, God*. Whence God is concerned with all things, the mind with the soul, the soul with the air, and the air with matter. Thus he spoke. From which it seems clearly explained that the celestial nature is the vehicle of the Word, just as the air is the receptacle of the celestial nature, by means of which it is introduced into the body, where it tends toward both vivification and generation.

We conclude, therefore, that that portion of nature which is called passive or moist is the celestial spirit, which Physicians call by another name, the *radical moisture* <term>radical moisture: the vital fluid or "lamp oil" of life in medieval medicine</term>, but truly they called the divine fire acting upon it the "innate heat" and the invisible fire, from which Zoroaster and Heraclitus of Ephesus taught all things were born: and this fire is the efficacy of the breath of life, which God is said to have breathed into created things, when it was said in the birth of the world, *increase and multiply*. By the power of this breath all things multiply themselves. But truly, because *God placed his tabernacle in the Sun*, according to the sentiment of the royal Psalmist; (for there is nothing in the circle of the firmament that bears a greater likeness to God than the glorious light of the sun, since every thing claims as much of God for itself as it has light) hence the Philosophers concluded that the soul of the world was located in the Sun, which soul (as explained above) the Cabalists understood through the angel Metattron or Michael, the presiding governor of the Sun. Therefore, from the storehouse of the sun by the most occult operation of Michael, such sparks or Phoebean seeds <note>Solar seeds; "Phoebean" refers to Phoebus Apollo, the sun god.</note> are daily disseminated into this lower world through the fiery breathing-holes of the Sun, which are emitted from the interior vessels of the sun like male sperm from its seminal vessels into the worldly womb, namely the air, and in the moment of emission they mix with the moist nature of the ether, or the passive sperm, not otherwise than the sperm of the male uses that of the female as a vehicle. Whence it is brilliantly explained by the wise that the air is filled everywhere with these solar seeds: like a certain great sea with tiny little fish.

Now indeed we must declare how these solar seeds are attracted into the human body, by means of which man lives, and are said by the Wise Man to be *the Sun and man, generating man*. This invisible fire, therefore, this active nature, imbuing all things with life, making all things sprout and vegetate, swimming in its nearest and more worthy spirit, and again both of these having fallen from heaven into the sublunary spirit or air, that is, into their general vehicle, are carried here and there by the breath of the East wind, present to all things, nourishing all things, and intoxicating them as if with the nectar of life. Thus we have God everywhere present and assisting in the heavens and on the earth, sitting on the highest and deepest throne and tribunal of his handmaid, Nature, and assisting all things; thus we draw our daily bread, thus the blessing of the Word, thus the food of life daily: For since according to that axiom of Parmenides, *nature rejoices in nature*, the power of life situated in the center of the heart, by a certain magnetic force, yearns to attract its like to itself: Hence it is that that author, a most profound inspector into the mysteries of nature, falls into a sentiment of such wonder: *O celestial nature, nature of truth, multiplying by the nod of God*. And again: *O strong nature, nature conquering and overcoming, and making its own natures rejoice*. This is that special and spiritual nature to which God gave power over the violence of fire, etc. By which he seems to suggest that by means of this celestial nature, the vital spirit and the flame enclosed in it are increased and multiplied, since by its power not only life, but also the fruit of generation is produced unto infinity: Nay, truly greater mysteries are revealed in the union of the fire of human life, or the microcosmic nature, with the celestial fire, or the active nature of the macrocosm, since by a link of this kind the universal nature of the world has communication with that of man, by means of which they can perform stupendous things in natural magic; Moreover, the reason by which the appetite of human life is fulfilled in the attraction of its like, namely the worldly nature, is the heart, which through its parts both simple and organic [operates...]

For it utilizes simple fibers of all kinds, so that by the contraction of the straight ones, and the dilation of the oblique and transverse ones, the heart—drawing with it the air from the lung through the venous artery <note>original: "arteriam venosam"; likely the pulmonary vein</note> and its branches as the celestial food of life—attracts and sucks it into its left ventricle. This air, introduced with its celestial treasure and clothed in divinity through the two mitral valves (open outward, closed inward), is so prepared by the chemistry of nature that its impure and smoky part is separated from the subtle part. The way it was first introduced in its gross substance by inhaling, it is expelled by exhaling. A separation of this kind occurs in the same way that those skilled in chemistry extract oil or essence from vegetables, namely by means of a cooling vessel, in which the pure oil is revealed in a purer portion of water, and the grosser portion of water is rejected as a useless thing; or rather, as the essence of spices extracted by means of water is separated from its superfluous aquatic menstruum <note>a solvent</note> or vehicle in a Bain-Marie <note>a water bath</note>. This cooling vessel or warm bath is the Pericardium itself, a portion of which is always filled with water, in which the bottom of the heart—or the natural Alembic <note>a chemical still</note>—swims, and in which an extract of this kind is perfected. Indeed, the subtle portion of the air serves as a vehicle for the fiery spirit of heaven (which is the matter of life), just as that spirit is the receptacle for reason, and reason for the mind. This is confirmed by this discourse of Hermes Trismegistus: <margin>Pimander 10</margin> *The mind is in reason, reason in the soul, the soul in the spirit or thin air, and the spirit in the body; and the spirit, diffused through the arteries and the blood, moves the animal on all sides—that is, by means of the celestial fire by which it is driven and agitated.* And elsewhere he says, *that God is concerned with all things, the mind with the soul, the soul with the air, and the air with matter.* Therefore, once this preparation is made—namely, by separating the gross from the subtle, so that the internal agent may act and move more freely in its spirit—it is collected and purified in the sanctuary of the heart. Through three other semilunar valves, open inward but closed outward, it is placed into the sheath of the aorta or great artery (which is the sanctuary of life), from which it is dispersed everywhere through the entire body to aptly perform the functions of life and generation. And from this most essential substance the internal man is fabricated, just as the external man is made from the subtle part of the four elements, as has been explained more than enough in our treatise on seed.

### CHAPTER V.

#### ->How there are three motions or actions of the heart, which correspond<-
#### ->to the three regions of the macrocosm.<-

Just as three properties are counted in the macrocosm <note>the universe</note> according to its three regions—namely, the *angelic*, which is to understand and act according to the pleasure of the divine mind; the *celestial*, which, by God's command, bestows the power of living upon creatures; and the *elementary*, in which simple bodies are disposed by divine ordinance—so also we observe in the microcosm <note>the human being</note> that action is threefold, corresponding to those three regions of the world: namely, the *intellectual* (which Physicians also call "animal") corresponding to the angelic heaven; the *vital*, to the ethereal heaven; and the *natural*, to the sublunary or elementary region. Truly, however, both Physicians and Philosophers have restricted these three actions, both in the macrocosm <margin>Galen, *On the Affected Parts*, 5; *On the Difference of Symptoms*; Avicenna, *First of the First*, doctrine 6.</margin> and the microcosm, into a double property: that which pertains to the highest region of either world they have called *voluntary*, while the lower (which concerns both the vital or celestial region and the natural or elementary region in both worlds) they have named *involuntary*. From these things it is right to elicit in the first place that, just as God, by means of angels, acts upon the heaven and the elements originally and according to His will—which, whether willing or unwilling (that is, involuntarily), are forced to receive the acts ordained by God and move according to them—so also those things which are ordained and acted upon by the supreme mind of the microcosm in its highest region are called *voluntary*, as they proceed from the principle and first act, and consequently are not involuntary, since nothing pre-existed before them. Whence it follows that there is nothing that can compel divine actions. Thus they are concluded to be voluntary and not involuntary. Such, therefore, are the super-celestial and divine actions in the macrocosm, and such are those intellectual and animal actions derived from the mind in the microcosm: namely, voluntary and not coerced. For thus in the summit of the natural macrocosm we see the *primum mobile* <note>the "first moved" sphere of the heavens</note> situated, to which the will is referred, as it is moved according to the divine will by means of His ministers; and all the various creatures of the ethereal heaven are revolved by a violent and involuntary motion by this kind of will; and again, the elements and things made of elements are snatched up by the motion of the celestial bodies. Whence both the motion and action of the celestial and elementary things are snatched and carried toward the voluntary motion of the first mover, which is why their motion and action is called involuntary. By the same reasoning, Physicians and Philosophers have observed that the vital and natural actions in man receive their powers from the motion and incitement of the intellect, and by the virtue of the mind's motion, they are twisted and agitated whether they will or no. Whence they concluded that actions of this kind are voluntary, as they are incited not by their own, but rather by a hidden and excited motion, not otherwise than in the macrocosm the stars and elements are said to be moved and driven by their intelligences, whose internal act or first mover is GOD.

Hence, therefore, an answer is given (unless I am mistaken) to that doubt agitated among the Princes of physicians and philosophers: namely, whether the brain or the heart is to be preferred in generation. In this, Aristotle and the rest of the Peripatetic school strenuously defend that the Heart obtains the first place in generation; to whom Hippocrates is opposed, asserting that the Brain is the first member in generation, and he seems to support this opinion of his with a certain experiment, because he observed that the head of a chick first appeared in the egg. And Isaac <note>likely Isaac Israeli the Elder</note> seems to agree with this opinion of Hippocrates, insofar as he considered man to be like an inverted tree, and consequently the brain to be most like its root. But we shall approach this sentiment of Hippocrates for this reason...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Heart.
## Z 4
<meta>catchword: faith,</meta>

Therefore, it must be established that it is certain beyond question that the principle must be placed before that which begins in time; yet the brain is the receptacle of voluntary action, which precedes involuntary action (such as that of the heart) in no other way than God precedes the creature, or as the first act or motion precedes secondary acts and motions. From the preceding will, therefore, proceed all voluntary actions, inasmuch as they are compelled to move at the instance of the preceding will; but voluntary motion descends from the brain and, by involuntary motion, causes the heart and liver to move regarding their functions, not otherwise than the lower spheres are accustomed to be moved or twisted by a quasi-involuntary motion from East to West at the motion of the *Primum Mobile* <note>The "First Moved" sphere in Ptolemaic astronomy which drives all other celestial bodies.</note> (to which the brain is compared). But let us return to the matter at hand.

<margin>Avicenna, *On the Medicines of the Heart*, chapter 7.</margin>
They have made this involuntary action in the heart (which they call "vital") consist of a threefold motion, corresponding to the three kingdoms or heavens of the greater world <note>The Macrocosm or Universe.</note>. The first of these consists only in the **dilation** <term>diastole: the expansion of the heart</term> of the heart, in which action the spirit in the heart is affected by good passions, such as joy, hope, and others; and these kinds of sympathetic passions, full of pleasure, tend toward the empyrean heaven or the intellect of the microcosm <note>The human being as a miniature universe.</note>. The last consists in the opposite act, namely, in **contraction** <term>systole: the shrinking of the heart</term> alone, in which action the spirits destined for life are disturbed by malignant passions, namely fear, sadness, etc. And these kinds of antipathetic passions, burdened with vexations, look toward the elementary heaven of the microcosm, which is subject to dark changes. The middle motion between these two extremes consists in both contraction and dilation, the action of which participates in both extremes; for by dilation the heart draws the food of life from the Mind, not otherwise than the Sun draws from the Word <note>The Logos or Divine Reason.</note>, and by contraction it disperses it to the lower parts. Therefore, through dilation it draws the benevolence of life from God by expanding itself, and through contraction it communicates it with the lower and natural parts by contracting itself; but concerning these things we shall treat more extensively in the following chapter (God willing).

### CHAPTER VI.

->*Concerning the mysteries of the involuntary actions in the heart, and how we may elicit from them the threefold angel of man and their nature.*<-

The mysteries of the involuntary actions of the heart are to be admired if we explore the matter a little more accurately and to the very core: for if, in the first place, we contemplate only the disposition of the heart's dilation, we shall perceive from the effect that it is occupied solely with super-celestial blessedness, since by its mediation the spiritual eyes of the heart are, as it were, opened. The spiritual heart (I say), or rather the center-point of the heart, looking away from darkness by its dilation, rejoices in super-celestial vision; it exults in speculating upward upon the divine Idea of the Divine Mind; and by this kind of contemplation, it allures the whole of human life from lower things to higher ones. Thus, the whole man is snatched from the cares of the evil demon to the happiness of the good angel and is raised on high, inasmuch as by the mediation of this kind of cardiac action, Saints John and Paul were snatched up into the third heaven, where they confess to have seen things by no means to be revealed to the world. For in the spacious dilation of the heart, the celestial spirits of life enclosed in the heart seek their freedom; they strive to visit their celestial brothers wandering everywhere in the air, in whose light they behold not only the fountain of the soul, but also the Mind within it, and the Word in the Mind, and in the Word and through the Word, God the Father, surrounded on all sides by a choir of graces and the service of archangels, and they are ravished by that sight. This also seems to be confirmed by these words of the divine Synesius <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and bishop.</note> speaking of the Mind: *Yet there is, there is some light in the eyes of the work; there is also in those who, recalling Him with their eyes, have a certain power, when having emerged from the waves of life they enter the holy path to the palace of the Parent. Blessed is he who, after labors, after bitter earthly cares, having entered the ways of the mind, has seen the depth, with divine light shining forth.* And elsewhere: *From the perennial fountain of good things, having conceived prayers suppliantly, ascend to the Parent, and do not delay; leaving the earthly earth, soon indeed, a goddess joined with the Father, you shall exult in God.* But truly this power of dilating the heart is seen to be proved by its effect, since by its mediation good and delightful passions are introduced to the soul, by reason of that hidden vision tending toward joy and blessedness, which, although it cannot be discerned by a man seeing spiritually on account of the shadow of his flesh, yet his internal spirit seems to exult with affection. Whence it happens that joy, hope, confidence, love, mercy, and humanity follow this action of the heart, which actions are pious, placid, and closest to divinity. Therefore Solomon feels this concerning the dilation of the heart, as also concerning its contraction, in these words: *The exaltation of the eyes is the dilation of the heart; the lamp of the wicked is sin* <note>original: "Exaltatio oculorum est dilatatio cordis, lucerna impiorum peccatum" - a variation of Proverbs 21:4.</note>, as if he had said, the eyes of the celestial spirits contained in the heart are exalted to God by the dilation of the heart, but truly by its contraction, their lamp is sin, that is, darkness and error. Whence also God said: *Who is this who applies his heart that he may approach me?* <note>Jeremiah 30:21</note> which speech can indeed be turned to this sense: Who is he who, by the power and fear of me, and by hope, charity, and joy, will so adapt his heart that he may reach the vision of me? For by good passions and habits the heart is dilated, but by evil and impious ones it is constricted. Hence David says in exultation: *My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and give praise in my glory.* <note>Psalm 108:1</note> That is, my heart is dilated, and by dilation it is made ready, so that by the vision of Thee, who art my glory, I may sing and exult; here, therefore, is the joy of the spirits on account of the heart's dilation, which arose from the intuition of the divine Mind, by the mediation of which the entire spirit of the body is refreshed. Whence the Wise Man says: *A glad heart cheers the face, but by sorrow of the mind the spirit is cast down* <note>Proverbs 15:13</note>, which can indeed be interpreted in this manner: A dilated heart cheers the spirit through the vision of invisible joy; but by the contraction of the heart, sorrow and sadness are produced, which oppress the spirit of life. The Psalmist feels this disposition when he says: *Set your hearts upon his virtue*, that is, spread out and open your hearts, so that you may exult in the Lord. From these things we see that the action of the heart in expansion is the origin of good and pious passions, because through it the celestial spirits, enclosed in the chamber of the heart for the benefit of life, are refreshed by the copious expansion of the heart and by the vision of the mind—both macro- and microcosmic. By this, they are snatched upward from the cares and vexations of earthly disturbances to the contemplations of celestial and <term>supersubstantial</term> <note>Beyond material substance; divine.</note> things, as if by a divine rapture: and in an ecstasy of this kind, they feel no small delight; indeed, Paul and John sometimes experienced this kind of heart action in an instant, when they saw wonderful and ineffable things even unto the third heaven. Therefore, good passions follow such an action of the heart, namely joy or gladness, love and charity, faith, hope, mercy, humanity, piety, humility, etc., all of which tend toward God and divinity and are numbered among the virtues. But the vision by means of which these good passions are rendered conspicuous to the body (though not always) is that of the soul, or the spirits of life, whose seat is in the heart. The eye of the soul, however, by which it beholds God, is the human mind, free from every stain and contagion of the body, to which the Idea of God adheres no differently than a ray of the Sun to the sun, or the image of a thing to a mirror; the gaze of the mind is reason, and its vision is the intellect. It happens, therefore, sometimes, that some of these passions arise in men defiled by sin—namely joy, gladness, hope, love, humanity, etc. But in these, the vision which is the cause of these passions is not discerned because of the darkness of the body weighing down the soul. But in Holy men and Prophets, that blessed vision is very often revealed, as in Paul, John, Elijah, Ezekiel, and others of this kind; which indeed did not happen unless a suitable preparation preceded it. Whence it is required that he who desires to see the vision of God distinctly should have healthy eyes with which to look rightly; and those are said to have healthy eyes whose souls are purged of mortal desires and removed from them. Nor can anyone rightly look spiritually unless he fixes the eyes of his contemplation in the light of God; he sees, therefore, through that contemplation, how great are the joys, how great the gladness, how great the serenity, and how great the delight. Health makes that gaze secure, the aspect makes it right, and the vision makes it blessed: wherefore the soul itself, free from all dregs and washed of stains, then holds itself most freely in itself, and fears nothing for itself or for whatever is done by any fault of its own. And then, with a certain immense and incredible joy or confidence, it proceeds into God, that is, into the contemplation of truth. Thus the soul is first healed; once healed, it finds the valves of the heart open; through them its aspect or vision goes out; having gone out, it is introduced to the divine object; having been introduced, it is refreshed and recreated.

But just as the soul or spirit of life (by means of those intellectual faculties) has its affections by which it is exercised regarding virtues, so also there are present at times passions contrary to them, by which it is disturbed and vexed; and these are called the vices of the spirit or passions depressing the soul. And just as the good passions of the soul or virtues arise from the expansion of the heart, so also its evil passions or vices are accustomed to proceed only from the contraction of the heart—namely sadness, despair, fear, hatred, envy, anger, fury, shame, etc. For where the heart inclines more to contraction than expansion, there the spirit is too much imprisoned in the abyss of the heart, so that they can very rarely reach the vision of the divine mind. Whence the melancholic, furious, and sorrowful soul of life looks toward lower things, since the way to higher things is closed to it, and much more so to those supreme things; it has visions of Demons and is deprived of the divine vision. And so, stirred by passions of this kind, it affects the nature of a <term>cacodemon</term> <note>An evil spirit or demon.</note> no differently than it used to put on the angelic nature in its blessed vision; for, being now deprived of divine grace, it seems to taste the bitterness of darkness and to be subjected to the rage of elementary demons, to be vibrated and agitated by hypochondriac winds and turbulent waves of the air, and to be afflicted by mania, insanity, fear, sadness, despair, fury, and the like, and is accustomed to be deluded by false and deceptive visions. Hence it is said: *He shall give thee a trembling heart, and failing eyes, and a soul consumed with sorrow, and*

<margin>Deuteronomy 28:67 <note>original: "Deut. 28. 67."</note></margin>

<margin>Job 21:4</margin> *My spirit is narrowed within me.* And the royal Psalmist says: *My spirit is consumed and I become like those descending into the sepulcher*, that is, my spirit is covered over with darkness; Wherefore the Wise Man also says, *that the way of the impious is dark, and they know not where they may fall*, whence we find it written elsewhere: *Their soul fails and is provoked even unto death*. Moreover, the reason for this error of the soul is due to the hindrance of its vision; for it is blind because of the darkness of the closed heart, and it cannot see, and this is gathered from many places in the sacred scriptures: *Blind (says GOD) the heart of this people, lest they understand with their heart.* And elsewhere: *All saw him and were troubled, etc.* and when the wind ceased they were even more amazed among themselves, for their heart was blinded, that is, they could not see the vision of truth because of the contraction of the heart. And elsewhere: *This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.* And elsewhere: *They did not glorify Him as God, or give thanks, but they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened.* And elsewhere: *According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God.* From which it is explained clearly enough that these passions—namely, fear, error from lack of vision, sadness or sorrow of the soul, despair and distrust, the narrowing of the spirits, the darkness of the soul, and the deceptive delusions of its failure, perversities or obstinacy, blindness, and its separation from divine contemplations—proceed from this dark and ill-fated action of the heart, namely, its long-lasting contraction; that is, when it is inclined more toward contraction than toward dilation, whence it happens that the spirit of life is covered in darkness, and does not know how to judge rightly of divine things, according to that saying of the Wise Man; *The body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that muses upon many things, and we hardly guess aright at the things that are upon earth, and with labor do we find the things that are before us, but who shall search out the things that are in heaven, and who shall know your counsel, unless you give wisdom, and send your Holy Spirit from the highest, etc.*

We conclude, therefore, that by the first passions arising from the dilation of the heart, the ethereal spirits in the heart adhere to super-celestial things, but by the last ones derived from the contraction of the heart, they are made close to sublunary <note>earthly/material</note> things: Thus we also see the celestial nature participate at will sometimes in the empyrean <note>highest heaven</note> nature, and sometimes in the elementary nature; if its spirits descend downward, it mingles itself with wicked demons, but truly visiting the super-celestial kingdoms, it participates in the angelic nature. This same ratio exists between the spirit of life in man, and his intellectual spirit in the brain, and that natural spirit in the liver; for as the spirit of life vivifies invisibly, so that natural spirit in the liver causes visible growth. Whence it is denoted that it belongs to the part of the flesh and the elementary kingdom: But that action of the heart, which is in the middle between these two extremes, is that which participates equally in both extremes, so that it may serve only the necessity of life, and in this work is the relation of the middle to both extremes, namely, of the nature of the middle heaven or ether to that nature of the empyrean or angelic heaven, and again its respect to the elementary nature: From the super-celestial heaven, therefore, it draws the intellectual spirit; the ethereal part holds the vital soul in itself, and is carried in the sublunary air with its super-celestial soul, and finally is enclosed in the opaque body for the complete composition of man. Hence it is that by the motion of the heart, which is the seat of the middle spirit—namely, by Diastole <note>expansion</note>—the soul dilates itself, so that it may incessantly attract to itself its like, both the rational from the empyrean heaven wandering everywhere in the air, and the vital from its ethereal kingdom, that is, from the higher regions (which action is completed by the dilation of the heart), as well as by its Systole <note>contraction</note> by means of which, by contracting, it separates the impure from the pure. Whence it is clear that the action of life imitates the action of the World Soul, or the primary emanation from Jehovah which the ancients (skilled in occult Theology) called the World Soul and the Messiah, that is, the power of the Tetragrammaton <note>the four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>, which the Cabalists made the angel Metatron or Michael, who has command over the malignant angels who are enemies of human life: By the dilation of its principal organ, therefore, the soul attracts friendship and the gifts of life and reason from heaven, namely, by means of the Diastole motion, as a bellows draws air to itself, by which it provides the food of life to the wasting fire; following which it may always burn in its vigor, where the breathing man is like the soul of life, the agitated bellows are likened to the lungs, and the air drawn into the bellows is the same in kind as that drawn into the lungs; as therefore the air drawn by a man by means of bellows nourishes the flame of an external and artificial fire, so also similar air drawn by the heart by means of the lungs preserves life and succors the fire of internal life and the natural flame with successive replenishment, by the growth and preservation of which man proceeds and progresses in his state of living. The soul is therefore, in this nod of life, the internal agent or formal principle as far as we are concerned, just as its internal agent is the mind or the word. The instrumental causes are the heart and lung, the material cause is the essential part of the air, and the effect is life, whence it follows that the involuntary motion called Diastole, through the dilation of its organ, attracts the benevolence of God (which, as sacred Scripture testifies, *is life and being*), and Systole, by contracting, expels the useless parts of the introduced air, not otherwise than a flame of fire selects for itself the pure from that air blown to it by bellows for its nourishment, but expels the impure and superfluous in the form of useless smoke: The heart, therefore, is to be cared for above all things, just as the Wise Man teaches us...

# Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book IV.

<margin>Proverbs 4:23.</margin> The Wise Man says in a discourse of this kind: *Keep thy heart with all diligence, for out of it proceed the issues of life.* <note>Original: "Omni custodia conserua cor tuum, quia ex illa vita procedit."</note> From this, therefore, a great mystery in nature is explained: namely, that in this motion of life, measured by the nature of the pulsation, it is necessary that an equality be created. This is no different than how we see the ethereal heaven hold an equal position between the empyrean <note>The highest heaven of pure fire/light</note> and the elementary realms, since the temperament of life and the elements consists of such a quality. For if the equality of this motion is corrupted, or fails in its beat, it is necessary that an error also occurs in the bond of the four elements, which is the **quintessence** <note>The "fifth essence" or ether that binds the four physical elements</note>; for this quintessence in its nature agrees with every quality of the elements, and consequently lives peacefully with them, binding them to one another in harmonious peace.

For the strength of life lies as much in the unequal attraction of light similar to itself as in the expulsion of the superfluous darkness of the opposite nature. Hence it happens that when the **systole** <note>The contraction of the heart/lungs; the out-breath</note> is weakened, while the **diastole** <note>The expansion of the heart/lungs; the in-breath</note> remains in its native state, nature is burdened with superfluities. In this case, there is a strong introduction of waste but a weak expulsion of it, so that although the natural heat may be at its natural level, nevertheless sooty and empty vapors tend to produce **orthopnea** and **dyspnea** <note>Technical terms for difficulty breathing while lying down and general shortness of breath</note> and act preternaturally. Even in these cases, or without them, fevers are excited because of the rot contracted from corrupt, useless, and empty air remaining in the body. This air ought to be expelled through expiration, but by its thickness, it tends to suffocate and block the convenient passages of life, and by its useless nature, it easily turns to corruption.

From this comes an equality of pulses combined with swiftness, due to the narrowing and compression in the blockage; hence the origin and beginning of fevers and acute diseases, whether putrid or contagious, which physicians to this day have not perceived. For where the expulsive force is not in the celestial fire of life, there **Michael**—who is the Prince of Life and the expeller of malignant spirits—rests from his office (by Divine will) on account of the sins of men. Whence demons contrary to nature, who dwell in the superfluous and least useful air (that is, the more "empty" air), take possession of the human spirit. Thus they become the authors of breathing difficulties, febrile conditions, or other diseases, according to the winds and elements most agreeable to these wicked demons.

This, therefore, is the inequality of the action of life, or of the celestial action. Since this balance is disposed by nature in both the **macrocosm** <note>The universe</note> and the **microcosm** <note>The human being</note>, it is necessary that if men depart from this nature, the habit of life behaves not naturally, but preternaturally. Furthermore, if the motion of the systole is longer and more lasting in its time than the diastole, it follows that wicked spirits and adversaries of life hold great dominion over such a sick person; for little food of life is attracted, but much superfluous air is retained with its spirits, the children of darkness, and consequently enemies to life and light. Diseases of this nature are for the most part "cold" diseases, or indeed mixed and melancholic diseases.

Whence it is evident that the motion of the heart, tending toward the exact disposition of a healthy life, ought to be equal in Diastole and Systole. The middle point between these two motions is that rest which refers to the nature of the middle heaven, in which there is an equal portion of **radical moisture** and **innate heat** <note>The two fundamental fluids/forces believed to sustain life in medieval medicine</note>. In their equality consists the Sabbath or rest of life. Just as the systole relates to the aerial or elementary heaven, the Diastole dilates and extends itself toward that super-celestial or empyrean realm (from which intellectual spirits descend), by means of which motion the intellectual light of God and the vivifying spirit of nature is enticed and attracted into the chamber of the heart.

In the strength of the Diastole, therefore, Michael performs his office in the expulsion of wicked and useless spirits from the human heaven, who without his assistance would bring ruin to life and its functions. The Diastole joins forces to forces by a natural path; hence nature rejoices in its own nature and is exalted; hence animal life is continued and preserved. The Diastole brings in and introduces confused and unrefined matter into the left ventricle of the heart; the Systole purges and prepares it, and finally expels the thick dregs; while the rest between these two retains the tested and purified matter as most suitable for the functions of life. And this exact operation of nature consists in the equality of these motions, which also denotes the concord of the elements and the firmness of the bond of nature, which is made through that virtue of life derived from heaven. But if there is inequality in the progress of these motions, it argues for an inequality of the elements and a violation of that natural bond, which infirmities follow—which are nothing other than distempers arising from the inequality of motion.

Here, however, a question may arise: in the beginning of life, does the Diastole or the Systole claim the first place? To this doubt we can respond, and not without consideration, that the Diastole claims preeminence in life, because it is necessary that attraction occurs before any expulsion is made, or before any expulsion can be possible. This is proven from the words of Holy Scripture, where we find: <margin>Genesis 2:7.</margin> *God breathed into the face of the earthly Adam the breath of life, who then was made into a living soul.* From this it is clear that the inspiration and the elevation of the lung were prior to the expiration or the depression of the lung, and consequently that the motion of the Diastole was prior in its act to that of the systole: for it is necessary that bellows first receive air before they can breathe it out.

We have gathered a certain notable observation concerning life or death in the extreme danger of the sick from the action of these heart motions as they relate indifferently to one another. For both I and others have noticed, in the extreme danger of death and in the "last gasp," as it were, that if the inspiration or motion of Diastole is long, and the systole very short, the patient often lives, where the disease is from a defect of innate heat. The reason for this is at hand: namely, because the native heat still left in the body of the sick person acts strongly in attracting its like to itself, and by that which is thus attracted, its failing vigor is so multiplied and refreshed that it is now able to resist the wicked spirits opposed to life, and thus is mostly restored to former health. But if the motion of the systole, by which expiration occurs, is long, and the Diastole short and sudden, this indeed is the greatest sign of death, since the native heat, already weak, [spends] its strength even more in the strong expulsion of superfluities...

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Heart.

<note>The author is discussing the "combustion" of the vital spirit in melancholic temperaments.</note> It weighs upon and consumes [the spirit] through heat, and because of its weakness in attraction, it seizes almost nothing celestial for itself by which it might be refreshed and increased; hence it happens that it is gradually extinguished. From this also arises the reason for the double respiration in Melancholics: namely, because the inhaled air or "sooty wind" is not totally exhaled, whereby the fullness hinders inhalation, forcing nature to redouble its force and action. So we also see that when the stomach is filled with vapors, the swallowing of food is hindered, so that one must swallow two or three times before the sustenance can be drawn down through the esophagus to the bottom of the stomach by means of the straight fibers.

Finally, upon these foundations, we can firmly consider, first, what kind of angels those are who have power over the internal man, likewise how many they are, and what their offices are. We have spoken abundantly of these in the preceding booklet on the *Mysteries of the Sperm*, and also in our *Genethlialogical* <note>Relating to the calculation of horoscopes or nativities.</note> treatise (which we dealt with in the *Technical History of the Microcosm*). Thus, as we see three actions occurring in the heart—of which the highest consists only in **dilation**, the middle in **dilation and contraction** together, and the lowest in **contraction** alone—so also it is very easily discerned that each of these actions has a respect or relation to the three regions of the world: namely, the **Empyrean** or super-celestial, the **Ethereal** or celestial, and the **elemental** or sublunary.

For pious, good, and just passions (which are produced by the dilation of the heart) belong to the angelic nature, and consequently are governed by the "super-fatal" angel <note>An angel existing above the realm of Fate or destiny.</note>, the guardian of the mind, whose proper dwelling is in the super-celestial kingdom. By means of this angel (as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on theurgy and the soul.</note> testifies), we perform such things as he brings into the mind, and he governs us to that extent, until we exchange the dominion of the sacred prefect for a demon. Then this angel, yielding to God, ceases from the work or leads to the same.

Furthermore, the actions of a balanced life (which are excited by the equal dilation and contraction of the heart together as if by instruments) proceed primarily from the **Olympic** or "fatal" angel (having dominion in the celestial world). This angel is subject to that angel who is the guardian of the mind, and he has care of the soul or life in no other way than his superior is the director of the mind. Whence the aforementioned Iamblichus says (wrongly attributing only a single demon to the internal man): <margin>Iamblichus</margin> *This demon existed in the archetype before the soul fell into generation; as soon as the soul received him as a leader, the demon stands by it, the fulfiller of lives, and binds the descending soul to the body. He himself cares for its common animal nature, directs the soul's own life, and whatever we reason, he provides the principles of reasoning; we do such things as he brings into the mind, and he governs us, until, purified by sacred works, we have God as our leader instead of a demon, etc.*

And certainly, we most rightly acknowledge with Iamblichus that the later actions are ascribed to the primary angel or the angel of the mind. But that he is also the *immediate* guardian of life, we utterly deny, because we see that the actions of life and mind are sometimes different. Whence the "middle soul" is said by the **Platonists** to neglect the mind and adhere to the animal soul or sublunary nature. For if only a single angel were attributed to the mind, the soul, and the spirit, it would follow that the operations of one and the other would always be in agreement. Experience teaches us this is false, demonstrating that Sadness, Joy, Hope, Despair, Envy, and Hatred are entirely opposites; of these, a single action—namely, dilation—is derived from the super-celestial nature, while contraction is derived from the sublunary.

We conclude, therefore, that the angel of the mind is one, and the angel of the soul is another. But we say the angel of the soul is subject to the angel of the mind in no other way than the soul itself is subject to the mind, of which it is the vehicle. And although the celestial angel or "Olympic demon" has that angel of the mind as his prince, yet he is sometimes found rebellious and perverse toward his prince, according to that saying: <margin>God. Job 4:17-18</margin> *Behold, those who serve him are not stable and firm, and in his angels he found wickedness.* <note>original: "Ecce qui serviunt non sunt stabiles & firmi, & in angelis suis reperit Deus pravitatem." A reference to the Book of Job.</note>

Hence the Platonists recognized three things in the internal man:
1.  The **Mind** (*Mens*), which is his highest part, corresponding to the Empyrean heaven.
2.  The **Spirit** (*Spiritus*) in the middle, the vital soul linking the lowest with the highest, whence it participates in both. They want this portion to differ from the supreme one as life differs from intellect in spiritual things, and as the heart differs from the brain in material things (which are vessels fit to receive these two gifts of the heavens). It also differs from the lower as celestial things differ from elemental ones.
3.  The **Animal or Sensible Soul**, which is composed of elemental spirit.

They conclude, therefore, that the **Mind** never consents to evil, always resists error, and exhorts to the best things. But the lowest portion is always submerged in evil, sin, and concupiscence, and draws toward the worst; for Paul felt this when he said: *I see another law in my members, and leading me captive in the law of sin.* <note>Romans 7:23</note> They say the Mind is never damned, but when its companions are punished, it departs unharmed to its own region. They believe the **Middle Spirit**, since it is free by nature, can adhere to either extreme at will. They say that if this middle nature constantly adheres to the higher (the Mind), it is finally united to it and blessed until it passes to God. But if, neglecting the Mind, it inclines to the lower portion, they assert it is depraved and corrupted until it becomes an evil demon.

From these things, it is gathered that the portions of these three natures in one man are diverse from each other, and consequently, they have leaders of various conditions presiding over them. Of these demons, the one who possesses the care of the lower portion is the worst, and is, as it were, a born **evil genius**, just as the superior is called his **good genius** or **Archangel**. We could expand this discourse infinitely, for the field of discussion is so wide; but truly, since other things call us away, leaving the spiritual heart and its actions, we shall say a few words about the material heart.

### CHAPTER VII.

->*Concerning the material heart, its instruments, and the method of its nutrition.*<-

Those of us learned in the experience of anatomy <note>The author refers to the practice of dissection and physical observation</note> observe that, just as the left ventricle of the heart is occupied with invisible spirits and directs its entire intention toward the creation of those vital forces, so too is it the duty of the right ventricle not only to build, support, and repair the material elements of the heart, but also to establish, nourish, and maintain the "fan" <note>original: *flabellum*; referring here to the lungs, which act as a cooling bellows for the heart</note> of the same in a healthy state. For that same motion in the heart which proceeds toward its dilation, called **Diastole**, besides the introduction of aerial spirit, draws blood from the *vena cava* into its right ventricle. During the time of rest, that introduced blood is prepared and thinned; its denser and heavier part passes through a small branch of the *vena cava* ascending toward the base of the heart—which is called the **coronary**—to the nourishment of the heart's substance. By means of this small branch, the venous blood ordained for nourishment is dispersed through the entire material heart, not unlike how, on the opposite side, a small branch proceeding from the **aorta** (before it exits the heart) imbues it with the invisible spirits of life. This latter process serves the vivification <note>giving of life/animation</note> of the substance, just as the branch from the *vena cava* serves those natural parts destined for nutrition.

However, the thinner portion of the blood prepared and thinned within the heart is transferred through three semi-lunar valves, by means of the "arterial vein" <note>The pulmonary artery</note>, into the substance of the lung (the heart's fan) for its growth, preservation, and nutrition, where it disperses itself everywhere through small branches or streams. In this manner, this principal organ is established and repaired, assisted in its work by the lung. The heart, therefore, prepares for itself both the spiritual and material nourishment by which it is sustained and exists in its state, and it preserves its instruments or bellows in their being, without which it is plainly crippled and deficient in its work.

Therefore, while these organs of life persist in their integrity, the entire "microcosmic machine" <note>The human body viewed as a miniature universe</note> is both irrigated by the spirits of life and everywhere vivified and illuminated by the rays of native heat. This is no different than the presence of the Sun; because the Sun draws from God, as from a fountain, its very being by which the entire world is sustained, so the heart draws its life, its being, its light, its spirit, and its whole self from God, and thereafter liberally nourishes everything contained within its world. Just as that Sun of the visible world (which **Plato** calls the *visible son of God*) is the exemplar of His invisible Son, or the uncreated spirit and light or emanation, so also the visible heart has its own spiritual counterpart in whose likeness it is formed. We call the invisible part the spirit of the thing, in which the soul dwells, just as the mind dwells in the soul, and the Word dwells in the mind—to speak with **Hermes Trismegistus**. And it is from this that the mystical teachers of the Hebrews and the doctors of the **Cabalists** agree: namely, that all lower things are representations <margin>of higher things; and as it is done below, so it is also acted above.</margin> But now, in this place, we shall briefly and somewhat abruptly dissolve our discourse on the heart, so that with a gentle leap we may pass across to the mysteries of the brain.

### CHAPTER I.

->*Wherein the Brain in the microcosm is compared to the Empyrean Heaven of the Macrocosm, both in its position and its function.*<-

---

<margin>Psalm 68:34 <note>The verse refers to God riding upon the "heavens of heavens."</note></margin>
<margin>Pimander 12.</margin>
<margin>Pimander 10. <note>Refers to the "Poimandres," a foundational text of Hermeticism attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note></margin>
Mercurius Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> recognized that the Mind is the presiding ruler of the vital soul; he also says that the celestial or vital soul has the same relationship to the elementary spirit (which is subject to it) as the soul has to the Mind, to which it usually offers similar obedience. Plotinus <note>original: "Photinus" - likely a variant or error for Plotinus, the major Neoplatonic philosopher.</note>, therefore, along with the other Platonists, recognized and established three parts in the internal man: namely, the highest, the lowest, and the middle. By that highest part, they understand the divine element, which they called the Mind or the illuminated Intellect, and they made this Mind the superior portion of the internal man. This is what Moses intended to signify by the "breath of life" <note>original: "vitarum spiraculum"</note> breathed into us by God or by His spirit. 

Just as in the external man the brain claims the third or highest place for itself—being enclosed on all sides by a bony, almost stone-like fortress—so also the interior of the brain is the intellectual world, in which Mind and Reason reign. This is no different from how the Word of God and His rational creatures (namely the angels) have their seat in the third or highest heaven, which is therefore called "intellectual and rational" by Bede, Isidore, and others. The spiritual brain is, as it were, the soul to that material brain; and just as we find in Holy Scripture that Mount Zion is the holy rock in which God dwells, so also within the walls of this towering rock, the illuminated Intellect has its seat and dominion in its empyrean spirit. 

For as the Empyrean Heaven <note>The highest heaven in ancient cosmology, believed to be composed of pure fire or light and the dwelling place of God.</note> relates to the celestial and Elementary realms, so also must the spiritual brain be considered in respect to those spiritual regions subject to it, namely the Thorax <note>the chest</note> and the abdomen. For just as God is said to have His habitation in the heaven of heavens of the macrocosm <note>the great world/universe</note>, so the Mind, or the breath of life, possesses its throne in the highest region of the microcosm <note>the little world/human being</note>, namely at the very summit of the whole body. 

Insofar, then, as the spiritual brain is the seat of intellect and reason, it is certain that it claims for itself that very place in the microcosm which the spirit of the Empyrean heaven holds in the macrocosm. Furthermore, it is said that God breathed the breath of life into Adam’s face—not into his chest or belly, but into the highest portion of man, which He chose as the seat for His divine breath, like the "heaven of heavens of old" in which He Himself sits. 

From these points, we think it has been explained clearly enough that the brain holds the primary place not only in location, but also in dominion and dignity, over both the heart (situated in the middle region of the microcosm) and the liver (which is the prince of its lowest region). This is because the rational soul of the brain has power over both the vital soul (whose palace is the heart) and the natural soul which reigns in the liver. Hence, Mercurius Trismegistus says: *Whichever souls the Mind presides over, it illuminates them with its brightness, resisting their evil habits.* From this he concludes elsewhere that a soul deprived of the presence of the Mind is able neither to do nor to say anything. Thus it is clear that, as the Mind excels the soul in dignity, it follows that its dwelling place—namely the brain—must be placed many degrees above that soul. From which it is right to gather that the brain in the microcosm has the same status in its arrangement as the empyrean heaven has in the greater world.
