### Chapter II.

### *Concerning the mystery of the choroid plexus, and the wonderful effort of nature in the reduction of material and coarse blood into that which is subtle and spiritual; by which we are taught that her endeavor is to lead earthly things back into a celestial nature.*

Those more skilled in Anatomy, equipped with a most relevant observation, say that the choroid or "choriform" plexus in the brain—which Laurentius <note>André du Laurens (1558–1609), a prominent French anatomist</note>, on account of its stupendous structure, called the *wonderful* network, and Columbus <note>Matteo Realdo Colombo (1516–1559), an Italian anatomist who described pulmonary circulation</note> called the *reticular plexus*—takes its origin from the "wonderful network" <note>original: *rete mirabile*</note> woven from the *pia mater* <note>The delicate innermost membrane surrounding the brain</note>. For it is composed of a labyrinthine texture of small veins and arteries running through a small portion of thin membrane. Regarding its position, we are taught that this membrane or web is located in the anterior ventricles of the brain, in which it floats upon the clear fluid contained within them, not unlike how we see the heart swimming in the fluid of the pericardial sac. 

They believe this plexus is useful for expiration, inspiration, and the breathing of air into the anterior ventricles; for the brain moves through contraction and expansion <note>original: *Systole & Diastole*</note> just like the heart. This occurs so that the animal spirits <note>The "fine" fluids believed to carry thought and sensation</note>—which are still coarse and like smoke while contained in this plexus—may be cooked, prepared, altered, and thinned before they reach the "natural sense" or third ventricle. In that place, the preparation of said spirits is finished and perfected, so that they may be passed to the fourth or final ventricle. Columbus, among others, therefore concludes that the use of these parts is destined chiefly for the generation of the animal spirits.

In the second book of this work, where we treated the mysteries of the blood—specifically in Chapter 3, in which we explained the chemical laboratory of Nature in the microcosm <note>The human body viewed as a miniature version of the universe</note> with its vessels—we demonstrated that there are three evident vessels or organs. By their mediation, Nature always separates the pure juice from the impure in a subtle manner and transmits each separated element of the mass into its own proper receptacle. Each of these vessels has preeminence over the other according to the dignity of its work: namely, the liver (which is the second vessel of natural Alchemy) over the stomach (which is its first vessel); and the heart (which is its third vessel) over the liver; and these choriform plexuses (which are held in the highest place of nature's laboratory) over the heart. 

For the stomach—which is nature's circulatory vessel, placed in the lowest part or the viscera (not of horses, but of humans) for the purpose of purifying its subject—is that hidden organ in which the first extraction of pure chyle-like nourishment from the impure fecal matter occurs. Their final separation happens in the intestines through a filtration performed by the mesenteric vessels. This is no different than how we see a skilled chemist, using a preceding circulation in a bath, separate and extract the spirit of wine <note>Alcohol/Ethanol</note> with its phlegm from its dregs. 

And just as we see this "water of life" <note>original: *aqua vitæ*</note>, still impure and mixed with its own wateriness, placed in a second vessel and exposed to the dew of the bath so that the purer spirit of wine may be divided from its impure and watery parts, so too is the chyle-like matter (divided from the earthly dregs by the filter) cooked in its second vessel—the liver—which is more tender and delicate than the first. This is done by the mediation of the visceral vapor surrounding the liver. In this cooking, the watery mass is separated from that which is airy or bloody, and is expelled downward into the "sea of the bladder" through the kidneys. The coarse blood, likened to coarse air, is poured out everywhere through the body to nourish its coarse members.

Furthermore, for an even more exact purging of the spirit of the vein from its wateriness, it must be placed into a third vessel more worthy than the others: the heart. From there, as that blood of the first preparation rises through the ascending *vena cava*, a portion of it is sent into the right chamber of the heart. There, it is circulated by the fire of the "third regime" (likened to the heat of the sun) and thinned into a more fiery nature, so that the blood thus purified may serve as light food for the lungs. It behaves like the pure, visible spirit of wine, while the "airy dregs" (which are also thinned and purified by this kind of boiling) run to the nourishment of the vessel itself, namely the heart. 

From these things, it should be noted:
1. The dregs of the first operation in the stomach are **earthy**, and their receptacle is the colon.
2. The dregs of the second operation (in the Liver) are **watery**, and their receptacle is the bladder; this is called the serum of the blood.
3. The dregs of the third operation are **air**, and are useful for the nutrition of the heart's substance.
Finally, the purified portion of both the arterial and venous blood ascends to the brain and constitutes those reticular plexuses or textures there.

Here it must be observed with diligence: just as the elements of wine naturally seek the regions destined for them by nature—as has been proven by us through experience and explained in the physical history of the macrocosm and microcosm, where we depicted water floating on earth, air above water, fire above air, and the quintessence or celestial element above fire (an enclosed experiment whose subject was wine, which I once dedicated to our most Serene King, not without his great admiration)—so also the celestial part of the blood seeks the third and highest region of man by a natural inclination. The fiery part holds the middle region, and the lowest region contains the air. These, descending invisibly through the great artery into the arterial seminal vessels, produce the seed of the sperm, which is the soul, or the internal man being generated. From this it is clear that the effigy of this generated being was first invisibly depicted or fabricated in the spiritual workshop of the brain of both parents before it was brought forth into a visible act. Do we not also forge visions and strong imaginations, both in sleep and in waking, which arise from the false air inspired through the nostrils, or from that air enclosed in ill-tempered blood? Therefore, the Wise Man wishes this to be understood concerning spiritual generation where he says: <margin>Wisdom 4:1.</margin> *Chaste generation is immortal in memory, for it is known before God and men.*

### Chapter IV.
#### *On the most spiritual regeneration, which produces the infants of reason and intellect.*

**J**ust as the intellect and reason are far more eminent in dignity than sense and motion, so it is necessary that a twofold spirit—one more worthy than the other—be required to perform these two functions of the soul. For one shall behave as the soul to the body, and the other as the body to the soul. For as sense and motion are closest to corporeal things (since they are immediately concerned with bodies), so also reason and intellect are neighbors to the spiritual things of the highest kind and are occupied in the contemplation of **Ideas**. Therefore, for sense and motion, animal spirits of a coarser disposition are required, whereas for reason and intellect, thinner and purer ones are needed. Thus, as the ethereal spirits relate to those empyrean and supracelestial ones, or as the airy ones relate to the ethereal, so also those animal spirits which work to fulfill the duties of sense and motion relate to those which are occupied with rational and intellectual matters. For the spirits of the heaven in the **macrocosm** <note>The universe as a whole.</note>—the empyrean spirits (which are also called intellectual)—are related to the animal spirits in the **microcosm** <note>The human being as a "little world."</note> in respect to the purity of both.

From this it is clear that the entire animal spirit, or **animal sperm** (which is invisible), is prepared in the **choroid plexus** and perfected in the third ventricle. In every way, it is assimilated to the visible sperm destined for material generation. Just as visible sperm is composed of a coarse part, called *sperma*, and a most subtle part, called *semen*—the former concurring to the constitution of the body or the external man, the latter to the soul or the internal man—so indeed the invisible or animal sperm is fused from a coarse spirit (which is more concerned with the senses) and that most subtle spirit (which tends toward the operations of the intellect). Therefore, from the **quintessence** <note>The "fifth element," the purest and most refined part of a substance.</note> alone of this spirit or animal sperm is the reason or intellect excited; and from both together, motion and sense are driven.

The sperm of motion and sense is therefore prepared by the choroid plexus and finished in the third ventricle. Passing through the opening from the third ventricle to the fourth between the *nates*—namely, through the "anus" <note>An anatomical term for the opening into the cerebral aqueduct.</note>—this whole animal sperm is sent in. Its more spiritual part is separated by hidden organs and reserved in the cell of memory. The remainder is diffused through the nerves into the whole body to produce the faculties of sensing and moving. For the spirit primarily enters the nerves by penetrating them to provide the faculty of the senses: namely, to the optic nerves for the sake of seeing; to the fifth pair of nerves for the sake of hearing; and to the third pair, by which taste operates; and so in the rest. From here also, motion and touch are bestowed upon every member of the body, both through the said nerves and especially through the sixth pair (which carries the power of both sense and motion to all the viscera of the thorax and abdomen), and through the spinal cord, the root of which begins in the *calamus scriptorius* <note>Latin: "writing pen"; a pen-shaped structure in the fourth ventricle of the brain.</note>, that is, in the posterior angle of the fourth ventricle.

That this kind of spirit destined for sense and motion is of a more servile and inferior condition than that of reason or intellect is clearly delineated by this: namely, because reason, shining in the light of the **agent intellect** through the middle of the "theater of the brain," sits in the tribunal chair like an upright judge. It commands like a king in his kingdom and judges concerning the desired object: whether it be useful or not? Whether it should be pursued with hatred or affected with love? The common spirit, however, fills the place of a messenger, who carries the commands of reason downward through the mediation of the nerves to the muscles. Finally, the muscles, agitated by the animal spirits and as if illuminated by intellectual rays, strive to perform and fulfill the commands of their prince or queen. Whence it is evident that the spirits of reason are more worthy than the rest, and hold eminence over the other species of animal spirits, no differently than the spirit of the Sun over those of the other stars, or as the element of fire possesses dominion over the other elements. The more subtle (I say) and more imperial part of the first animal sperm is reserved in the sanctuary of memory for the use of royal reason; and that part, thus enclosed in the hidden chest of memory, is again prepared into a sperm of the highest degree of spirituality by the most secret ways and means.

### CHAPTER V.

#### *Concerning certain organs found in the Brain which refer to those of Carnal generation: And how it is probable that they contribute to the generation of the third or supreme order.*

Those well-versed in anatomy recognize, and we also understand, being taught by experience, that behind the "furnace" <note>likely referring to the third ventricle or the heat of the vital spirits</note> at the edge of the brain toward the cerebellum, and at the boundaries of the posterior part of the third ventricle, certain prominent parts are seen, bearing the likeness of testes or testicles. Whence they have not undeservedly claimed the name of "testes" from the Anatomists. Near these testes, two other small parts present themselves, a little larger and more elevated than the former, which because of their shape are called the *clunes* <note>buttocks; referring to the corpora quadrigemina</note>. Between these is situated that hole or entrance which leads from the third to the fourth ventricle (where the seat of memory is), and this passage is marked with the name of the *anus* because of its similarity to the same. Furthermore, in the anterior part of the testicles extending toward the third ventricle, another small portion of the brain presents itself, which expresses the image of the female pubes or *vulva* not unsuitably, but indeed quite elegantly. Moreover, near this small body, a somewhat hard gland is seen, different in color from the substance of the brain—that is, somewhat yellowish—covered by a certain thin membrane; and this gland is attached to the *torcular* <note>the "wine-press" or confluence of sinuses</note> and has the shape of a penis or virile member. From all of these things, one may see (and it is so named by similarity) that around this same location of the brain, all the members of generation are present, or at least the likenesses of the genital members: namely the testes, buttocks, anus, vulva, and the penis itself. These are arranged among themselves in this place no differently than the members destined for carnal generation in the lowest region of the body.

As for the utility of these parts thus arranged in the brain, authors seem to disagree and are hardly consistent with themselves. For Columbus <note>Matteo Realdo Colombo (c. 1516–1559), a famous Italian anatomist</note> thought the penis was ordained by nature for the division of vessels. Others feel it was created by nature so that through it, like a stopper, the animal spirits or sperm of the first degree might be enclosed in the fourth ventricle. Others say it is for preserving the species of memory, etc. Concerning the use of the other small parts, they could judge nothing at all, and (as if nature had made anything in vain) they treated them as if useless and superfluous. Regarding the use of the penis according to Columbus's opinion, certainly its shape, varied color, the covering of the thin membrane, and finally its attachment to the *torcular*, must denote some other hidden use than merely being ordained for the division and partitioning of vessels, or serving as a stopper according to the opinions of others, since we see that office performed in many parts of the body by a mechanism far different from this. Furthermore, why do these small parts agree so much in location, shape, and arrangement with the testes, anus, buttocks, and vulva placed near them, unless they have a hidden relationship to those instruments of bodily generation—not only in shape, but also in action and property? Or, since the other members are arranged according to the disposition of this penis or "little rod," why is some particular use attributed to this one and not to those, since nature has made nothing in vain?

Indeed, I, instructed by probable demonstration, have been forced into this opinion: namely, that the buttocks and anus, as well as the testes and the rod, have a secret power in spiritual and rational generation. Specifically, the anus and buttocks serve for the secretion of the coarse animal sperm from the subtle part of the same, after that spiritual sperm of the first degree has been completed in the third ventricle. Its thicker part is extended for sense and motion through the nerves and spinal marrow; the subtle part is hidden and reserved in the secret chests of memory, which is contiguous to the *torcular* to which the penis is attached. Whence perhaps this thin or intellectual sperm, penetrating through secret and inscrutable passages in the testes, is rightly prepared in them, conducted to the surface of the *torcular*, and once conducted, is cast by the penis into the vulva...

...produced images of this kind in the brain for the same reason, since the form of an external thing paints the image of the internal. For in this way, God is declared through his creatures—that is, through demonstration *a posteriori* <note>reasoning from effects back to causes</note>—and in this same way the soul is depicted through its body; for as has been frequently alleged above: *All lower things are representative of the higher, etc.* As it is below, so it is conducted above. Whence by the "higher heaven" the spirit of a thing is denoted, and by the "lower" its internal or visible part; for there is nothing external and visible which does not have its internal and invisible likeness from which it proceeds. For the Apostle says: <margin>To the Hebrews 11</margin> *It has always been done in the world through the Word of God, so that from those things which could not be seen, those things which can be seen were made.* Finally, three such generations in the body are declared by their effect: for the effect of the bodily seed is the visible or elementary man; the effect of the invisible generation of the first degree is the "phantastic" <note>the faculty of phantasia or mental imaging</note> and that which is depicted in the imagination, whose species <note>mental forms or appearances</note> are diffused everywhere into the body through both the internal and external senses, as well as through motion. This "infant" is a medium between the sensible and the intelligible, just as the heaven of the macrocosm is situated as a medium between the elementary and the ethereal realms. For the generated body is an element; the procreated phantastic part is likened to the matter of heaven; and finally, the offspring of reason or intellect possesses an angelic composition within itself. Thus, an element is reduced into heaven by dissolution, and the nature of heaven puts on an angelic form by refinement and purification: not otherwise than how the thick and elementary blood of the liver, with that first and ethereal blood of the heart, produces by refinement the "animal seed" of the first degree—that complex choroid <note>the vascular membrane in the brain</note> which is made from vein and artery. And this same substance is reduced to its ethereal likeness, through the *rete mirabile* <note>the "wonderful net," a network of blood vessels at the base of the brain</note>, by refinement into the spiritual seed of the final degree. We have here, therefore, a sensible generation attributed to the body, we have that phantastic one assigned to the imagination, and finally, the generation destined for reason claims the highest place for itself. But Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with Hermetic philosophy</note> also seems to declare this clearly in these words: *The idea of the body is air; of air, the soul; of the soul, the intellect; and of the intellect, God. God, therefore, is around all things; the intellect or mind is around the soul; the soul is around the air; and the air is around matter. Through matter, he denotes the effect of the first generation; through air, the phantastic faculty, in which spirit the soul acts, penetrating by refinement to the intellect, which reaches to divinity itself.*

### CHAPTER VI.

#### *On the excellence of the eye, and on the notable mystery of the pupil.*

<margin>Numbers 22</margin>
<margin>Matthew 13:13</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 4:25</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 15:3</margin>
<margin>Job 10:4</margin>
How great is the nobility of the eyes, how great their power, and how great and many are the mysteries to be contemplated in them—and that they are as much spiritual as they are corporeal—we are taught even by the Holy Scriptures. Indeed, the difference in the nature of the eye is no less than that between this temporary bread and that spiritual bread which is the Word; or between heaven and earth. This we also draw from Genesis chapter 3:5, where it is said: *that the eyes of the man and the woman shall be opened. You shall be as Gods, knowing good and evil.* And elsewhere: *The eyes of Balaam were uncovered by Jehovah, so that he might see the angel.* The Evangelist also speaks of this kind of dull and clear vision from the admonition of Christ: *I speak to them in parables because seeing they do not see, etc. But blessed are your eyes because they see.* From this it is clear that eyes are both spiritual and corporeal. Hence, eyes are attributed to God himself, no differently than bread is to angels. Whence it is said: *Let your eyes, O Jehovah, look toward what is right.* And elsewhere: *The eyes of Jehovah are in every place, watching the good and the evil.* And Job declares best what kind of eyes God has: *The eyes of God (he says) are not of flesh, nor do they see as those mortals do.* And the Psalmist says: *The eyes of God see all things, and nothing can be hidden from them.*

By these things it is clearly explained that all the mysteries in the world are comprehended in the essence of the internal eye, since it has familiarity with God, with angels, and even with whatever secrets are in the worldly spirit. Do we not also see in the contemplation of the greater world <note>the macrocosm</note> two eyes in it, conducting and governing the entire mass of the visible world and all its members? Namely, the Sun, which the Platonists not inaptly called the right eye of the world, and the Moon its left. And yet we recognize that in the visible sun there is an invisible eye of the world, which is also called the invisible light of the world by the Holy Scriptures, inasmuch as He "set his Tabernacle in the Sun." For it is not the solar mass that illuminates the world and beholds all things in it, but it is that divine mind which, descending from its Empyrean and supernatural throne, established its natural Tabernacle in the center of the sun (as a more worthy substance), providing it the power of seeing, illuminating, and quickening. By a plainly similar reason, it is not the human eye that sees, but that spirit—illuminated by the intellect or mind from the Empyrean seat of reason, carried down on wings—penetrates through the visual organs or optic nerves and descends into the orbs of vision. In their centers—namely, the crystalline humors <note>the lenses of the eyes</note>, as seats more suitable for its clarity—it builds its palaces, from whose centers, through the pupils of the eyes, its power...

# Section I. Portion III. Part III. Book V.

they emit a bright light in order to see some object, no differently than the mundane Sun sends its rays to the earth or a portion of a cloud. These rays, moreover, flashing with the invisible brightness of the mind and leaping forth from the center of the **crystalline humor** <note>The lens of the eye, then thought to be the primary organ of vision</note>, gradually and step-by-step dilate themselves, no differently than two lines of an angle proceeding from the point of the angle are observed to be more distant from each other the further they tend in length from the center. Whence it happens, that the base of these rays thus ejected is formed and terminated in the object seen, while the cone is in the center of the eye; and from this we can divinely contemplate that just as the point, or unity, of that pyramidal motion is in the middle point of the crystalline humor, so truly its final multiplicity is in the object seen. Thus it is also concluded, that the first agent in that center or point has the closest relation with God, inasmuch as He is the One and the **monad** <note>The indivisible mathematical and spiritual unit</note>, who immerses Himself through His emanation into multiplicity, just as the reason of the mind here moves from the center, or middle point, or cone of the pyramid to its base; in which emanation it always immerses itself more and more into the depth of matter, until it reaches the base of the pyramid. For thus was the world made, and into its fabric the divine spirit immersed itself more and more deeply from the center of unity into the mundane multiplicity. As we see, therefore, in the emission of solar rays, that in the object where the base of the pyramid is, the superficial rays concur and are reflected back into the center of the base, where both extremes meeting together in the middle, with equal and even resistance, radiate in a direct motion to the center of the sun (which motion is called the **axis of the pyramid**, that is, the formal line tending through the middle of the pyramid from the center of its base to its cone). But this is also confirmed in what we see in a **round concave mirror**, where all the exterior rays are contracted in the center, and through their resistance in it, the entire species <note>The visual image or "form" of the object</note> seen appears to leap out from it along a straight line. In plainly the same way, the matter holds for the rays reflecting from the center of the eye to the base, and from the base through its center to the cone; because by this straight reflection, the truth concerning the external nature of the object is reported—or rather, by a certain retrograde reflection, that image of truth is brought back, concerning which the reason judges. According to this, it instructs the natural soul either with hatred or love, or appetite, or loathing, or neutrality, and through its messengers instructs all the members of the body, either to avoid the thing seen or to embrace it with love.

Therefore, the first **animal seed**, or the **animal spirit** <note>The "spiritus animalis," a subtle fluid believed to carry nerve impulses</note> of the first degree, prepared in the **choroid plexus** <note>A network of blood vessels in the brain</note>, whose function is to serve the senses and motion, is a messenger sent from the intellect to conduct this kind of inquiry. It carries the mandate of the mind to the crystalline palace of the eye, and that mandate in this **microcosm** <note>The "little world" of the human body</note> is like the Word of God in the **macrocosm** <note>The "great world" of the universe</note>, surrounded on all sides by intellectual light and divine splendor. This is the first act of both life and vision, which placed its tabernacle in the microcosmic eye no differently than the Word of Jehovah in the sun. Therefore, the spiritual seed of the second degree or purification is the immediate vehicle of this intellectual light or splendor, which is carried upon the wings of the former no differently than the celestial spirit or soul is carried upon those of the air or wind. For this spirit is extracted from the cream of the **vital spirit** flowing abundantly and swimming in the **rete mirabile** <note>Latin: "wonderful net"; a complex of arteries at the base of the brain</note>; this cream, floating on top and made invisible by purification, relates to the gross animal spirit as the **ether** (in which super-celestial gifts abound) relates to the air. For in it, not only life, but also the splendor of the intellect holds dominion. And this is the reason why the images in the pupil of the eye are perceived as living and sparkling; this is because of the copious presence of these flashing rays, which are nonetheless observed to be absent and failing in men near the extreme danger of death for three days before their passing. This is considered by physicians to be a most certain sign of following death, the reason for which is readily apparent: namely, because due to the weakness of nature, the animal faculty is unable to prepare and purify its seeds, by means of which the intellectual splendor ought to be carried and conducted to the crystalline seat of vision. This same thing is also the cause why the sight of those suffering from an external and long-lasting disease is so weak and dull that it cannot look at light or tolerate the rays of the sun; namely, because nature, weakened by sickness, works only slowly and feebly in the manufacture of the animal spirits. Consequently, the divine splendor of the mind is emitted only sparingly to the crystalline mountains or watchtowers of the eyes. Whence it happens, that due to the lack of this shining soul, the eyes are rendered tender and infirm.

# On the Mystical Anatomy of the Brain.

It is observed that quartan fevers <note>A form of malaria where fever recurs every fourth day, historically attributed to "melancholy" or spiritual oppression.</note>, which are usually produced by the most wretched attacks of besieging malignant spirits, are driven away and cured; this could certainly not be accomplished unless a great celestial power and efficacy were present in this stony part <note>original: "parti petrosæ," likely referring to the petrous portion of the temporal bone at the base of the skull.</note>, as we shall explain more extensively elsewhere. But truly, as far as the cure of Epilepsy is concerned, it has been observed by some diligent investigators that in the skulls of certain hanged men (which they say happens and is found only in those who die a violent death) a certain whitish cross is found in some small part of this intact bone, of approximately this size, + <note>original: "crux quædam albicans"</note>, which contains within itself the specific faculty for curing Epilepsy. Indeed, they are accustomed to hold that little portion at a great price, and they believe that no small virtue and the most hidden properties are contained in a transverse bone of this kind.

Furthermore, the Philosophers who are most highly versed in the hidden mysteries of nature have made mention of a certain bone hidden in the human body, which they themselves called *Luz* <note>A legendary bone in Jewish tradition, often identified with a vertebra or a bone in the skull, believed to be indestructible.</note>, concerning whose internal property the ancients certainly declared great and stupendous things. For these things are written concerning it: *There is in the human body a certain very small bone, which the Hebrews call Luz, the size of a peeled chickpea, which is subject to no corruption, nor is it even conquered by fire, but is always preserved unharmed; from it, just as a plant grows from a seed, our animal body will sprout again in the resurrection of the dead.* And they conclude that these virtues are declared not by mere reason, but by experience. And certainly, this is that wonderful little portion in man which never departs from the human body, and through it, it shall remain as a guardian until the final day.

These things have come into my mind to write to you (kind readers), so that you may understand that not all things are known to men of common understanding; indeed, as you yourselves may ingenuously confess, more things are hidden from men than have been revealed to them up to this time. I wish, therefore, that you would receive this anatomy of mine in good part and with serene countenances, and I implore you to read, re-read, and consider everything point by point before you rashly and ill-advisedly condemn these labors of mine, which (in my opinion) are by no means to be lightly rejected. For you have everything we have said and committed to writing confirmed both by reasons drawn from the foundations of philosophy, and by the testimonies of philosophers and Theosophists <note>term: Theosophists (those who study divine wisdom through direct spiritual insight)</note>, and indeed even by the Holy Scriptures. Nor is it enough to say that this teaching of ours should be rejected or cast aside because it seems new, and has been very little revealed or publicized until this day; rather, we think it should be weighed all the more in the scales of justice, the more we perceive the treatment of philosophy and medicine among us to be uncertain and deceptive. In our next treatise, however, which discusses the causes of diseases, we hope to make all these things clearer—indeed, to make them so evident that we believe no one endowed with a sound mind will doubt these matters any longer. In the meantime, we pray from the heart for sound minds in sound bodies <note>original: "mentes sanas in corporibus sanis"</note> for you.

-> THE END. <-

That your letter (given on short notice) reached my hands so suddenly, Most Excellent Sir, has left me with no small joy and bathed me in unexpected delight. Yet, I would not have you think I emerged happy and cheerful simply because of their welcome presence; for as soon as I noticed the *Apology* <note>Kepler's *Apologia Tychonis contra Ursum*, a defense of Tycho Brahe's system</note> attached to them, I perceived that your indignation against me had flared up publicly. Indeed, my sadness would be increased and doubled, had I not sensed that you—without being called or incited to do so—had dipped your finger, armed for the violation of an honest reputation, into my works with rash desire. But because your *Apology*, appearing recently in public like a state envoy, seems in that very act to excuse its master to me and to the world, a provident caution warned me, and a forced necessity urged me, to sharply accuse him in my *Analytical Discourse*. Truly, by Hercules, you say you wonder what necessity drove me to respond to your *Analytical Discourse*, since you promised nothing, asked nothing, and objected to nothing. Is it thus, my Johannes, that you play with us? Do you not know that I am still able to judge colors? Or do you think I am composed of a spirit entirely devoid of feeling or not at all subject to the touch of a tongue—as if I do not know how to feel the hard blows of words and the burning wounds of writing? But who, by curiously judging or carefully deliberating on this matter, could conceive in his mind that a man so exalted by the light of the mind, second to none in mathematical science <term>Mathesis: the Greek-derived term for the mathematical sciences</term>, most celebrated throughout almost all of Europe for his various gifts of soul, and singing the *Harmony of the Heavens* <note>A reference to Kepler's work *Harmonice Mundi*</note> in his own divine mathematical way, had fallen into such an antipathy of character? Who would think that, by way of comparison and with no evident cause preceding it, he would bruise a man plainly unknown to him—one who had not struck him or offered just occasion—with a leafy club of words, as it were, and pursue him with the thick and hostile heels of malevolence? And did you think you would carry off my insults with impunity? Or did you believe the vexation of such a great injury should be passed over in silence, and not washed away by a pen imbued with the sharpness of truth? For what mortal would not strive to repair his reputation and dignity, wasting away under the aspersions of insolence, by a mutual effort and restore it with the Balm of Truth? Since even the fly is endowed with its own anger, and the little worm with gall...

# PREFACE

...fortified against the invasions of enemies and the insults of opponents, which must be repelled in every way, as if declaring this by a certain natural instinct. But truly, you dream of yourself standing in the pulpit as is your custom, and you do not blush to assert that you spoke from there as if to instruct your readers; as if this were a just and fit excuse for the insult offered to Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the ancient astronomer whose harmonic theories Fludd defended.</note> and Robert, by means of which you might securely—and with no further question to be made in this matter hereafter—produce the established foundations of their science onto the public stage like a victim offered up to your will. 

What? Is it because that once great and royal Ptolemy (now buried in the earth by a small cruelty of fate) cannot plead his own cause with a living voice or repel the injuries and crimes of error brought against his honor and dignity? Did you therefore think in your mind that Robert—who survives Ptolemy in life, though not in glory—would not descend into the cause of his own harmony on his own behalf? Did you think he would not manfully stand against Johannes, even if he attacked bravely, even if Johannes had turned out far more learned in the matter of symphony, and even if he were thronged by a whole choir of auditors and disciples and accompanied by the entire crowd or troop of his sect? 

Behold, then, and see: contrary to your expectation (for you say I have arisen unexpectedly from the crowd, though it was not by my own will, but by a just reason impelling me to a contest of this kind), I appeared at the last two Spring Fairs; I have, I say, come forth into the public view under the title of the *Analytical Discourse*. <note>original: "Discursus Analytici". This refers to Fludd's published response to Kepler.</note> For hey there, you! You who began the comparison—the offspring of our present contention—and who first cast laws upon the speech in my *Harmony*; you who inquire into the deeds of another's business more curiously than is fair, with the subtle gaze of Lynceus <note>A mythological figure famed for keen sight.</note> and the manifold eyes of Argus <note>The hundred-eyed giant of myth.</note>: do not be annoyed or ashamed if I have destined a profusion of wordy coins of the same condition—returning like for like, as they say—as payment for a slanderer or detractor. For this is a Christian admonition: that we should not do to another what we do not wish to be done to ourselves. We also find it commanded in the scriptures that an eye should be restored for an eye, blood washed away with blood, and wordy reproaches sometimes repressed with the like; for it is said that poison is expelled by poison, and a scorpion crushed into a pulp heals the wounds of its own sting.

Truly, I was not thinking of building or contriving any opposition to you or your *Harmony* <note>Refers to Kepler's *Harmonice Mundi* (The Harmony of the World).</note> out of any malice stirred up against you, nor was I driven to such an end by the stings of envy. Rather, a double occasion invited me, and a twin caution persuaded me, to boldly plead my cause against the one casting errors upon me. First, I wished to show the learned of the world how easy it is for one skilled in Philosophy—and how light a task even for one endowed with mediocre gifts of wit—to defend the foundations of his Philosophy, however much they are besieged and attacked by words smeared with insult. This is especially true since they are fortified by a triple demonstration, like an invincible faction of armed men: armed, I say, with the most powerful reasons of Physics <term>Physica: Natural philosophy or the study of the physical world</term>, thronged by the frequent authority of both Philosophers and Theosophists <term>Theosophia: Divine wisdom or mystical insight into the nature of God and the universe</term>, and finally (which is more effective than any argument) derived and confirmed by a most certain choir of ocular conclusions from the hidden mystery of the five elements and their spiritual operations. 

Secondly, I acted so that I might point out to the reader, borne aloft on the wings of justice, that it is just as possible for me, Robert, to reject and make vile the laws of Johannes's *Harmony* with closed eyes and a hardened heart, as it is for you, Johannes, to refute or inflict injuries upon his own. For it is not difficult for one who is willing to fashion lies and things least consistent with the truth—supported by some probability of the most perverse opinions and arguments—which may seem either new to the ear or arduous beyond the reach of common thought. Nevertheless, if these things are inspected a little more accurately, they are judged not only evident to be discovered, but possible, indeed easy, to be done. Therefore, of Physics...

-># PREFACE<-

...you have attempted to overturn the foundations of Robert <note>Robert Fludd (1574–1637), the English physician and mystical philosopher</note> with your cunning and mathematical subtlety. If, indeed, with equal art and with reasons gushing forth from the storehouse of nature, I have set out to tear down those of Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), the famed astronomer</note> by a mutual effort, would anyone consider Johannes to be stirred to unjust indignation—even beyond the measure of the deed—as a supporter (familiar to scholars who struggle with wordy swords in the "Castle of Minerva" <note>A metaphorical reference to academic debating halls or the goddess of wisdom's stronghold</note>), when like is returned for like, and it is deemed fair and honorable?

But at the end of your *Apology* <note>Kepler's *Apologia*, published in 1622 as a defense against Fludd</note>, you say that you were provoked by frequent injuries, and that you had cause to break out in anger here and there. By Hercules, you are singing my own song! I, who have been struck by a double blow, having only struck you once while you were striking me twice, would have had a double reason for anger compared to your single one—had I not listened to you yourself on page 50, where you kindly asserted that the jests and jokes of debaters were merely "sauces" <note>original: *embammata*; a culinary metaphor for the flavoring of a speech</note>.

Just as I have been present at two of your "Philosophical Banquets" by invitation, I discovered there that the arrangements of the feast were not so much composed of physical harmony as they were seasoned with the bitterness of words. So too, I feel you are burdened at my own meal and table—not dissimilar, though only once invited—more by indignation and weariness than by the food, despite the palate's pleasure; and thus I see that both of us are inclined toward peace and quiet.

Therefore, let the vessels of ill-will be hastily removed, and let the harmful cups of this enmity be banished into exile beyond the Hyperborean mountains <note>The far north; a classical metaphor for a remote, unreachable place</note>. Let us, finally appeased, conclude these complaints—or rather, if you please, these philosophical brawls. Let us approach friendship according to your wish; let us cement it, though it began from a dispute (albeit a philosophical one); let us indulge it and, I say, give it the loosest of reins. To correspond almost word-for-word with your speech delivered on page 50:

Behold, you find me mitigated and appeased by your fairness; nor do I see (provided you act with justice and goodness) what shall hinder us in the future from cultivating a literary friendship. Let whatever "Talent" <note>A biblical reference to the Parable of the Talents; a gift or skill given by God</note> each has received from God be contributed to the praise of the Creator and the instruction of one's neighbor, without the disparagement of the other. Whatever well-written things one finds in the other, let him receive and enjoy them with a grateful heart and with veneration for the spirit of the Giver.

Indeed, I judge him truly worthy to suffer the extremes—if there is anything more extreme than the last—who, without being forced or incited, rejoices in preferring quarrels and contentions over the peaceful contemplation of God and Nature. Whoever of us, therefore, shall attempt in the future to resist the rules of this friendship previously offered by you, let him be deservedly struck down.

But in the meantime, I would have you know this: just as I have resolved to think nothing toward your ruin hereafter, nor to act against the laws of your *Harmony* <note>Kepler's *Harmonice Mundi* (The Harmony of the World)</note>, so also God knows better than that I should allow, through the slightest negligence of my own, even a tiny bit of indignity or the smallest grain of insult to be suffered by my *Harmony* or my *Physical Works*. On the contrary, if anything in your *Apology* should look unfavorably upon any part of them, I shall not cease to wash it away entirely with arguments drawn from the fountain of truth (by your leave, and with the bonds of our friendship remaining safe). In which business, nevertheless, I hope Johannes will admit the effectiveness of what Robert, in this his *Reply* <note>original: *Replicatione*; Fludd's formal response</note>, desires neither to twist into a "serene brow" <note>A calm or deceptive appearance</note> with you (as he says on page 4), nor to hurl back at anyone except the one who strikes.

While Fludd agrees to peace, he maintains his right to defend his own philosophical works against Kepler's previous criticisms using "the fountain of truth."</summary>

# REPLICATION TO THE APOLO-
### GY TO THE FIRST ANALYSIS.

Whether Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler</note> in his comparison seems to accuse me of ignorance, albeit secretly, I willingly leave to you, Reader, who weighs all things in the scales of justice. And who in this deceitful world is to be found so just, and so sincere in the truth of a matter, that when comparing his own work with another's, he does not usually prefer his own, or place it before another’s, however much more excellent the other may be? Johannes made a voluntary Comparison between his own *Harmony* and that of Robert <note>Robert Fludd</note>. What then is more to be expected, than that Johannes, being closest to himself, should bestow extraordinary honors upon his own *Harmony*, while contaminating Robert’s with the most depraved opinions? He attempts with his mathematical subtleties to make those things appear as lies which are most truly offered by us and are felt to be easy in practice. But even now, the outcome will prove the deeds. For

> On page 41, he breaks out into these words: *I have detected more of the divine works in my harmonies than you have in yours, you who indulge in private conceptions of the world, confirmed by no sense-perception.*

But because I would least wish the Reader to be burdened by a multitude of pages on my account, I set out here to recite and re-measure those small portions of Johannes’s Comparison in few words—those which cast I know not what errors upon me—so that it may be more clearly shown to the benevolent and just Reader that a just occasion was offered to me for repelling the insults of an attacker, and for washing away and wiping off my dignity, which had been defiled by the openings of envy, as if by the waves of truth. These are his words:

> Text 10. *Therefore, in his work there are many pictures; in mine, there are mathematical diagrams provided with letters.*

What is this? Or why this Comparison between pictures and mathematical diagrams, unless he would thereby intimate to the world the vanity of pictures and the utility of mathematical diagrams?

> Text 11. *Let him see that he himself is greatly delighted by the dark riddles of things, while I strive to bring into the light of the intellect those very things involved in obscurity. The former is indeed familiar to the Chemists, Hermeticists, and Paracelsians; the latter is the proper possession of Mathematicians.*

Here it seems to be made known to the world that my *Harmony* is useless because it is involved in dark riddles; and thus he unjustly endeavors to draw the learned away from my *Harmony* with his most depraved opinions. But indeed, so that his own might be held in respect and honor, he says that it is open, clear, and entirely devoid of parabolic shadows.

> Text 12. *Where he treats the same material as I do, this is the difference between us: that he takes his from the ancients, while I dig mine out from the nature of things and establish it from the very foundations. He uses what he has received, confused because of the varying opinions of those handing them down, and uncorrected. I proceed by a natural order, so that all things are amended according to the laws of nature, and confusion is avoided.*

He seems to preach much about himself in this place, most welcome Reader, but if you look into the matter a little more accurately, you will feel that while mountains are promised, scarcely little hills are produced. But meanwhile, it must be gathered from the above how austere a judge and how unjust an arbiter he is toward me (the cause having been least heard, or being entirely ignored by him).

> Text 13. *Where I expressly refute the ancients who differ concerning the causes of consonances, there he follows the roll of the dice without hesitation, and does not even think about the truer causes.*

Go on then, fix the wordy trophy of your victory: but meanwhile I warn you to beware, lest you be deceived by your incomplete knowledge of the causes of consonance; for I perceive clearly enough from your writings that you have not yet tasted the sweetness of the Heliconian fount, nor ever visited Parnassus, the seat of the Muses. But go on, I say, with your Comparison, which (on page 5 of this work) you are eager to call a comparison and not an accusation.

> Text 14. *Where he introduces Music into the world. Here indeed the difference between us is immense. First, those Harmonies which he intends to teach are mere symbolisms, concerning which I say the same as I do of the symbolisms of Ptolemy: that they are poetic or oratorical rather than Philosophical or Mathematical.*

I see, by Hercules, that Johannes holds my *Harmony* to be poetic symbolisms rather than philosophical ones for this reason: because he observed that its basis is that Chaos alleged by Ovid, and the Waters, Light, and darkness so often sung of by Homer and Hesiod, and indeed by Virgil. But truly, no wise man will think that there is no Chaos, no waters, or Light, or darkness, simply because they were celebrated by the Poets. Finally, all Philosophers, both pagan and Christian, confess that these are the original subjects of Physics. What, therefore, shall hinder the foundations of my *Harmony*, if they be held as symbolisms, from being philosophical symbolisms?

# Reply of Robert Fludd

...more than those of Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler</note>, which are founded upon a circle in the soul and its divisions; he proves this necessarily follows (on pages 16 and 17) because the soul is the image of God. From this, he seems to say that all figures of Geometry are derived in a plane. Is this anything more than symbolic and parabolic? For the Soul is called a Circle, and even God himself is so called, but in an analogical and plainly metaphorical way. Yet I do not wish nor desire to detract anything from Johannes’s laws of Harmony, since number is also said to have been the principal model in the mind of the Creator for things to be created. But in what way? Clearly, insofar as through number, God is declared to be infinite; for nothing is more infinite than number. Also, through number, the immutability of God is declared, insofar as nothing is more immutable than number and its properties. Number therefore suggests a simple God, while being immutable; it suggests a wise God, while being foreknowing; it suggests an incomprehensible God, while being infinite; and it suggests a wonderful and singular God, while being these three. And this is the reason why Theology chose the triple number <note>The Trinity</note> as primary and most perfect, wishing to express God as the first form of all things, arguing from there that He is the origin of forms and of Light. Furthermore, His greatness is explained through number, whence the triangle is ascribed to Him by Mathematicians, as that figure is not resolved into others and is subject to no principles, but is the principle in every composition of geometric figures and the end in their resolution; for the square, the pentagon, and the remaining figures proceed from it and return into it. It is therefore like the first form, from which matter received its being, and without which it cannot exist. Furthermore, form is incapable of receiving accidents. From these things, therefore, it is clear how God or the Mind itself (which participates in God) is called by the Sages <term>Sophis</term> <note>The wise or the philosophers</note> a number, or a circle, or a triangle—not because He is truly so, but through similitude, and is so called in parabolic speech. Therefore, if there be a symbol of my Harmony, it is indeed a philosophical one, just as I confess that of Johannes to be a mathematical one; and this I hope is without injury to either his Harmony or mine.

> Text 15. *In his first Volume he distributes the world into three regions, where according to that most famous axiom of Hermes <note>The Emerald Tablet: "As above, so below"</note>, he makes the upper things similar or analogous to the lower. But for this analogy to succeed through all things, the things being compared on both sides must often be dragged in by the hair.*

But now, let the Reader most easily perceive where this Comparison of Johannes is heading: let him see whether this is properly a comparison, as he himself said, or an accusation. He proceeds, however, and deals with me liberally thus:

> Text 17. *He, trusting in the ancients, believed the force of Harmonies to be from abstract numbers. I am satisfied if he demonstrates a concordance between any parts, however he may encompass them with numbers, with no care for what kind of units are accumulated in that number. I nowhere teach to seek harmonies where the things between which there is Harmony cannot be measured by the same measure of quantity.*

But here, good Johannes, you have wandered "by the whole sky" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "to be completely mistaken"</note> in this assertion of yours, as is clearly explained in my analytical Demonstration. There, I proved first of all that you have not at all understood the physical sense of my Harmony, and also that the units of my harmony—taken in an external and mathematical way in the **mundane monochord** <note>A single-stringed instrument used as a metaphor for the proportions of the universe</note> (which I fashion as the axis of each Pyramid, where the degrees of form and matter are best explained)—are ordered well, harmonically, and in just proportion to worldly things according to the pleasure of your Plato and Proclus. I shall not despair of demonstrating this clearly enough in this little Treatise. Observe again, good Reader, with what importunity he presses me:

> Text 18. *Furthermore, he divides the whole world into three equal parts by reason of the semi-diameter, knowing well enough that those parts are not at all equal. But he does so only because the first unit is the elementary world, the second the ethereal world, and the third the empyrean: and truly, units cannot be depicted otherwise than by equality of lines.*

Here Johannes finds much error in the poor application of units; indeed, he seems to recognize none except those depicted in the equality of lines. He is a man strenuous in Mathematics <term>Mathesi</term> and so addicted to geometric demonstrations that he has forgotten truly physical and formal Units determined by no dimensions. If it please you, Reader, to read my analytical demonstration in this context, I beseech you to deign to do so. Who, then, from this speech of his, would not choose to call it a refutation rather than a Comparison?

You will observe that Texts 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, and 25 are of this same condition and "flour" <note>of the same sort</note>, if you inspect them with a just mind. Finally,

> Text 26. He concludes thus: *From these few things I think it is established that, although to understand the mysteries joined to the most profound Philosophy which Robert treats, a knowledge of Harmonic proportions is altogether necessary: nevertheless, he who has learned my entire work will still be not a little further from those most perplexed mysteries than they themselves have receded from the most accurate certainty of mathematical demonstrations.*

From these things, therefore, as I believe is not hidden from the Reader, Johannes has attempted not a comparison, but indeed an express refutation of my Harmony and Physics through the entire discourse of his Appendix, and has tried it with every effort; although he seems to deny this in many places of his Apology, among which I have proposed to recite some here:

> *I have long since asked of you, Robert, that you hold me excused from the crime of detraction or malevolence. I thrust no disgrace upon either you or Ptolemy because you use symbols demonstrating nothing directly. Page 31.*
> *I have instituted a comparison, not an accusation, for the instruction of the Student of Philosophy. Page 5.*
> *In the title of the Preface: I wonder what necessity drove you to respond, to whom I first promised nothing, asked nothing, and objected to nothing. Page 3.*

# Regarding the Defense of Analysis II and III

*I have done you no wrong, Robert; I have fixed no mark of envy upon your work, but have written of the work for the Reader according to its own nature. Page 11.* <note>Fludd is quoting Kepler's previous arguments back to him to refute them.</note>
*You complain that I attempt to expose your ignorance and lack of skill to the world. You are clearly deceived, or you deceive yourself. I, as I said, compare my things with these so that I may instruct the Reader. Page 14.*
*I say that no injury is done to your teaching by my comparisons, while I call my harmonic boundaries "Mathematical," but yours "enigmatic," "pictorial," and "Hermetic." Page 33.* <note>Hermetic refers to the mystical tradition of Hermes Trismegistus, which Fludd followed.</note>
*I do not refute your things, Robert; but I compare mine, so that the Reader may know what to seek from you, and what from me. Page 37.*
*In vain do you fortify yourself, Robert; I do not come as an attacker, but as a guest greeting you from a distance. Page 40.*
*This desire of yours for vengeance could have found more excuse than now, when, having used mere comparisons, I have built a fence for the sake of the Reader between your Harmony and mine. Page 47.*

But now to you, Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler</note>, I shall turn the thread of my speech, and I will say boldly that my Physics <note>Natural philosophy</note> pertains neither to you nor to your mathematical Harmony; therefore, the mark of envy is to be assigned to you rather than to me, you who began this kind of contention or dispute between us, and first cast your speech against my Physics. Therefore, let the eye of the reader and of justice be witness, to whom I commend my present case, whether that speech of yours brought forth on page 41 be fitting or not. *Nor now* (you say) *ought I to wink and remain quiet, but rather demonstrate my indignation, because I see you provoked by an emulation of injury (which you imagine for yourself from the fact that I gave God His due, having performed my duty by distinguishing between your things and mine); by the slight offense of this,* you say, *driven by thoughts of revenge, you are carried away crosswise, etc.* You are deceived and you deceive, Johannes: for I do not burn with emulation, nor do I envy your virtue; indeed, I would rather praise it, were it not that I perceived you, being not at all called upon or previously provoked by me, to be carried away crosswise against me and my Harmony. For I was attempting to move nothing against you or your dignity or Harmony by my own appetite, but was compelled and provoked—as becomes a wise man—to repel another's violence with my own strength, and I have undertaken to defend with the utmost effort my fortification against the attempts of an invading enemy. Let the vice of envy and emulation, therefore, be cast upon you, who began these philosophical complaints: for truly, as far as I am concerned, I praise your inventions in mathematical matters, and in astronomical matters I do not envy your success; but I only ask of you, since you are eminent in both morality and learning, that you do not consider it fair or honest to cheaply disparage anyone as your equal in omniscience without reason, or to affect his teaching with reproach and calumnies, unless you have been first summoned by him into the philosophical or at least the mathematical arena. But I proceed thus to your Defense.

### ->In the Defense of Analysis II<-

Whether I long to claim any glory for myself in this Analysis, I commit to the Reader, who is borne up on the wings of justice: who will without doubt find this assertion of yours as true as those words of yours: *Putrefactions, Calcinations, Sublimations, and Reverberations* <note>Technical terms from alchemy/chemistry</note>, as they pertain to the matter or subject of your Defense or my Analysis.

### ->In the Defense of Analysis III<-

I do not wish to dispute further concerning the sense of words or their grammatical application. For let that which was said by you suffice: namely, that you place no part of the distinction in the number of words. I shall therefore gird myself rather for the material parts of this section of your Defense, the primary intention of which concerns the contraction or dilation of speech in teaching regarding both Harmonies, and similarly in the method of explaining means <note>Mathematical ratios</note> and the more convenient and fitting discovery or demonstration of the *Diapason* <note>The musical octave</note> consonance.

As for the copious flow of words, I acknowledge it to be very necessary and useful for public professors, who are accustomed to preach the art they deal with from the pulpit to their auditors, so that they may, first of all, explain and demonstrate the secrets of the Art they profess with a multitude of words and circumlocutions to make it easier for the auditors to grasp, and secondly, so that they do not let the space of the appointed hour pass by in vain. I do not, therefore, envy Johannes's abundance of words; indeed, I rather praise it. Yet it does not follow that Robert's succinct method of demonstrating in musical matters and his indications through figures <note>Illustrations/diagrams</note> are to be entirely rejected or neglected. For he <note>Fludd refers to himself in the third person</note> never exercised a public profession of Mathematics, nor did he propose to exercise it; for although (I confess) the condition and office of a Public Professor is highly laudable and most worthy of reverence, I nevertheless feel myself neither ready nor fit for such business, being impatient of labor and not at all excelling in volubility of tongue. Nor certainly (thanks be to God) does such necessity compel me that I should spend my diligence on any work or condition adverse to my nature or inclination for the sake of acquiring food and clothing, since my once-dearest Father, distinguished with the honor and title of *Knight* <note>Latin: Equitis aurati</note>, having held offices in the state of no low condition, and being fortunate enough in riches and possessions, left me a portion or patrimony (though not so great, yet sufficient for the youngest born), by means of which I am able to lead and conduct a life quite elegantly and sumptuously by myself without the protection of any Profession or Art. And although of Medicine...

# Robert Fludd’s Reply
<meta>catchword: high</meta>

I now embrace this profession willingly and gladly, as a science most full of the mysteries of nature and divinity. However, I acknowledge that I am more often absent from its practical application than engaged in it, because the peaceful contemplation of God and Nature calls me away, for the most part, from worldly affairs. This, therefore, is the reason why I have dealt only succinctly with various sciences (the fruits of my youth). By contracting them into brief summaries <note>original: "Epiromas," likely meaning epitomes or abridgments</note>, I did not intend to instruct merely raw and fresh students in the manner of a Professor, but rather to advance those moderately versed in Physics and the liberal arts toward perfection in them. Succinctly, I say, I have vividly delineated the matter to the eyes through writings and pictures, so that the one might supply the defect of the other, and the mystery of Science might be more quickly drawn out by the diligent Searcher. 

But this John <note>Johannes Kepler</note> seems to mock those who strive to teach the eye instead of using a multitude of words, considering very little that sight is more excellent than all the senses and more existing through itself: for a thing seen is accustomed to make stronger impressions on the mind than that explained by words alone. We say, therefore, that the marrow of an art, explained by both pictures and words, is more quickly grasped by a scholar than if it were only thrust into the ears by speech. I praise John’s wordiness, insofar as he is a Professor; likewise, I am neither ashamed nor annoyed by Robert’s succinct way of writing, interspersed with demonstrations by pictures. 

As for what pertains to the harmonic means and the discovery of the octave <term>Diapason: the interval of an octave, considered the most perfect consonance</term> consonances, and also the revelation of the keys of B-flat and B-natural <note>original: "b. b." referring to the soft and hard 'b' in the hexachord system</note> from the foundations of Nature: since you, John, value my knowledge in Music and Mathematics so little, I shall speak of them below in their proper place. I hope to make the literate world perceive with open eyes both that I am not entirely ignorant of the nature and condition of John’s foundations, and that he has erred by "the whole heaven" <note>a Latin idiom meaning "entirely" or "diametrically opposed"</note> in his rash judgment of my works. Yet you will perceive that I do not, according to my promise, bring anything against you or the laws of your *Harmony*. For you should know that I have not done this foolishly (however much I have been harassed by insults in this *Apology* of yours), because throughout this little treatise of mine, I study to soften you with the sweetness of morality rather than to inflame you with indignation or anger.

### ->In the Apology to Analysis IV.<-

And certainly, I distinguish natural Music from artificial Music not without justice, although both are produced from the same foundations. For we do not call a house, or a clay vessel, or glass "natural things" simply because they are all derived from the same natural base—namely stones, wood, clay, herbs, and sand—but rather "artificial," insofar as the foundations of nature (the elements) are so mixed, composed, and shaped according to the Artist’s pleasure by the industry of art. From these things, therefore, the Reader may gather whether I am a difficult man in such an assertion, or not?

### ->In the Apology to Analysis V.<-

Regarding the manifold division of your time; regarding your wonderful experiment between the heavy and sharp string constituting the sound of the Octave, by which you say you measure the space between the contraction and dilation <term>systole and diastole: the rhythmic beating of the heart</term> of the human pulse; whether the measure of the beat <note>original: "tactus," the basic unit of time in Renaissance music</note> has no place, as you say, in the Harmonies of the Planets; whether the Harmonic proportions of the Planets consist in the length of their periodic times, or not; whether the Harmonies are to be sought in the real motions of the Planets as they appear from the center of the Sun; whether the motion of the *Apogees* <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the center</note> is not physical—concerning all these things, I say, sharp and tedious Disputations and controversies could be made. 

But I do not intend to judge or discuss them in this place, lest I bring boredom to the Reader above all, or become a troublesome scholar to you by inciting you to further anger. Whether the time of duration can be considered in the Harmonies of the Planets, as in human song: you deny it, and yet they are distinguished from one another by time, namely the duration of motion, nor, as it seems to me, do they relate to only one respect of time. But I acknowledge all these things (to speak with your own mouth) *have been thoroughly poured into the divine power of Robert’s genius*. But whether Robert is deceived or not in these matters, I do not wish to inquire too curiously, nor to contend further with you, since these things pertain to your *Harmony*, against which, according to my promise, I do not wish to produce anything adverse hereafter, lest I render you more resentful or stir you to new anger.

### ->In the Apology to Analysis VI.<-

Tones can be called dissonant intervals in one respect, but consonant in another; therefore, I have not denied the assertion of the ancients in this either. For according to Guido the Monk <note>Guido of Arezzo, the 11th-century music theorist</note>, Consonance is as it were "sounding together": which cannot be a Consonance unless two voices sound at the same time. Yet the tone is counted among the Consonances, of which he himself makes 8 in number. Furthermore, practice has taught me that a low string with a B-flat produces a sound with another in B-natural, and although that collision is somewhat raw and harsh, yet by a sudden inclination, that agreement is made pleasant in identity. Moreover, we see two tones of the same interval produce sounds differing in number. Nor do I play with ambiguity here (as you say) since both the tone and the interval are sounds and harmonize with each other; for otherwise a Tone would not be called a consonance, and thus a tone sounds identically with a tone. Nor do I argue that there is a difference in the species of interval between tone and tone, since I have said that the tone of one string...

# On the Defense against Analysis VII, VIII, and IX.

...produced a unison symphony corresponding to the other by an identity of proportion, but in number. Whence I affirmed that it is a consonant interval in one respect, although in another respect it is dissonant. In the *barbitos* <note>A multi-stringed ancient Greek instrument similar to a lyre</note> the truth of this matter is most easily explained.

### On the Defense against Analysis VII.

Pythagoras would never have arrived at the mystery of this science without the practical experience of the hammer-strikes <note>Refers to the legend of Pythagoras discovering musical ratios by listening to blacksmiths' hammers</note>. Furthermore, we read that Tubal Cain, the primary inventor of Music, was highly skilled in the practice of musical instruments; Ptolemy also is said to have been by no means ignorant of the practice of Music. Therefore, I do not exclude these men from the theory of Music; on the contrary, I confirm them in it all the more.

Finally, stirred by I know not what wrath, you break into this exclamation: *“O wretched little Philosophers, who thrust their speculations about the work of Creation upon us, when they themselves have created nothing.”* And indeed, Johannes, you who are so strenuous—I will not say a wretched little Philosopher—and so great a Mathematician, what in the name of God have you created? Do you truly know what creation is, what the forging of the world is, or what God has left in the power of men? With whom did He permit His Wisdom to remain perpetually, to instruct him in all things, and to teach him what is acceptable to God, and how the world was made? Or do you know what Robert <note>Fludd refers to himself in the third person</note>, being a man created in the image of God, is capable of? To what extent he is engaged in the true practice of Creation? Or do you think his science is imaginary, or uncertain in the manner of common Mathematics (I except yours here)? Do you believe that infallible demonstrations of his Mosaic science—indeed, even ocular ones—are lacking? You are deceived, you are deceived, Johannes, and you wander through your entire external heaven, even though you believe you perceive the positions and harmonic motions of the Planets from afar through your clear optics <note>A jab at Kepler’s reliance on telescopes and mathematical observation</note>. You do not know how to judge the internal mind of man or his more occult actions. Therefore, I will boldly say: if Johannes abounded in as much skill in his Art as Robert does in his, he would insist upon a better and more correct state of worldly Harmony than currently exists. And I confess that I exult in this: that I am worthy to be numbered among the disciples of Moses, from whose Theosophical and Philosophical art all other sciences are derived—indeed, even that most holy and only true Astronomy and Astrology in which few are engaged, which neither your Proclus nor Copernicus ever tasted, or ever seem to have tasted. Therefore, I pray, do not cry out against men not so well known or familiar to you by calling them "wretched little philosophers" at your pleasure, nor judge that no one is to be compared to you. I know indeed and confess that you are well-versed in common Mathematics; I praise your industry and magnify your invention, nor do I deny that perhaps a common pleasure can be found in it. But yet, it must be felt as unseemly in your acquired glory that you do not hesitate to so easily condemn men unknown to you for the crime of ignorance. But I acknowledge your bitterness, since I see you wrote this passage in anger.

### On the Defense against Analysis VIII.

Here I will leave you hidden in your corner, since your musical instruments and that new subject of your comparison pertain to nothing. For either you have added superfluous things, or you have alleged them for the sake of mocking; I disregard both and value them at a straw.

### On the Defense against Analysis IX.

You say that Pythagoras *“considered the strikes of the hammers before the causes of Music were discovered,”* and yet you conclude that *“Robert has today handed down new instruments.”* But Robert seems to reply that although those instruments may be new in habit or shape, the causes of their Harmony are most ancient and extracted from the very bowels of nature. Then you assert that *“because his book lacks my instruments, you have provided the causes of consonances to your Reader.”* I respond that I have accomplished this same work for the Reader (but under another form), though in words not so copious. But I would wish you to candidly confess here: do no accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not change the essence of a thing</note> (as you say) *“except those quantitative and mathematical ones concur in the true explanation of a physical thing?”* Then you proceed by affirming *“that among accidents the first genus is quantitative, and this you learned from Aristotle; all others you say are posterior.”* I ask, therefore, what quantity does the substantial form admit, which is the first act and principle of motion, stripped of every external accident? Or what do you make of formal quality? After this, you say that *“harmony requires both mathematics and physics for the discovery of causes.”* This is denied, because it is in the nature of harmony to seek its own causes: indeed, by the very revelation of its own hidden nature through its admirable motion in the fabric of the world, both old and new—that is, in both the macrocosm and the microcosm—it is accustomed to manifest the causes of harmony even to scientific eyes, with no recourse had to mathematical things. Yet I do not deny that Nature can, in a certain way, also indicate through mathematics, though not so openly and naturally. Furthermore, let this also be said by me without offense: that my sacred Physics is the same as your Metaphysics.

That Robert uses the word "Harmony" in the broadest sense (as he says), I do not blush, since I recognize a single soul of the world expanded everywhere, which seems to pluck the string of the world's harmony (which is the universal spirit), whose instrument is the entire aggregate of the world itself. It is not an error to me that I have placed Music among the Liberal Arts, although it is but the husk and shadow of true formal Music. For who will rightly affirm...
