# Reply of Robert Fludd

Who will claim that the exterior is to be preferred to the interior, or the circumference to the center, or corporeal things to the spiritual, or the coarse to the subtle? I do not rest (as you seem to suggest) in sensible Music <note>Music perceived by the physical senses, like hearing a lute.</note>, but in the elementary music entirely, for in those elements dwells the "pulsing form." Nevertheless, I say that formal Music possesses formal and internal sounds, just as we say material music has external ones: for the voice of the spirit is one thing, that of the body another; one is of God, another of an Angel, and another of man. In this, I seem to differ neither from my beloved Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the mysteries and mathematics.</note> nor indeed from the Holy Scriptures. The world will see in the future (I hope) that I am no more ignorant of the logic of concords and discords than Johannes himself, nor less versed in the Harmony of Plato, Porphyry, Iamblichus, or Proclus. And as you say you have corrected their dogmas according to the prescription of Catholic doctrine, so indeed I, insofar as I am a Christian, shall not follow them in all things.

I say that the Music is truly the same in all things, just as the Soul of the World <note>Latin: *Anima mundi*; the vital force connecting all living things to the cosmos.</note> is the same generally speaking; but in truth, regarding the voices: different sounds are produced according to the proportion of the agent's action upon the patient <note>The "agent" is the force acting, the "patient" is the object being acted upon.</note>. For example, the same stroke makes a different sound in copper, tin, iron, lead, and in the earth, but in the air it is scarcely heard. Furthermore, a strong stroke gives a stronger sound in the same subject, and a weaker one a more feeble sound; for a more obedient spirit renders a younger and more insensible sound, so that corporeal things rightly agree with corporeal, and spiritual with spiritual. Do you see here how "equivocal" my Harmony is, as you call it? But I say that all Music consists of sounds, though some are sensible, while others are by no means subject to the senses. And although I grant that these voices—whether sensible or not—can be demonstrated well enough by mathematical proportions, nevertheless such an indication is more analogical, symbolic, and accidental than that Physical <note>In the 17th-century sense: relating to the study of nature and its actual substances.</note> indication in which the thing itself is explained in its own nature as it is. For nature is closer to its own nature than to something foreign, and rejoices more in real substance than in imaginary accidents. I do not condemn the mathematical arts, my Johannes; indeed, truth compels me to praise and extol them. Yet, in the demonstration of nature, I am compelled to prefer nature itself and its real physical motions—which distinguish the degrees to the eyes—above all mathematical things. For who cannot, by an imaginary way or perhaps by chance or analogy, rightly and infallibly declare the form or the motion and act of form in nature everywhere through the industry of Mathematics?

->*In the Apology to the Tenth Book of the Annals*<-

Here, you Johannes, *say that my book abounds with copper-plate engravings by my own admission.* I confess it, and I did not feel angered by it. But I wonder what delight moved you, or what necessity in your comparison, that you threw out words about my pictures and your diagrams—since this would be familiar to any reader—unless it is because you yearn to prefer your diagrams to my pictures. If that does not follow, then what you said was superfluous and useless to your comparison.

You conclude, Johannes, too pompously, as it seems to me, and boastfully, with these words: *Allow me even now to bring forth a clearer voice. He who loves the certainty of Mathematical Disciplines will gain more utility in learning the harmonic part of Mathematics from my harmonic work than from that of Robert Fludd. But truly, the mind of mystic philosophy (which is accustomed to be delivered through enigmas) desires to feed its eyes on pictures; what it seeks it will not find in my book.* To which I reply: by the sole contemplation of my monochord <note>A single-stringed instrument Fludd used to diagram the proportions of the entire universe.</note>, by rightly applying it to the world and the soul of the world, I could (if I wished) explain and teach more of the internal harmonic truth to readers in the space of a single day—provided they were at least moderately versed in Philosophy—than Johannes could with his many inventions. But I see very well that Johannes has read nothing but the titles of the books and their chapters, or in reading them has taken for enigmas those things which are truly very clear and transparent to one who looks closely, and are confirmed and demonstrated by visual conclusions. Indeed, I see no reason why Johannes should proclaim my "enigmas" to the world and yearn to publish everything written by me as obscure and parabolic, while his own is brilliant and manifest. Yet it is certain and well known by some who have experienced it, that men here in England versed in both Theology and Philosophy—indeed, even some Nobles of both the highest and lowest rank—have, by the mere reading of my books and by well observing the connection and link of the passages, become so learned in my Physical works that, having neglected and almost condemned the Peripatetic <note>Aristotelian philosophy, which Fludd viewed as outdated and "heathen."</note> philosophy of the heathens, they have trumpeted the praises of my philosophy (perhaps beyond my merits) and have seemed to delight wonderfully in its contemplation. I refer myself, therefore (in the manner of Johannes), to those who do not look only at the titles, but immerse themselves in the true marrow of the work before they judge it. And they will see, I hope, that the matter is far otherwise, and further removed from enigmas than Johannes injuriously and unjustly seems to trumpet—whose only argument, and one he sings so often, is: *What Robert wrote are dark enigmas and hieroglyphics, while I strive to bring things wrapped in obscurity into the light of understanding.* As if he were saying: "Come, embrace my doctrine, for it is clear, easy, transparent, and pleasant; flee that of Robert, for it is enigmatic, Hermetic, and dark." But Robert denies this argument of yours, and says there is greater difficulty in perceiving the foundations of your Harmony, as we shall declare below, than those of mine, if the matter is properly considered.

# Regarding the Defense against Analysis XI and XII

### On the Defense against Analysis XI

You believe you burden and vex me greatly here with these terms: "Hieroglyphic" and "enigma," and you even have me as a supporter of your view, since I have used hieroglyphics in my writings. It is granted that I said my *Musical Temple* <note>A complex diagram in Fludd's work representing the harmonic structure of the universe.</note> stands in the place of a hieroglyphic sign. But I would especially want the reader to understand that a hieroglyphic either remains veiled in its own darkness and mystery, or it is revealed and manifested once its curtain or veil is drawn back, its interior disclosed, and its meaning explained through letters and interpretations. I say that the *Musical Temple*, without the keys and notes expressed within it, would be a hieroglyphic image and a thing as obscure as the pyramids of Memphis; but with the keys and notes expressed in it, it differs not at all from the Musical System of Guido <note>Guido of Arezzo, the medieval inventor of modern musical notation.</note> and others most well-versed in music. Furthermore, we have demonstrated every part of it through letters and writings, and the same holds true for my other pictures. Here, therefore, Johannes, you have a Hieroglyphic that is open and not hidden.

And how, I pray, do the mathematical images explained in your books differ from such hieroglyphics, if they were not demonstrated and explained by letters and writings? Furthermore, if the reader looks at your *Prodromus* <note>Kepler's *Mysterium Cosmographicum*, often called the *Prodromus*.</note>, he will find new pictures there that are closer to hieroglyphic characters than mine are. Therefore, these words and terms of yours are empty; and consequently, what you have written in so many lines should be ignored and rejected with a single word. Furthermore, if I have brought forward the opinions of wise men—both Theosophers and Philosophers—concerning the approval of silence and secrecy, I did not do this to excuse myself for my "enigmatic" writings, but rather against your assertion, as you seemed to condemn parabolic writings and enigmas.

Hence, you seem to affect a threatening tone here, and try to strike fear into me with "foot-and-a-half long" words <note>original: "verbis sesquipedalibus" - a Horace reference meaning long, pompous words.</note>. These are your words: *“I would wish you to look back at yourself more diligently in the future, lest you harm your own reputation. For as far as I am concerned, I have no need of either your recantation or your contrary praise. Nor will you achieve by this persistence that I should refuse to skirmish with you, as often as I can do so without expense to myself and with some profit to the reader.”* These are your words; to which I reply: My reputation (I warn you here) is by no means placed in your power, such that you could harm it either with your elegance or your mathematical demonstrations. Behold, therefore, Robert in the philosophical arena (if you should attempt anything against him) ready to repel any injury offered by you. There you will find me not disturbed by fear of your words, nor stunned into a stupor, but armed partly with the shield of truth and partly with the sharp darts of wit. Where should I look for such philosophical virtue in you? I shall see by what means I might be forced either to recant the things I have alleged, or to hold you and your power in philosophical matters in such great admiration with unworthy praises. Good God, what boastful words these are—how unbecoming of a man of such fame and learning! And I would not want you to think that I brought anything forward against you to prevent you from skirmishing with me; on the contrary, I have rather expected the force of your divine genius to be driven from that region. And if in the future you test my Works with an even more scrupulous inquiry, I would have you expect that I shall repay you with the same coins of lashes, or at least similar ones; let this be the pledge of my promise. And believe for certain, that I lack neither the power to perform it, nor indeed the will (once the bonds of friendship offered by you and reciprocally accepted by me have been violated).

Finally, you conclude this section of the Defense with these words: *“I fear, as the nation is perverse today, lest that iniquity should extend itself beyond words into deeds themselves, if some of the readers believe you rashly without inspecting my text.”* I wish, Johannes, that you had lowered this tragic curtain, or folded up this theatrical veil, so that I might discern whether this was said by you in good or bad faith. What, my Johannes, have you now suddenly changed from a Mathematician into a Chemist? Do you now delight in speaking enigmas, you who just now rejected parables? Is it because I said, with the Holy Scriptures, that the secrets of the sciences are acquired through the attainment of the Holy Spirit, that you therefore speak perversely of me in an enigma, as if some knowledge could be acquired through new inventions without the assistance of the Holy Spirit? I see that you have been goaded into anger by the heels of this Analysis of mine; therefore, I willingly forgive the things said by you while you were incensed.

### On the Defense against Analysis XII

Pythagoras refused to admit the interval of a semitone into Harmony, because a superparticular ratio <term>A ratio where the numerator is one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3:2 or 4:3)</term> cannot be divided into equal parts. And Ptolemy and Proclus themselves, although they seem to agree on this—that a semitone cannot properly be given—nevertheless attempted to divide the whole tone into unequal parts, the larger of which they called the *Apotome*, and the smaller the *Leimma* <note>original: "Lemna"</note>. But the perfection of Pythagoras in the science of Music is hidden from no one of sound mind. However, as regards the definition of the Semitone, which you call "incorrect," and whether two major tones are given or not, and similarly regarding other matters alleged by you here: because I shall speak of them below, God willing, I will omit them in this place. But I will say here, that he who seems to quibble over the minutes of a Semitone—in which little or almost no perceptible error is found—yet can find no fault in things more clear and open, I rightly call "scrupulous" <note>In the sense of being overly concerned with tiny details (scruples).</note>; for he who busies himself so sharply with "scruples," or rather with imperceptible minutiae, desires to appear more than he truly is.

But here you make your entrance into my inquiry made into your works, which I did for no other reason...

# Reply of Robert Fludd
<note>original: "Replicatio Roberti Flud"</note>

...I have done this only to show you that it is just as easy for me, through a scrupulous investigation, to notice the slips or errors in your writings as it is for you to find them in mine. You should not believe this was done out of envy or arrogance, but rather in the manner of debaters, whose role it is to argue for and against any proposed matter; a task begun by me and brought to its conclusion. Regarding those things which pertain to your Harmony set forth in this analysis, I shall say nothing, but we think there are three main points to be treated by us. The first is to explain my opinion on the natural foundations of your Harmony—a work I would not have approached had I not been invited and incited by these words of yours on page 17, line 11: *“Now go, Robert, and first overturn these parts of nature: undermine these foundations: then finally deny that I have fulfilled my promise or proceeded naturally.”* The second is that I may sustain, in a few brief words, certain assertions in philosophy put forward by me (which you attempted to subvert in this part of your Defense). The third is to show myself, against your allegations, to be sufficiently well-versed in the Harmony of the ancient Philosophers, and consequently to demonstrate clearly that my Harmony is not so imperfect, nor so destitute of true demonstrations, nor so hidden and veiled in hieroglyphics and enigmas as you, Johannes, strive to imply in many places.

As for the natural foundations of your Harmony, you seem to explain them in these words on page 16, near the end: *“It is clear (I say) that I have unearthed the causes of this matter from the nature of things. Do you wish to know, then, what that nature of things is? The human soul is a part of nature: in the Soul shines the circle with its divisions through regular planes <note>Kepler refers to Euclidean geometry and the "constructible" polygons</note>, because the soul is the image of God. From the division of the circle, which occurs in the very essence of the soul, the terms of intellectual harmonies are established—in the world, according to Proclus; in the intelligible world, according to Iamblichus; and according to me, in the Divine mind, of which the human mind is a copy here, retaining the character of geometrical things from the birth of man from his Archetype. Furthermore: Hearing is a part of nature, and it bears witness to sounds and their quantities, which the common sense represents to the intellect. If a proportion is found in these that already shines in the intellect from its origin, these sounds are judged to be harmonic: from this arises the delight taken in them. This is the case in general. Now specifically, a part of the nature of intelligible things is the Triangle, a part is the Quadrilateral, and so on for the rest; and each distinguishes the circle into parts, which by their quantity or length become the terms of some harmonic proportion. To the number of consonances thus established follow the remaining Natural things which are present in artificial song.”* Now go, Robert, etc., as was said before.

Behold, my Johannes, your Robert stands ready to show you courteously, in succinct words—yet not in hieroglyphics or parables—what he thinks of these foundations of your Harmony.

As it seems to me, from these foundations of your Harmony, many-sided questions and doubts arise that are not easily resolved: namely:

> I. *Whether the human soul is a part of nature.*
>
> II. *Whether the Circle with its divisions through regular planes shines in the Soul, because the soul itself is the image of God.*
>
> III. *Whether from the division that occurs in the very essence of the soul, the terms of intellectual harmonies are established in the divine mind, as Johannes Kepler wishes: of which the human mind is a copy here, retaining the character of Geometrical things from the birth of man from his Archetype?*
>
> IV. *Whether Hearing is a part of nature, and bears witness to sounds and their qualities, which the common sense represents?*
>
> V. *If a proportion (from the aforesaid) were found shining in the intellect from its origin, whether the sounds should be judged harmonic, and whether delight arises from them or not?*
>
> VI. *Whether a part of the nature of intelligible things is the triangle, a part the quadrilateral, and whether each divides the circle into parts which are, by their quantity or length, terms of some harmonic proportion; and whether to the number of consonances thus established follow the remaining Natural things which are present in artificial song?*

Regarding the most important of these questions, my Johannes, in order—not to contradict you in anything, or to bring any harm to your Harmony, but solely for the sake of debating, and as a Philosopher provoked by a Philosopher to the resolution of certain questions beyond his own opinion—I thus begin:

### ->Is the human Soul a part of Nature?<-

->This question is held by me in the negative, contrary to your expectation:<-

1. Because Nature, insofar as it is the universal soul, has the character of a whole, and is not divided into essential parts, as Plato testifies.
2. Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus"</note> says that the Soul, namely the human mind (which he did not hesitate to call the nature of God), is no more separated or divided from God than a ray of the Sun is from the Sun.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense (Apologia) against criticisms found in the "Annals," specifically focusing on the nature of the Soul and its relationship to God and Nature. The author uses scholastic syllogisms to argue against the idea that the soul is a "part" of nature or contains geometric divisions.</meta>

# In Defense against the 12th Book of the Annals.

3. Plato, along with Aristotle, seems to affirm that the Creator of all things possessed the Soul as a total entity before any division. And Plato called this soul the Universal Nature.
4. Plato says that the Soul, when separated from bodily laws, is not a number possessing quantity, nor is it divided or multiplied into parts, but is uniform.
5. And Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized theurgy and the soul's ascent.</note> seems to agree that the Soul, although it appears to have all reasons and forms within itself, is nevertheless always determined according to some single thing.
6. Finally, Pythagoras and all other philosophers endowed with some divinity recognized God to be one and invisible. Thus, therefore, we dispute by Syllogism:
> That which was a total entity before any division is not a part of any thing,
> But the Soul was a total entity before division,
> Therefore it cannot be a part of nature.

The Minor premise is proved by the third axiom cited above.
But if you say to the Major premise that the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in scholastic texts.</note> understood this to be about the Soul of the World <note>original: "Anima mundi"</note> or the total soul, while you speak of the human soul: We reply with the fourth axiom, that the Soul separated from bodily laws is not a number, nor is it divided. But that Soul of the world, which according to Plato and following axiom 3 is nature itself, is separated from bodily laws; therefore, the human soul cannot be counted as a part of it, since it is indivisible, as shown by axioms 2, 3, and 4.
Or otherwise I shall deal with you thus, taking an argument from your own mouth:
> The Image of God is not a part of any thing,
> But indeed, by your own concession, the human soul is the image of God,
> Therefore it is not a part of Nature.

The Major premise is evident, because God is one and indivisible, according to axiom 6.
The Minor premise is your own assertion, as declared in the second question, and the discourse of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus.</note> concerning the vastness of the Mind declares this. Axiom 2.
Now indeed we shall hasten to the second question;

### Does the Circle with its divisions through regular planes shine forth in the Soul, for the reason that the Soul is the Image of God?

Supported by the strongest votes of the Philosophers and incited by them to this, I will not hesitate to deny even this Question. Namely because:
1. First, Plato says that the Soul separated from bodily laws is not a number having quantity, whence it is neither divided nor multiplied. But it is uniform, returning into itself, and rational, surpassing all bodily and material things.
2. Aristotle and Plato say that the Creator retained the soul as a total entity before division: and Pythagoras makes it one within itself, and says that it has its unity in the intellect.
3. Pythagoras, writing to Eusebius, recognizes God to be unity and indivisible, and says that duality is the Devil and evil, for in it is multitude and materiality. And Plato wishes all good to be one: but he wishes Evil to be on account of confused multitude.
4. Cicero says that there could be no perfection of order in all parts of the world, unless they were made continuous by one single divine and continuous spirit.
5. God can neither be defined, nor divided, nor composed. — Francesco Giorgio <note>A Venetian Franciscan friar (1460–1540) known for his Christian Kabbalah and Neoplatonism.</note>.
6. God infused in all things is called by the Platonists the Soul of the World, which they say has the character of the whole, insofar as being universally diffused He fills and invigorates all things.
7. God is neither a "what," nor a "what kind," nor a "how much," insofar as no category <note>term: predicamentum (a logical category of being, such as substance or quantity)</note> comprehends Him. — Scotus <note>Duns Scotus, the medieval scholastic theologian.</note>.
8. The Pythagoreans and Platonists, enclosing the Soul within 7 limits, say that in the first limit it rests in the highest intellect, and then they say it is made one and the same with it.
9. Just as all numbers are in unity, just as all lines of a circle are in the center, just as the powers of the limbs are in the soul, so God is said to be in all things and all things in God. — *The Art of Chemistry* <note>original: "Ars Chym."</note>.
10. Hermes Trismegistus says that God is the center of every thing, whose circumference is nowhere.

Thus, therefore, we argue upon these Axioms of the Philosophers against your assertion.
Argument I.
> That which, taken by itself, is not a number nor has quantity, certainly does not receive within itself a quantitative figure (such as a circle).
> But the Soul, separated from bodily laws, is not a number, nor has it quantity,
> Therefore the Soul does not receive a quantitative figure (such as a circle) within itself from its origin, and consequently, the circle does not shine forth in it at all.

<summary>The author argues that the human soul is an indivisible unity and the image of God, rather than a part of nature or a divisible geometric entity. Drawing on a wide range of authorities from Plato to Hermes Trismegistus, he concludes that the soul cannot contain quantitative shapes like circles because it exists beyond the laws of matter and number.</summary>

# Robert Fludd’s Reply

The major premise is evident in this: that which is not a quantity cannot receive quantities, just as "one" does not admit a multitude, and consequently, is not a number.

The minor premise is confirmed by Axiom 1, and similarly by 2 and 3, by which the Soul is proved to be "one." If you respond that the Soul, as you define it, is not exempt from these laws because it is specifically a human soul; I say that you have understood the very essence of the soul—as appears from what follows—which, when existing in a human, does not differ from the soul of the Great World <note>The Macrocosm or the Universe</note>, which is the subject of Axiom 1 in the second question, and by Axiom 2 of the first, where it is proved that the essence of the soul cannot be divided from God. Or otherwise thus:

> If the Soul be the image of God, it is neither a quantity nor a number,
> But, by your own confession, it is the Image of God,
> Therefore it is neither a number, nor does it admit quantity.

The major premise stands because God is neither a "what," nor a "what kind," nor a "how much" <note>original: "nec quid, nec quale, nec quantum"</note> per Axiom 7, insofar as He is outside and above every category <term>predicamentum: the Aristotelian categories of being</term>.

Furthermore, as pertains to the confirmation of your opinion (proving the soul to be the image of God), that is corroborated by Axiom 7, which testifies that the Soul sometimes rests in God, and is made one with Him at the highest limit of its essence. And by Axiom 2 in Question 1, the mind is not divided from God.

> If a circle with its divisions through regular planes from the origin reflects in the Soul, as if in gods, then the Soul is divided or multiplied.
> But the Soul is neither divided nor multiplied, Therefore [it is not a circle].

The major premise stands because if a circle fills the soul—whence it is called a "circle" by the Platonists (albeit in metaphorical speech)—and that circle is divided into parts by regular planes, it follows that the Soul is also divided by the division of that circle.

The minor premise is confirmed by Axiom 1; moreover, through Axiom 2, it is clear that the Creator obtained the Soul as a certain "total thing" before any division, whence from the beginning neither did a circle shine within it, nor did it admit the division of a circle through regular planes. But this is declared even more clearly by the following argument:

> The human soul (even by your agreement) is the image of God,
> But God can neither be divided nor composed of parts,
> Therefore neither can the human soul.

The major premise stands from what has been conceded.

The minor premise is declared first by Axiom 3, where Pythagoras makes God indivisible. Then by Axiom 5. Furthermore, the Platonists call God the "Soul of the World," from which Hermes Trismegistus says the human soul can no more be divided than a ray of the Sun from the Sun. And this also agrees with the Holy Bible, where we find that God is the Sun providing man's life and glory. From these things, therefore, I infer that if the Soul is the image of God, it follows that its divine essence is the same as God's, through which it is also made one with God.

Finally, that axiom of Cicero denotes that God is a single and continuous—that is, not divided—spirit, by means of which there is a perfection of order in all parts of the world. And this Spirit, as has been said, the Platonists take for the Soul of the World, and they say it has the nature of a "whole," insofar as it is universally diffused, fills all things, and governs and continually preserves them through the virtue which it liberally pours into created things daily from the perennial fountain of its spirit. Yet it is not as if a circle reflected in Him, or in His "breath of life" <note>original: "inspiraculo"</note>, imparting life and fiery love to the waters; for the human soul is also continuous, but it is said to be in all things, or all things in it, just as numbers are in unity, as all straight lines of a circle are in the center, or as the powers of the limbs are in the soul. For just as Unity is the common measure, fountain, and origin of all numbers, containing every number joined uniquely within itself—the principle of all multitude, yet in itself indivisible and lacking multitude, always the same and immutable—so in like manner created things relate to the Creator. And just as the individual human soul exists as the ruler of its body, being whole in the whole body and present in every part, so similarly God is everywhere in this world and presides over all creatures in it. And this is what Hermes seems to declare clearly when he defines God as the center of every thing, and elsewhere: *whose center is everywhere, whose circumference is nowhere.* Since, therefore, a center is a point scarcely imaginable, and a point is the smallest part of quantity, it does not seem likely that the largest and most capacious figure of Geometry <note>the circle</note> could be received within its being, much less be divided into smaller parts; and yet from that point, majesty and power shine forth unto infinity—namely, from a center where no periphery is found, because in Himself is all that is, and outside Himself He emits the rays of life at His pleasure unto infinity. And this is the reason why he affirms that He truly can neither be defined, divided, nor composed, and yet He has all these properties in metaphorical speech—in which sense He is also said to hear, speak, be angry, see with eyes, and touch with finger and hand. However, I think it escapes no one endowed with reason that this discourse is metaphorical and drawn from likeness. And this same thing can be said of the Soul; wherefore Iamblichus speaks not unwisely in these words: *The soul, although it seems to have all reasons and species, yet it is always determined according to a certain "one."*

These things being so, there is no need to proceed to the explanation or refutation of the four following questions: for when the cornerstone of any structure is weak or fashioned from shifting sand,

# In Defense against the 12th Analysis
->Cc<-

breath, it must of necessity melt away and be reduced to nothing by itself, so that the entire edifice collapses of its own accord, with no force pushing it, and is brought to nothing.

But nevertheless, God knows me better than to think I would do any violence in this place to the principles or foundations of Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler</note>; rather, I hope—indeed, I know—that he used metaphorical speech there, where he says that the human Soul is a part of nature, and that in it shines a circle with its dimensions through regular planes, etc. Yet I shall not imagine his Harmony to be merely symbolic or poetic, as he does mine. For who can explain the wonders of God, or of Nature, or of the first-born wisdom, except through similarities to created things? Since God is known through His creatures to be immense, ineffable, unthinkable, beyond all imagination, beyond all thought, beyond all intellect and essence, unnamable, to be preached only by silence in the heart, an incomprehensible depth, an indivisible Trinity, and an immutable essence. Of this, therefore, our very image is the **Universal Soul**: whence it is impossible to truly know or imagine that a circle can be found in God, or in that "breath of life" which He communicated to man, except in a certain allegorical respect; much less that Geometric figures could be found or represented in it by any real or spiritual impression, except by speaking through <term>analogy</term> <note>original Greek: ἀναλογίαν</note> and likeness. The Philosophers, therefore, spoke of God according to their own capacity and not truly as He is, nor could they judge concerning divine mysteries, which are indeed beyond all imagination, beyond all intellect, beyond all essence, and are incomprehensible. For God the Creator is enclosed within Himself, and no one can know the Father except through the Son, nor are His mysteries to be revealed except through His own Spirit. Yet it is granted to Physicists <note>Natural philosophers</note> and to Mathematicians to elicit prior causes by looking at subsequent effects. For Physicists, through the proper adaptation of the grades of matter to the form in the pure spirit and the elements—as of the passive or female to the active and male—derive the harmony of the world from the throne of God. Mathematicians, through Arithmetical and Geometric proportions with proper numbers and measures, attempt this same thing not foolishly. Physicists describe the spirit of God as being most thin and simple, closest to the source; Mathematicians rise up from the multitude toward God by the way of Geometry—namely, from the body to the surface, and from that through lines to the point of the angle—or they seek the Harmony of the world from the division of the circle into a triangle, quadrangle, etc., and by the apt application of these to the parts of the world; or by the Arithmetical way through regression from number and multitude to unity. Physicists seek to strip away the form and lay aside the confusion of matter, because they believe that by this path there will be an entrance to the knowledge of God, whose seat is indeed "inaccessible light," and they conclude that the more light something has in itself, the more it can claim God for itself; and by these steps they truly perceive and gather the Harmony of the world. Mathematicians seek to demonstrate this same thing through the simplicity of solid figures, through the mean square and resolution into the root. Therefore, a Physicist is not to be despised by a Mathematician because he does not use the Mathematician's invention to demonstrate Harmony, nor the Mathematician by the Physicist, even if he is not so well-versed in physical demonstration; for one travels from Prague toward Rome by various routes that do not differ in their result. Let us therefore join Mathematics to Physics, so that virtue thus united may be stronger and more powerful to perfect this work; for a great power and a literal ocean of disciplines is required for the description of the world's Harmony, and yet at the end of our searching we shall perceive ourselves to be as remote from the investigation of God's mysteries as at the beginning, for as the Prophet says, the mystery of God is a "great sea" into which many rivers have entered.

The Philosopher Simonides, when asked by the tyrant Hieron what God was, requested the space of one day for the resolution of this question. Returning the next day into the tyrant's presence, he was urged a second time to answer his question, but he requested two more days to explain the matter; finally, when the term ended and the tyrant pressed him more often to give an answer to his doubt, the Philosopher used to double his days every time. At last, when the tyrant diligently inquired into the reason for this, he is said to have received this response: "Because," he said, "the more I revolve this matter with myself again and again by thinking, the more obscure and mystical it indeed becomes to me." The Holy Scriptures also testify to this same thing: for, as God is said to be "clothed in light," so indeed is that Light inaccessible. And hence in Wisdom chapter 9 we find that no one knows the counsel of God, nor can think what God wills: because the reasonings of mortals are timid, and their thoughts unstable. The High Priest Moses seems to confirm this best in very few words, Deuteronomy 29:29: "The secret things of God no one knows, but they belong to God; however, the things revealed are known to us and to our children." Wherefore it is manifest that it is impossible to arrive at the knowledge of the hidden mysteries of God even through subsequent effects, unless it be through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. But let us hear what the Philosophers say for you, among whom I shall here recite the opinions of your Proclus.

First, Proclus seems to assert that the division of the soul is not according to matter or inferior things, but proceeds from an efficient cause: he therefore divides it through its perfect measures of all things, looking toward which it was necessary for the Creator to divide this universality in a similar way into intelligible patterns; and he affirms that this division into a multitude is gathered through a harmonic order assimilating the diverse parts.

Plato asserts that the Soul is both divisible and indivisible—namely, he makes it divisible when not separated from bodily laws; but truly he describes it as not being a number having quantity, and consequently, it is neither divided nor multiplied into parts.

Aristotle says (with whom Plato also agrees) that the Creator constituted the Soul as a certain whole before division.

# The Reply of Robert Fludd

Francesco Giorgio of Venice <note>Francesco Giorgio (1465–1540), a Franciscan friar and author of *De Harmonia Mundi*, who sought to harmonize Christian theology with Neoplatonism and Cabala.</note>, who wrote wonderfully and divinely concerning the **Harmony of the World**, says that the substance of the soul is a certain unique thing having parts simultaneously—namely, unity and multiplicity gathered from a marvelous Harmony. He says that whoever wishes to perceive the soul rightly must not apply the limit of their industry or labor to mathematical contemplations, but must elevate themselves as much as possible toward the place most suitable for the animal substance <note>In this context, "animal" refers to *anima* (soul), meaning the "soul-substance."</note>, and weigh in just balances that there is a threefold whole: one which is before its parts, another consisting of the parts themselves, and the last within each of the parts. The whole that arises from the production of parts is not consumed but remains; for that which gives the parts is good, and the composition of the parts is not even dissolved, for such dissolution is characteristic of a malignant spirit and not a good one. Whence it happens that the whole which precedes the parts survives and remains, but that which is of the parts is dissolved and perishes through the dissolution of the parts. For that which is from the parts is lower, and Plato designates this through those circles into which the soul is divided. He concludes, therefore, that the Soul is both unique and multiple, having its unity in the intellect and its quality of multitude insofar as it has respect for lower things. Therefore, the soul existing by itself is unique and simple, but descending toward lower things, it is said to be divided. And this is the principle of generation and corruption in lower things. Hence Pythagoras says, writing to Eusebius: **God is in unity, but in duality is the Devil and evil**, since in duality there is material multitude.

Hence it is clear how varied are the opinions of writers concerning the division of the Soul, as some wish it not to be according to matter, while others wish it so insofar as it participates in material things. For in truth, the inner soul (which is God himself) neither suffers nor admits divisions; therefore, its division is in respect to the matter in which it resides, and not from its own essence, which is the same as God, from whom it first emanated according to that saying of **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a foundational text for Renaissance magic and alchemy.</note> in the *Pimander*: "Mind indeed is born from the very essence of God, if indeed he has any essence; therefore it is by no means divided from the essence of God, but is connected to it in the same way that light is to the body of the Sun." This Mind is God in men, and for that reason, some among the number of men are Gods. Thus he spoke. From these things, it is clear that division exists in the multitude which is in matter, and not in the essence of the form. Thus we see infinite rays of the Sun mingle themselves with the spirit of the world, distinguishing it into infinite parts, while nevertheless those rays are not divided or distinguished from the solar body.

Plato, as was said above, seems to divide the Soul into circles, and elsewhere he called the soul a circle. But **Aristotle** is said to have rejected Plato’s propositions, not to refute what was written by him, but to condemn those terms which sound common and yet have another meaning; he did this so that some might not fall into errors through the metaphorical writings or terms frequently used by Plato (in which he used to enclose and hide a profound meaning). Francesco Giorgio of Venice provides an example of this. When they read in Plato, he says, that the soul is a circle or a number, it is not to be believed that this was said according to material mathematics or common arithmetic. Similarly, when he says that all things are nothing but one, it is not to be understood as one composite thing or any particular thing, but all things are called "one" insofar as they have the power of existing through the One, just as all numbers have their being from the **Unity** expanded into them.

By a clearly similar reason, God is called a **Circle** by the Platonists, which takes its origin from nowhere else but itself, and tending toward itself, leads all things with it. And yet by them and by Hermes Trismegistus, He is called the **Center** of every thing. Furthermore, the same Hermes, as Francesco Giorgio of Venice testifies, explains the **Trinity** under the riddle of the **Sphere**, when he says that God is a Sphere whose center—that is, the Father—is everywhere, or the circumference—that is, Wisdom and the Son—is nowhere, because he is incomprehensible, and yet he comprehends all things; but truly the mutual respect of harmony and the bond of love between the center and the circumference, which occurs through the regularity of the proportions of similar radii, is denoted by the **Holy Spirit**. This Spirit is called that **Golden Chain** in the world, preserving all the joints of the world (namely the elements) in peace and concord by its amorous embrace; that is, imparting the fiery vigor of life and the amorous power of multiplication to the waters (namely the mundane spirit), and filling all things with its harmony in the vast hollow of the world, lest a vacuum should again be given in the nature of things. This interpretation of the circle also seems to be confirmed by that passage of Ecclesiasticus: "I alone," says **Wisdom**, "have compassed the circuit of heaven, and I have penetrated even to the depth of the abyss." Furthermore, it is said that by the **Word of the Lord** the heavens were established, and by the **Spirit of his mouth** all their power. That the periphery of this circle is beyond human grasp is clear from these words of the holy man Job (ch. 11:8-9): "The Wisdom of God is not to be found; it is higher than the heavens, and deeper than the lowest grave; its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea." You see here, therefore, how enigmatic is the sense of the Philosophers, and how removed from common understanding, when they name God or the Soul a Circle, or say that a Circle is within them.

Indeed, through the **Harmony** of the same Word leaping forth from the bonds of darkness and overcoming the marks of death, all things shall return to the Unity from which they previously regressed, according to that saying of Saint Paul previously cited, by which we are openly taught that not only men, but also all other things are led to their true harmonies through the blood of Christ. His words are of this kind: "Making peace through the blood of his Cross for all things which are on earth and which are in the heavens." This, I say, is the extension of the Son (namely Wisdom) from the center (namely the Father), whom the **Cabalists** <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), which Fludd integrated into his Christian Hermeticism.</note> called the **Dark Aleph** <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, used here to represent the hidden, unmanifested God (*Ein Sof*).</note> (namely the hidden God), so that the Son (namely Light or the Word) leaping forth from this Center in every direction as if into a circle, is called by them the **Luminous Aleph**, that is, the revealed God; concerning which enough will be said copiously below. And the Platonists received this Wisdom of the Hebrews, and the Messiah of the Christians, and the Cabalists—

# In Defense of the Twelfth Book of the Annals
## Cc 2

...the [Angel] Metatron <note>original: "Mittatron"; in Jewish mysticism, the highest angel and celestial scribe</note>, and the Word of the Prophets and Apostles as the true Soul of the World, which they said harmoniously filled all the intervals of the world in the triple, its square, and its cube: namely 3, 9, 27. This formal and most perfect proportion acted upon that material one—2, 4, 8—as the active upon the passive, the male upon the female, form upon matter, and perfection upon imperfection. Therefore, the active Spirit of Wisdom, namely the angel Metatron, strikes through the aforementioned proportions of perfection into the passive spirit of the world, which receives the measures—that is, the impressions of harmonies—from the striking spirit, just as a string from a Musician, or a pipe from a blower. But the pipe itself, namely the instrument, is the vast cavity of the World itself, which when the soul has struck it, it fills with divine breath, just as the force of the blower fills the hollow of the pipe with his spirit.

And here it is demonstrated clearly enough in passing that, just as the proportion of harmony (namely of sounds and chords) was in the pipe or the string and not in the blower or the player, so also the circles—from whose parts you say harmony arises in the soul—that very harmony or the proportions constituting it were in the thing measured, and not in the measurer; that is, in the numbered and not the numbering, as I shall immediately show in a physical manner.

But let us return to the matter: just as the Platonists reduced every act of worldly Music to the cube of the triple [27]; so, to explain the harmony of the world, they expressed three groups of nine <note>enneads</note> concurring in the composition of that cube in a twofold way: either, namely, insofar as this cube of the triple is 27, or by adding three nines gathered into one—999—they produced or arranged them from right to left in this manner: 999. By the cube, therefore, they attempted to demonstrate the worldly Harmony mathematically, proving the harmonic proportions of form through its parts in the world, as we shall declare below.

And Pythagoras, most skilled in numbers, intended this same thing when he asserts that perfect harmony is completed through cubes: whence the Pythagoreans called cubes "harmony," because among other figures they have angles proportionally equal in sides and surfaces. But Plato and the Cabalists seem to include admirable mysteries of worldly harmony, both metaphysical and physical, in this series of nines, 999: for according to the Arithmetic <note>Algorithm</note> of the Arabs and Hebrews, the first number toward the right is a simple number contained under the number ten, to which, because of its simplicity, they attributed the formal essence and the nine Orders of Angels, which are in the intelligible world; the second group of nine, which is of tens, and in which there is composition, they applied to the nine auricular heavens; and the last, which is of hundreds, in which the composition is still more material and compact, to the nine degrees of generable and corruptible things in the elementary world. All these terminate in man, who is like a passage and medium through which those things pass to celestial things, and from them are exalted again to intelligible things. And through these intervals perfectly filling the world, so that no vacuum or emptiness is left in the nature of things, the most exact Harmony of the Sages, both of the world and of the soul, is drawn out; but to specify these things exactly with the Philosophers and Mathematicians is a most difficult matter.

Truly the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah</note> demonstrated this threefold division not by numbers, but by analogy or likeness: for there are three things, it says, which correspond and are shaped according to the pattern of the Archetype (the primary Idea): namely, the Tabernacle of God prepared by Moses, the Temple of Solomon, and the Human Body. These correspond to the three aforementioned numbers in the Macrocosm <note>the great world/universe</note>: namely the vocal or operative, which is drawn from measure to the elementary world; the formal, which is elicited from the vocal to the celestial; and the rational, springing from the formal to the intelligible.

For the Tabernacle represented by Moses seems to symbolize the three worlds in both the macrocosm and microcosm in this way:
*   **The first portion**, which is not covered but lies open to the air, is exposed to winds, rain, hail, snow, and other atmospheric impressions in the sublunary world, and is in perpetual change and alteration; and to this place the common crowd and animals have access, and there was a constant change of life and death because of the continual sacrifices offered there. This portion of the Tabernacle denotes the **Elementary World**, which is composed of thicker waters as a fluid substance, unstable and least remaining in the same state; whence this is properly called the World of shadows and darkness, where the Tempter and prince of darkness has his dwelling and dominion. Thus it is subject to death, corruption, and changes. In man himself, this is denoted by his **body**.
*   **The second part**, gleaming with gold and adorned by the lampstand with seven points (which without doubt are symbols of the 7 heavens of the Planets), denotes the **Celestial World**, which participates in light and darkness, corresponding to water and fire: whence by the Hebrews the Heaven is called <term>אשמים</term> <term>Eschamaim</term> <note>Heaven</note> from <term>אש</term> <term>Esch</term> <note>Fire</note> and <term>מים</term> <term>maym</term> <note>Water</note>: whence ether is also called as if *aeth-aer*, that is, fiery air. And hence it is that although this part is imbued with body, yet because of the prevailing disposition of the lucid form in it and a certain intellect governing it (as the rational soul governs the body), it does not submit itself to corruption. In man, such is his **soul or spirit of life**.
*   **The third part** of the Temple is the **Holy of Holies**, showing the super-celestial or intellectual World in the macrocosm, totally forged from perfect and intelligible light and fire: and it is the seat of the Angels ministering before God, the great Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter divine name YHWH</note>. And this is denoted by those two golden Cherubim, who, elegant and extending their wings toward the altar and the Mercy Seat, cast a shadow.

This World, therefore, moves the celestial one, and that in turn moves the Elementary. The Super-celestial World is thus male to the Celestial, upon which it acts as a male upon a female, whose universal matrix is the Sun, which fills the other stars with its Light; and likewise that Celestial is male to the Elementary, whose matrix is the Earth itself. In a similar way, such is the respect or comparison between the outer part of the Tabernacle and the human Body, likewise between its middle and gilded part and the human Soul, and finally between the Holy of Holies of the tabernacle and the Reason, Intellect, and Mind in man. And hence it is that man is also called by the Apostle the "Temple of the Holy Spirit."

-># Reply of Robert Fludd<-

And from this it arises that, through that respect which is held toward the number 999, the division of the fruits and goods of the earth was made in the Mosaic law: for one hundred portions were destined for the people, and a tenth part for the men of the Church, from which part again a tenth portion was extracted for God himself. Thus, the hundreds—as numbers more material, coarse, and immersed in the multitude—are referred to the people, the commoners, and the profane; the tenth to the priests; and the unity to God, who, existing as all in all, is nevertheless nothing but unity. From these things it is clear that all things are nothing but one when viewed in respect to God, but by the reasoning of the human grasp, they seem to be many and manifold.

And so, as far as the Philosophers are concerned, the Soul and God himself seem to be a Circle, receiving divisions into themselves from which they desire to draw out sciences and find various formulas of worldly Harmony. But I wish they would rightly understand what Jeremiah says on this matter in chapter 9: *Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong in his strength, nor the rich in his riches, but in this, that he knows and understands God.* <note>Jeremiah 9:23-24</note> But the truly wise say one thing and understand another, as has been proven before. But to proceed in this Discourse and open the mystery of the ternary number <note>The number three</note> with a wider gap, the Cabalists and the Wise Men of the Hebrews say that this number 999 is found in the Hebrew letters of the strongest intelligence, <term>מטטרון</term> <note>Metatron: In Jewish mysticism, the highest angel and celestial scribe.</note> Metatron, whom they called the Prince of Faces, because he has the office of introducing before the face of the Lord those whom he wishes to be called; others take him for that Soul of the World described by the Platonists. This Metatron, namely the Soul of the World, was (according to the tradition of the Sages) the first created thing, retaining in himself the perfection of all other Creatures: whence it seems to me that he was that Wisdom of which it is said in Ecclesiasticus chapter 1: *Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from everlasting:* as will also appear from what follows.

The more secret Theologians and those most expert in the true Cabala have said that just as the Mind has dominion over the human Soul, so also Metatron presides over the celestial world (in which the Sun resides), and the soul of the Messiah over the angelic world, and Adonai over the Archetype itself. And just as the light of the soul is the active intellect—that is, the Mind itself—so also the light of the Angel Metatron or the Soul of the World is *Shaddai* <note>original: "Sadai"; a Hebrew name for God, often translated as Almighty.</note>, and the light of the soul of the Messiah is *El Chai* <note>original: "El chai"; meaning "The Living God."</note>, and the light of Adonai himself is *En Soph* <note>original: "En soph"; the Infinite or Boundless nature of God before manifestation.</note> signifying the infinity of the Divinity. Therefore, the Soul of the World or Metatron—whose light is that Soul of the Messiah or the power of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note>, in which is the light of the living God, in which is the light of *En Soph*—is the point beyond which there is no progression. From these things it is clear that in Metatron himself (the soul of the world, the wisdom created before all things and existing in eternity with God) is the power of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Whence concerning him (as the Sages have explained), God intended when he spoke to the Israelites in these words, Exodus 23: *Behold, I send my Angel before thy face, who shall keep thee in the way; listen to his voice, and do not provoke him, for my name is in him:* This is the Tetragrammaton, which is the Symbol of the Trinity. Behold, therefore, how powerful and close to God the Creator himself is that soul of the world, and how profoundly it sees; from *En Soph* or the infinity of the divinity itself, it draws the origin of that spiritual and fiery Harmony, which is the active and formal harmony in the world, signified by the Platonists through the ternary numbers 1, 3, 9, 27, or 999. Its harmonic acts are imprinted upon imperfect matter through the binary number 1, 2, 4, and 8, according to the Philosophers, following the dignity and proportion of the matter in its purity, subtlety, thickness, or opacity; by these, it fills the worldly spirit with its lucid virtue, whether by thinning it through subtlety or thickening it through coagulation. And just as through the act of this universal soul the unity of deformed and dark *hyle* <note>Matter or primordial substance.</note> is divided into a multitude—just as we perceive the Sun with our eyes dividing the worldly spirit into infinite parts with its rays—so also the Platonists understand all those parts created in the beginning by illumination to be joined to one another by that fiery love (which is also called the "glue" or the fiery bond of nature), joining its creating form with the things created in material multitude by a harmonic knot: as we see in numbers that 3 joins 2 to 4, and 6 joins 4 to 8, and so in the rest. And from here arose the invention of the triple means, namely the Harmonic, Geometric, and Arithmetic, among which the harmonic is truly natural and pertains to physics; the others look to mathematics rather than to nature. From here, therefore, is derived the invention of the Platonists and Pythagoreans regarding the Heptachord <note>A seven-stringed musical scale.</note>, where they make their mixtures of odd numbers with even numbers, denoting thereby the "unions" of progression—that is, the proportions of the harmonic bond made between male and female, light and darkness, matter and form, heaven and earth, creator and creature. This is done either by counting upward from the lowest base of the multitude toward unity (simplicity), like Aristotle and the Peripatetics, who used to outline Nature and its consensus through *a posteriori* demonstrations—that is, they ascended in their demonstration from the nature of sensible things through the explanation of the mysteries of the elements and the principles of lower things up to the celestial machine and no further, and this through the quaternary number, which is corporeal, material, and sensible (which number, according to the doctrine of Pythagoras, participates in matter and body just as the ternary number participates in form). Or, it is done by descending through *a priori* demonstration from the supreme Creator of all things to the lowest grade of creatures, and this through the ternary number, in the manner of the order of the Sephiroth <note>The ten attributes/emanations in Cabala.</note>, first from the intellectual heaven into the ethereal, and from that into the elements (the elementary heaven). And from there I have derived my natural Demonstrations, from the composition of two pyramids—one formal and one material—disposed in a transverse way. From these, the grades and bonds of watery matter and lucid form in worldly nature—that is, the intersections of the worldly monochord <note>A single-stringed instrument used by Fludd to illustrate the musical proportions of the universe.</note> with their intervals linked to each other by a harmonic bond—are drawn forth, concerning which I have written more copiously in my Physics.

# In Defense of the 12th Analogy
## Cc 3

We have dealt with this in the physical *History of the Macrocosm* <note>referring to Fludd's earlier work, *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*</note>. From this, it should be noted in passing how varied are the methods of philosophizing among men, and how divided is the discovery of the true worldly Harmony. Some begin through numbers, and of those, some start with the number two <note>the dyad</note>, like the **Peripatetics** <note>followers of Aristotle</note>; others with the number three <note>the triad</note>, like the **Platonists**, of whom the latter desires to demonstrate matter through form, while the former strives to explain the mysteries of form through matter. The **Pythagoreans** used both formulas. The **Cabalists**, **Sages**, and **Hermeticists** undertake to achieve this through the real and living speculation and observation of the actions and passions of nature. Yet all have acknowledged and confessed that **Golden Chain** <note>original: *Catenam illam auream*</note>, whose first link they believe is bound and fixed to the Throne of Jove; declining downward from that point and stretching through all the vitals of nature even to the center of the world, it delineates the consonances and intervals of worldly harmony with its joints, and Jupiter himself strikes and compels the harmonic string of the worldly instrument to vibrate in symphony.

This, I say, is that **Jacob’s Ladder**, by means of which the Angels—that is, the divine minds of men—incline themselves from heaven and ascend to heaven with admirable harmony. The instrument of this harmony, I say, was that stone of Jacob, a pillow possessing and representing the likeness and harmony of the whole world, which was indeed called the "House of God." Its image was that tripartite Tabernacle of Moses described by us before and related to the three regions of the World. Indeed, in that **Microcosm** <note>the human being as a "little world"</note>, the true temple of God, the true harmony of the world is beheld with living eyes: the ratio of formal numbers, the primordial consideration of the dyad and triad, the clear disposition of darkness and light, the union of passive nature with the active, the progression of element into element according to the laws of nature, the ratio of the perfection of the number three, and the production of that number seven springing from the admirable bond of matter and form (that is, 4 and 3), the explanation of the Sabbath day (namely, rest in the Lord), and the lucid demonstration of the 7 steps of Jacob’s Ladder. These steps are: the way through the earth, through the thick water, through the impure air, through the thick fire, through the ether of life (which is the fifth element or fiery and pure air), through the purely fiery heaven (the sixth element), and finally to the ineffable revelation of the divine essence and majesty, where inexplicable rest, peace, Sabbath, and glory are most clearly explained for eternity; for Jacob said: *God is here, and I knew it not.*

Here, therefore, is explained the true harmony of the world; here is the first illumination of the divine philosophers and the discovery of the science of Music, which they adapted to the external numbers and figures of Mathematics, just as we have declared that the secrets of both the archetypal and typical world are drawn out according to the model of Solomon’s Temple or the Mosaic Tabernacle. But this is usually done in a symbolic or analogical manner, when it occurs through the numbers of common Arithmetic, the external figures of Geometry, or through visible things; for there is no true or certain vision in corporeal things, which "seem to be and are not." Rather, the certainty of all visions is in the center of the form—namely the intellectual center—since in the "womb of form," **Wisdom** (that is, the **Word**, the **Light of the Messiah**) is said to shine back, just as it is said to be in **Metatron** <note>a supreme angel in Kabbalistic tradition</note>, the soul of the world.

From these things, therefore, it stands clearly enough (unless I am mistaken) that when Philosophers have said God is a Circle, or that a Circle is in the soul, dividing it into Geometric parts (namely triangle, quadrangle, pentagon, etc.), that, my Johannes, is said only in an analogical and metaphorical way. And yet I still hope that I shall achieve so much before the world that, because we are now joined in literary friendship (as I hope), I may bring it about that we both agree on the same foundations of Harmony. Thus it will appear to the world that there is no need for further contention between us, but that we may rest together in peace, as becomes good Christians.

You, therefore, say that the human Soul is a part of nature, and that in the soul a circle shines back with its divisions through regular planes, because the mind is the image of God. But I say that the Soul, insofar as respect is had for its essence, cannot be divided from nature as a part from the whole, according to that saying of **Hermes Trismegistus** in *Pimander* 12: *The Mind is by no means divided from the essence of God, but rather connected to it in the same way that Light is to the body of the Sun.* For we see the solar rays are joined with the solar body and are not truly to be divided, since the essence of Light is one and not divisible into parts. But indeed, in respect to us who are occupied in the multitude, we say the Soul of this person differs from that of another in number and species, while nevertheless all souls have a continuous relation to the one soul of the world or **Metatron**, as the light of the Sun to the Sun.

There is, therefore, truly plurality in matter and not in form, which is nothing other than a continuous emanation from God (namely the Word), imparting life and essence to all Creatures. By the withdrawal of this, life is taken away, according to Psalm 104: *When God gives to the Creatures they gather; when He opens His hand they are filled and satisfied with good; when He hides His face they are troubled; when He takes back His spirit they expire and return to dust; when He sends forth His spirit they are recreated.* And Job chapter 12:10 says: *In God’s hand is the soul of every living thing, and the spirit of all flesh.* And Psalm 146: *The kindness of God preserves all things forever.* And elsewhere it is said that God is the Sun, giving life and glory. For God, as has been said, is present everywhere by His essence throughout the world, and dwelling in His Metatron, and clothed in Light (as the Holy Scriptures say), He fills all things and continually preserves them by His presence. Hence all works in creation were called "good," which had been esteemed "evil and void" before Creation; this goodness arose from God (who is the sole and highest good) and from participation in His essence. By this "glue" and harmony, all things in the world are connected in concordant peace and eternal bonds.

I conclude, therefore, that as the essence of God is indivisible, so also Nature itself, which is His emanation into the world, is in every way a single form and indivisible in itself. And insofar as God is divisible into three Persons (arguing from the offices and properties produced for the perfection of this world), so also the soul is said to be divided into various parts, whence sometimes it is sense, now...

# Reply of Robert Fludd

memory, sometimes imagination, then reason, intellect, Mind, etc. Those who choose to consider the Soul as it is placed within perishable things will notice with their bodily eyes that it is distinguished from the body and its properties. But he who returns into himself and toward his own center, neglecting the external world as if it were a deceptive shadow, and penetrates his own interior entrances—he indeed will perceive with spiritual eyes that there is neither division nor quantity within the soul. Nor can numbers or geometric figures be investigated within God (who is above "how much" and "what kind," and with whom the essence of the soul is continuous). But regarding this, the Cabalists <note>Jewish mystics whose teachings Fludd integrated into his Christian Hermeticism</note> spoke of the circle of *Metatron* <note>original: "Mettatron"; a high archangel in celestial hierarchy</note> (in whose image the human soul is made, since it is of the same essence and continuous with it), affirming it to have been a certain green line surrounding the vast cavity of the world, whence it is also called by them *Kether Elyon* <note>original: "Cheterelion"; Hebrew for "Supreme Crown," the highest Sephirah or emanation of God</note>, that is, the supreme crown. And Moses seems to support their opinions by saying that the Spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters, and as another adds, imparting fiery force to them by a peripheral motion. Yet, the soul of the world is not a circle for that reason, nor is a circle within it; rather, the soul itself, by its own circular motion, terminates and contains the world as if through the most capacious figure, just as it also divides the light from the darkness. Therefore, the circle and its imaginary divisions exist in the created passive spirit, and not in the creating soul.

But truly, insofar as the soul through its essence fills the triple and formal steps of the harmonic scale, and is said to be present everywhere and to comprehend all things, the thing comprehended is nonetheless not otherwise than the nature and essence of the comprehender, just as the Creature is in the essence of the Creator. But the mundane Circles are said to be in the radiant soul, just as darkness once illuminated is in the light, or mundane water is in fire; so also a multitude can be said to be found in light—namely, in the matter comprehended by Light—even though that Light is individual, unique, and indivisible in itself. Therefore, the circle is not in the essence of the soul, but in that material thing, namely the mundane spirit, to which the soul gives being, and which it embraces on all sides like a circle; yet in that circle is found neither center nor circumference, according to that passage of Job cited above, chapter 11:9: *The wisdom of God is not to be found, for it is higher than the highest heavens, and deeper than the lowest grave; its measure is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.*

We agree, therefore, on this: that the universal Spirit of the world (once empty and covered in darkness, now made by the very *Yod* <note>The Hebrew letter representing the beginning of the Divine Name</note>, or God previously hidden but now revealed by revelation, or the Word (which is the Light and life of the world), and by the wisdom created before all things, which Solomon says is in itself brighter than the Sun and Stars) was reduced into a spherical figure filling the vast cavity of the world, sustained by the power and virtue of the act—namely, the soul of the world—and enclosed like something terminated and finite within an indeterminate and infinite thing. Thus, this circular spirit is enclosed by the fiery soul of the world surrounding it, with whose parts the fiery force and symphonic love of that soul is mixed in the smallest degree, just as the human soul is in the whole being and in every part of the whole. I acknowledge also, that by the art of Mathematics <note>original: "Matheos"; referring to the mathematical study of the spheres</note>, this substance can be partitioned and distinguished into parts by an imaginary way and conceived in the mind, both by arithmetic numbers and geometric figures, by which we can arrive at the knowledge of the perfection of God and nature through demonstration, either *a posteriori* or *a priori*. However, Mathematicians and Philosophers ought to know that they labor in mathematics for that goal because, in truth, neither numbers nor external figures exist in the mundane soul considered by itself (since it is continuous and devoid of division), but demonstrations are made through analogy or likeness. For the true subject of Physics and its harmony is Spirit (or Water) and Light (or soul)—that is, matter and form. Therefore, in a mathematical manner, Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler</note> has well described the harmony of the visible world, but in a more abstract reason; and in a physical manner, Robert <note>Robert Fludd himself</note> has explained his Harmony, but in a more concrete reason. Since, therefore, both of us are firmly established upon the same foundations of nature, I do not see why Robert can justly reject Johannes’s mathematical way in describing the Symphony of nature, or likewise why Johannes should repudiate Robert’s physical path in the explanation and demonstration of his Harmony, since (I say) the foundations are the same, the object and goals are the same, and only the progress in demonstrating is different.

But where you seem to assert that those divisions and intervals of Harmony were in the archetypal world from the beginning, and were infused from there into the human soul, I say that no division occurs in the divine essence, as it is indivisible, nor can it receive impressions of circles or figures (except when speaking metaphorically). For it is like a *Diapason* <note>The musical interval of an octave, representing perfection and return to unity</note> of the most perfect and complete consonance, which, arising from its own power, returns into it again, and remains this one thing. And the soul behaves likewise, according to that saying of Plato mentioned above, insofar as it is free from bodily laws; since it is a ray of that divinity from which it arose. Whence it should be known that, just as in the nature of things the Sun is an entire whole and one without division, yet it emits infinite rays (which are of the same essence as their whole) into the spirit of the world, distinguishing it into infinite species; or as unity in Arithmetic is indivisible, yet from it a multitude flows by itself: so also God, who is always one and the same and in every way indivisible, is dispersed into a multitude—that is, into matter and its parts—while this "One" remains itself and indivisible. Whence He is called by Philosophers versed in Theology the "Being of beings" and the "Father of creatures." He is therefore one infinite and indivisible thing insofar as He is considered in and by Himself, and yet again He is divided into harmonic parts and proportions as far as we and common understanding are concerned, insofar as life and being send out their rays from a single center, as it were, to infinite points of the circumference, attributing life to every proportion and creature of the world, and distinguishing one from another. Whence all things are said to live in God and exist in Him—that is, they are thought to derive life and existence from His essence. And this was the reason why Democritus and Orpheus and many of the Pythagoreans, considering things in a common way, asserted that all things are full of Gods.
