# In Defense against the 12th Analysis
## Cc 4

...they have declared, showing from there that every creature possesses its own proper and peculiar God; yet, judging with their interior eyes, they concluded that all these Gods had a relation to the one Jupiter, just as all the rays of the Sun are referred back to the single Sun. Whence we find in Exodus 20: that none is to be worshiped except the one God, who is elsewhere called the God of Gods <note>original: "Deus Deorum"</note>; and elsewhere: *You alone, O Jehovah, are God.* It does not follow, therefore, that because the Holy Spirit is in every man, providing the power and virtue of living and reasoning, that there are many Holy Spirits or that the Holy Spirit is divided into parts, insofar as the essence of God is not divisible. Yet it is certain that men are, as it were, infinite, and truly distinct and divided from one another in terms of matter—which alone expands into multitude—and not in form, which is always continuous with its own luminous source.

But to transcend now to more particular matters, let us inquire for a moment whether the method of investigating natural Harmony among the Philosophers most skilled in nature was varied or not, and whether they observed a single path or one method? And if not, it must be asked why a new system of worldly harmony should not be granted to Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler</note> and Robert <note>Robert Fludd</note> as much as to any of those who applied their efforts to the investigation of the World’s Harmony.

We read first of all that Terpander <note>A Greek poet and musician of the 7th century BCE</note>, discovering the seventh string (that is, the heptachord), finally equated it to the number of the 7 planets. Others among the ancients found a fourfold kind of Harmony in both the Macrocosm and Microcosm fitting the elements: namely, they judged the **Dorian** mode to harmonize with Water and Phlegm, the **Phrygian** with Fire and Choler, the **Lydian** with Air and Blood, and the **Mixolydian** with Earth and Black Bile. Similarly, Nicomachus <note>Nicomachus of Gerasa, a mathematician who wrote on the music of the spheres</note> assigned the Tetrachord discovered by Mercury to the 4 elements; of which he claimed the single string *Hypate* resonated with and indicated Earth, *Parahypate* or *Mese* Water, *Nete* or *Diezeugmenon* or *Hyperbolaion* Fire, and *Paranete* Air. Others, looking to the number and power of the heavens, assigned the **Dorian** to the Sun, **Phrygian** to Mars, **Lydian** to Jupiter, **Mixolydian** to Saturn, **Hypophrygian** to Mercury, **Hypolydian** to Venus, **Hypodorian** to the Moon, and **Hypomixolydian** to the starry sky. Some again make the space lying between the Earth and the Moon the interval of a Tone. (Here indeed Johannes would mock me, by Hercules, I know, if he had found a tone of such great length in my Harmony!) Then from the Moon to Mercury he makes half that space a semitone, and as much from there to Venus. From there to the Sun he establishes a triple tone and a half, as it were, a <term>Diapente</term> <note>A perfect fifth</note>. From the Moon to the Sun, making two and a half, a <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>A perfect fourth</note>. From the Sun to Mars they again have as much interval as from the Earth to the Moon, making a tone. From there to Jupiter half of that, making another semitone, and as much from there to Saturn, constituting a semitone, from which to the orb of the stars there lies again the space of a semitone. Thus from the Sun to the starry heaven is a *Diatessaron*, namely of two tones and a half; but from the earth a perfect <term>Diapason</term> <note>An octave</note>, namely of six whole tones. According to others, from the proportion of the motions of the Planets to each other and with the eighth heaven, there results a Harmony, as they say, the sweetest of all; the proportion of Saturn to Jupiter is a double sesquialtera <note>5:2 ratio</note>, Jupiter to Mars a sescupla <note>6:1 ratio</note>, of that to the Sun, Venus, and Mercury (who complete their journey equally) a double proportion <note>2:1</note>, of those to the Moon a twelvefold proportion <note>12:1</note>, and of Saturn to the starry orb a thousandfold and two-hundredfold. Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, the famous occultist</note> maintains that Saturn, Mars, and the Moon have more of "voice" than of "concord," and says that Saturn has sad, hoarse, deep, slow sounds, as if compressed toward the center. Mars has harsh, sharp, threatening, swift, and angry voices. Between these, the Moon observes a middle ground. Jupiter, the Sun, Venus, and Mercury possess concords. Jupiter therefore claims for himself deep, constant, intense, sweet, cheerful, and pleasant concords. The Sun, venerable, pure, and sweet ones. Venus, lascivious, luxurious, and voluptuous ones. Mercury, more relaxed, manifold, and joyful with a certain vigor. From these particular concords and proportions, the tone obeys the nine Muses: Jupiter has the grace of the eighth and fifth voice, that is, the *Diapason* and *Diapente*; the Sun obtains the melody of the eighth voice, the *Diapason*. Similarly, the fifteen tones of the <term>Disdiapason</term> <note>A double octave</note>. Venus holds the grace of the fifth voice, the *Diapente*. Mercury has the *Diatessaron*, the grace of the fourth voice. And so with the rest.

Plato and Pythagoras draw the demonstrations of their Harmony from the reasoning of numbers and proportions and their mutual concatenation. Aristotle attempts to explain this matter through physical principles and things derived from principles. Likewise, there are others who imagine the Harmony of the human Soul to consist of the due temperament and proportion of its virtues and operations, which are the Concupiscible, the Irascible, and the Rational; the proportions of which they say are of this kind: namely, that the Rational and Concupiscible have the proportion of a *Diapason*, but to the Irascible a *Diatessaron*; and the Irascible to the Concupiscible has the proportion of a *Diapente*. And there are other various inventions of this kind according to the minds and intentions of Philosophers and Mathematicians philosophizing in diverse ways.

From these things, therefore, it clearly appears that it is as permissible for Johannes, according to the concept of his soul in his mathematical way, to proceed in the demonstration of worldly Harmony, as it is for Robert to explain the laws of his natural Symphony according to his own invention and imagination; since it is established by the testimony of the aforementioned that it is a common and familiar thing among Philosophers to commit the mysteries of nature to writing in their own manner and peculiar method.

But now, my Johannes, since it has not entered my mind to make a further inquiry into the laws of your Harmony because of the friendship once kindly contracted between us, it occurs to me at this point to bring forth a few but sufficiently clear words about my own Worldly Harmony and its proportions, and likewise to lightly introduce a comparison here between its proportions and those of Plato, whereby...

# Robert Fludd’s Reply

->308<-

...let me declare to you and to the world in succinct speech that Robert, in the discovery of his Harmony and the arrangement of its proportions, has not erred as gravely as you perhaps thought at first glance. But before I descend into the discourse of my own Harmony, I shall now speak of the Harmony of the ancients, compelled to do so for a twofold reason. First, to indicate to the learned that I am not entirely as ignorant of the Harmony of the ancients as I have been proclaimed to be by Johannes <note>Johannes Kepler</note> in many places. Second, so that I might more rightly and easily adapt the proportions of their Harmony to my Monochord of the World, by which you (most esteemed Readers) might more rightly judge that comparison of mine.

We find it committed to writing, according to both the Pythagoreans and the Academics <note>Followers of Plato</note>, that both the world and its souls were to be described most fittingly through harmonic proportions. And since three kinds of melodies—that is, genres of harmony—were chiefly in use and practice among the ancients: namely, the **Diatonic**, which proceeds by Tone, Tone, and Semitone <note>The steps of a musical scale</note> constituting the consonance of a *Diatessaron* <term>Diatessaron: An interval of a perfect fourth</term> in all tetrachords (originally discovered for the arrangement of the four elements), which genre is somewhat harsh but natural; the **Chromatic**, receding from the natural Diatonic and sounding softer, which decreases by a semitone, a semitone, and three semitones, which joined together also make a *Diatessaron*; and finally the **Enharmonic**, which is sung in all tetrachords by a *Diesis* (which is here taken for half a semitone) and a *Diesis* and a *ditone* <note>A major third</note>, all of which added together likewise measure out the consonance of a *Diatessaron*.

From these, the divine Plato chose the **Diatonic** for describing his harmony of the world and the soul, because he perceived that genre to be more natural, simple, and noble, and consequently more disposed of itself to originally depict and describe the symphonic duties and harmonic proportions of the world and the soul—that is, the links of watery matter and lucid form, or of the passive and active—within each thing by itself and between them. He was moved all the more toward this choice because it was noticed through diligent observation by him and Timaeus of Locri that this genre has in its nature a certain governance of rational life, just as that Harmonic genre presides over all life adapted to the body, and the Chromatic has respect for the ideal-corporeal. But since among these properties of the soul, reason is more eminent and noble, and this Diatonic genre is more natural in its arrangement, he therefore chose it above the others for this inquiry into his mundane Harmony.

But truly, as the ancients proceeded through tetrachords <note>Four-note scales</note> in this, so Plato—in imitation of Nicomachus—expanded it to a **Heptachord** <note>A seven-stringed scale</note> and to seven limits for a better and more proportional demonstration of his Harmony, beginning from unity and doubling up to the binary cube (namely, 8), and then afterwards tripling up to the cube and solid of the ternary <note>The number 3</note>. According to the proportion of such numbers, the Academics thought the fabric of both the soul and the world was arranged and brought to completion, following those ancient teachings of Pythagoras. He equated the proportions of the ternary number to the soul, as if to masculine active perfection and light, and those of the binary to matter, as if to feminine, passive imperfection and water. From the conjunction of these—namely, from matter and form—all things in this world were procreated and propagated. Therefore, those most skilled in the science of numbers adapted the **Monad** <note>The number 1</note> to God the Creator, the **Dyad** or Duality to matter, the virgin **Triad** to the forms themselves, and the **Heptad** <note>The number 7</note> to life and man.

And hence Plato ordered his Diatonic Harmony to the Heptachord, because he adapted it to the relationship between both worlds—namely, the soul and corporeal substance—the proportions of which he deduces from the aforementioned 1, 2, and 3. The cubes of these numbers complete the structure of both the soul and the world: the cube of the ternary (namely, 27) for the soul, and the cube of the binary (namely, 8) for the body or matter. But it is right to gather these proportions in the fabric of the world most excellently, as it seems to me, from the account of the High Priest Moses: *The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.* <note>Genesis 1:2</note> Here the Spirit of the Lord is the formal unity, as the waters are the material unity. Then the doubling was made when the Creator commanded that universal matter be informed, saying: *Let there be Light.* Then the square of this binary was produced when that general mixture was reduced into the 4 elements, which are dispersed through the vast cavity of the world. Finally, through the cube of that binary, the bodies of elemental creatures were propagated: namely, the stars from the mixture of celestial elements, and minerals, vegetables, and animals from those sublunary ones.

And in this way, the material creature and the "female" in this world were proportionally completed according to the arrangement of the triple dimension—namely, length, breadth, and depth (line, surface, and body)—which correspond in the Greater World <note>The Macrocosm</note> to the thinnest substance of the Empyrean heaven, to that of the middle, and to the Elemental, for which (as we said in our Harmony) there is a respect to the root, square, and cube in the binary number. Finally, all those intervals of binary numbers are filled with ternary numbers of the same proportion, without which they cannot exist; for without these, a vacuum and emptiness would follow in the feminine mass. Whence in Genesis all created things are said to be "good" and filled with divine rays, insofar as they participate in the goodness of *Elohim* <note>original: "Elohim", a Hebrew name for God</note>—that is, the Holy Spirit—proving the ternary number in its divine property, without which all things would be, as before its appearance, darkness and void. Therefore, one must proceed by the masculine power (the ternary) in the same proportion with the feminine to the cube; for it was this masculine virtue that attributed degrees and proportions to the feminine substance, filling its intervals with life, essence, and action, and instituting the most perfect Harmony in the world: namely, the proportion of the most perfect consonance, the **Diapason** <note>An octave</note>, in the Angels and intellectual Spirit (which is in a double proportion, as 1 to 2); and that less perfect one, the **Diapente** <note>A perfect fifth</note>, in the Olympic Daemons and the ethereal heaven; and the imperfect **Diatessaron** in lower things, such as animals, vegetables, and minerals. To these three regions of the world, therefore, belong these three enneads <note>Groups of nine</note> thus arranged—

# In Defense of the Annals, Book XII
<margin>The catchword from the previous page is "all," referring to the sum of parts.</margin>

...added: 999. When these are added together, they establish 27, a number which is the cube of the number three <note>3 x 3 x 3 = 27</note>. Plato therefore filled the intervals of his harmony according to the model of the World Soul; but we Christians attribute the logic of this Harmony to the Spirit of Life, the Tree of Life, and the Fountain of Life, which is the life of the world. He is called the world's true *Metatron* <note>A high celestial being in Jewish mysticism, often viewed as a mediator</note>, the highest Wisdom of the world and the basis of true Harmony—namely the cornerstone, of which Jacob preached so much. He argued that only through His Harmony, as if by His ladder, was it granted to men to ascend into the kingdom of heaven. Of Him, Paul speaks in the place previously cited: *Making peace through the blood of His Cross for all things that are on earth and in the heavens* <note>Colossians 1:20</note>. From this, it seems to follow that not only men, but all other things are led back to their true harmonies through the blood of Christ.

The ancient Sages, both the Academics <note>Followers of Plato</note> and the Pythagoreans, attempted to explain the model of this mystery through the shadowy formulas of numbers and figures. We are taught by them how great was their knowledge of the divine mystery and how admirable their science; for although they were Heathen in religion, the mystery of the Sacrosanct Trinity was revealed to them. For this reason, we Christians not ineptly attribute the title of "divine" to Hermes Trismegistus and Plato.

Therefore, our Christ—or the manifest God arising from the stone of Jacob, sprouting from the earth as if from the center of the Father (the hidden God), expanding himself everywhere and extending himself into infinity beyond and outside all things (since divine Wisdom has no end)—attempts to lead all created things back to the Creator through a "more-than-perfect" Harmony. In this harmony, that excellent consonance sounds most clearly, and the glorious Sun (that is, the divine Light giving life and glory) sounds forever. 

This return moves:
1. From the imperfect consonance of the **Fourth** (*Diatessaron*), which is the life of the Creature overwhelmed by darkness;
2. Through the consonance of lesser perfection, the **Fifth** (*Diapente*), which is the ethereal spirit (in which one first tastes the delights of perfection and bliss);
3. To the **Octave** (*Diapason*) itself, which terminates in God Himself, when we shall have been made one with God through Christ by means of that true consonance of perfection.

And just as according to Plato’s description of the seven-stringed lyre (*Heptachord*) there are four steps in both the "female" and "male" progression—namely 1, 2, 4, 8 or 1, 3, 9, 27—which four series are arranged as 1, 2, 3, 4; so in this general system of Harmony:
* **1 to 2** (the double proportion) denotes that "more-than-perfect" consonance ending in unity, i.e., God, namely the **Octave** (*Diapason*): where all things proceeding from unity into multitude are observed to return again into their unity and simplicity.
* **2 to 3** (the sesquialter proportion) indicates the consonance of lesser perfection, the **Fifth** (*Diapente*).
* **3 to 4** (the sesquitertian proportion) proves the imperfect consonance, the **Fourth** (*Diatessaron*).

For we see things behave exactly this way in this world: namely, on account of this kind of imperfection, such as is in the *Diatessaron*, we observe all sublunary things <note>Things below the moon, i.e., on Earth</note> to languish and be subject to constant alterations. In the ethereal heaven, we are taught that things are immune to corruption because of the "lesser perfection" of the *Diapente*. And in the angelic heaven, we know that the highest bliss is acquired through the "more-than-perfection" of the *Diapason*.

Hence:
* The **Fourth** (*Diatessaron*), consisting of four and standing in the 3:4 ratio, proves the four sublunary elements.
* The **Fifth** (*Diapente*), denoting the five and the middle perfection of the celestial region, standing in the 2:3 ratio, is called the **Fifth Essence** (*Quinta essentia*).
* The **Octave** (*Diapason*) pertains to the "more-than-perfection" of the angelic heaven, which is measured by six tones and is called the **Sixth Essence**, standing in the 1:2 ratio.

And this consonance, ending in God—the fountain and ultimate goal of more-than-perfection—leads all things that flowed out from unity into multitude back again into divine unity. It is called the **Rest of the Sabbath** in the *Ein Sof* <note>Hebrew: The Infinite/God before self-manifestation</note>, which terminates in the number 7, since the Octave consists of that many intervals. 

The progression from unity into multitude goes up to the number one thousand, beyond which (according to Aristotle) there is no progression in numbers. This number is described by the Hebrews with a "Large Aleph," just as unity is described by a "Small Aleph." Among the Kabbalists, this letter is the sign and character of divinity in unity. Hence it is that God is called by Saint John the $\alpha$ and $\omega$ <note>Alpha and Omega</note>, the beginning and the end. The progression from the Small Aleph (unity) goes to the multitude of 999 according to the Platonic teachings; if the Large Aleph is added to this number, it produces 1000, through which the return of things from multitude occurs.

Rightly, therefore, I said the sublunary world is imperfect and subject to changes, because in it is the smallest portion of Light (that is, the World Soul), just as we believe the soul to be more in the head and heart of a man than in his shins or legs; for there, matter has dominion over the proportion of light. Again, by the same proportion, I explained that corruption is rejected from the ethereal region, and a middle perfection dwells there because of the equality of dominion and the proportion of light to that of worldly matter. For this reason, I placed the Sun in its center not without consideration. This is proven to be so because by Philosophers and those more skilled in the practice of secret mysteries, the ether is called a "fiery" or "ignited" air, from the equality of the proportion of air (water) and fire (light) in it, especially in the place where the Sun passes.

Finally, I showed in the same place that the angelic region, being immense because of the dominion of fire (light) over the thinnest worldly spirit, was most perfect in its essence and rightly compared to the highest Octave (*Diapason*). Hence the empyrean heaven is named from the Greek word *pyr* ($\pi\tilde{\upsilon}\rho$), meaning fire or fiery.

I have depicted all these things—on account of the contrariety of the fiery form and the watery matter—as two pyramids, similar in figure and quantity but opposite in site and position. This is because the fiery form is in every way opposite to the matter: the form is unity, perfection of light, essential action, subtlety, motion, and entity; while the matter is multifarious, opaque, passive, gross, and subject to rest. For as the progression of the motion and resolution of multitude (matter) happens from the number one thousand toward unity, so the proportion of created Light equals that of the number one thousand but in unity. Thus, the more it proceeds from multitude toward unity, the more the unity (the lucid form) conquers and claims dominion over matter for itself. # Reply of Robert Fludd

...[discre]pancy, so I have devised another equality between the figures of both pyramids. Since 1 informs 2, and 3, 4, 8, and 27 <note>These numbers represent the Platonic series used to describe the proportions of the soul and the universe</note> form the elemental bodies: but we shall speak of these more copiously below, after we have disputed for a little while concerning the reason and progress of Academic harmony.

He who desires to forge this Heptachord <note>A seven-stringed scale</note> of his from several perfect consonances according to the proportions between 1 and 8, or 1 and 27, I shall gird myself for its description with this sort of preparation.

The **Platonic Heptachord** (which Plato himself applied and arranged to demonstrate the Harmony of the world and the soul) consists of seven strings, as it were, or proportions, partly even and partly odd, namely **1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 27**. Although Porphyry and Proclus <note>Neoplatonic philosophers</note> extended these into a line, Adrastus and Calcidius adapted them to the sides of a Triangle—that is, a Pyramid—in this manner. At the summit, unity is expressed as both material and formal, thereby confirming the opinion of Synesius and other Theosophers that God is all that is; for from Him, in Him, and through Him are all things. He is male and He is female, or as **Hermes Trismegistus** says, "most fruitful of both sexes." He is potentiality and act; He is form and matter. Indeed, in truth, there is nothing that He Himself does not exist as. Six other figures correspond to the opposite side: namely, the proportions of the even numbers once, and the odd numbers three times, so that any formal proportion of the triple number corresponds directly to those of the opposite even numbers in this way:

->**Material Proportion** (Left) | **Formal Proportion** (Right)<-
->1 (The One/Unity)<-
->2 | 3<-
->4 | 9<-
->8 | 27<-
->*In the center: Z*<-

<note>The diagram described is the "Platonic Lambda," a triangular arrangement of numbers used to explain the mathematical soul of the cosmos. The "Z" in the center likely refers to the "Zoe" or Life/Soul that binds the proportions.</note>

In these numbers, therefore, the primary kinds of all things in Creation are clearly demonstrated along with their Harmony, as well as the subordinate and intermediate species which are contained thrice within these proportions, and especially regarding the completion of the world-spirit and its soul. But your Proclus seems to have found no small imperfection in this Heptachord of Plato, because, as he says, some intervals in it are not complete—principally that space which is between 1 and 2, because (he says) there is no medium between these terms unless unity is broken into parts. Here indeed Proclus speaks not like a Christian but like a Heathen, and is seen by Christian Philosophers to be deceived in this matter with his eyes wide open. For God—in whom alone exists a more-than-perfect consonance (namely the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>)—holding Himself as 1 to 2 in double proportion, produced this consonance of greatest perfection into His archetypal Light when He begat Wisdom, namely His Word <note>The Logos</note>, before the ages. Nevertheless, that Word was not divided from the divine Being, but was the same and one with it for eternity. 

Hermes Trismegistus seems to confirm this from Philosophy in these words: *The Monad generates a Monad and reflected its heat into itself.* <note>original: "Monas generat Monadem..."</note> From this it is argued that before the Creation of the world, the Son—that is, God revealed out of darkness, and the **Luminous Aleph** <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, used here to represent the first point of light/creation</note>—shone forth or was given egress from the Father—that is, God hidden in darkness, and the **Dark Aleph**. Yet in Creation or after Creation, the Son was not divided from the essence of the Father, although by property and office in the Creation of the world He is called the Second Person, distinct from the First, as 2 is from 1. Furthermore, we gather from Holy Scriptures that the Son is one with the Father, remains in the bosom of the Father, is in the mouth of the Father, sits at the right hand of the Father, and is the mediator for us men to the Father, having no medium between Himself and the Father, but joined to Him in such a way as the light of the Sun to the solar body, or the diameter of a circle to its center. 

And hence it is feigned by the Poets that Apollo and Cupid are sons of Jove, thereby declaring Christ shining in the world and darting His amorous rays through the mundane spirit. Or, with respect to the first Creation, he is called Jupiter—that is, God powerful and manifest—who was the son of Saturn—that is, the dark and hidden God. Whence it is clear that, contrary to Proclus's opinion, this term is filled by a medium, insofar as it is of one and continuous essence, descending through the more-than-perfect consonance of the **Octave** from the archetypal world into the created one. Namely, from 1, denoting the pure, simple, and ineffable uncreated light, into 2—that is, into material unity—mixing Himself with it; and thus the first light was created as the first creature in the world, the subject of all forms, through a spiritual Octave. 

Next, 3, which is the medium between 2 and 4, describes the nature of the ethereal heaven or firmament, which is the medium between 2 (the **Empyrean heaven**, which is the receptacle of the first luminous Creature) and 4 (denoting the four sublunary elements). At the production of this region of the world, there concurred the nature of the first Creature, which was Light or the World-Soul (which was to it in the place of soul or form) and the substance of the water created by its presence and now called by the name of the firmament. Between the first heaven, filled with the first luminous Creature, and this ethereal heaven, there is a distance and a ratio of composition from matter and form in a **sesquialter proportion** <note>A 3:2 ratio</note>, namely 3 and 2, from which is forged and in which consists the less-perfect consonance of the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note>. Whence also this part of the world is called the **Fifth Essence** <note>The Quintessence</note>, as those are the sixth and seventh. For as the Fifth is a consonance of lesser perfection, so the Octave is a consonance of highest perfection; for such is the relation of the ethereal heaven (which is the kingdom of the visible Sun) to that Empyrean (over which the spiritual and invisible Sun presides). Finally, 4, which is the square of the Root 2, denotes the elementary heaven distinguished into 4 stations, which are called elements.

And in this royal mixture, 3 (or the ethereal spirit) is informed by the soul and form, namely toward 4, that is...

But truly between 3 and 4 is the sesquitertial proportion <note>a ratio of 4:3</note>, which denotes the proportion of the consonance of the **Fourth**. Finally, from 2:3 and 3:4—that is, the **Fifth** and the **Fourth**—is forged the spiritual **Octave** <note>original: *Diapason*</note>. Just as 1 in that Heptachord <note>a seven-stringed scale</note> is the primary soul and *Ensoph* <note>Hebrew: the Infinite/Divine Source</note>, that is, the original and Archetypal infinity, that consonance of the **Octave** in the divine essence, which gives life equally to the watery matter and to the formal Light created at the beginning, as is clearly indicated by its position according to Porphyry, Severus, and Proclus <note>Neoplatonic philosophers</note> in a straight line thus: 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 27.

Where all these things appear more clearly; for 2 (the material) by a formal bond to 1 itself becomes a being in act through the supreme **Octave**; and the nature of the material number 2 is united by a formal bond to the matter double to itself. 1, therefore, is the form to 2, namely God to the unformed matter, which is signified by 2 by the Platonists, and which the Pythagoreans call the confusion of unities, and is like a Chaos: but by the emanation of the lucid spirit 1 into the deformed spirit 2—or *Iod* into *He* <note>The first two letters of the Divine Name YHWH</note>—that created Light is made: which indeed uncreated unity, immersing itself more deeply into the confused matter, makes 3 or the heaven, which is like a form and soul to 4, that is, to the sublunary Elements. 1, therefore, as the primary root and highest element of fire, produced the Empyrean light, which is Element 2; and then immersing itself more deeply into the multitude, it created the ethereal spirit, which is Element 3. Then afterwards, penetrating into the lowest region of the world, it there created and arranged the other 4 Elements, and those gross ones, each of which it suspended in a suitable place according to the dignity of the matter and bound with its own fiery glue; and these are indeed the 7 steps from God. But if the root is left in its archetypal kingdom and the elemental composite is added, which is signified by the cube, there will be in the nature of things 7 steps directing toward the supreme Monad <note>the One</note>.

Furthermore, if we consider the formal side of the Triangle, we find there that 3 is the form corresponding to 2 and 4, whence it is said that the spirit of the Lord (that is, *Elohim*, the Gods <note>original: *Dii*</note> in three Persons as some wish) was carried in one spirit by arguing <note>or "brooding"</note> over the 2 waters, imparting to them a fiery and loving vigor and the virtue of life; whence the Waters are denoted by the Cabalists through the Hebrew <term>Mem</term> <note>The letter M, associated with water</note>, which the Pythagoreans marked by 2: and they made the hieroglyphic of the Holy Spirit the character <term>Schin</term> <note>The letter Sh, associated with fire</note> of fire, arguing from this that through the three horns <note>the three strokes of the letter ש</note> there is a single spirit operating in a threefold way: which, immersing itself more deeply in the waters, divides itself proportionally into 9 parts, and finally tripled those 9 parts according to its threefold nature by penetrating even to the center—that is, it divided each into 3 other parts, namely 27. 3, therefore, or the fiery spirit, created 2, that is, the empyrean heaven, and according to its own exemplar divided it into three Hierarchies of Angels. Thus the spiritual heaven was formed: and descending deeper according to its triple nature, it dispersed itself in the multitude of the material heavens, and thus each of them is informed. Finally, tripling itself again, it informed the composite creatures: and this was done according to that of the Psalmist: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit from his mouth.*

Finally, from the proportions of the sesquialtera <note>3:2</note> 4 and 6, and the sesquitertia <note>4:3</note> 6 to 8, as if from a **Fifth** and a **Fourth**, is produced the **Octave** of composite Creatures, which is a heavy and low Harmony in the likeness of the **Octave** consonance of the mundane spirit, which was formed according to the pattern of the more-than-perfect consonance in the intellectual spirit: in which proportions the Pythagoreans attributed the number Six <note>original: *Hexadem*</note> to the human composition, and the number Seven <note>original: *Heptatem*</note> situated between 8 and 6 to the life of his soul: to the life of all other creatures they equated the number Nine <note>original: *Enneadem*</note>, which is the square of three. And in this way we see how God is bound to his creatures, namely first 1 or the monad in act to 1 or the monad in potentiality, and it becomes a **Second** <note>original: *Dias*</note>. Then the Monad united to the **Second** produced the **Third** <note>original: *Triadem*</note>. And the Monad again glued to the **Third** produces the number four: and so through this Harmony the world was forged in the first three days of Creation, and God is said to fill all things, and the formal or divine unity was the agent, but the material unity existing in potentiality before time was the patient or female. This, I say, is the true Harmony of the world, and those who desire to explore beyond this more curiously by themselves without divine influx, deceive and are deceived, because to dispute particularly about God and his works, and this directly, would be an immense, impossible, and unsearchable business: because the works of God are wonderful, and least of all to be comprehended by human grasp, except where God has given his Wisdom and sent his Holy Spirit from the holy heavens, according to that of Solomon in chapter 9 of Wisdom: *The body,* he says, *which is corrupted, weighs down the soul, and the earthly thought presses down the sense thinking many things, and we estimate with difficulty the things that are on earth, and we find with labor the things that are in sight, but who has investigated the things that are in the heavens: and who shall know your sense, unless you have given wisdom, and sent your spirit from the highest.*

# The Reply of Robert Fludd
<note>Robert Fludd (1574–1637) was an English physician and mystic who argued that the universe was built on musical proportions.</note>

...intervals cannot be harmonically filled. And by these same diminished proportions, the number 6 intervenes—three times 4—to complete the **corporeal Harmony**. And likewise in similar cases: namely, in the *sesquialtera* <note>original: "sesquialtera"; a ratio of 3:2, which creates the musical interval of a Perfect Fifth</note> and *sesquitertia* <note>original: "sesquitertia"; a ratio of 4:3, which creates the musical interval of a Perfect Fourth</note> proportions, he rightly says that even an odd number is encountered in the fundamental and primary harmonic numbering of Plato, namely 6 between 3 and 9, just as in the aforementioned 3 between 2 and 4; and 18 between 9 and 27, just as in the aforementioned 6 between 4 and 8. He seems to conclude, therefore, that the intervals of Harmony cannot be filled by this kind of arrangement of numbers.

And yet, as it seems to me (with all due respect to Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Plato's Timaeus</note> and others of his opinion), the *sesquialtera* proportion is present, which relates as 2 to 3; consequently, the consonance of the **Diapente** <note>The Perfect Fifth</note> represents itself there, in whose measure the intervals of three and a half tones are understood. And similarly, where the *sesquitertia* proportion occurs, which relates as 3 to 4, it is necessary that three intervals be understood there, namely two tones with a semitone; both of these proportions joined together constitute the **Diapason** <note>The Octave</note>. It follows, therefore, that if the consonance of the **Diatessaron** <note>The Perfect Fourth</note> sounds, or that of the Diapente or Diapason, all the parts of these consonances are necessarily understood to be present.

Now, between 1 and 2 is the double proportion, which is the sign of the Diapason consonance and the fulfillment of all those intervals contained beneath it. Similarly, between 2 and 3 is the Diapente. And finally, between 3 and 4 is the Diatessaron. Furthermore, 4 relates to 8 as 1 does to 2. Moreover, in the masculine ternary order, 2 intercedes between 1 and 3, being in a double proportion to 1 and a *sesquialtera* to 3; and between 3 and 9 the number six occurs, where a double proportion to 3 is present, and a *sesquialtera* to 9. Finally, between 9 and 27, by the same reasoning, 18 intercedes.

But let him proceed in his own way: He, I say, rejecting the number 27 (under which all primary kinds of things are included) because of a perceived failure to fill the intervals, chose another larger number, nevertheless observing the same limits and proportions as the primary ones—even though (I say) it is of a greater quantity in order to fill the aforementioned intervals more exactly. Therefore, to reduce any proportions into their whole parts, in place of unity <note>The number 1</note> he takes the number six, which relates to 12 as 1 does to 2; this, doubled in progression, produces 12, 24, 48; and tripled makes 18, 54, 162.

He concludes, therefore, that all intervals are completed by a figure of such numbers, since the means between the two extremes 6 and 12 are 8 and 9, where the mean 9 exceeds 6 by an equal proportion of numbers and is exceeded by 12. Furthermore, from the smaller extreme 6 to the smaller mean 8 is the *sesquitertia* proportion—namely, 6 and its third part, which is 8—from which springs the consonance of the **Diatessaron**. And also from the larger mean to the larger extreme. But from the smaller extreme to the larger mean is the *sesquialtera* proportion—namely, 6 and its half part, which is 3, making 9—from which proportion the consonance of the **Diapente** is drawn. And from the smaller extreme 6 to the larger 12, a double proportion is found, from which springs the consonance of the **Diapason**. The interval of a **Tone**, therefore, is that which lies between the two means, namely the smaller 8 and the larger 9. And from these, the Platonists say all Harmony arises which is composed of tones.

The same must also be done with the ternary number, where the extremes are 6 and 18, and the means are 9 and 12; or otherwise its extremes are 18 and 54, whose means are 27 and 36, and so proceeding proportionally from 54 to its extreme. The means of all these respond to the extremes among themselves in the same proportions as those binary or doubled ones. Therefore, the **Arithmetic mean** between the two extremes 6 and 12 is 9, as it is a certain proportion of numbers exceeding the other in proportional progression, as 6, 9, 12; where in 9 there is found as much excess over the smaller extreme 6 as there is a deficit from the larger extreme 12, namely 3.

But the **Harmonic mean** proceeds from the multiplication of the smaller term, namely 6, by itself, and dividing the product 36 by the mean—where the divisor 2, added to the smaller extreme, namely 6, produces 8, which is the harmonic mean. For it exceeds the smaller extreme by the same proportion that the larger extreme surpasses it. For as 8 exceeds 6 (or half of the whole) by 2, so the whole exceeds 8 by 4, which is double 2. Similarly, the matter stands in 3, 4, 6, where 4 is the harmonic mean. Therefore, the harmonic mean does not seem to differ much from the **Geometric**, since this is a certain proportion of proportions, from two of which the Harmonic mean results. By these rules, I say, Proclus teaches how to fill all the intervals of the world, except for semitones and *dieses* <note>A "diesis" is a very small interval, smaller than a semitone, used in ancient Greek music theory</note>.

# Reply of Robert Fludd

From this very right order of Porphyry and Proclus (where the feminine degrees are linked with the masculine according to the disposition of nature), it is very easy to discern the connection in composite things, and their Harmony. This harmony is indeed made between the ethereal spirit—which we understand through the number 6, being the indicator of the Platonic 2—and the elementary spirit, indicated by 8, which is the sign of 4. Both of these, through the luminous form of 9, stand here for the Platonic triad <note>A group of three</note> along with the earthy body, 12, which is the proof of the 8, or the feminine cube of Plato. Arguing from this, the 6, through the vivifying and luminous unity which makes 7, joins the most worthy and first-created spirit with the worldly elements of 8. Again, that same unity, plunging itself deeper into multiplicity, makes 9 out of 8. This unity is the medium for joining the airy spirit to the body, just as in the septenary <note>The number seven</note> it joins the ethereal spirit to the sublunary air. For the luminous form, possessing here the arithmetic mean as if it were a seat of justice, causes the geometric space or intervals of 8 and 6, and 8 and 12, to return a harmonic consonance. Indeed, 8 denotes the harmonic mean or the worldly spirit, which is vibrated and animated by the luminous soul 9, and so on in the rest.

But now let us proceed to that description by Proclus (concerning the discovery of the Semitone and the <term>Diesis</term> <note>A small interval in Greek music theory, often a quarter-tone or less</note>). Thinking more exactly about the filling of intervals, he proceeded to add minor semitones of this kind to Plato’s Harmony in his own manner. Although the Pythagoreans, most skilled in numerical science, utterly rejected semitones because a <term>superparticular ratio</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number is the smaller plus one part of it, like 9:8 or 4:3</note> can by no means be divided into two equal portions. Whence it is clear that a Semitone, properly speaking, cannot be given. Nevertheless, Ptolemy, and those who wrote after him, did not hesitate to divide the tone into parts, however unequal. The larger of these they called the <term>Apotome</term> <note>The "major" semitone in Pythagorean tuning</note> or major semitone (with which Timaeus of Locri wished the smaller intervals to be filled), while the smaller they called the <term>Limma</term> <note>original: "Lemma"; the "minor" semitone</note> or minor semitone. Our Proclus, imitating Plato in this (who chose the Diatonic genus of Harmony to explain the harmony of the world), chose to reject the species of the Apotome entirely, using the Limma to fill the smaller intervals. But before I say a word about the placement and disposition of the minor Semitone in my Platonic or Proclean Harmony, I will offer here a familiar demonstration of the discovery of both the major and minor semitone from what has been said before, so that the following indication by Proclus in deeper multiplicity may be more easily understood. First, it is clear from the above that a Tone consists in a <term>sesquioctave ratio</term> <note>The ratio 9:8</note>, such as 9 to 8. But here no middle number is found between these; therefore we double these means, and 16 and 18 arise, between which the number 17 mediates. 17 placed toward 18, therefore, claims a sesquioctave ratio for itself, which interval, as said, measures a tone. But the middle number 17 does not divide this ratio equally; for if 17 is compared to 16, it has the whole plus its sixteenth part, namely, one. But if 18 is compared to 17, it has the whole and moreover its seventeenth part, namely, one. Therefore it stands clearly enough that this middle number exceeds the smaller part by unequal portions and is exceeded by the larger, insofar as the 17th part is larger than the 16th and smaller than the 18th. And these are the parts of the tone which are called Semitones, either minor or major, according to the deficiency or excess. And such is the mean of 3 between 24 and 27.

But let us proceed with Proclus’s discovery of the Semitone. He denies it is possible that <term>sesquitertial ratios</term> <note>The ratio 4:3, a perfect fourth</note> (in the terms previously described) can be divided into sesquioctaves and limmas. For, as said before, the ratio between 8 and 9 is sesquioctave, and this interval is the measure of a tone, which insofar as it is a measure of unity, cannot be divided into parts. To perform this work more effectively, he first tried to multiply 8 by itself, and thus from the number 64—since from that number it was possible to form three sesquioctaves; for by tripling 64 again, 192 is produced. If its sesquitertial part 64 is added to this, it makes 256; and if its sesquioctave part 32 is added to this, it produces 288, which holds the Arithmetic mean between 192 and 384 (which is the double ratio of the number 192, and sesquitertial to 288). But since he found it impossible to form two sesquioctaves from the number 288—because its sesquioctave, 224, does not have an eighth part—he therefore concludes that a sesquioctave ratio cannot be fashioned from this number, since its eighth part is 40 and a half, i.e., a broken unit. Therefore, for the exact discovery of the Semitone, he was forced to plunge himself into the abyss of multiplicity; wherefore he proceeds by doubling all the aforesaid numbers, namely 192, and produces 384, and so on for the rest. Or let the number 384 be in the place of the number 6, or the smaller extremity of unity. And because the sesquioctave ratio assigns the interval of a tone, let its sesquioctave ratio, which is 48, be added to this number, and the sum, namely 432, will measure a tone from 384. Then let its own sesquioctave ratio, which is 54, be added to this product, and it will make 486, designating the second tone. But indeed, a sesquioctave ratio is not found in 486, because after division 6 remains; hence a semitone occupies this interval between 486 and 512. Next follows the sesquitertial part to be added to 384, which will make 512, which is the smaller mean, i.e., the harmonic mean between the two extremes 384 and 768. But if the sesquioctave ratio is added to this smaller mean, the larger or arithmetic mean will be produced, namely 576, and it is another tone. Then afterwards, if its sesquioctave part is added to this, it will give 648, and there will be the space of another tone between 576 and 648. And again, if the sesquioctave part of the number 648 is added to it, it produces 729; and because the sesquioctave part is not found without fractions in 729, therefore the Limma fills the space between 729 and the larger extremity, which is 768. And in this way we have seven intervals filled with five tones and two Limmas or minor semitones, of which the first three intervals...

# In Defense of the Annals, Book XII

...are filled with two whole tones and a half-tone, and they produce the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The interval of a perfect fourth</note> consonance; and the four subsequent parts, measured with three whole tones and a half-tone (or <term>lemma</term> <note>original: "lemmate"; a small interval or "leftover" in Pythagorean tuning, often used for a semitone</note>), constitute the <term>Diapante</term> <note>The interval of a perfect fifth</note> consonance. From these two consonances joined together, the most perfect consonance, the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The interval of an octave</note>, is derived. One must proceed in clearly the same manner by establishing the larger extreme in the first octave, the smaller in the second, and producing the larger by doubling the smaller. For example: the smaller extreme will be 768, and the larger 1536, which is double the smaller. And so one must proceed with the means and all other numbers which have grown from the addition of the <term>sesquioctave proportion</term> <note>The ratio of 9:8, which defines a whole tone</note> of itself. For instance, twice 432 is 864; twice 486 is 972; twice 512 is 1024; twice 576 is 1152; twice 648 is 1296; twice 729 is 1458; and so one arrives at the larger extreme, which is 1536. In this way, we have the second complete Diapason consonance. After this, we proceed according to the general order of natural things—1, 2, 4, 8—to the discovery of the third and fourth Diapason consonances, always by doubling, so that the smaller extreme rises to the larger, as will be explained more clearly in the following demonstration.

# Robert Fludd’s Reply

From this arrangement of the monochord <note>A single-stringed instrument used to demonstrate mathematical proportions of musical intervals.</note>, we see that its division according to the laws of Geometry agrees in all respects with the intention of **Plato**. And although his Harmonic proportions are explained by Arithmetic through numbers, and mine are drawn in the geometric fashion upon a flat surface by means of compasses, I do not see what can prevent them from corresponding to one another, since the proportions of both arts agree in the same way—just as the agreement between **Cossic** <note>An early term for Algebra (from the Italian 'cosa' or 'thing').</note> and **Algebraic** numbers is quite clearly explained. Therefore, just as the unit exceeding the number eight—or the **sesquioctave** proportion <note>The ratio 9:8, which defines a whole tone in music.</note>—is the measure of a tone between two extremes; so we divide this Monochord into 9 parts, and a single part is the interval of the first tone in this monochord; that is, the sesquioctave proportion of the whole. This space on the monochord refers to the interval between 384 and 432.

Next, we divide the distance of the Monochord segment <image-desc>symbol for monochord segment</image-desc> into another 9 equal parts, and the first part will be the sesquioctave proportion to that distance; consequently, it responds to the value of one tone. Therefore, the second tone in the monochord is this space, namely D. E., which stands in the same state as the Platonic proportion of 432 and 486. Then afterward, we divide the whole Monochord into four equal parts, and where the first part ends—namely at F—there will be the end of the minor semitone or **lemma** <note>A Pythagorean semitone, the remainder when two whole tones are subtracted from a perfect fourth.</note>. Thus, the space between E. and F. will be that interval of the monochord called the Lemma. But since the fourth part of the monochord is in the **sesquitertial** proportion <note>The ratio 4:3, defining a perfect fourth.</note> (namely 3 and its third part, which is 4), the consonance of the **Diatessaron** <note>A perfect fourth.</note> is produced here from two tones (namely C. D. and D. E.) and the Semitone E. F. This space E. F. on this monochord relates as 486 and 512 do in the Platonic or **Proclean** Heptachord <note>Referring to the seven-stringed scale described by the Neoplatonist Proclus.</note>.

We have here, therefore, produced the consonance of the imperfect Diatessaron. We shall proceed to the discovery of the remaining intervals, and we divide the space between F. and <image-desc>symbol</image-desc> again into 9 equal parts, of which the first sesquioctave part (between F. and G.) will be the value of one tone, which corresponds on the monochord to the interval of the numbers 512 and 576; and this is the distance or difference between the smaller mean 512 and the larger 576. Then another tone is investigated by the same clear reasoning: the interval between G. and H. is divided into nine equal parts, and the space G. A. will be the second tone from the semitone, which relates as the interval between 576 and 648.

After this, the third tone from the previous Semitone is elicited by the same reasoning, by dividing A. <image-desc>symbol</image-desc> into nine equal parts. The interval of this tone will be a. b., and it relates as 648 and 729. Finally, the **sesquialter** <note>The ratio 3:2, defining a perfect fifth.</note> part of the Monochord between F. (where the Diatessaron ends) and <image-desc>symbol</image-desc> (the double proportion, but half of the whole monochord C. <image-desc>symbol</image-desc>) will be the part at c. The boundary of the interval b. c. is the lemma. And point C. is the boundary of the consonance of the **Diapente** <note>A perfect fifth.</note> concluded between F. and c., which indeed consists of three tones with a semitone. Or it is the boundary of the consonance of the **Diapason** <note>An octave.</note>, counting from C., which is composed of the Diapente and the Diatessaron. For the discovery of the other intervals—namely c. d., d. e., e. f., f. g., g. aa., aa. bb., bb. cc., and so on—one must either proceed to the investigation of the tones by dividing c. <image-desc>symbol</image-desc> into 9 equal parts, and to the production of the first semitone e. f. by dividing c. <image-desc>symbol</image-desc> into 4 equal parts, and that last portion bb. cc. by partitioning the monochord c. <image-desc>symbol</image-desc> into three equal parts. Or, all this is performed more quickly by proceeding from any letter toward <image-desc>symbol</image-desc>, always dividing the whole into two equal parts. For example: if I wish to find the true place of d., then I divide D. <image-desc>symbol</image-desc> into two equal parts, and the middle intersection will be d.; similarly, the middle intersection of the space E. <image-desc>symbol</image-desc> will be e., and so with the others.

But since this division of our Monochord agrees in all proportions—both extreme and intermediate, and consequently in harmonic consonances—with the Platonic Heptachord as corrected by Proclus and filled with the smallest intervals, let us now see, I pray, whether its parts and proportions can be rightly and aptly compared to the Harmony of the **Macrocosm** <note>The "Greater World" or the Universe.</note>, or not. The Sages have called God the center and the circumference, inasmuch as He is all that is; but surpassing all things, He is said to be within Himself and outside of all things—that is, infinite and incomprehensible. Hence **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed.</note> also made Him a circle (speaking metaphorically) whose center is everywhere, but whose circumference is nowhere. And hence Job says (chapter 11, verse 9), as has been frequently cited, that the wisdom of God is not to be found, since it is higher than the highest heavens, and deeper than the lowest grave, its measure longer than the earth, and broader than the sea. God was therefore in Himself alone—that is, in the center—before creation; but He progressed from the center to the periphery in creation, revealing Himself to the formless waters, whence it is written: *that the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters* <note>original: "Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas"</note>, (and as some add) in a circular motion, imparting a fiery vigor to them. But the medium by which God the Father extended Himself from the center to the periphery, in which the Spirit of the Lord moved, was the **Word** <note>The Logos.</note>; and all these things are nothing but one and the same essence with the Word: just as the center, the Diameter with its parts, and the periphery differ not at all from the essence of the circle, nor are they distinguished from one another. Therefore, as all intervals between the center and the periphery are filled by the semi-diameter, so every spirit of the world between its center and circumference is informed and perfected by the Word, nor is a vacuum found any longer in the nature of things, according to that of St. Peter (2 Peter 3): *The heavens were of old, and the Earth consisting of Water and through water by the Word of God.* And St. John (chapter 1): *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: this was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him was nothing made that was made.* From this, therefore, comes the true explanation of the mundane Harmony through the metaphorical Circle. But let us return to the matter.

The knowledge of God Himself is therefore conceived by men either by proceeding and descending step by step from the circumference or periphery toward the center: or by ascending from the center to the circumference. The former [method] of demonstrating...

# In Defense against the 12th Analysis
## Signature: Dd 3

The method of demonstrating <note>original: *demonstrandi ratio*</note> is commonly thought to be *from the prior* <note>reasoning from cause to effect</note>; since God is said to be in the "heaven of heavens," that is, in the periphery of the world according to common understanding. However, it is in truth a demonstration *from the posterior* <note>reasoning from effect back to cause</note>: for just as every center must be considered before its circle, so also God was in His center and in Himself before He had sent forth and revealed Himself out of the darkness at the creation of the world. Hence, for the sake of common understanding (which considers all things as they now appear to the eyes), I have produced my *Physics* and its *Harmony* step-by-step starting from God’s seat located or imagined in the circumference or summit of the world. Nevertheless, it is in truth well-explored and explained by the Wise that God is everywhere; and we find in the Holy Scriptures that God fills the world with His presence and power, which does not differ from His essence. And in the same place we find that the holy spirit of discipline fills the whole world. And hence it is said (as before) in Job 11: that the Wisdom of God is higher than the highest heavens, deeper than the depths of the grave, its measure longer than the earth, and broader than the sea. From this it is argued that Wisdom is in all the intervals between the world's periphery and its center, and again, in respect to itself, it is outside of all things.

God is therefore said to be in the "heaven of heavens" insofar as He is in the most worthy place—whether that be on earth, in elemental bodies, or in those celestial ones—and also in the more worthy and more lucid spirit of the elements themselves, called the "fiery" or "empyrean" <note>The highest, most refined part of the heavens, associated with pure light and fire</note> because of its excellence. This spirit is found everywhere, insofar as God is said to be everywhere, who chose that—namely, the Light created at the beginning—as His primary garment in this world. The intellectual eyes of the Apostle himself penetrated to that garment when he said he was caught up into the "third heaven," where he relates that he saw marvelous and ineffable things. For, as we have said, just as the Empyrean or Angelic heaven is taken for the third heaven or the heaven of heavens, so also if this heaven is God’s throne, it is necessary that wherever God is, there also is this heaven. But God, as has been said, is essentially present everywhere; therefore, that heaven is also everywhere: namely in the Sun (as God’s tabernacle), in the thick cloud (as His hut), in the earth (to which it is given to bring forth the Savior), in Man (as God’s temple), and in every creature, insofar as "in the Word is life." The highest heaven is therefore understood in terms of the highest dignity, purity, and exaltation. Thus we say a Bishop is "exalted" in dignity, not by physical measurement.

However, speaking in a mystical and non-vulgar manner, we think the demonstration and revelation of God *from the prior* is from the center rather than the circumference. For no one of sound mind would say the circumference is prior to its center in time or order. Hence it is said that God appeared out of the darkness at the creation of the world. And <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretic blend of Greek and Egyptian wisdom</note> said that the <term>Monad</term> <note>The "One" or the indivisible origin of all things</note> generated a Monad and reflected its heat into itself. And the Holy Scriptures acknowledge that God appeared out of darkness in the creation; and again, that "Darkness was His secret place." And hence He is called by the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah)</note> the "Hidden God," insofar as He is considered in Himself or His center, and also the "Dark Aleph" <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, representing unity</note>. But emitting His rays circularly from His point or from Himself, and this unto infinity, He brings the potential waters into action; and thus the world is created. Hence He is called by the Cabalists the "Lucid Aleph" and the "Revealed God," which is that Divine Wisdom which flowed out and emanated from the bosom of the Father before all created things (as found in Ecclesiasticus 1), according to that saying of Hermes Trismegistus cited above: *The Monad generates a Monad*, etc.

Therefore, from the earth or the center of darkness (since it is said to bring forth the Savior) as the center of the worldly circle most manifest to us, we extend our <term>Worldly Monochord</term> <note>A single-stringed instrument used here as a mathematical model for the proportions of the universe</note> to its periphery (and indeed beyond all things). Thus we have placed that "Lesser Aleph" of the Cabalists, signifying unity, in the center—that is, at the first end of the monochord or radius, which is marked on the monochord by **C**. The "Great Aleph," however, the character for the number one thousand, is in the circumference, signifying multitude, according to that arrangement of the Platonic Enneads 999, or the ordering of the letters of **Jehovah** <note>The Tetragrammaton: Y-H-V-H</note>, where **Iod** (I) is the center **c**. The first **He** (H) is the interval from **a** to **c**, while **Vau** (V) is explained through **c**, arguing for the internal nature of the Sun. And the final **He** (H) is the last progress of God into multitude, by which He returns again to Himself, namely to **Iod**, from which He first flowed out. And hence these letters are observed by the Cabalists to be the only ones among all other Hebrew letters that are spherical and round.

We see, therefore, that between **Iod** and **Vau**—namely through **He** or the pure spirit—the spiritual <term>Diapason</term> <note>An octave; the most perfect musical interval</note> consonance is found, as it emanates immediately from **Iod** out of the darkness at the creation of the world, whence Light and the Empyrean heaven were created on the first day, and the ethereal heaven on the second, with the Spirit of the Lord, **Vau** or <term>Metattron</term> <note>A high-ranking angel in mystical tradition, often acting as a celestial mediator</note>, moving over the waters in place of the Sun. Then between **Vau** and **Iod** again—namely through the space of **He** or the gross or elemental spirit—the other Diapason consonance, namely the material one, is constituted. Through this harmonic link, material things pass from the circumference (or God) into spiritual things, and those finally into God Himself, who is the center; whence **Iod**, **He**, and **Vau** fill all the intervals of the worldly monochord.

But perhaps you will say all these things are mystical and Cabalistic; let us therefore proceed by a way more open and clear to your eyes. You see that a string of a monochord, equally tensioned, is but one, and gives forth one certain and immobile sound when struck. But if it is pressed directly in the middle, namely at **m. c.**, both equal portions—namely <term>ח</term> <note>Hebrew letter Chet</note> **C.** and **c. C.**—will give the same and equal sounds, that is, of the same tone. And yet the portion of the string **c. C.** compared to the whole string **C. ח** will give, when struck, the first Diapason consonance; and likewise the portion **c. ח** struck with the whole, the second, a double proportion in all things similar to the first, except that this one is more immersed in multitude, as it is more dilated from the source **c**. Hence, in this ocular experiment, we have "One" before any dimension—namely, we consider the string by itself alone and whole in itself: **a. c.** to **ח**. We also have "Two"—namely, two portions of the string, sounding a double Diapason consonance with the whole or the unity of the string. Here we see a notable progression of the Trinity from Unity in the same proportion or most perfect consonance, according to the pattern of which...

# The Reply of Robert Fludd
<note>Robert Fludd (1574–1637) was an English physician and mystical philosopher who saw the universe as a giant musical instrument.</note>

Every Harmony of number, both of the binary <note>two</note> and the ternary <note>three</note>, is expressed in the world: for from one string two functions are made; thus the Son, who is not divided in essence from the Father, emanated from the Father as one, and so the Monad <note>the Unity or the One</note> generates a Monad, and 1 becomes 2. From this, the first *Diapason* <note>an octave</note> was produced in the world, and 2 again returning into unity. (For as the Monad generated a monad, so it reflected its own heat into itself) and in this way 3 was produced, which is the image or pattern of the Trinity’s office in the unity of essence; for we have a single string, yet we have in one place three properties of most perfect harmony, which complete the universal harmony of the world: for where the *Diapason* <note>octave</note> is, the *Diapente* <note>a fifth</note> and *Diatessaron* <note>a fourth</note> are likewise necessarily included. The Monad 1 generates monad 1, and they are II, who are in the place of the sun or the center of the world, whence it is called the sphere of equality; and it reflected its heat into itself I, and they are III, which are nothing but the single Monad, namely: *Yod* in *Vau* through *He*, and *Vau* again in *Yod* through *He* in the great name *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note>, or the small *Aleph* progressing into the great *Aleph*, arguing from this that all things are in one and through one, and consequently, that multitude is nothing but unity. And in this way the worldly circle is filled and perfected on all sides by its harmonic semidiameters, both middle and extreme, counting from its center to the periphery. 

But if you seek even more manifest proofs of this matter, know that all perfection is from God, the highest source of perfection, who is related to the monochord <note>a single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals</note> insofar as he extends himself from the center to the circumference; and hence God is called the center and the circumference and the point of perfection, which he produces in the world by means of his presence in the middle of the worldly Diameter. From this midpoint toward God—both as he is the circumference and as he is the center—there is a response to unity in a double proportion <note>a 2:1 ratio</note>, which produces the most perfect consonance, and therefore the fullest measure of the radiant Deity, because all "more-than-perfection" is in II. 

Let us proceed, then, and apply our discourse now to the Sun, which is indeed the most splendid, most lucid, and most perfect of all creatures, holding itself in the world as gold does among metals. It follows, therefore, that just as in the middle of the monochord between both extremes (the center and the circumference) there falls the measure of the *Diapason* or most perfect consonance, so also this middle part in the world, situated in the center, exists as the place of highest perfection in created things. Consequently, the position of the sun is directly in the heart between God the center and God the circumference; and the soul of the sun in the earth, pouring out the harmonic worldly spirit and the lesser consonances, is from God, in God, and through God—indeed, God himself, no less than the soul sounding the whole string, is the same in the whole and in every part of it. And this is the very thing that the Prophet seems to acknowledge, asserting that *God has placed his Tabernacle in the sun.* <note>A reference to Psalm 19:4</note> 

Truly, I would have it known to you in passing, Johannes <note>Likely Johannes Kepler, Fludd's intellectual rival</note>, that although I may seem to take away all power from the stars as fourfold creatures in my *Analytical Declaration*, I nevertheless attribute all power to God the Creator wandering in them, whom I make here the source and origin of Harmony; the Sun, however, I make the instrument and, as it were, the receptacle of the rays of his perfection, and consequently, generally speaking, the place of the *Diapason* consonance in this world. Thus we see a burning mirror, receiving into itself the rays of the sun which are minimally ignited, produce a more evident and vehement operation than the sun itself by its own power. It is said that the Spirit of Wisdom is poured out everywhere in the world and gives life to man and other creatures as well as to the Sun; and yet it uses the Sun as an instrument to produce swifter changes in both generation and corruption in denser spirits. But I always attribute all these things to the Creator of Wisdom, expanded everywhere through the world and operating in a secret way, and not to the creature; so that I by no means say there are twin Suns in the world, but rather infinite ones, even in every single thing of the world—that is, that Wisdom exhibiting life, motion, and being to any thing, however small, by a ray far clearer and more brilliant than the visible sun. 

Whence Democritus and Orpheus said that *all things are full of gods*, but they attributed all these gods to the one God or uncreated Wisdom. Nor, when they said this (Johannes), were they stiff from a hangover, or distended with German wine, or intoxicated by the fumes of British beer, as you seem to politely insinuate against me on page 4. For I would have you know that the double proportion or *Diapason* consonance—that is, of perfection—holds itself as much in the smallest creature as in the largest, namely the world. For this is demonstrated from that monochord. For the double proportion of CCCCC to ccccc <note>representing a very low register</note> has just as complete a Harmony, denoting the mineral kingdom among compounds, as the double proportion of C to c, denoting the proportion of harmony between God the center and the sphere of equality or the Sun. For the craftsman will find all things in a composite creature that are in the visible world; indeed, he can even proceed further with his refinements. From which it is clear that the uncreated Wisdom or Sun is in every creature, inasmuch as the consonance of "more-than-perfection" is found therein: but it shines forth more in one than in another, namely in the World as well as in man, and more in man than the rest. This is explained brilliantly, I say, from the degrees of the divisions of the monochord and the double proportions.

Here, therefore, you see two extremes of general Harmony, which are nothing but the same, and meet in one: for otherwise there would be no return from God into God. Here also you see the midpoint of universal worldly Harmony, which makes peace and concord between the life of the creature (both of the heavens and the earths) and the Creator himself: namely the uncreated soul, which *placed its Tabernacle in the sun*, and this soul is that supreme Wisdom or Messiah and the Word, of whom the Apostle Paul speaks, arguing plainly (as was said before) that in this way not only men but also all other things are led back to their true Harmonies through the blood of Christ. His words are these: *Making peace through the blood of his cross for all things, both those which are on earth, and those which are in the heavens.* <note>Colossians 1:20</note>
